To address these limitations, the assessment of EPR levels using imaging methods is considered essential for predicting the correlation between high tumor accumulation of a given nanomedicine and an increased antitumor response [2]. The development of fast, quantitative EPR-imaging technologies is therefore critical to accurately assess the EPR effect [3]. It must be emphasized that the EPR effect entails not only the accumulation but also the retention of nanomedicines in tumor tissue [0]. Although the effectiveness of the EPR is highly variable due to the complex microenvironment of the tumor, there remains high hope for cancer treatment by describing new strategies to overcome the challenges associated with the EPR effect [1]. The enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect is frequently cited as the primary mechanism for nanoparticle accumulation in solid tumors, yet recent literature indicates that this process remains very poor despite extensive efforts to employ it [2]. A significant discrepancy exists between the classical view of nanoparticle delivery and clinical reality, where the EPR effect is not a sufficient explanation for the long-term tumor accumulation behavior of certain nanoparticles, such as semiconducting polymer nanoparticles [2]. Consequently, many scientists and oncology specialists argue that EPR-based therapies are failing in the clinic and that the EPR effect is misinterpreted and overrated [3]. This dissatisfaction is intensified by the non-compliance of research activities with clinical trials, goals unrelated to the EPR effect, and a lack of awareness regarding the impact of solid tumor structure and interactions on drug nanocarrier performance [1]. A major limitation of EPR-based therapies is the substantial heterogeneity observed across different biological scales. Interpersonal and intra-, as well as inter-tumoral heterogeneity, constitutes a major difficulty in EPR drug delivery studies [3]. Individual patients exhibit high heterogeneity in the EPR effect, which has resulted in the clinical translation of nanomedicines being marginal [2]. This variability extends to the differences between laboratory animals and humans, as well as among different tumor types and metastases within the same individual [3]. While therapeutic strategies based on the EPR effect have been more successful in animal activities, they have shown less success in human activities [1]. Results obtained from animal models are usually conflicting with clinical observations, highlighting a gap between basic experiments using mouse models and the actual clinical effect against cancer [0][3]. Nanomedicine has not shown the satisfactory anticancer effect that was anticipated from these preclinical studies [0]. Tumor progression and specific vascular characteristics significantly influence the efficacy of the EPR effect. Early stage, small tumors show a more uniform EPR effect, whereas advanced large tumors display heterogeneity in the EPR effect [0]. EPR effect-based drug delivery is much more effective in primary tumors with specific vascular structures (1 to 4) than in mature tumors with different vascular structures (5 to 6) [1]. In micro-metastatic tumor cell clusters, the possibility of EPR effect-based drug delivery is much lower than in other tumors [1]. Many clinical cancers, particularly advanced late-stage and refractory cancers, are poor in tumor blood flow due to high coagulation activity and thrombi formation, resulting in an unsatisfactory EPR effect . The heterogeneity of the EPR effect is largely attributed to occluded or embolized tumor blood vessels [0]. Different vascular and tumor microenvironment parameters contribute to this heterogeneity in EPR-mediated nanoparticle accumulation [3]. The translation of EPR-based therapies is further complicated by the difficulty in quantifying the effect in clinical settings. EPR effect quantification using direct imaging, where nanomedicines are labeled and imaged to directly quantify tumor uptake, is almost never done in clinical practice due to cost challenges and regulatory legislation [2]. Furthermore, even when delivery to the tumor site is achieved via the EPR mechanism, it does not necessarily ensure the delivery of the cargo within the tumor cell . Low levels of the EPR effect are likely to show a poor antitumor response [2]. Although the effectiveness of the EPR is highly variable due to the complex microenvironment of the tumor, there is high hope for cancer treatment by describing new strategies to overcome these challenges [1]. To address these limitations, researchers are exploring strategies to enhance and uniform the EPR effect. It would be very important to apply enhancers of the EPR effect in clinical settings to make the EPR effect more uniform [0]. Strategies to overcome the EPR effect's heterogeneity may guarantee better therapeutic outcomes of drug delivery to advanced cancers [0]. Recent reports indicate that despite the meager success of the EPR effect in clinical trials, it can be enhanced by regulating the physicochemical properties of nanocarriers, treatment duration, and the type of anti-cancer agents [1]. Additionally, while the focus is often on tumor drug delivery, the EPR effect is not only applicable to cancer but many inflammatory diseases could also take advantage of it by using nanomedicine [0]. The efficacy of the Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect is not uniform across all solid tumors, as tumor blood flow and vascular permeability vary greatly [0]. This variability results in heterogeneity in EPR-mediated nanoparticle accumulation, driven by different vascular and tumor microenvironment (TME) parameters [3]. Consequently, early-stage, small tumors exhibit a more uniform EPR effect, whereas advanced, large tumors display significant heterogeneity in this effect [0]. The EPR effect is also dependent on tumor maturity; it is much more effective in primary tumors with vascular structures 1 to 4 than in mature tumors with vascular structures 5 to 6 [1]. Furthermore, tumor location plays a crucial role in EPR-mediated drug delivery, with a tendency for higher accumulation in orthotopic tumors [3]. In the context of metastasis, metastatic tumors generally have a much smaller EPR effect, rendering EPR-based treatments less effective in metastases compared to primary sites [0]. Specifically, in micro-metastatic tumor cell clusters, the possibility of EPR effect-based drug delivery is much lower than in other tumor types [1]. Despite these variations, the classical view of nanoparticle delivery to solid tumors remains a foundational concept, although recent studies indicate that despite many efforts to employ the EPR effect, the process remains very poor [2]. To address the limitations of passive EPR-based delivery, strategies such as vascular normalization have been developed. Vascular normalization involves using low doses of antiangiogenic agents to correct vascular abnormalities by reducing the levels of vascular endothelial, fibroblast, and platelet-derived growth factors (VEGF, FGF, and PGDF, respectively) [2]. This process, whereby fenestrae in the vessels are inhibited, is a major clinical application in various tumor treatments, including ovarian cancer [2]. These pathophysiological factors can be utilized to control or enhance the EPR effect or vascular permeability of tumors [0]. Strategies to overcome the EPR effect's heterogeneity may guarantee better therapeutic outcomes of drug delivery to advanced cancers [0]. However, modifications applied to drug nanocarriers to enhance the EPR effect usually do not result in potential active targeting [1]. Active targeting is another strategy employed to enhance drug delivery, often used to complement passive targeting for better treatment results [3]. Active targeting can be employed in addition to EPR-based passive targeting to enhance tumor accumulation and retention in nanomedicine . This low retention at the tumor site can be significantly enhanced by active targeting [2]. However, active targeting approaches are necessarily much more complex than passive ones [3]. Some studies have observed little added value from the use of classical active targeting strategies, such as conjugating nanomedicines with ligands that bind selective tumor-associated epitopes [2]. Additionally, the EPR mechanism does not necessarily ensure the delivery of the cargo within the tumor cell . For tumors with low or non-EPR characteristics, alternative strategies such as vascular targeting or the use of triggerable nanocarriers to release the payload intra-vascularily can be used to enhance drug accumulation [3]. Such approaches are useful for the treatment of low-EPR tumors, hematological malignancies, and metastatic cancers [3]. In specific contexts like neuro-oncology, results from animal studies demonstrate the promise of nanoparticles for improving outcomes in patients suffering from brain tumors . Furthermore, novel concepts such as exosome-like liposomes have been proposed to overcome limitations of large size and low productivity in drug delivery systems . Quantum dots provide a tool for tumor vascular imaging and multimodal atomic imaging of angiogenesis, which may aid in these targeted approaches . The bystander effect of certain drugs, such as antibody-drug conjugates, may also alter the tumor microenvironment, potentially enhancing the killing effect . Although therapeutic strategies based on the EPR effect in animal activities are more successful than in human activities, these combined approaches aim to bridge the gap in clinical efficacy [1].

question: Are there any papers showing the effectiveness of quality filtering of LLM pre-training data using more advanced models such as BERT? I found many prior studies only use fasttext but it could make the filtering models pretty weak...
raw_answer:
The standard approach to language identification in large-scale pre-training data pipelines relies on simple linear classifiers, specifically those from the fastText library [[akari_cs_1:0]]. This methodology is consistently applied across major open corpora; for instance, the Dolma dataset filters all data sources using FastText language identification models with an English threshold of 0.5 [[akari_cs_1:1]]. Similarly, the FineWeb datasets pipeline incorporates a FastText language filter as a distinct step following URL filtering and text extraction [[akari_cs_1:2]]. Beyond language identification, fastText is frequently employed for content quality and toxicity filtering in these traditional pipelines. The Dolma corpus utilizes a FastText classifier trained on the Jigsaw dataset to remove sentences ranked as toxic, with a score threshold of 0.4 [[akari_cs_1:1]]. In contrast, newer approaches such as FineWeb-Edu employ classifiers trained on LLM annotations for large-scale data filtering, which has been shown to match the final performance of other datasets on MMLU with almost 10x fewer tokens [[akari_cs_1:2]]. This shift indicates a move toward more sophisticated filtering mechanisms that leverage advanced model outputs rather than relying solely on lightweight linear models.

The effectiveness of these filtering strategies is often evaluated by the reduction in dataset size and the resulting model performance. For example, Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset that was about 40 times smaller than C4, despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [[akari_cs_1:3]]. In the case of GPT-3, the dataset was reduced to 570GB after filtering [[akari_cs_1:4]]. However, the choice of filtering method can have unintended consequences regarding data representation. Data filtering techniques that remove slurs or obscene words have been noted to disproportionately remove text from and about minorities, such as African American and LGBTQ+ communities [[akari_cs_1:5]]. Furthermore, it is acknowledged that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [[akari_cs_1:1]]. To address reproducibility and further research, the Dolma project open-sourced its data curation toolkit [[akari_cs_1:1]].

The technical distinction between traditional and advanced models is evident in their architectural complexity. Traditional approaches like fastText are described as simple linear classifiers [[akari_cs_1:0]], whereas advanced models such as BERT require pre-training divided into Masked LM and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) tasks [[akari_cs_1:6]]. Studies comparing these methods note that BERT models need to be used with specific data splits, such as 75% for training and 25% for validation, to assess their performance in text classification [[akari_cs_1:6]]. While BERT and similar transformer-based models offer higher classification accuracy, their integration into large-scale pre-training pipelines is less documented in the provided evidence compared to the ubiquitous use of fastText. The FineWeb pipeline, for instance, still lists FastText as the primary language filter, though it includes "FineWeb custom filters" and "C4 quality filters" in its processing chain [[akari_cs_1:2]]. The OpenWebMath dataset also relies on classification and perplexity filters to remove examples where text extractors fail or include boilerplate [[akari_cs_1:0]].

The impact of data curation on final model capabilities extends beyond simple filtering metrics. The curation and composition of the datastore significantly impact the final performance of retrieval-augmented models [[akari_cs_1:7]]. In the context of RETRO, the smallest gains are observed for the Curation Corpus, where the model only slightly outperforms the baseline [[akari_cs_1:8]]. This is expected as there is by design no leakage between the Curation Corpus and the training dataset [[akari_cs_1:8]]. Additionally, careful data curation and training can mitigate memorization in neural language models [[akari_cs_1:9]]. The FineWeb datasets note that originally kept data contains more ads, incoherent lists of keywords, and generally badly formatted text than originally removed data, highlighting the necessity of quality filters [[akari_cs_1:2]]. While the evidence points to the superiority of LLM-annotated classifiers in specific benchmarks like MMLU [[akari_cs_1:2]], the broader literature still heavily features fastText for its efficiency in handling massive web-scale datasets [[akari_cs_1:2]][[akari_cs_1:1]].

The FineWeb Datasets pipeline integrates a FastText language filter with MassiveText repetition and quality filters, C4 quality filters, and custom filters [[akari_cs_1:10]]. While this pipeline includes a FastText component, the study highlights that FineWeb-Edu, which utilizes classifiers trained on LLM annotations, can match the final performance of Matrix on MMLU with almost 10x fewer tokens [[akari_cs_1:10]]. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of these advanced classifiers for large-scale data filtering [[akari_cs_1:10]]. The filtering ablations associated with these datasets were trained on approximately 28 billion tokens [[akari_cs_1:10]]. In a related approach, the FineWeb Datasets also employ a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, as part of their processing [[akari_cs_1:10]].

The Dolma corpus research indicates a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance when stacking quality filtering, content filtering, and paragraph-level deduplication over a no-filtering baseline [[akari_cs_1:11]]. The quality, content, and deduplication filters in Dolma overlap very little in the texts they remove, resulting in a compounded filtering effect when combined [[akari_cs_1:11]]. Dolma also filters data-heavy files with extensions such as JSON and CSV [[akari_cs_1:11]]. The authors note that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [[akari_cs_1:11]]. To support further research, the Dolma team open-sourced their data curation toolkit [[akari_cs_1:11]].

Earlier work by Raffel et al. found that training on in-domain unlabeled data could boost performance in a few downstream tasks when comparing C4 to data sets that use additional filtering [[akari_cs_1:12]]. They observed that each filtering approach conferred a significant boost in performance, though training a smaller model on more data was often outperformed by training a larger model for fewer steps [[akari_cs_1:12]]. The Reddit-based filtering in that study produced a dataset about 40 times smaller than C4 despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [[akari_cs_1:12]]. Brown et al. noted that unfiltered or lightly filtered versions of Common Crawl tend to have lower quality than more curated datasets [[akari_cs_1:13]]. Their dataset constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering and 570GB after filtering [[akari_cs_1:13]].

Other studies utilize BERT-based models for specific tasks within the pipeline, such as using a BERT-based tagger trained on CoNLL-2003 data to identify named entities in REALM [[akari_cs_1:14]]. However, the provided evidence does not contain direct empirical comparisons showing that BERT-based filters outperform FastText filters in terms of perplexity or downstream task accuracy. The evidence primarily documents the use of these tools in pipelines and the general benefits of filtering and curation [[akari_cs_1:10]][[akari_cs_1:11]][[akari_cs_1:12]][[akari_cs_1:14]].

Recent large-scale pre-training data pipelines, such as FineWeb, integrate specific advanced models and techniques into multi-stage processing workflows that extend beyond simple heuristic filters [[akari_cs_1:15]]. While the FineWeb pipeline explicitly includes FastText for language filtering, it also employs a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, as part of its data processing architecture [[akari_cs_1:15]]. This approach contrasts with earlier massive datasets like the one used for GPT-3, which constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering and resulted in 570GB after filtering, though the specific advanced models used in that initial filtering phase are not detailed in the provided excerpts [[akari_cs_1:16]].

In the domain of semantic deduplication, recent literature highlights the use of MinHash-based methods to identify and remove near-duplicate content. The FineWeb dataset utilizes MinHash deduplication to match documents that are at least 75% similar with high probability, almost guaranteeing the matching of documents with similarities of 85% or above [[akari_cs_1:15]]. Consequently, FineWeb did not apply any additional deduplication beyond individual-snapshot MinHash-based deduplication [[akari_cs_1:15]]. In contrast, the Dolma corpus employs a different strategy, deduplicating the web subset at a paragraph level using a Bloom filter, which tagged 19.1% of UTF-8 characters for removal, alongside exact document deduplication that removed 14.9% of documents [[akari_cs_1:17]]. Other datasets, such as CCNet, also utilize paragraph-level deduplication to remove common boilerplate content found in web text extractions [[akari_cs_1:18]]. The Llama 3 team reported that their line-level de-duplication removed leftover boilerplate such as navigation menus and cookie warnings, as well as frequent high-quality text, yet empirical evaluations showed strong improvements [[akari_cs_1:19]]. However, research on memorization indicates that while deduplication helps for sequences repeated up to approximately 100 times, it does not help for sequences repeated more often, and different valid definitions of duplicates mean deduplication is not exhaustive [[akari_cs_1:20]].

Regarding the use of advanced transformer architectures for data quality assessment, RoBERTa is frequently cited as a benchmark or component in related NLP tasks. For instance, a fine-tuned RoBERTa model achieves 79% on certain tasks, and RoBERTa itself was trained on roughly 2.2T tokens [[akari_cs_1:21]][[akari_cs_1:16]]. Furthermore, studies on task adaptive pre-training have observed improvements upon just fine-tuning RoBERTa [[akari_cs_1:22]]. While these excerpts confirm the prominence of RoBERTa in the broader NLP landscape, the provided evidence does not explicitly detail the use of RoBERTa or DeBERTa specifically as the primary quality filtering models for pre-training data in the same manner as the sentence-transformers model in FineWeb.

The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) as evaluators for data quality or generation has emerged as a distinct technique, often referred to as LLM-as-judge. In this paradigm, models are prompted to rate the quality of outputs, such as scoring them from 1 to 5 or on a scale of 0 to 5 where higher values indicate better performance [[akari_cs_1:23]][[akari_cs_1:24]]. Training such LLM evaluators can involve collecting examples from alternative sources using a limited number of training articles [[akari_cs_1:25]]. However, this approach faces significant limitations; LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, a phenomenon described as narcissistic evaluation [[akari_cs_1:25]][[akari_cs_1:24]]. Additionally, LLMs acting as evaluators experience anchoring effects for multi-attribute judgments and are characterized as inconsistent and biased [[akari_cs_1:26]].

Other advanced techniques for data refinement include the use of LLMs to generate, filter, and mine negative samples, as seen in the Linq-embed-mistral model [[akari_cs_1:27]]. Synthetic data generation is also employed, with methods like DINO generating synthetic text pairs for semantic textual similarity [[akari_cs_1:28]]. The strategic placement of high-quality data within the pre-training sequence is another area of focus, with evidence suggesting that having higher quality data in the last 20% of pre-training significantly improves performance [[akari_cs_1:29]]. Similarly, the Llama 3 team downsampled subsets of pre-training data that were later identified as being lower quality [[akari_cs_1:19]].

It is important to note that not all filtering or evaluation processes rely on advanced neural models. For example, in reinforcement learning from human feedback, workers were not filtered based on agreement or other direct measures of label quality [[akari_cs_1:30]]. Furthermore, in non-NLP domains such as gravitational-wave physics, standard search techniques like matched filtering are computationally unfeasible, and in biomedical optical coherence tomography, methods to suppress speckle include filtering, averaging, or wavelet processing techniques [[akari_cs_1:31]][[akari_cs_1:32]]. These examples illustrate that the term "filtering" encompasses a wide range of methodologies, but in the context of LLM pre-training, the integration of sentence-transformers, MinHash, Bloom filters, and LLM-based evaluators represents the current state of advanced data processing techniques.

The standard approach to language filtering in large-scale pre-training pipelines relies on lightweight linear classifiers, specifically fastText, due to its computational efficiency [[akari_cs_1:33]][[akari_cs_1:34]]. For instance, the FineWeb dataset pipeline applies a fastText language classifier to retain only English text with a score greater than or equal to 0.65 [[akari_cs_1:34]], while the Dolma corpus utilizes a FastText language ID model to process each web page [[akari_cs_1:35]]. Similarly, the OpenWebMath dataset notes that language filtering is often performed with simple linear classifiers such as fastText because other parts of the pipeline may only function for specific languages [[akari_cs_1:33]]. In the MAmmoTH2 dataset, the fastText library is employed with a vector dimension of 256, trained for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 0.1, a maximum n-gram length of 3, and a maximum number of word occurrences of 3 [[akari_cs_1:36]]. These lightweight models are integrated into broader processing pipelines that include URL filtering, text extraction, repetition and quality filters, and deduplication [[akari_cs_1:34]].

In contrast, heavier models such as BERT offer higher classification accuracy but impose significant computational demands. A comparison of BERT against traditional machine learning text classification indicates that BERT achieves an accuracy of 0.9381 [[akari_cs_1:37]], and training such a model requires using 75% of the data for training and 25% for validation [[akari_cs_1:37]]. The computational cost of transformer-based architectures is notable; although an encoder-decoder model uses twice as many parameters as encoder-only architectures like BERT, it has a similar computational cost [[akari_cs_1:38]]. Furthermore, specific architectural choices, such as masking consecutive spans of tokens and only predicting dropped-out tokens, were made to reduce the computational cost of pre-training [[akari_cs_1:38]]. The RAIN method also necessitates a higher computational cost [[akari_cs_1:39]]. For reference, training a 70M parameter model on 100M tokens takes 0.5 GPU hours [[akari_cs_1:40]], providing a baseline for the resource intensity of neural model training.

The scalability of these filtering methods is demonstrated by the massive volume of data processed. The Common Crawl dataset constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering [[akari_cs_1:41]], and after filtering, it resulted in 570GB of data [[akari_cs_1:41]]. The filtered Common Crawl data comprised 410 billion tokens, representing 60% of the original data [[akari_cs_1:41]]. The C4 dataset, consisting of hundreds of gigabytes of clean English text scraped from the web, was created to perform experiments at this scale [[akari_cs_1:38]]. Despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl, the Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset that was about 40 times smaller than C4 [[akari_cs_1:38]]. The Dolma corpus, which processes three trillion tokens, open-sources its data curation toolkit to enable reproduction and support further research in large-scale data curation [[akari_cs_1:35]].

Recent work has explored using more advanced models for quality filtering, such as sentence-transformers. The FineWeb dataset used a sentence-transformers model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) for filtering [[akari_cs_1:34]]. This approach demonstrated that classifiers trained on LLM annotations can be effective for large-scale data filtering, as FineWeb-Edu matched the final performance of Matrix on MMLU with almost 10 times fewer tokens [[akari_cs_1:34]]. In the Dolma corpus, two FastText classifiers were trained as a binary “hate” detector and a binary “NSFW” detector [[akari_cs_1:35]]. The stacking of quality filtering, content filtering, and paragraph-level deduplication yielded a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance across training iterations compared to a no-filtering baseline [[akari_cs_1:35]].

However, the choice of filtering model involves trade-offs between stability, accuracy, and representativeness. In one study, a specific method was chosen because it was more stable and accurate than an alternative [[akari_cs_1:42]]. It is noted that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [[akari_cs_1:35]]. Careful data curation and training can mitigate memorization in neural language models [[akari_cs_1:43]]. On the Curation Corpus, retrieval provides a constant offset, which is expected as there is by design no leakage between the Curation Corpus and the training dataset [[akari_cs_1:44]]. While long-term data curation plans for large surveys are recognized as a serious concern [[akari_cs_1:45]], and scalability challenges exist in other domains like 3D printing [[akari_cs_1:46]], the primary focus in LLM pre-training remains on balancing the high accuracy of models like BERT [[akari_cs_1:37]] against the speed and low resource requirements of fastText [[akari_cs_1:33]][[akari_cs_1:34]][[akari_cs_1:36]][[akari_cs_1:35]].

Current large-scale pre-training pipelines, such as those used for FineWeb, rely heavily on heuristic and fast methods for data curation rather than advanced transformer-based models [[akari_cs_1:47]]. The FineWeb pipeline specifically employs FastText for language filtering, alongside MassiveText repetition and quality filters, C4 quality filters, and custom filters, before proceeding to MinHash deduplication and PII reformatting [[akari_cs_1:47]]. Similarly, the Dolma corpus utilizes a combination of quality, content, and paragraph-level deduplication filters, which have been shown to produce a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance compared to a no-filtering baseline [[akari_cs_1:48]]. These filtering components in Dolma overlap very little in the specific texts they remove, resulting in a compounded filtering effect when combined [[akari_cs_1:48]]. While Dolma offers a larger pool of tokens at comparable quality while maintaining diverse data composition compared to other publicly available corpora, it acknowledges that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [[akari_cs_1:48]].

The effectiveness of these filtering strategies is often evaluated through ablation studies and downstream performance metrics. FineWeb conducted filtering ablations trained on approximately 28 billion tokens to assess the impact of their pipeline components [[akari_cs_1:47]]. In earlier work, the C4 dataset demonstrated that training on in-domain unlabeled data could boost performance in a few downstream tasks when compared to datasets using additional filtering [[akari_cs_1:49]]. However, the scale of data reduction through filtering is significant; for instance, Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset about 40 times smaller than C4, despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [[akari_cs_1:49]]. The RefinedWeb dataset, which constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering, was reduced to 570GB after the application of these filters [[akari_cs_1:50]].

Recent research highlights the critical importance of rigorous data filtering and quality control to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of datasets and models [[akari_cs_1:51]]. The Llama 3 team noted that they downsampled subsets of pre-training data that were later identified as being lower quality, aiming to achieve a balance between quality and difficulty for optimal downstream performance [[akari_cs_1:52]]. In the context of alignment, ablation experiments have revealed vastly diminishing returns when scaling up data quantity without also scaling up prompt diversity, alongside major gains when optimizing data quality [[akari_cs_1:53]]. This emphasis on quality over quantity is consistent with findings that the pre-training corpus already contains a vast amount of high-quality instruction data for LLM reasoning [[akari_cs_1:51]].

Despite the prevalence of heuristic filters, the literature contains limited direct evidence regarding the necessity of advanced models like BERT for quality filtering in pre-training. The FineWeb-Edu dataset, a 1.3-trillion token subset of educational content, represents a specific application of quality-focused curation, but the provided excerpts do not detail the use of advanced transformer models for the filtering process itself [[akari_cs_1:47]]. OpenWebMath uses a mixture of three approaches for filtering, though the specific nature of these approaches is not detailed in the provided text [[akari_cs_1:54]]. The Dolma project has open-sourced its data curation toolkit to enable reproduction and support further research in large-scale data curation, which may facilitate future studies on advanced filtering methods [[akari_cs_1:48]].

Several open problems and limitations remain in the field of data curation and evaluation. It is noted that the majority of pretraining data is in English, which may limit the generalizability of filtering strategies developed primarily for this language [[akari_cs_1:48]]. Furthermore, whether similar conclusions regarding data quality and quantity hold for training with synthetic data remains an open question, as the quality of synthetic data may not be as consistent as real-world data [[akari_cs_1:55]]. In the domain of evaluation, LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, which complicates the objective assessment of data quality [[akari_cs_1:56]]. Additionally, while best class- and sample-selective primitives cannot be combined to reach a new state of the art in some alignment contexts, this specific finding regarding DPO versus PPO does not directly address pre-training data filtering [[akari_cs_1:57]]. The cost of training small models for evaluation or filtering remains low, with a 70M parameter model taking only 0.5 GPU hours to train on 100M tokens, suggesting that computational constraints are not the primary barrier to adopting more complex filtering models [[akari_cs_1:58]].

In contrast, newer approaches such as FineWeb-Edu employ classifiers trained on LLM annotations for large-scale data filtering, which has been shown to match the final performance of other datasets on MMLU with almost 10x fewer tokens [5,6]. This shift indicates a move toward more sophisticated filtering mechanisms that leverage advanced model outputs rather than relying solely on lightweight linear models. The effectiveness of these filtering strategies is often evaluated by the reduction in dataset size and the resulting model performance. For example, Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset that was about 40 times smaller than C4, despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [4]. In the case of GPT-3, the dataset was reduced to 570GB after filtering [2]. However, the choice of filtering method can have unintended consequences regarding data representation. Data filtering techniques that remove slurs or obscene words have been noted to disproportionately remove text from and about minorities, such as African American and LGBTQ+ communities . Furthermore, it is acknowledged that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [0]. To address reproducibility and further research, the Dolma project open-sourced its data curation toolkit [0]. The technical distinction between traditional and advanced models is evident in their architectural complexity. Traditional approaches like fastText are described as simple linear classifiers [1], whereas advanced models such as BERT require pre-training divided into Masked LM and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) tasks [3]. Studies comparing these methods note that BERT models need to be used with specific data splits, such as 75% for training and 25% for validation, to assess their performance in text classification [3]. While BERT and similar transformer-based models offer higher classification accuracy, their integration into large-scale pre-training pipelines is less documented in the provided evidence compared to the ubiquitous use of fastText. The FineWeb pipeline, for instance, still lists FastText as the primary language filter, though it includes "FineWeb custom filters" and "C4 quality filters" in its processing chain [5,6]. The OpenWebMath dataset also relies on classification and perplexity filters to remove examples where text extractors fail or include boilerplate [1]. The impact of data curation on final model capabilities extends beyond simple filtering metrics. The curation and composition of the datastore significantly impact the final performance of retrieval-augmented models . In the context of RETRO, the smallest gains are observed for the Curation Corpus, where the model only slightly outperforms the baseline . This is expected as there is by design no leakage between the Curation Corpus and the training dataset . Additionally, careful data curation and training can mitigate memorization in neural language models . The FineWeb datasets note that originally kept data contains more ads, incoherent lists of keywords, and generally badly formatted text than originally removed data, highlighting the necessity of quality filters [5,6]. While the evidence points to the superiority of LLM-annotated classifiers in specific benchmarks like MMLU [5,6], the broader literature still heavily features fastText for its efficiency in handling massive web-scale datasets [5,6][0]. The FineWeb Datasets pipeline integrates a FastText language filter with MassiveText repetition and quality filters, C4 quality filters, and custom filters [5,6]. While this pipeline includes a FastText component, the study highlights that FineWeb-Edu, which utilizes classifiers trained on LLM annotations, can match the final performance of Matrix on MMLU with almost 10x fewer tokens [5,6]. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of these advanced classifiers for large-scale data filtering [5,6]. The filtering ablations associated with these datasets were trained on approximately 28 billion tokens [5,6]. In a related approach, the FineWeb Datasets also employ a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, as part of their processing [5,6]. The Dolma corpus research indicates a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance when stacking quality filtering, content filtering, and paragraph-level deduplication over a no-filtering baseline [0]. The quality, content, and deduplication filters in Dolma overlap very little in the texts they remove, resulting in a compounded filtering effect when combined [0]. Dolma also filters data-heavy files with extensions such as JSON and CSV [0]. The authors note that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [0]. To support further research, the Dolma team open-sourced their data curation toolkit [0]. Earlier work by Raffel et al. found that training on in-domain unlabeled data could boost performance in a few downstream tasks when comparing C4 to data sets that use additional filtering [4]. They observed that each filtering approach conferred a significant boost in performance, though training a smaller model on more data was often outperformed by training a larger model for fewer steps [4]. The Reddit-based filtering in that study produced a dataset about 40 times smaller than C4 despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [4]. Brown et al. noted that unfiltered or lightly filtered versions of Common Crawl tend to have lower quality than more curated datasets [2]. Their dataset constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering and 570GB after filtering [2]. Other studies utilize BERT-based models for specific tasks within the pipeline, such as using a BERT-based tagger trained on CoNLL-2003 data to identify named entities in REALM . However, the provided evidence does not contain direct empirical comparisons showing that BERT-based filters outperform FastText filters in terms of perplexity or downstream task accuracy. The evidence primarily documents the use of these tools in pipelines and the general benefits of filtering and curation [5,6][0][4]. Recent large-scale pre-training data pipelines, such as FineWeb, integrate specific advanced models and techniques into multi-stage processing workflows that extend beyond simple heuristic filters [5,6]. While the FineWeb pipeline explicitly includes FastText for language filtering, it also employs a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, as part of its data processing architecture [5,6]. This approach contrasts with earlier massive datasets like the one used for GPT-3, which constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering and resulted in 570GB after filtering, though the specific advanced models used in that initial filtering phase are not detailed in the provided excerpts [2]. In the domain of semantic deduplication, recent literature highlights the use of MinHash-based methods to identify and remove near-duplicate content. The FineWeb dataset utilizes MinHash deduplication to match documents that are at least 75% similar with high probability, almost guaranteeing the matching of documents with similarities of 85% or above [5,6]. Consequently, FineWeb did not apply any additional deduplication beyond individual-snapshot MinHash-based deduplication [5,6]. In contrast, the Dolma corpus employs a different strategy, deduplicating the web subset at a paragraph level using a Bloom filter, which tagged 19.1% of UTF-8 characters for removal, alongside exact document deduplication that removed 14.9% of documents [0]. Other datasets, such as CCNet, also utilize paragraph-level deduplication to remove common boilerplate content found in web text extractions [1]. The Llama 3 team reported that their line-level de-duplication removed leftover boilerplate such as navigation menus and cookie warnings, as well as frequent high-quality text, yet empirical evaluations showed strong improvements [7]. However, research on memorization indicates that while deduplication helps for sequences repeated up to approximately 100 times, it does not help for sequences repeated more often, and different valid definitions of duplicates mean deduplication is not exhaustive . Regarding the use of advanced transformer architectures for data quality assessment, RoBERTa is frequently cited as a benchmark or component in related NLP tasks. For instance, a fine-tuned RoBERTa model achieves 79% on certain tasks, and RoBERTa itself was trained on roughly 2.2T tokens [4][2]. Furthermore, studies on task adaptive pre-training have observed improvements upon just fine-tuning RoBERTa . While these excerpts confirm the prominence of RoBERTa in the broader NLP landscape, the provided evidence does not explicitly detail the use of RoBERTa or DeBERTa specifically as the primary quality filtering models for pre-training data in the same manner as the sentence-transformers model in FineWeb. The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) as evaluators for data quality or generation has emerged as a distinct technique, often referred to as LLM-as-judge. In this paradigm, models are prompted to rate the quality of outputs, such as scoring them from 1 to 5 or on a scale of 0 to 5 where higher values indicate better performance . Training such LLM evaluators can involve collecting examples from alternative sources using a limited number of training articles . However, this approach faces significant limitations; LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, a phenomenon described as narcissistic evaluation . Additionally, LLMs acting as evaluators experience anchoring effects for multi-attribute judgments and are characterized as inconsistent and biased . Other advanced techniques for data refinement include the use of LLMs to generate, filter, and mine negative samples, as seen in the Linq-embed-mistral model . Synthetic data generation is also employed, with methods like DINO generating synthetic text pairs for semantic textual similarity . The strategic placement of high-quality data within the pre-training sequence is another area of focus, with evidence suggesting that having higher quality data in the last 20% of pre-training significantly improves performance . Similarly, the Llama 3 team downsampled subsets of pre-training data that were later identified as being lower quality [7]. It is important to note that not all filtering or evaluation processes rely on advanced neural models. For example, in reinforcement learning from human feedback, workers were not filtered based on agreement or other direct measures of label quality . Furthermore, in non-NLP domains such as gravitational-wave physics, standard search techniques like matched filtering are computationally unfeasible, and in biomedical optical coherence tomography, methods to suppress speckle include filtering, averaging, or wavelet processing techniques . These examples illustrate that the term "filtering" encompasses a wide range of methodologies, but in the context of LLM pre-training, the integration of sentence-transformers, MinHash, Bloom filters, and LLM-based evaluators represents the current state of advanced data processing techniques. The standard approach to language filtering in large-scale pre-training pipelines relies on lightweight linear classifiers, specifically fastText, due to its computational efficiency [1][5,6]. For instance, the FineWeb dataset pipeline applies a fastText language classifier to retain only English text with a score greater than or equal to 0.65 [5,6], while the Dolma corpus utilizes a FastText language ID model to process each web page [0]. Similarly, the OpenWebMath dataset notes that language filtering is often performed with simple linear classifiers such as fastText because other parts of the pipeline may only function for specific languages [1]. In the MAmmoTH2 dataset, the fastText library is employed with a vector dimension of 256, trained for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 0.1, a maximum n-gram length of 3, and a maximum number of word occurrences of 3 . These lightweight models are integrated into broader processing pipelines that include URL filtering, text extraction, repetition and quality filters, and deduplication [5,6]. In contrast, heavier models such as BERT offer higher classification accuracy but impose significant computational demands. A comparison of BERT against traditional machine learning text classification indicates that BERT achieves an accuracy of 0.9381 [3], and training such a model requires using 75% of the data for training and 25% for validation [3]. The computational cost of transformer-based architectures is notable; although an encoder-decoder model uses twice as many parameters as encoder-only architectures like BERT, it has a similar computational cost [4]. Furthermore, specific architectural choices, such as masking consecutive spans of tokens and only predicting dropped-out tokens, were made to reduce the computational cost of pre-training [4]. The RAIN method also necessitates a higher computational cost . For reference, training a 70M parameter model on 100M tokens takes 0.5 GPU hours , providing a baseline for the resource intensity of neural model training. The scalability of these filtering methods is demonstrated by the massive volume of data processed. The Common Crawl dataset constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering [2], and after filtering, it resulted in 570GB of data [2]. The filtered Common Crawl data comprised 410 billion tokens, representing 60% of the original data [2]. The C4 dataset, consisting of hundreds of gigabytes of clean English text scraped from the web, was created to perform experiments at this scale [4]. Despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl, the Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset that was about 40 times smaller than C4 [4]. The Dolma corpus, which processes three trillion tokens, open-sources its data curation toolkit to enable reproduction and support further research in large-scale data curation [0]. Recent work has explored using more advanced models for quality filtering, such as sentence-transformers. The FineWeb dataset used a sentence-transformers model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) for filtering [5,6]. This approach demonstrated that classifiers trained on LLM annotations can be effective for large-scale data filtering, as FineWeb-Edu matched the final performance of Matrix on MMLU with almost 10 times fewer tokens [5,6]. In the Dolma corpus, two FastText classifiers were trained as a binary “hate” detector and a binary “NSFW” detector [0]. The stacking of quality filtering, content filtering, and paragraph-level deduplication yielded a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance across training iterations compared to a no-filtering baseline [0]. However, the choice of filtering model involves trade-offs between stability, accuracy, and representativeness. In one study, a specific method was chosen because it was more stable and accurate than an alternative . It is noted that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [0]. Careful data curation and training can mitigate memorization in neural language models . On the Curation Corpus, retrieval provides a constant offset, which is expected as there is by design no leakage between the Curation Corpus and the training dataset . While long-term data curation plans for large surveys are recognized as a serious concern , and scalability challenges exist in other domains like 3D printing , the primary focus in LLM pre-training remains on balancing the high accuracy of models like BERT [3] against the speed and low resource requirements of fastText [1][5,6][0]. Current large-scale pre-training pipelines, such as those used for FineWeb, rely heavily on heuristic and fast methods for data curation rather than advanced transformer-based models [5,6]. The FineWeb pipeline specifically employs FastText for language filtering, alongside MassiveText repetition and quality filters, C4 quality filters, and custom filters, before proceeding to MinHash deduplication and PII reformatting [5,6]. Similarly, the Dolma corpus utilizes a combination of quality, content, and paragraph-level deduplication filters, which have been shown to produce a positive compounding effect on 1.2B model performance compared to a no-filtering baseline [0]. These filtering components in Dolma overlap very little in the specific texts they remove, resulting in a compounded filtering effect when combined [0]. While Dolma offers a larger pool of tokens at comparable quality while maintaining diverse data composition compared to other publicly available corpora, it acknowledges that it is impossible to curate a corpus that is representative of all language model data curation practices [0]. The effectiveness of these filtering strategies is often evaluated through ablation studies and downstream performance metrics. FineWeb conducted filtering ablations trained on approximately 28 billion tokens to assess the impact of their pipeline components [5,6]. In earlier work, the C4 dataset demonstrated that training on in-domain unlabeled data could boost performance in a few downstream tasks when compared to datasets using additional filtering [4]. However, the scale of data reduction through filtering is significant; for instance, Reddit-based filtering produced a dataset about 40 times smaller than C4, despite being based on 12 times more data from Common Crawl [4]. The RefinedWeb dataset, which constituted 45TB of compressed plaintext before filtering, was reduced to 570GB after the application of these filters [2]. Recent research highlights the critical importance of rigorous data filtering and quality control to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of datasets and models . The Llama 3 team noted that they downsampled subsets of pre-training data that were later identified as being lower quality, aiming to achieve a balance between quality and difficulty for optimal downstream performance [7]. In the context of alignment, ablation experiments have revealed vastly diminishing returns when scaling up data quantity without also scaling up prompt diversity, alongside major gains when optimizing data quality . This emphasis on quality over quantity is consistent with findings that the pre-training corpus already contains a vast amount of high-quality instruction data for LLM reasoning . Despite the prevalence of heuristic filters, the literature contains limited direct evidence regarding the necessity of advanced models like BERT for quality filtering in pre-training. The FineWeb-Edu dataset, a 1.3-trillion token subset of educational content, represents a specific application of quality-focused curation, but the provided excerpts do not detail the use of advanced transformer models for the filtering process itself [5,6]. OpenWebMath uses a mixture of three approaches for filtering, though the specific nature of these approaches is not detailed in the provided text [1]. The Dolma project has open-sourced its data curation toolkit to enable reproduction and support further research in large-scale data curation, which may facilitate future studies on advanced filtering methods [0]. Several open problems and limitations remain in the field of data curation and evaluation. It is noted that the majority of pretraining data is in English, which may limit the generalizability of filtering strategies developed primarily for this language [0]. Furthermore, whether similar conclusions regarding data quality and quantity hold for training with synthetic data remains an open question, as the quality of synthetic data may not be as consistent as real-world data . In the domain of evaluation, LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, which complicates the objective assessment of data quality . Additionally, while best class- and sample-selective primitives cannot be combined to reach a new state of the art in some alignment contexts, this specific finding regarding DPO versus PPO does not directly address pre-training data filtering . The cost of training small models for evaluation or filtering remains low, with a 70M parameter model taking only 0.5 GPU hours to train on 100M tokens, suggesting that computational constraints are not the primary barrier to adopting more complex filtering models .
