The Self-Instruct framework aligns language models with self-generated instructions by allowing the model to generate instructions for new tasks until it stops its generation, reaches its length limit, or generates specific termination tokens [0,1]. This approach distinguishes between generating classification instances with an output-first approach and generating non-classification instances with an input-first approach [0,1]. In the context of mathematical reasoning, WizardMath empowers large language models via reinforced Evol-Instruct, while Xwin-Math leverages GPT-4-turbo for data synthesis [4,5]. MetaMath bootstraps mathematical questions for large language models, and merging all augmented data together for fine-tuning is better than merging answer augmentation and rephrasing augmentation data, demonstrating the effectiveness of specific augmentation strategies in improving mathematical reasoning ability [6]. The STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner) framework bootstraps reasoning by sampling 10,000 problems from the dataset for each outer loop iteration on arithmetic [7,8]. This method relies on the principle that generating step-by-step "chain-of-thought" rationales improves language model performance on complex reasoning tasks like mathematics or commonsense question-answering [7,8]. Similarly, Orca employs progressive learning from complex explanation traces of GPT-4, observing that for analytical and reasoning tasks, Vicuna performs significantly worse, retaining only 62% of ChatGPT quality as opposed to 85% for open-ended generation . Orca notes that Vicuna performs poorly on sophisticated reasoning tasks in this benchmark , whereas ChatGPT shows superior logical reasoning capabilities compared to Orca . Constraint-based and retrieval-augmented approaches also contribute to handling hard reasoning problems. Self-RAG learns to retrieve, generate, and critique through self-reflection, with hard constraints yielding specific performance metrics in its evaluation . Socratic Models compose zero-shot multimodal reasoning with language, finding that formulating video Q&A as reading comprehension directly leverages the extent to which large language models are capable of logical reasoning by connecting commonsense relationships with knowledge learned from Internet-scale data . These models can provide meaningful results for complex tasks across classically challenging computer vision domains without any model finetuning . ViperGPT utilizes visual inference via Python execution for reasoning, a simple approach that requires no further training and achieves state-of-the-art results across various complex visual tasks . Despite these advancements, limitations persist in generating and solving the hardest problems. REBASE demonstrates a significant advantage on harder problems, specifically levels 3-5 . However, across the board, existing schemes provided small gains on hard problems, and future work should work to develop new ways of using test-time compute which can circumvent this limitation . Simply prompting existing LLMs to correct their own mistakes tends to be largely ineffective for obtaining performance improvements on reasoning problems . While chain-of-thought has been shown to perform well in complex reasoning tasks that cannot be fully addressed by model- or data-scaling , the reliance on proprietary models for data synthesis, such as GPT-4-turbo in Xwin-Math [4,5], highlights a dependency on external high-quality sources. Models pre-trained on code can leverage code generation to answer challenging reasoning tasks even when the original task does not directly involve code . Furthermore, LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generation, a bias noted in the context of iterative refinement methods like Self-Refine . Recent models like LLaVA-OneVision highlight strong performance in complex tasks such as multi-image reasoning, identifying differences, and understanding 3D environments . Empirical studies indicate that fine-tuning language models on synthetic data yields significant improvements in reasoning capabilities, particularly for unseen in-context learning and algorithmic-reasoning tasks [3]. Models trained on such synthetic datasets have been shown to generalize reasonably well to realistic data scraped from the Internet [3]. In the domain of mathematical reasoning, merging all augmented data for fine-tuning has proven more effective than merging only answer augmentation and rephrasing data, highlighting the specific utility of SV and FOBAR augmentation methods [6]. Furthermore, the use of high-quality mathematical tokens, such as those found in the MathMix dataset which contains both natural and synthetic data, has been utilized to finetune models like GPT-4 . Similarly, the Minerva model, a PaLM variant finetuned on billions of tokens of mathematical documents, reported dramatically improved performance on problems requiring quantitative reasoning . The generation of hard reasoning problems often involves specific sampling and filtering strategies to ensure data quality and difficulty. For instance, in the STaR framework, 10,000 problems are sampled from the dataset for each outer loop iteration on arithmetic tasks [7,8]. To maintain diversity and quality, new samples are generated with a temperature of 1.0, and duplicate question-answer pairs are discarded . The WizardMath method employs a scoring mechanism where the similarity between problems is rated on a scale from 1 to 10, with 1 indicating completely different tasks and 10 indicating identical tasks [4,5]. This method, known as Math Evol-Instruct, has been demonstrated to be as scalable and effective as DART-Math for large-scale synthetic data generation [4,5]. Additionally, Xwin-Math leverages GPT-4-turbo for its data synthesis process [4,5]. In MetaMath, reasoning paths are filtered to retain only those with correct answers [6]. Measuring the difficulty of these synthetic problems is crucial for calibrating model performance. One approach assigns a given question to one of five difficulty levels based on an estimate of question difficulty . Another metric, Intra-Task Difficulty, denotes the inherent learning difficulty of a single task . Empirical analysis shows that the performance of sampling and the REBASE method is comparable on easy problems, specifically levels 1-2 . However, REBASE demonstrates a significant advantage on harder problems, specifically levels 3-5 . This distinction is important because challenging tasks like mathematical reasoning degrade fastest under certain conditions, such as quantization . The impact of synthetic hard problems on model training is further evidenced by the exposure of models to difficult problems that would otherwise not appear in their finetuning datasets [7,8]. Generating step-by-step "chain-of-thought" rationales improves language model performance on complex reasoning tasks such as mathematics or commonsense question-answering [7,8]. Despite these advancements, simply prompting existing LLMs to correct their own mistakes tends to be largely ineffective for obtaining performance improvements on reasoning problems . In contrast, using synthetic data for supervised finetuning significantly improved model performance on unseen tasks [3]. Evaluations based on synthetic data have shown strong correlation with real human judgements [3]. While synthetic data offers benefits, there are considerations regarding data contamination and model scale. One notable exception to contamination concerns was LAMBADA, which appeared to have substantial genuine contamination, yet the impact on performance was very small, with the clean subset scoring within 0.5% of the full dataset . The quality of synthetic text generation has improved over smaller models, increasing the difficulty of distinguishing synthetic text from human-written text . However, Vicuna performs poorly on sophisticated reasoning tasks in certain benchmarks . To address this, strategies such as upsample mathematical data have been employed to improve the model's mathematical reasoning performance . Additionally, rendering results injected into the context allow even small language models armed with Mind's Eye to achieve performance comparable to models 100 times larger [3]. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution to address challenges such as data scarcity, privacy concerns, and high costs in AI development [3]. However, ensuring the factuality, fidelity, and lack of bias in synthetic data remains a critical challenge [3]. The quality and diversity of synthetic data are heavily dependent on the performance of the back-translation method used [3]. Furthermore, the diversity of synthesized data is heavily influenced by the seed data, and although synthesized data can be generated at any scale, the high rate of hallucination can lead to significant quality degradation . This dependency on seed data and generation methods creates a risk of mode collapse, where the diversity of the generated samples diminishes, a limitation analogous to the collapse of diversity in amplification processes observed in other technologies . Bias propagation is another significant limitation, as the training or inference procedure itself may amplify bias beyond what is present in the training data . While some studies suggest that the lack of observed bias may reflect limitations of the measurement rather than an underlying fact about the models , specific biases have been documented in evaluation processes. For instance, LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generations, with GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 showing opposite biases in this regard . This self-recognition bias persists even when models are fine-tuned on tasks unrelated to self-recognition, such as length, vowel count, and readability score . Additionally, the difficulty of distinguishing synthetic text from human-written text has increased with larger models like GPT-3, which improves the quality of text generation and adaptability . A major open challenge is the "ceiling effect," where models struggle to generate problems harder than their own capability or to improve performance on difficult reasoning tasks through simple self-correction. Simply prompting existing LLMs to correct their own mistakes tends to be largely ineffective for obtaining performance improvements on reasoning problems . Similarly, across the board, current schemes for using test-time compute provide only small gains on hard problems, indicating that future work must develop new ways to circumvent this limitation . While methods like REBASE demonstrate a significant advantage on harder problems (levels 3-5) compared to easy problems (levels 1-2) , the general difficulty of scaling to complex reasoning remains. The data quality distribution for Complex Reasoning tasks, which are often constructed through multi-turn dialogues, is spread over a wider area, highlighting the challenge of maintaining data quality in these task types . Current approaches to generating hard reasoning problems often rely on proprietary LLMs and manual prompt engineering to elicit high-quality outputs . For example, Xwin-Math leverages GPT-4-turbo for data synthesis [4,5], and other strategies involve synthetically constructing different slices by taking weighted mixtures of domains from labeled examples . In some cases, new samples are generated with specific temperature settings, and duplicate question-answer pairs are discarded to manage diversity . While models finetuned on such synthetic data can generalize reasonably well on realistic data scraped from the Internet [3], and performance remains competitive even without labeled data in some settings , the reliance on manual prompt engineering and proprietary models limits the scalability and reproducibility of generating truly hard problems. The high proportion of synthetic data in high-quality knowledge sets, such as the 99.8% found in LLaVA-OneVision , underscores the field's dependence on these generation pipelines, yet the inherent limitations in bias, diversity, and the ceiling of model capability remain unresolved open problems.

plan.goal: Define the core methodologies and taxonomies for generating synthetic data, distinguishing between simple augmentation and complex reasoning-focused synthesis.

question: What are some of the key advantages and challenges of building multilingual evaluation datasets by translating existing English datasets into other target languages? Or more specifically, how do these translated datasets impact the quality and reliability of cross-lingual evaluations, and what potential pitfalls should be considered when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks?
raw_answer:
The creation of multilingual datasets frequently relies on translation as a primary method, with approximately 20% of surveyed datasets involving translation in their creation [[akari_cs_10:0]]. This approach is particularly prevalent in research focused on cross-lingual transfer, where datasets used translation at a rate of 61.9%, significantly higher than datasets with other motivations [[akari_cs_10:0]]. Among the various platforms utilized for this purpose, Gengo and One Hour Translation are identified as the most highly used for translation-based multilingual dataset creation [[akari_cs_10:0]]. While machine translation baselines have obtained the best results in some experimental contexts [[akari_cs_10:1]], the reliance on computationally intensive translation models at training or test time remains a significant methodological consideration [[akari_cs_10:1]].

A critical distinction exists between machine translation (MT) and human translation strategies, each presenting unique challenges for data quality. Machine translation systems, such as those based on the sequence-to-sequence framework which has demonstrated success in natural-language sequence transduction [[akari_cs_10:2]], often introduce "translation artifacts" into datasets [[akari_cs_10:3]]. These artifacts can result in "translationese," a phenomenon where hidden linguistic cues in translated text render the task easier than it would be with natural text [[akari_cs_10:3]]. Consequently, recent investigations have revealed that these artifacts compromise the reliability of examples, prompting recommendations for authors to benchmark the presence of such issues and report on geographical invariance [[akari_cs_10:3]]. In specific tasks like open-retrieval question answering, the discrepancy between human and machine translation suggests that even state-of-the-art translation systems struggle to translate questions precisely enough to retrieve an evidence paragraph [[akari_cs_10:4]]. Furthermore, errors in automatic query translation can affect later layers in the pipeline, indicating that translation quality directly impacts downstream performance [[akari_cs_10:4]].

The performance of translation-based methods varies significantly across languages and tasks. For instance, in the XOR QA benchmark, the translation approach outperformed the multilingual one in Arabic, Bengali, Finnish, Japanese, and Korean, but performed poorly in Telugu [[akari_cs_10:4]]. This variability highlights that approaches relying too heavily on the availability of high-quality machine translation will fail to generalize across the world's languages [[akari_cs_10:5]]. Additionally, there is a consistent trend indicating that translation into English is often stronger than translation from English [[akari_cs_10:6]]. In contrast, human translation offers the potential for higher fidelity but introduces different complexities. In the multilingual extension of the COPA dataset, researchers asked carefully chosen human translators to perform culturally-sensitive translation, which involved paraphrasing, substituting original concepts with similar ones, or leveraging phonetically transcribed loan words [[akari_cs_10:7]]. However, human translation is not without its own pitfalls; if human translation tasks are not carefully curated, they can also lead to translation artifacts [[akari_cs_10:3]]. Moreover, while fluency is a common objective of machine translation, it may be less important than comprehensibility for users [[akari_cs_10:7]].

The economic and methodological costs of translation-based dataset creation are substantial. Multilingual dataset creation is often more expensive than English dataset creation [[akari_cs_10:0]]. This cost is partly driven by the need for high-quality translation resources, as automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [[akari_cs_10:7]]. To mitigate these issues, some researchers advocate for native data collection methods. For example, the TyDi QA benchmark avoided data collection procedures reliant on translation and multilingual modeling to greatly mitigate the risk of sampling bias [[akari_cs_10:5]]. This approach stands in contrast to methods like MONOTRANS, which is competitive with joint learning but requires performing additional steps to transfer models to every other language [[akari_cs_10:8]]. The XNLI dataset was designed to address the lack of standardized evaluation protocols in cross-lingual understanding, noting that having a stronger encoder in English positively impacts transfer results on other languages [[akari_cs_10:1]].

Despite the prevalence of translation, there are indications that it may not be the optimal strategy for all scenarios. Results from the T5 model suggest that scale and English-language pre-training may be insufficient to match the performance of more sophisticated methods [[akari_cs_10:9]]. Transfer learning has become apparent in experiments with smaller datasets, where its importance is more pronounced [[akari_cs_10:10]]. Furthermore, techniques such as dropping adapters in the last layer have achieved considerable improvements in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance [[akari_cs_10:11]]. These findings suggest that while translation is a dominant method for creating multilingual benchmarks [[akari_cs_10:0]], its limitations regarding generalization [[akari_cs_10:5]], translation artifacts [[akari_cs_10:3]], and performance variability across languages [[akari_cs_10:4]] necessitate careful consideration when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks.

The process of translating existing English datasets into other target languages introduces specific artifacts that compromise the linguistic fidelity and representativeness of the resulting benchmarks. Recent investigations into cross-lingual modeling have revealed "translation artifacts" in datasets where machine translation systems are used, or where human translation tasks are not carefully curated [[akari_cs_10:12]]. These artifacts are not merely theoretical concerns; for instance, "translationese" results in hidden linguistic cues in translated text that render the task easier than a natural translation would [[akari_cs_10:12]]. The discrepancy between human and machine translation suggests that even state-of-the-art translation systems struggle to translate questions precisely enough to retrieve an evidence paragraph, indicating a fundamental limitation in preserving semantic precision during the translation process [[akari_cs_10:13]].

A primary consequence of these translation artifacts is the introduction of source-language structural biases, making the target language data less representative of its native usage. The process of translation—including human translation—tends to introduce problematic artifacts to the output language such as preserving source-language word order [[akari_cs_10:14]]. Each of these issues makes a translated corpus more English-like, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches by creating a dataset that is structurally closer to the source language than to the target [[akari_cs_10:14]]. This phenomenon is particularly problematic because literal translation of datasets is sometimes impossible or undesirable due to culture-specific concepts in the source that may be missing or unnatural in the target [[akari_cs_10:15]]. Consequently, if evaluation data is automatically translated, there is no trivial way of exposing cultural biases introduced by the projection process, leaving researchers without a straightforward method to assess the cultural validity of the benchmark [[akari_cs_10:15]].

The impact of these artifacts on data quality varies significantly across resource levels, with low-resource languages facing compounded challenges. For low-resource languages, the data quality is poor, and parallel sentences are often misaligned, which exacerbates the issues introduced by translation [[akari_cs_10:16]]. Approaches that rely too heavily on the availability of high-quality machine translation will fail to generalize across the world's languages, as the necessary parallel data for trustworthy translation systems is often lacking in these contexts [[akari_cs_10:14]]. While adapters mostly improve performance in cross-lingual transfer, they fail to do so for low-resource languages such as Urdu, Swahili, Thai, and Greek, suggesting that the translated data in these languages may not support effective model adaptation [[akari_cs_10:17]]. Furthermore, results indicate that datasets constructed via translation are challenging even in English, but especially in low-resource languages, highlighting the uneven distribution of difficulty and quality across the multilingual spectrum [[akari_cs_10:12]].

Despite the prevalence of machine translation, the reliability of these methods remains a subject of ongoing scrutiny and mixed results. Automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data, indicating that the translation process itself can degrade the utility of the dataset for model training [[akari_cs_10:15]]. While machine translation baselines obtained the best results in some experiments, these approaches rely on computationally-intensive translation models either at training or at test time, posing significant practical constraints [[akari_cs_10:18]]. There is a consistent trend of improvement across all datasets as the model scales, with a tendency for translation into English to be stronger than translation from English, suggesting an asymmetry in the quality of cross-lingual transfer that affects the reliability of translated benchmarks [[akari_cs_10:19]].

To address these quality concerns, researchers have proposed specific methodological standards for dataset construction and evaluation. Authors of future multilingual datasets that use any translation methods are encouraged to report and detail their geographical invariance and to benchmark the reliability of examples and presence of translation artifacts [[akari_cs_10:12]]. However, translation artifacts in these datasets remain unclear in many existing works, and future studies can further quantify the quality of each translation method, the distribution of translation artifacts and mistakes, and the impact of such artifacts on final downstream task performances using meta-annotations [[akari_cs_10:16]]. A pilot study suggests that translation quality can reflect the target task performance if workers who copy from MT systems are filtered, and can serve as a good proxy for languages without specific language qualifications, offering a potential path to mitigating some quality issues [[akari_cs_10:16]].

In the context of bias and fairness, the translation process poses additional risks to the preservation of linguistic diversity and social identities. Surveys of bias and fairness in machine learning offer important broad-stroke frameworks but are not specific to linguistic tasks or contexts, leaving a gap in the understanding of how translation specifically impacts bias [[akari_cs_10:20]]. It is crucial to avoid flattening linguistic style and variation or erasing social group identities in post-processing, as translation can inadvertently homogenize the linguistic features necessary for fair evaluation [[akari_cs_10:20]]. For example, Wan et al. (2023) evaluated gender bias in LLM-generated recommendation letters through linguistic style and lexical content, highlighting the need to monitor how such stylistic elements are preserved or altered during translation [[akari_cs_10:21]]. Additionally, mathematical constraints such as $r(f) \leq r(g)$ have been proposed in the context of gender bias mitigation for fairer instruction-tuned machine translation, indicating that formal methods are being developed to address specific bias artifacts introduced by translation [[akari_cs_10:22]].

The reliability of cross-lingual evaluation metrics is fundamentally compromised when datasets are created through translation, as the resulting "Translationese" introduces hidden linguistic cues that render tasks easier than they would be with natural text [[akari_cs_10:23]]. This phenomenon results in a corpus that is markedly different from purely native text, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches by making the translated data more English-like [[akari_cs_10:24]]. Consequently, automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data, highlighting a discrepancy between the utility of translated data for training versus its fidelity for evaluation [[akari_cs_10:25]]. When evaluation data is also automatically translated, there is no trivial way to expose the cultural biases introduced by the projection process, as cross-lingual countermeasures are culture-agnostic and disparity persists even when languages are sampled equally [[akari_cs_10:25]].

Empirical evidence indicates that cross-lingual performance is heavily dependent on the quality of the translation system, with the TRANSLATE TEST approach yielding the best cross-lingual results in evaluations of sentence representations [[akari_cs_10:26]]. However, the reliability of these evaluations is further complicated by the fact that translation artifacts and geographical invariance are often not detailed, making it difficult to benchmark the reliability of examples [[akari_cs_10:23]]. In the context of question answering, manual quality assessment by native speakers on translation samples is necessary to mitigate these issues, yet such rigorous checks are not always standard [[akari_cs_10:27]]. For instance, in the MKQA benchmark, questions are translated into the target language at train time, a process that may introduce inconsistencies if not carefully managed [[akari_cs_10:23]].

The correlation between performance on translated datasets and native data is not uniform across all model types or evaluation metrics. While the average absolute value of the Pearson correlation coefficient between perplexity and performance on other benchmarks is notably high at 0.7895, the correlation between the perplexity of quantized LLMs and their performance remains poorly understood [[akari_cs_10:28]]. In the specific case of quantized models, the correlation between downstream performance and dataset size becomes stronger as quantization becomes more extreme, increasing from $R^{2}=0.24$ for W8 to $R^{2}=0.63$ with W4 [[akari_cs_10:29]]. This suggests that the reliability of evaluation metrics may vary depending on the model's architectural constraints and the specific quantization strategy employed.

Discrepancies in model rankings across languages are evident in various evaluation settings. For GPT-4 results alone, translated responses show superior performance over generated responses in Chinese, indicating that the evaluation metric may favor translated outputs [[akari_cs_10:30]]. In contrast, when using Large Language Models and Reward Models to evaluate multilingual performance, the LLM and RM agree on the ranking of model quality over internal metrics on average across languages [[akari_cs_10:29]]. However, win rates in these evaluations are based on ranking preferences alone, which may not capture the full nuance of cross-lingual performance [[akari_cs_10:29]]. Furthermore, the use of default multilingual models like LASER2 for all languages in benchmarks such as MTEB may obscure language-specific variations, especially since retrieval and clustering tasks in that benchmark are English-only [[akari_cs_10:31]].

The reliability of evaluation is also affected by the specific configuration of the evaluation process. For example, the effect of the number of evaluation samples ($k_{\mathrm{eval}}$) on evaluation reliability is significant, with $k_{\mathrm{eval}} = 100$ chosen to balance cost and reliability in some studies [[akari_cs_10:32]]. In other contexts, such as the evaluation of evaluator LMs, settings are not exactly fair compared to other ranking models, and the purpose is often to check generalization rather than to claim state-of-the-art positions [[akari_cs_10:33]]. Additionally, the inconsistency of LLMs as evaluators is a known issue, with models like GPT-4 prompted to produce scores for Coherence, Consistency, Fluency, and Relevance in a single generation, which may introduce biases [[akari_cs_10:34]]. These factors collectively demonstrate that while translated datasets provide a scalable method for creating multilingual benchmarks, they introduce specific reliability challenges that must be addressed through careful benchmarking, manual assessment, and awareness of translation artifacts [[akari_cs_10:23]][[akari_cs_10:25]].

The reliance on translation as a primary method for constructing multilingual benchmarks introduces significant methodological flaws that compromise the validity of cross-lingual evaluations. A central issue is the phenomenon of "translationese," where translated text retains hidden linguistic cues from the source language, rendering the evaluation task artificially easier than it would be with naturally generated text [[akari_cs_10:35]]. This process systematically makes translated corpora more English-like, which can inflate the apparent performance gains of transfer-learning approaches by masking the true difficulty of the target language [[akari_cs_10:36]]. Consequently, questions in recent multilingual question answering datasets, such as those derived from Lewis et al. (2020), Artetxe et al. (2020), and Longpre et al. (2020), are often translated from English, leading to an inherent English-centric bias in the evaluation items [[akari_cs_10:37]].

This English-centricity limits the generalizability of findings because translated data often fails to capture linguistic phenomena that are typically absent in English but problematic for NLP models in other languages [[akari_cs_10:36]]. For instance, translated sentences can be opaque without specific cultural context, a limitation highlighted by Peskov et al. (2021) [[akari_cs_10:38]]. To address these gaps, benchmarks like TYDI QA explicitly aim to mitigate sampling bias by avoiding data collection procedures that rely on translation and multilingual modeling [[akari_cs_10:36]]. Similarly, XOR-TYDI QA remedies the issue of English-centric questions by annotating questions directly from native speakers of diverse languages [[akari_cs_10:37]]. In contrast, datasets that do rely on translation, such as XNLI, argue that this approach ensures data distributions are maximally similar across languages, which is a trade-off for ecological validity [[akari_cs_10:39]].

The use of automatically translated data can also degrade model performance and evaluation reliability. Research indicates that automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [[akari_cs_10:38]]. Furthermore, the best cross-lingual results in certain evaluations are obtained by the TRANSLATE TEST approach, suggesting that models may be exploiting the specific artifacts of the translation process rather than learning robust cross-lingual representations [[akari_cs_10:39]]. This reliance on translation patterns is compounded by the fact that many existing datasets are automatically induced or translated from English data, meaning that prior surveys estimating resource availability based on dataset counts can be misleading due to varying quality [[akari_cs_10:40]]. The availability of NLP researchers fluent in specific languages highly correlates with the availability of datasets, creating a disparity where languages with fewer fluent researchers are underrepresented or represented only by low-quality translated data [[akari_cs_10:40]].

Data leakage represents another critical failure mode in translated benchmarks, particularly when large-scale retrieval or training corpora are involved. Evaluation data can partially leak into training and retrieval data despite the use of deduplication techniques, allowing models to dramatically exploit such leakage [[akari_cs_10:41]]. The slope of the bits-per-byte metric can indicate how much a model exploits this evaluation leakage, highlighting a risk that is particularly relevant when translated data is used for both training and evaluation [[akari_cs_10:41]]. While some studies attempt to control for biases by randomizing the order of model outputs [[akari_cs_10:42]], the fundamental issue of uncontrolled biases in automatic evaluators remains, as these biases can be significantly gamed by AI systems in ways that human biases would not [[akari_cs_10:43]].

The structural bias in multilingual evaluation is further evidenced by the dominance of English in bias and fairness research. Many surveys focus solely on bias issues in LLMs for English, with additional languages considered only in the context of machine translation or multilingual models [[akari_cs_10:44]]. This focus overlooks global bias, which is a property of an entire span of text, such as the sentiment of several generated phrases [[akari_cs_10:44]]. There is no substitute for a larger representation of minority cultures in the data used for training and evaluation, yet the current landscape is constrained by the difficulty of crowdsourcing for non-English languages and the high reliance on machine translation systems on English-centric platforms [[akari_cs_10:38]][[akari_cs_10:40]]. Providing details about data can help alleviate issues related to exclusion and bias, but the current reliance on translated data often obscures these issues [[akari_cs_10:40]].

Specific benchmarks illustrate the scale of this reliance. For example, the Llama 3 model training data includes 34.6% translated reasoning data, indicating a significant portion of the training signal is derived from translation [[akari_cs_10:45]]. In contrast, smaller datasets like QA@CLEF have only 200 evaluation questions for each language without training data, highlighting the scarcity of native, high-quality evaluation resources [[akari_cs_10:37]]. When evaluating cross-lingual transferability, models like multilingual BERT trained jointly on 15 languages are used, but methods like CLWE perform poorly, suggesting that simple transfer strategies may not overcome the limitations of translated data [[akari_cs_10:46]]. The mean performance metrics in such studies can be skewed by these underlying data quality issues [[akari_cs_10:46]]. Ultimately, while translation facilitates the creation of multilingual benchmarks, it introduces pitfalls such as data leakage, overfitting to translation patterns, and English-centric bias that limit the reliability of cross-lingual evaluations [[akari_cs_10:35]][[akari_cs_10:36]][[akari_cs_10:37]].

To mitigate the risks associated with translation-based dataset creation, researchers are encouraged to report on geographical invariance and benchmark the reliability of examples to detect translation artifacts [[akari_cs_10:47]]. A primary concern is that "translationese" introduces hidden linguistic cues that can render tasks easier than they would be in natural text [[akari_cs_10:47]]. This phenomenon results in a corpus that is markedly different from purely native text, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches [[akari_cs_10:48]]. Consequently, automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [[akari_cs_10:49]]. If evaluation data is also automatically translated, there is no trivial way to expose cultural biases introduced by the projection process [[akari_cs_10:49]]. Furthermore, translation-based approaches can result in data that does not reflect native speakers' interests [[akari_cs_10:50]].

To address these issues, several benchmarks employ human-in-the-loop verification and native speaker assessment. In MKQA, queries are localized to 25 languages by bilingual translators [[akari_cs_10:47]]. Similarly, XOR QA performs manual quality assessment by native speakers on 50 translation samples [[akari_cs_10:51]]. The XNLI dataset utilized annotators who recovered the English consensus label 85% of the time on original English data and 83% of the time on translated French data [[akari_cs_10:52]]. In XNLI, the premise and hypothesis pair is translated from English to other languages, and the label is reused for the translated pair [[akari_cs_10:49]]. While human evaluation correlates with the sacreBLEU metric with a correlation coefficient of 0.79 [[akari_cs_10:50]], the quality and diversity of synthetic data ultimately depends on the performance of the back-translation method [[akari_cs_10:53]].

Hybrid approaches and specific data collection strategies are also employed to reduce bias. TyDi QA avoids data collection procedures reliant on translation and multilingual modeling to greatly mitigate the risk of sampling bias [[akari_cs_10:48]]. This approach presents the first public large-scale multilingual corpus of information-seeking question-answer pairs [[akari_cs_10:48]]. In contrast, MKQA uses a "translate train" method where questions are translated into the target language at train time [[akari_cs_10:47]]. XOR QA focuses only on answerable queries [[akari_cs_10:47]]. The Llama 3 model incorporates a mix of data sources, with 34.6% of the overall distribution being translated reasoning data, alongside 2.4% human annotations and 44.2% data from other NLP tasks [[akari_cs_10:54]]. For quality control, Llama 3 prompts its checkpoint to rate each sample on a three-point scale for general English data regarding accuracy, instruction following, and tone/presentation [[akari_cs_10:54]].

The choice of translation platforms and the broader context of dataset availability also influence best practices. Gengo and One Hour Translation are the most highly used platforms for translation-based multilingual dataset creation [[akari_cs_10:50]]. However, multilingual dataset creation is often more expensive than English dataset creation [[akari_cs_10:50]]. Prior surveys estimating resource availability based on dataset counts can be misleading because many datasets are automatically induced or translated from English data, leading to variable quality [[akari_cs_10:50]]. The availability of NLP researchers who are fluent in specific languages highly correlates with the availability of datasets [[akari_cs_10:50]]. In the MTEB benchmark, while multilingual MPNet provides the overall strongest performance on multilingual classification and STS [[akari_cs_10:55]], retrieval and clustering tasks remain English-only [[akari_cs_10:55]].
answer_official_all: The creation of multilingual datasets frequently relies on translation as a primary method, with approximately 20% of surveyed datasets involving translation in their creation [0]. This approach is particularly prevalent in research focused on cross-lingual transfer, where datasets used translation at a rate of 61.9%, significantly higher than datasets with other motivations [0]. Among the various platforms utilized for this purpose, Gengo and One Hour Translation are identified as the most highly used for translation-based multilingual dataset creation [0]. While machine translation baselines have obtained the best results in some experimental contexts [2], the reliance on computationally intensive translation models at training or test time remains a significant methodological consideration [2]. A critical distinction exists between machine translation (MT) and human translation strategies, each presenting unique challenges for data quality. Machine translation systems, such as those based on the sequence-to-sequence framework which has demonstrated success in natural-language sequence transduction , often introduce "translation artifacts" into datasets [3]. These artifacts can result in "translationese," a phenomenon where hidden linguistic cues in translated text render the task easier than it would be with natural text [3]. Consequently, recent investigations have revealed that these artifacts compromise the reliability of examples, prompting recommendations for authors to benchmark the presence of such issues and report on geographical invariance [3]. In specific tasks like open-retrieval question answering, the discrepancy between human and machine translation suggests that even state-of-the-art translation systems struggle to translate questions precisely enough to retrieve an evidence paragraph [6]. Furthermore, errors in automatic query translation can affect later layers in the pipeline, indicating that translation quality directly impacts downstream performance [6]. The performance of translation-based methods varies significantly across languages and tasks. For instance, in the XOR QA benchmark, the translation approach outperformed the multilingual one in Arabic, Bengali, Finnish, Japanese, and Korean, but performed poorly in Telugu [6]. This variability highlights that approaches relying too heavily on the availability of high-quality machine translation will fail to generalize across the world's languages [4]. Additionally, there is a consistent trend indicating that translation into English is often stronger than translation from English . In contrast, human translation offers the potential for higher fidelity but introduces different complexities. In the multilingual extension of the COPA dataset, researchers asked carefully chosen human translators to perform culturally-sensitive translation, which involved paraphrasing, substituting original concepts with similar ones, or leveraging phonetically transcribed loan words [5,7]. However, human translation is not without its own pitfalls; if human translation tasks are not carefully curated, they can also lead to translation artifacts [3]. Moreover, while fluency is a common objective of machine translation, it may be less important than comprehensibility for users [5,7]. The economic and methodological costs of translation-based dataset creation are substantial. Multilingual dataset creation is often more expensive than English dataset creation [0]. This cost is partly driven by the need for high-quality translation resources, as automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [5,7]. To mitigate these issues, some researchers advocate for native data collection methods. For example, the TyDi QA benchmark avoided data collection procedures reliant on translation and multilingual modeling to greatly mitigate the risk of sampling bias [4]. This approach stands in contrast to methods like MONOTRANS, which is competitive with joint learning but requires performing additional steps to transfer models to every other language [1]. The XNLI dataset was designed to address the lack of standardized evaluation protocols in cross-lingual understanding, noting that having a stronger encoder in English positively impacts transfer results on other languages [2]. Despite the prevalence of translation, there are indications that it may not be the optimal strategy for all scenarios. Results from the T5 model suggest that scale and English-language pre-training may be insufficient to match the performance of more sophisticated methods . Transfer learning has become apparent in experiments with smaller datasets, where its importance is more pronounced . Furthermore, techniques such as dropping adapters in the last layer have achieved considerable improvements in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance . These findings suggest that while translation is a dominant method for creating multilingual benchmarks [0], its limitations regarding generalization [4], translation artifacts [3], and performance variability across languages [6] necessitate careful consideration when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks. The process of translating existing English datasets into other target languages introduces specific artifacts that compromise the linguistic fidelity and representativeness of the resulting benchmarks. Recent investigations into cross-lingual modeling have revealed "translation artifacts" in datasets where machine translation systems are used, or where human translation tasks are not carefully curated [3]. These artifacts are not merely theoretical concerns; for instance, "translationese" results in hidden linguistic cues in translated text that render the task easier than a natural translation would [3]. The discrepancy between human and machine translation suggests that even state-of-the-art translation systems struggle to translate questions precisely enough to retrieve an evidence paragraph, indicating a fundamental limitation in preserving semantic precision during the translation process [6]. A primary consequence of these translation artifacts is the introduction of source-language structural biases, making the target language data less representative of its native usage. The process of translation—including human translation—tends to introduce problematic artifacts to the output language such as preserving source-language word order [4]. Each of these issues makes a translated corpus more English-like, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches by creating a dataset that is structurally closer to the source language than to the target [4]. This phenomenon is particularly problematic because literal translation of datasets is sometimes impossible or undesirable due to culture-specific concepts in the source that may be missing or unnatural in the target [5,7]. Consequently, if evaluation data is automatically translated, there is no trivial way of exposing cultural biases introduced by the projection process, leaving researchers without a straightforward method to assess the cultural validity of the benchmark [5,7]. The impact of these artifacts on data quality varies significantly across resource levels, with low-resource languages facing compounded challenges. For low-resource languages, the data quality is poor, and parallel sentences are often misaligned, which exacerbates the issues introduced by translation [0]. Approaches that rely too heavily on the availability of high-quality machine translation will fail to generalize across the world's languages, as the necessary parallel data for trustworthy translation systems is often lacking in these contexts [4]. While adapters mostly improve performance in cross-lingual transfer, they fail to do so for low-resource languages such as Urdu, Swahili, Thai, and Greek, suggesting that the translated data in these languages may not support effective model adaptation [1]. Furthermore, results indicate that datasets constructed via translation are challenging even in English, but especially in low-resource languages, highlighting the uneven distribution of difficulty and quality across the multilingual spectrum [3]. Despite the prevalence of machine translation, the reliability of these methods remains a subject of ongoing scrutiny and mixed results. Automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data, indicating that the translation process itself can degrade the utility of the dataset for model training [5,7]. While machine translation baselines obtained the best results in some experiments, these approaches rely on computationally-intensive translation models either at training or at test time, posing significant practical constraints [2]. There is a consistent trend of improvement across all datasets as the model scales, with a tendency for translation into English to be stronger than translation from English, suggesting an asymmetry in the quality of cross-lingual transfer that affects the reliability of translated benchmarks . To address these quality concerns, researchers have proposed specific methodological standards for dataset construction and evaluation. Authors of future multilingual datasets that use any translation methods are encouraged to report and detail their geographical invariance and to benchmark the reliability of examples and presence of translation artifacts [3]. However, translation artifacts in these datasets remain unclear in many existing works, and future studies can further quantify the quality of each translation method, the distribution of translation artifacts and mistakes, and the impact of such artifacts on final downstream task performances using meta-annotations [0]. A pilot study suggests that translation quality can reflect the target task performance if workers who copy from MT systems are filtered, and can serve as a good proxy for languages without specific language qualifications, offering a potential path to mitigating some quality issues [0]. In the context of bias and fairness, the translation process poses additional risks to the preservation of linguistic diversity and social identities. Surveys of bias and fairness in machine learning offer important broad-stroke frameworks but are not specific to linguistic tasks or contexts, leaving a gap in the understanding of how translation specifically impacts bias . It is crucial to avoid flattening linguistic style and variation or erasing social group identities in post-processing, as translation can inadvertently homogenize the linguistic features necessary for fair evaluation . For example, Wan et al. (2023) evaluated gender bias in LLM-generated recommendation letters through linguistic style and lexical content, highlighting the need to monitor how such stylistic elements are preserved or altered during translation . Additionally, mathematical constraints such as $r(f) \leq r(g)$ have been proposed in the context of gender bias mitigation for fairer instruction-tuned machine translation, indicating that formal methods are being developed to address specific bias artifacts introduced by translation . The reliability of cross-lingual evaluation metrics is fundamentally compromised when datasets are created through translation, as the resulting "Translationese" introduces hidden linguistic cues that render tasks easier than they would be with natural text [3]. This phenomenon results in a corpus that is markedly different from purely native text, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches by making the translated data more English-like [4]. Consequently, automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data, highlighting a discrepancy between the utility of translated data for training versus its fidelity for evaluation [5,7]. When evaluation data is also automatically translated, there is no trivial way to expose the cultural biases introduced by the projection process, as cross-lingual countermeasures are culture-agnostic and disparity persists even when languages are sampled equally [5,7]. Empirical evidence indicates that cross-lingual performance is heavily dependent on the quality of the translation system, with the TRANSLATE TEST approach yielding the best cross-lingual results in evaluations of sentence representations [2]. However, the reliability of these evaluations is further complicated by the fact that translation artifacts and geographical invariance are often not detailed, making it difficult to benchmark the reliability of examples [3]. In the context of question answering, manual quality assessment by native speakers on translation samples is necessary to mitigate these issues, yet such rigorous checks are not always standard [6]. For instance, in the MKQA benchmark, questions are translated into the target language at train time, a process that may introduce inconsistencies if not carefully managed [3]. The correlation between performance on translated datasets and native data is not uniform across all model types or evaluation metrics. While the average absolute value of the Pearson correlation coefficient between perplexity and performance on other benchmarks is notably high at 0.7895, the correlation between the perplexity of quantized LLMs and their performance remains poorly understood . In the specific case of quantized models, the correlation between downstream performance and dataset size becomes stronger as quantization becomes more extreme, increasing from $R^{2}=0.24$ for W8 to $R^{2}=0.63$ with W4 . This suggests that the reliability of evaluation metrics may vary depending on the model's architectural constraints and the specific quantization strategy employed. Discrepancies in model rankings across languages are evident in various evaluation settings. For GPT-4 results alone, translated responses show superior performance over generated responses in Chinese, indicating that the evaluation metric may favor translated outputs . In contrast, when using Large Language Models and Reward Models to evaluate multilingual performance, the LLM and RM agree on the ranking of model quality over internal metrics on average across languages . However, win rates in these evaluations are based on ranking preferences alone, which may not capture the full nuance of cross-lingual performance . Furthermore, the use of default multilingual models like LASER2 for all languages in benchmarks such as MTEB may obscure language-specific variations, especially since retrieval and clustering tasks in that benchmark are English-only . The reliability of evaluation is also affected by the specific configuration of the evaluation process. For example, the effect of the number of evaluation samples ($k_{\mathrm{eval}}$) on evaluation reliability is significant, with $k_{\mathrm{eval}} = 100$ chosen to balance cost and reliability in some studies . In other contexts, such as the evaluation of evaluator LMs, settings are not exactly fair compared to other ranking models, and the purpose is often to check generalization rather than to claim state-of-the-art positions . Additionally, the inconsistency of LLMs as evaluators is a known issue, with models like GPT-4 prompted to produce scores for Coherence, Consistency, Fluency, and Relevance in a single generation, which may introduce biases . These factors collectively demonstrate that while translated datasets provide a scalable method for creating multilingual benchmarks, they introduce specific reliability challenges that must be addressed through careful benchmarking, manual assessment, and awareness of translation artifacts [3][5,7]. The reliance on translation as a primary method for constructing multilingual benchmarks introduces significant methodological flaws that compromise the validity of cross-lingual evaluations. A central issue is the phenomenon of "translationese," where translated text retains hidden linguistic cues from the source language, rendering the evaluation task artificially easier than it would be with naturally generated text [3]. This process systematically makes translated corpora more English-like, which can inflate the apparent performance gains of transfer-learning approaches by masking the true difficulty of the target language [4]. Consequently, questions in recent multilingual question answering datasets, such as those derived from Lewis et al. (2020), Artetxe et al. (2020), and Longpre et al. (2020), are often translated from English, leading to an inherent English-centric bias in the evaluation items [6]. This English-centricity limits the generalizability of findings because translated data often fails to capture linguistic phenomena that are typically absent in English but problematic for NLP models in other languages [4]. For instance, translated sentences can be opaque without specific cultural context, a limitation highlighted by Peskov et al. (2021) [5,7]. To address these gaps, benchmarks like TYDI QA explicitly aim to mitigate sampling bias by avoiding data collection procedures that rely on translation and multilingual modeling [4]. Similarly, XOR-TYDI QA remedies the issue of English-centric questions by annotating questions directly from native speakers of diverse languages [6]. In contrast, datasets that do rely on translation, such as XNLI, argue that this approach ensures data distributions are maximally similar across languages, which is a trade-off for ecological validity [2]. The use of automatically translated data can also degrade model performance and evaluation reliability. Research indicates that automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [5,7]. Furthermore, the best cross-lingual results in certain evaluations are obtained by the TRANSLATE TEST approach, suggesting that models may be exploiting the specific artifacts of the translation process rather than learning robust cross-lingual representations [2]. This reliance on translation patterns is compounded by the fact that many existing datasets are automatically induced or translated from English data, meaning that prior surveys estimating resource availability based on dataset counts can be misleading due to varying quality [0]. The availability of NLP researchers fluent in specific languages highly correlates with the availability of datasets, creating a disparity where languages with fewer fluent researchers are underrepresented or represented only by low-quality translated data [0]. Data leakage represents another critical failure mode in translated benchmarks, particularly when large-scale retrieval or training corpora are involved. Evaluation data can partially leak into training and retrieval data despite the use of deduplication techniques, allowing models to dramatically exploit such leakage . The slope of the bits-per-byte metric can indicate how much a model exploits this evaluation leakage, highlighting a risk that is particularly relevant when translated data is used for both training and evaluation . While some studies attempt to control for biases by randomizing the order of model outputs , the fundamental issue of uncontrolled biases in automatic evaluators remains, as these biases can be significantly gamed by AI systems in ways that human biases would not . The structural bias in multilingual evaluation is further evidenced by the dominance of English in bias and fairness research. Many surveys focus solely on bias issues in LLMs for English, with additional languages considered only in the context of machine translation or multilingual models . This focus overlooks global bias, which is a property of an entire span of text, such as the sentiment of several generated phrases . There is no substitute for a larger representation of minority cultures in the data used for training and evaluation, yet the current landscape is constrained by the difficulty of crowdsourcing for non-English languages and the high reliance on machine translation systems on English-centric platforms [5,7][0]. Providing details about data can help alleviate issues related to exclusion and bias, but the current reliance on translated data often obscures these issues [0]. Specific benchmarks illustrate the scale of this reliance. For example, the Llama 3 model training data includes 34.6% translated reasoning data, indicating a significant portion of the training signal is derived from translation . In contrast, smaller datasets like QA@CLEF have only 200 evaluation questions for each language without training data, highlighting the scarcity of native, high-quality evaluation resources [6]. When evaluating cross-lingual transferability, models like multilingual BERT trained jointly on 15 languages are used, but methods like CLWE perform poorly, suggesting that simple transfer strategies may not overcome the limitations of translated data [1]. The mean performance metrics in such studies can be skewed by these underlying data quality issues [1]. Ultimately, while translation facilitates the creation of multilingual benchmarks, it introduces pitfalls such as data leakage, overfitting to translation patterns, and English-centric bias that limit the reliability of cross-lingual evaluations [3][4][6]. To mitigate the risks associated with translation-based dataset creation, researchers are encouraged to report on geographical invariance and benchmark the reliability of examples to detect translation artifacts [3]. A primary concern is that "translationese" introduces hidden linguistic cues that can render tasks easier than they would be in natural text [3]. This phenomenon results in a corpus that is markedly different from purely native text, potentially inflating the apparent gains of transfer-learning approaches [4]. Consequently, automatically translated training data can lead to worse performance than native target language data [5,7]. If evaluation data is also automatically translated, there is no trivial way to expose cultural biases introduced by the projection process [5,7]. Furthermore, translation-based approaches can result in data that does not reflect native speakers' interests [0]. To address these issues, several benchmarks employ human-in-the-loop verification and native speaker assessment. In MKQA, queries are localized to 25 languages by bilingual translators [3]. Similarly, XOR QA performs manual quality assessment by native speakers on 50 translation samples [6]. The XNLI dataset utilized annotators who recovered the English consensus label 85% of the time on original English data and 83% of the time on translated French data [2]. In XNLI, the premise and hypothesis pair is translated from English to other languages, and the label is reused for the translated pair [5,7]. While human evaluation correlates with the sacreBLEU metric with a correlation coefficient of 0.79 [0], the quality and diversity of synthetic data ultimately depends on the performance of the back-translation method . Hybrid approaches and specific data collection strategies are also employed to reduce bias. TyDi QA avoids data collection procedures reliant on translation and multilingual modeling to greatly mitigate the risk of sampling bias [4]. This approach presents the first public large-scale multilingual corpus of information-seeking question-answer pairs [4]. In contrast, MKQA uses a "translate train" method where questions are translated into the target language at train time [3]. XOR QA focuses only on answerable queries [3]. The Llama 3 model incorporates a mix of data sources, with 34.6% of the overall distribution being translated reasoning data, alongside 2.4% human annotations and 44.2% data from other NLP tasks . For quality control, Llama 3 prompts its checkpoint to rate each sample on a three-point scale for general English data regarding accuracy, instruction following, and tone/presentation . The choice of translation platforms and the broader context of dataset availability also influence best practices. Gengo and One Hour Translation are the most highly used platforms for translation-based multilingual dataset creation [0]. However, multilingual dataset creation is often more expensive than English dataset creation [0].
