question: What are papers that train multilmodal language models that can input and output both text and images?
raw_answer:
The architectural landscape for multimodal language models is defined by a spectrum of design choices, ranging from modular compositions of separate pretrained models to unified single-transformer frameworks. Early approaches often relied on modular frameworks that leverage structured dialogue between multiple large pretrained models to make joint predictions for new multimodal tasks without requiring additional training [[weijia_cs_2:0]]. For instance, Socratic Models compose these models through language prompting to perform downstream tasks such as image captioning, where the language model can perform comparably on contextual captioning even without direct image input, relying solely on article text [[weijia_cs_2:0]]. In contrast, more recent foundational architectures integrate vision and language components more tightly, such as the architecture consisting of a Transformer-based pre-trained CLIP vision encoder, an MLP vision-language connector, and an LLM backbone [[weijia_cs_2:1]]. This specific structure underpins baselines like LLaVA-1.5, which is proposed as a simple, effective, and data-efficient baseline for large multimodal models [[weijia_cs_2:2]].

A critical distinction in this taxonomy is between models that primarily process visual inputs for understanding versus those that generate images. While large language models are typically defined by autoregressive, autoencoding, or encoder-decoder architectures trained on massive text corpora [[weijia_cs_2:3]], multimodal extensions must address the specific challenges of integrating non-textual data, as methods designed for single-modal targets do not inherently address multimodal settings [[weijia_cs_2:1]]. For image generation, diffusion models have emerged as a dominant paradigm, achieving image sample quality superior to current state-of-the-art generative models [[weijia_cs_2:4]]. These diffusion-based approaches often condition the image generator with a text caption using a noisy version of CLIP [[weijia_cs_2:4]], or utilize classifier guidance that combines the score estimate of a diffusion model with the gradient of a separately trained image classifier [[weijia_cs_2:5]]. However, integrating these generative capabilities into a unified language model presents architectural challenges; for example, unlike text-only generation which is inherently variable-length, token-based image generation produces fixed-size blocks of tokens corresponding to an image [[weijia_cs_2:6]].

Recent efforts aim to unify multimodal understanding and generation within a single model, moving away from separate encoders and decoders. CM3, a causal masked multimodal model, demonstrates that a single model can be prompted to recover the functionality of many other models, including image generation, image captioning, and unconditional image generation [[weijia_cs_2:7]]. In CM3, generated images show substantial improvement when grounded in ground truth text compared to unconditional image-infilling [[weijia_cs_2:7]]. Similarly, Chameleon, a mixed-modal early-fusion foundation model, performs non-trivial image generation all in a single model [[weijia_cs_2:6]]. Show-o further advances this unification by eliminating the need for a separate text encoder to extract text embeddings for text-to-image generation, instead inherently encoding text conditional information by itself [[weijia_cs_2:8]]. This contrasts with state-of-the-art diffusion models that typically require an additional text encoder [[weijia_cs_2:8]].

The choice of representation for image tokens within these unified architectures significantly impacts performance. Transfusion explores a model that can generate images and text on par with similar scale diffusion models and language models [[weijia_cs_2:9]]. However, training on quantized image tokens has been found to degrade text performance more than using diffusion on all three benchmarks [[weijia_cs_2:9]]. This highlights an open problem in the field, as it remains to be explored whether image generation and understanding can be as easily unified as text embedding and generation [[weijia_cs_2:10]]. While these models aim for generalizability and applicability [[weijia_cs_2:3]], and very large language models are considered an important ingredient in adaptable, general language systems [[weijia_cs_2:11]], the specific integration of high-fidelity image generation with robust text processing remains an active area of research. Practical implementations of these models also involve specific training configurations, such as a maximum token sequence length of 2048 and a per-GPU batch size of 8 in the case of CM3 [[weijia_cs_2:7]]. Furthermore, the application of these models extends to specific tasks like style similarity measurement, where images are generated using prompts in the format "A painting in the style of <artist_name>" using Stable Diffusion 2.1 [[weijia_cs_2:12]], and visual task transfer, as seen in LLaVA-OneVision which handles single-image tasks [[weijia_cs_2:13]].

Early-fusion architectures represent a significant approach to unifying multimodal understanding and generation, exemplified by Chameleon, which enables the early fusion of different modalities to generate both text and image tokens through the same manner of autoregressive modeling [[weijia_cs_2:14]]. Chameleon performs non-trivial image generation within a single model [[weijia_cs_2:15]] and outperforms models such as Flamingo and IDEFICS on tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering [[weijia_cs_2:15]]. The Chameleon-34B model, which was trained on 6.0T tokens with a 7B parameter count, achieves specific performance metrics including a score of 67.1 and 26.74 on evaluated benchmarks [[weijia_cs_2:16]]. While Chameleon unlocks new possibilities for multimodal interaction, as demonstrated by its strong performance on mixed-modal open-ended QA [[weijia_cs_2:15]], it has limitations, such as failing to correctly identify unusual aspects in certain contexts [[weijia_cs_2:14]].

In contrast, late-fusion or connector-based architectures, such as LLaVA, utilize simpler designs where vision tokens from pre-trained vision encoders are directly input into the language model [[weijia_cs_2:17]]. LLaVA passes all vision tokens through a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector to the language model, achieving high performance but at the cost of increased computational demands [[weijia_cs_2:17]]. This architecture is considered one of the simplest for Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and requires training only a simple fully-connected projection layer on merely 600K image-text pairs [[weijia_cs_2:18]]. The effectiveness of this approach is highlighted by LLaVA-1.5, which provides more detailed, visually-grounded responses for writing tasks with visual inputs than the original LLaVA [[weijia_cs_2:18]]. Visual instruction tuning plays an important role in improving an LMM's capabilities, as suggested by the results of these models [[weijia_cs_2:18]].

The LLaVA-OneVision model extends this line of work, utilizing datasets such as Single-image 3.2M and OneVision 1.6M for training [[weijia_cs_2:19]]. A similar conclusion is observed in this work: a large amount of visual instruction tuning data can significantly improve performance [[weijia_cs_2:19]]. Other models, such as CM3, operate with a maximum token sequence length of 2048 and use a per GPU batch size of 8 for every model [[weijia_cs_2:20]]. Flamingo, another representative model, achieves a score of 50.6 in specific evaluations [[weijia_cs_2:21]].

Recent advancements explore unified frameworks that handle both text and image modalities. The SHOW-O model aims to unify multimodal understanding and generation using a single transformer [[weijia_cs_2:14]]. Transfusion presents a multi-modal model that predicts the next token and diffuses images [[weijia_cs_2:16]]. In the domain of generative representational instruction tuning, it remains to be explored whether text embedding and generation can be as easily unified as in recent works [[weijia_cs_2:22]]. Socratic models focus on adapting pre-existing foundation models to capture new multimodal functionalities zero-shot without relying on additional domain-specific data collection or model finetuning [[weijia_cs_2:23]]. Instruction tuning has been shown to result in significant gains for knowledge tagging and image editing tasks [[weijia_cs_2:24]]. Training strategies often involve balancing different data sources, satisfying constraints such as $\alpha_{\mathrm{out}} + \alpha_{\mathrm{in}} + \alpha_{\mathrm{D}} = 1$ [[weijia_cs_2:25]], with specific weighting examples including an EW value of 8.75 [[weijia_cs_2:25]]. Evaluation of these models can be complicated by biases, where crowd-sourced annotators, GPT-4, and Claude-1 exhibit a distinct and notable preference for specific assistants [[weijia_cs_2:26]].

Multimodal language models that generate images primarily employ two distinct architectural strategies: discrete tokenization using vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAE) and continuous diffusion heads. In the discrete approach, images are represented as a series of discrete tokens, similar to text, allowing the language model to predict the next token in a sequence [[weijia_cs_2:27]]. This method utilizes discrete autoencoders, such as VQ-VAE, which introduce a quantization layer and regularization losses to map continuous latent embeddings to discrete tokens [[weijia_cs_2:28]]. For instance, the CM3 model uses image tokens from a VQVAE-GAN, where each image amounts to 256 tokens provided in the order they appear in the original HTML source [[weijia_cs_2:29]]. Similarly, the Chameleon model represents images as discrete tokens, noting that unlike text-only generation which is variable-length, token-based image generation produces fixed-size blocks of tokens corresponding to an image [[weijia_cs_2:27]]. The Show-o model also adopts this discrete approach, using the pre-trained MAGVIT-v2 to tokenize input images into discrete tokens for both multimodal understanding and generation [[weijia_cs_2:30]]. In some implementations, the token count for images can be significantly higher than for text; for example, one model reports an image having 2,308 tokens whereas the associated text contains an average of only 192 tokens [[weijia_cs_2:31]].

In contrast, other models utilize continuous diffusion mechanisms to output images. The Transfusion model combines next-token prediction for text with diffusion for images within a single multi-modal model [[weijia_cs_2:28]]. This approach incorporates bidirectional attention for the image generation component [[weijia_cs_2:28]]. Experimental results indicate that Transfusion scales significantly better than quantizing images and training a language model over discrete image tokens [[weijia_cs_2:28]]. Diffusion models have historically demonstrated strong performance in conditional image synthesis; for example, conditioning an image generator with a text caption using a noisy version of CLIP allows for state-of-the-art results [[weijia_cs_2:32]]. Classifier guidance, which combines the score estimate of a diffusion model with the gradient of an image classifier, requires training an image classifier separate from the diffusion model [[weijia_cs_2:33]]. By combining guidance with upsampling, sample quality on high-resolution conditional image synthesis can be further improved [[weijia_cs_2:32]].

The integration of these generation mechanisms into unified architectures presents specific challenges and characteristics. While CM3 is capable of generating semantically coherent images on-par with modern GANs, it notes that neither of its components is jointly modeling image tokens in the same way as text [[weijia_cs_2:29]]. In the Chameleon framework, the images generated are usually relevant to the context, making documents with interleaving text and images appealing to users [[weijia_cs_2:27]]. However, the process of generating these images can involve external tools; for instance, Chameleon uses OpenAI DALL-E 3 to generate images conditioned on captions and replaces the captions in original responses with those generated images [[weijia_cs_2:27]]. The computational cost of generation is also a factor, as generating 100 pages of content from a trained model can cost on the order of 0.4 kW-hr [[weijia_cs_2:34]].

Current research highlights ongoing limitations and open questions regarding the unification of these modalities. It remains to be explored whether image generation can be as easily unified as text embedding and generation in recent works [[weijia_cs_2:35]]. Furthermore, the role of vision-language models (VLMs) in the generation process varies; information from the VLM is more important for language models in generating image descriptions than captions [[weijia_cs_2:36]]. The quality and specificity of generated images depend heavily on the prompting strategy; for example, using Stable Diffusion 2.1 with a prompt in the format "A painting in the style of <artist_name>" generates specific outputs, such as always generating a version of Marilyn Diptych's painting for the prompt "A painting in the style of Warhol" [[weijia_cs_2:37]]. These results suggest that very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems [[weijia_cs_2:34]].

Evaluation of multimodal models that handle both text and image inputs and outputs relies on distinct benchmarks for understanding and generation, with recent work highlighting the difficulty in unifying these capabilities within a single framework [[weijia_cs_2:38]]. For multimodal understanding, models are typically assessed on visual question answering (VQA) and related tasks, where Show-o autoregressively predicts textual answers given an image and visual questions [[weijia_cs_2:39]]. Show-o achieves competitive performance on benchmarks such as POPE, MME, Flickr30k, and VQAv2, and performs better on the GQA benchmark, despite having a smaller model size [[weijia_cs_2:39]]. Similarly, the model achieves decent performance on the Flickr30k benchmark and performs much better on the VQAv2 benchmark [[weijia_cs_2:39]]. LLaVA-OneVision, a family of open large multimodal models, improves performance boundaries in three important vision settings, including multi-image tasks where it achieves a score of 43.0% [[weijia_cs_2:40]]. However, achieving ideal performance remains difficult for tasks requiring a combination of capabilities; for instance, correctly answering the attribute of an object in VQA does not guarantee an accurate depiction of that attribute in a detailed image description [[weijia_cs_2:41]]. While LLaVA-1.5 is not finetuned for multilingual multimodal instruction following, it is capable of following multilingual instructions [[weijia_cs_2:41]]. In contrast, Socratic Models demonstrate that language models can perform comparably on contextual image captioning even without input images, using only article text [[weijia_cs_2:42]]. The increased measured performance of Socratic Models, rising from 40.3 to 44.7 R@1, directly reflects the added benefits of incorporating language-based multimodal reasoning [[weijia_cs_2:42]]. Visual Programming (VisProg) shows strong zero-shot performance using a single-image VQA model for image understanding and an LLM for reasoning [[weijia_cs_2:43]]. Replacing the VILT-VQA model with a better VQA model for NLVR could improve performance by up to 24% [[weijia_cs_2:43]]. Chameleon unlocks new possibilities for multimodal interaction, as demonstrated by its strong performance on a new benchmark for mixed-modal open-ended QA [[weijia_cs_2:44]].

For image generation and alignment, evaluation often involves metrics such as the CLIP score and Inception score. The CLIP score reflects how well image features correspond to text features, allowing for the identification of high-quality data where images and text are closely related [[weijia_cs_2:45]]. To evaluate similarity between an input image and text, the CLIP model is used to extract features from both [[weijia_cs_2:45]]. In the context of diffusion models, conditioning an image generator with a text caption using a noisy version of CLIP is a standard approach [[weijia_cs_2:46]]. Data that can be classified well scores high on the Inception score of perceptual quality [[weijia_cs_2:47]]. While diffusion models produce diverse and high-quality images, they still fall short of GANs without expensive rejection sampling and special metrics to compensate for blurriness [[weijia_cs_2:46]]. CLIP is consistently biased towards image content, for instance retrieving images of a dog or a mother and baby in specific columns [[weijia_cs_2:48]]. The CLIP ViT-L model is utilized with a dimension of 70 in certain evaluations [[weijia_cs_2:48]]. In data curation for models like Llama 3, all image-text pairs below a certain CLIP score are removed [[weijia_cs_2:49]].

The representation of images within these models varies, impacting their ability to comprehend visual information. Show-o reveals that it is required to involve more image-text pairs for multimodal alignment and more image tokens to represent an image for better comprehending the image information [[weijia_cs_2:39]]. In CM3, image tokens from a VQVAE-GAN are provided in the order they appear in the original HTML source, amounting to 256 tokens for every image [[weijia_cs_2:50]]. Socratic Models utilize a prompt structure where the model acts as an intelligent image captioning bot, identifying objects in an image to generate a short caption [[weijia_cs_2:42]]. It remains to be explored whether image embedding and generation can be as easily unified as text embedding and generation [[weijia_cs_2:38]].

A primary constraint in the development of multimodal language models is the substantial computational cost associated with training and inference. Training large-scale multimodal architectures often requires significant hardware resources, as evidenced by experiments that normalize training time by linearly scaling to 256 GPUs [[weijia_cs_2:51]]. The computational burden is further compounded by architectural choices; for instance, using a base model to embed input data roughly doubles the computational cost [[weijia_cs_2:52]]. Similarly, in task composition frameworks like AdapterFusion, adding more tasks to the set of adapters results in a linear increase of computational cost for both training and inference [[weijia_cs_2:53]]. While some approaches attempt to mitigate this, such as RAIN, which necessitates a higher computational cost for self-alignment without finetuning [[weijia_cs_2:54]], others suggest that smaller models combined with advanced inference algorithms can offer Pareto-optimal trade-offs in cost and performance [[weijia_cs_2:55]]. However, these cost-efficiency strategies are often designed for single-modal targets and do not directly address the specific challenges present in multimodal settings [[weijia_cs_2:56]]. Furthermore, the choice of denoising objectives in unified text-to-text transformers is largely driven by their computational cost, with observations showing nearly identical step times for L-layer language models versus L+L-layer encoder-decoder models [[weijia_cs_2:57]]. At inference time, methods that utilize search can lead to performance gains but at the cost of increased inference-time compute [[weijia_cs_2:55]].

Hallucination remains a critical limitation for multimodal models, particularly when generating visual or textual outputs that may be factually incorrect. Large language models often generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect responses, a phenomenon commonly known as hallucination [[weijia_cs_2:58]]. In the context of visual instruction tuning, models like LLaVA-1.5 are not exempt from producing hallucinations and occasionally disseminating misinformation, necessitating caution in critical applications such as medicine [[weijia_cs_2:59]]. Although scaling model inputs to higher resolutions, such as 448^2, has been found to significantly reduce such hallucinations [[weijia_cs_2:59]], the issue persists. The unreliability inherited from the underlying models on which Socratic systems are constructed further limits their effectiveness [[weijia_cs_2:60]]. Additionally, the degree to which visual details are provided in captions is largely limited by the capabilities of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) [[weijia_cs_2:60]]. There is also evidence that alignment techniques may exacerbate this issue; for example, the factuality score of Llama-2-7b-chat (RLHFed) is lower than that of Vicuna-7b (SFTed), suggesting that RLHF might cause more hallucination [[weijia_cs_2:61]].

Maintaining coherence and reliability in long-context or multi-turn multimodal interactions presents additional open challenges. Current multimodal models often operate with limited sequence lengths; for instance, CM3 utilizes a maximum token sequence length of 2048 [[weijia_cs_2:51]]. The ability of models fine-tuned on limited data to engage in multi-turn dialogue remains an open question, as illustrated by the inquiry into whether a model fine-tuned on only 1,000 single-turn interactions can successfully handle multi-turn exchanges [[weijia_cs_2:62]]. In complex reasoning tasks, such as those involving Socratic models, the interaction relies on web crawlers and visual search to retrieve related frames based on language model responses, a process that is constrained by the reliability of the constituent models [[weijia_cs_2:60]]. The evaluation of these systems is further complicated by the fact that current measures of how well models perform a task have pointed-out limitations [[weijia_cs_2:63]]. While very large language models are considered an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems [[weijia_cs_2:64]], their application to multimodal settings requires further investigation, as few-shot recalibration approaches are only beginning to be applied to a broader set of models, including instruction-tuned and RLHF models, in multimodal contexts [[weijia_cs_2:65]].

While Chameleon unlocks new possibilities for multimodal interaction, as demonstrated by its strong performance on mixed-modal open-ended QA [0], it has limitations, such as failing to correctly identify unusual aspects in certain contexts . In contrast, late-fusion or connector-based architectures, such as LLaVA, utilize simpler designs where vision tokens from pre-trained vision encoders are directly input into the language model . LLaVA passes all vision tokens through a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector to the language model, achieving high performance but at the cost of increased computational demands . This architecture is considered one of the simplest for Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and requires training only a simple fully-connected projection layer on merely 600K image-text pairs . The effectiveness of this approach is highlighted by LLaVA-1.5, which provides more detailed, visually-grounded responses for writing tasks with visual inputs than the original LLaVA . Visual instruction tuning plays an important role in improving an LMM's capabilities, as suggested by the results of these models . The LLaVA-OneVision model extends this line of work, utilizing datasets such as Single-image 3.2M and OneVision 1.6M for training . A similar conclusion is observed in this work: a large amount of visual instruction tuning data can significantly improve performance . Other models, such as CM3, operate with a maximum token sequence length of 2048 and use a per GPU batch size of 8 for every model [1]. Flamingo, another representative model, achieves a score of 50.6 in specific evaluations . Recent advancements explore unified frameworks that handle both text and image modalities. The SHOW-O model aims to unify multimodal understanding and generation using a single transformer . Transfusion presents a multi-modal model that predicts the next token and diffuses images [2]. In the domain of generative representational instruction tuning, it remains to be explored whether text embedding and generation can be as easily unified as in recent works . Socratic models focus on adapting pre-existing foundation models to capture new multimodal functionalities zero-shot without relying on additional domain-specific data collection or model finetuning . Instruction tuning has been shown to result in significant gains for knowledge tagging and image editing tasks . Training strategies often involve balancing different data sources, satisfying constraints such as $\alpha_{\mathrm{out}} + \alpha_{\mathrm{in}} + \alpha_{\mathrm{D}} = 1$ , with specific weighting examples including an EW value of 8.75 . Evaluation of these models can be complicated by biases, where crowd-sourced annotators, GPT-4, and Claude-1 exhibit a distinct and notable preference for specific assistants . Multimodal language models that generate images primarily employ two distinct architectural strategies: discrete tokenization using vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAE) and continuous diffusion heads. In the discrete approach, images are represented as a series of discrete tokens, similar to text, allowing the language model to predict the next token in a sequence [0]. This method utilizes discrete autoencoders, such as VQ-VAE, which introduce a quantization layer and regularization losses to map continuous latent embeddings to discrete tokens [2]. For instance, the CM3 model uses image tokens from a VQVAE-GAN, where each image amounts to 256 tokens provided in the order they appear in the original HTML source [1]. Similarly, the Chameleon model represents images as discrete tokens, noting that unlike text-only generation which is variable-length, token-based image generation produces fixed-size blocks of tokens corresponding to an image [0]. The Show-o model also adopts this discrete approach, using the pre-trained MAGVIT-v2 to tokenize input images into discrete tokens for both multimodal understanding and generation . In some implementations, the token count for images can be significantly higher than for text; for example, one model reports an image having 2,308 tokens whereas the associated text contains an average of only 192 tokens . In contrast, other models utilize continuous diffusion mechanisms to output images. The Transfusion model combines next-token prediction for text with diffusion for images within a single multi-modal model [2]. This approach incorporates bidirectional attention for the image generation component [2]. Experimental results indicate that Transfusion scales significantly better than quantizing images and training a language model over discrete image tokens [2]. Diffusion models have historically demonstrated strong performance in conditional image synthesis; for example, conditioning an image generator with a text caption using a noisy version of CLIP allows for state-of-the-art results . Classifier guidance, which combines the score estimate of a diffusion model with the gradient of an image classifier, requires training an image classifier separate from the diffusion model . By combining guidance with upsampling, sample quality on high-resolution conditional image synthesis can be further improved . The integration of these generation mechanisms into unified architectures presents specific challenges and characteristics. While CM3 is capable of generating semantically coherent images on-par with modern GANs, it notes that neither of its components is jointly modeling image tokens in the same way as text [1]. In the Chameleon framework, the images generated are usually relevant to the context, making documents with interleaving text and images appealing to users [0]. However, the process of generating these images can involve external tools; for instance, Chameleon uses OpenAI DALL-E 3 to generate images conditioned on captions and replaces the captions in original responses with those generated images [0]. The computational cost of generation is also a factor, as generating 100 pages of content from a trained model can cost on the order of 0.4 kW-hr . Current research highlights ongoing limitations and open questions regarding the unification of these modalities. It remains to be explored whether image generation can be as easily unified as text embedding and generation in recent works . Furthermore, the role of vision-language models (VLMs) in the generation process varies; information from the VLM is more important for language models in generating image descriptions than captions . The quality and specificity of generated images depend heavily on the prompting strategy; for example, using Stable Diffusion 2.1 with a prompt in the format "A painting in the style of <artist_name>" generates specific outputs, such as always generating a version of Marilyn Diptych's painting for the prompt "A painting in the style of Warhol" . These results suggest that very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems . Evaluation of multimodal models that handle both text and image inputs and outputs relies on distinct benchmarks for understanding and generation, with recent work highlighting the difficulty in unifying these capabilities within a single framework . For multimodal understanding, models are typically assessed on visual question answering (VQA) and related tasks, where Show-o autoregressively predicts textual answers given an image and visual questions . Show-o achieves competitive performance on benchmarks such as POPE, MME, Flickr30k, and VQAv2, and performs better on the GQA benchmark, despite having a smaller model size . Similarly, the model achieves decent performance on the Flickr30k benchmark and performs much better on the VQAv2 benchmark . LLaVA-OneVision, a family of open large multimodal models, improves performance boundaries in three important vision settings, including multi-image tasks where it achieves a score of 43.0% . However, achieving ideal performance remains difficult for tasks requiring a combination of capabilities; for instance, correctly answering the attribute of an object in VQA does not guarantee an accurate depiction of that attribute in a detailed image description . While LLaVA-1.5 is not finetuned for multilingual multimodal instruction following, it is capable of following multilingual instructions . In contrast, Socratic Models demonstrate that language models can perform comparably on contextual image captioning even without input images, using only article text . The increased measured performance of Socratic Models, rising from 40.3 to 44.7 R@1, directly reflects the added benefits of incorporating language-based multimodal reasoning . Visual Programming (VisProg) shows strong zero-shot performance using a single-image VQA model for image understanding and an LLM for reasoning . Replacing the VILT-VQA model with a better VQA model for NLVR could improve performance by up to 24% . Chameleon unlocks new possibilities for multimodal interaction, as demonstrated by its strong performance on a new benchmark for mixed-modal open-ended QA [0]. For image generation and alignment, evaluation often involves metrics such as the CLIP score and Inception score. The CLIP score reflects how well image features correspond to text features, allowing for the identification of high-quality data where images and text are closely related . To evaluate similarity between an input image and text, the CLIP model is used to extract features from both . In the context of diffusion models, conditioning an image generator with a text caption using a noisy version of CLIP is a standard approach . Data that can be classified well scores high on the Inception score of perceptual quality . While diffusion models produce diverse and high-quality images, they still fall short of GANs without expensive rejection sampling and special metrics to compensate for blurriness . CLIP is consistently biased towards image content, for instance retrieving images of a dog or a mother and baby in specific columns . The CLIP ViT-L model is utilized with a dimension of 70 in certain evaluations . In data curation for models like Llama 3, all image-text pairs below a certain CLIP score are removed . The representation of images within these models varies, impacting their ability to comprehend visual information. Show-o reveals that it is required to involve more image-text pairs for multimodal alignment and more image tokens to represent an image for better comprehending the image information . In CM3, image tokens from a VQVAE-GAN are provided in the order they appear in the original HTML source, amounting to 256 tokens for every image [1]. Socratic Models utilize a prompt structure where the model acts as an intelligent image captioning bot, identifying objects in an image to generate a short caption . It remains to be explored whether image embedding and generation can be as easily unified as text embedding and generation . A primary constraint in the development of multimodal language models is the substantial computational cost associated with training and inference. Training large-scale multimodal architectures often requires significant hardware resources, as evidenced by experiments that normalize training time by linearly scaling to 256 GPUs [1]. The computational burden is further compounded by architectural choices; for instance, using a base model to embed input data roughly doubles the computational cost . Similarly, in task composition frameworks like AdapterFusion, adding more tasks to the set of adapters results in a linear increase of computational cost for both training and inference . While some approaches attempt to mitigate this, such as RAIN, which necessitates a higher computational cost for self-alignment without finetuning , others suggest that smaller models combined with advanced inference algorithms can offer Pareto-optimal trade-offs in cost and performance . However, these cost-efficiency strategies are often designed for single-modal targets and do not directly address the specific challenges present in multimodal settings . Furthermore, the choice of denoising objectives in unified text-to-text transformers is largely driven by their computational cost, with observations showing nearly identical step times for L-layer language models versus L+L-layer encoder-decoder models . At inference time, methods that utilize search can lead to performance gains but at the cost of increased inference-time compute . Hallucination remains a critical limitation for multimodal models, particularly when generating visual or textual outputs that may be factually incorrect. Large language models often generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect responses, a phenomenon commonly known as hallucination . In the context of visual instruction tuning, models like LLaVA-1.5 are not exempt from producing hallucinations and occasionally disseminating misinformation, necessitating caution in critical applications such as medicine . Although scaling model inputs to higher resolutions, such as 448^2, has been found to significantly reduce such hallucinations , the issue persists. The unreliability inherited from the underlying models on which Socratic systems are constructed further limits their effectiveness . Additionally, the degree to which visual details are provided in captions is largely limited by the capabilities of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) . There is also evidence that alignment techniques may exacerbate this issue; for example, the factuality score of Llama-2-7b-chat (RLHFed) is lower than that of Vicuna-7b (SFTed), suggesting that RLHF might cause more hallucination . Maintaining coherence and reliability in long-context or multi-turn multimodal interactions presents additional open challenges. Current multimodal models often operate with limited sequence lengths; for instance, CM3 utilizes a maximum token sequence length of 2048 [1]. The ability of models fine-tuned on limited data to engage in multi-turn dialogue remains an open question, as illustrated by the inquiry into whether a model fine-tuned on only 1,000 single-turn interactions can successfully handle multi-turn exchanges . In complex reasoning tasks, such as those involving Socratic models, the interaction relies on web crawlers and visual search to retrieve related frames based on language model responses, a process that is constrained by the reliability of the constituent models . The evaluation of these systems is further complicated by the fact that current measures of how well models perform a task have pointed-out limitations . While very large language models are considered an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems , their application to multimodal settings requires further investigation, as few-shot recalibration approaches are only beginning to be applied to a broader set of models, including instruction-tuned and RLHF models, in multimodal contexts .

question: How do machine unlearning methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from language models?
raw_answer:
Machine unlearning is defined as a technique that forces a trained model to forget a previously learned sample [[weijia_cs_3:0]]. The ultimate goal of this process is to obtain a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set [[weijia_cs_3:1]]. This objective stands in stark contrast to the broad goal of machine learning, as unlearning requires overfitting [[weijia_cs_3:1]]. The challenge of machine unlearning is particularly magnified in the realm of language models due to the enormity of the training data [[weijia_cs_3:1]]. While the quality of a model is strongly influenced by the quality of the dataset it is trained on [[weijia_cs_3:2]], unlearning seeks to alter this relationship by removing specific knowledge rather than adding new data.

Methodologically, unlearning approaches are categorized into exact and approximate types. Exact unlearning ensures that the unlearned model is behaviorally identical to the model resulting from retraining from scratch, denoted as the target model [[weijia_cs_3:3]]. However, such retraining is usually too costly in real-world deployment, leading researchers to focus on evaluating approximate unlearning algorithms [[weijia_cs_3:3]]. In the context of evaluation, the target model serves as the benchmark, with a score of 0.00 indicating perfect alignment with the retrained state [[weijia_cs_3:3]]. Approximate methods aim to mimic this target behavior without the computational expense of full retraining, though the performance of an unlearned model tends to decrease significantly with respect to the number of unlearning requests [[weijia_cs_3:3]].

Machine unlearning is distinct from knowledge or model editing, which is a related line of work aimed at understanding and manipulating models rather than preserving privacy [[weijia_cs_3:1]]. For instance, using logits to avoid network editing is an architecture-agnostic approach that differs from the privacy-focused goals of unlearning [[weijia_cs_3:4]]. Another related technique involves further fine-tuning large language models with alternative labels for specific tokens to perform unlearning [[weijia_cs_3:5]]. This fine-tuning approach contrasts with standard fine-tuning, which is typically used to increase model accuracy, such as the over 6 percentage point increase observed in agricultural domain applications [[weijia_cs_3:2]].

Despite these methodological distinctions, the efficacy of unlearning remains a subject of scrutiny. Studies emphasize that findings regarding the potential downsides of existing methods are not a criticism of the machine unlearning paradigm itself, but rather a call for better algorithms [[weijia_cs_3:3]]. For example, audits using MIN-K% PROB on an unlearned LLM trained to forget copyrighted books found that the model could still output related copyrighted content [[weijia_cs_3:5]]. This indicates that current methods may not fully achieve the goal of making the model indistinguishable from one trained without the target data [[weijia_cs_3:1]]. The field continues to explore these boundaries, with some taxonomies extending previous summaries to better categorize these approaches [[weijia_cs_3:6]].

Machine unlearning is defined as a technique that forces a trained model to forget a previously learned sample [[weijia_cs_3:7]]. In the context of large language models, the challenge of machine unlearning is magnified due to the enormity of the training data [[weijia_cs_3:8]]. The ultimate goal of this process is to obtain a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set [[weijia_cs_3:8]].

One specific methodological approach is Gradient Ascent (GA), which minimizes the likelihood of correct predictions on the forget set by performing gradient ascent on the cross-entropy loss [[weijia_cs_3:9]]. This method is distinct from other unlearning algorithms because it has access to both the forget and retain sets, attempting to balance the two losses in an unstable fashion [[weijia_cs_3:8]]. In evaluations such as MUSE, GA variants like GA_GDR are tested across specific epochs, such as epoch 7 and epoch 1 [[weijia_cs_3:9]]. Another approach involves further fine-tuning the LLMs with alternative labels for specific tokens, a novel method introduced by Eldan & Russinovich (2023) [[weijia_cs_3:10]]. This fine-tuning process may utilize specific hyperparameters, such as a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ [[weijia_cs_3:8]].

Weight pruning represents another technique, where large-scale generative pretrained Transformer-family models can be compressed to high sparsity via weight pruning in one-shot without any retraining [[weijia_cs_3:11]]. This contrasts with most existing pruning methods, which require extensive retraining following the pruning step to recover accuracy [[weijia_cs_3:11]]. Some pruning approaches allow for adjustable token pruning ratios during inference without retraining, offering flexibility in balancing efficiency and performance [[weijia_cs_3:12]].

The computational and implementation aspects of these methods are influenced by training dynamics and efficiency strategies. For instance, efficient finetuning can be depicted with a batch size of 1, a sequence length of 512, and gradient checkpointing [[weijia_cs_3:13]]. To further optimize memory usage, rematerialization-aware gradient checkpointing strategies have been proposed to eliminate redundant forward recomputation of FlashAttention [[weijia_cs_3:14]].

Despite these methodological advances, the effectiveness of unlearning remains a subject of scrutiny. Audits using MIN-K% PROB on an unlearned LLM trained to forget copyrighted books found that the model could still output related copyrighted content [[weijia_cs_3:10]]. A higher ROUGE-L recall value signifies a greater degree of overlap, which can indicate a higher likelihood of unlearning failure [[weijia_cs_3:10]]. In the MUSE evaluation, specific metrics such as NPO recorded a value of 0.59, while the Target metric recorded 0.00 [[weijia_cs_3:9]]. These results highlight potential downsides of existing methods, serving as a call for better algorithms rather than a criticism of the machine unlearning paradigm itself [[weijia_cs_3:9]]. The necessity for such methods is underscored by the fact that large language models memorize and leak individual training examples [[weijia_cs_3:15]]. While modified prompting language techniques have been shown to have limited effectiveness [[weijia_cs_3:16]], the focus of recent work remains on specific bias issues in LLMs for English, with additional languages considered for machine translation and multilingual models [[weijia_cs_3:16]].

Empirical evaluations of machine unlearning in language models reveal that current methods often fail to fully remove target knowledge, with most approaches revealing the membership of the forget set through either under-unlearning or over-unlearning [[weijia_cs_3:17]]. The MUSE framework formally defines different unlearning scopes and corresponding metrics to systematically evaluate these outcomes from both data owners' and deployers' perspectives [[weijia_cs_3:17]]. A primary metric for assessing the removal of specific content is the Min-K% Prob attack, which measures the probability of the model generating specific tokens from the forget set [[weijia_cs_3:18]]. In one study, the Min-K% Prob based attack achieved an AUC of approximately 0 on the target function, confirming the effectiveness of that specific unlearning method in preventing memorization [[weijia_cs_3:17]]. However, other audits using the MIN-K% PROB metric on LLMs trained to forget copyrighted books found that the models could still output related copyrighted content, indicating unlearning failure [[weijia_cs_3:18]]. This failure is further quantified by ROUGE-L recall values, where higher values signify greater overlap between the model's output and the target data, indicating a higher likelihood of unlearning failure [[weijia_cs_3:18]].

Membership inference attacks (MIA) serve as a critical evaluation approach to determine if a model is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. The ultimate goal of machine unlearning is to obtain a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. One evaluation approach proposed for the NeurIPS 2023 Machine Unlearning Challenge involves comparing the point-wise distribution of outputs of multiple unlearned and retrained models and performing membership inference attacks [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. In a membership inference attack, the adversary attempts to infer whether a specific point was included in the dataset used to train a given model [[weijia_cs_3:20]]. These attacks allow an adversary to detect the presence of a given example in a model's training set [[weijia_cs_3:21]]. To accurately measure privacy leakage, metrics should use strong attacks rather than incomplete evaluation methodologies that consider average-case success metrics like accuracy or ROC-AUC [[weijia_cs_3:22]]. While attribute inference is at least as difficult as membership inference, the focus remains on detecting specific training data presence [[weijia_cs_3:20]].

The challenge of machine unlearning is magnified in language models due to the enormity of the training data [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. Machine unlearning is a technique that forces a trained model to forget a previously learned sample [[weijia_cs_3:23]]. One approach involves further fine-tuning the LLMs with alternative labels for specific tokens [[weijia_cs_3:18]]. However, it is possible that unlearning algorithms only locally modify the model outputs around a particular query, creating a false promise of unlearning [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. Empirical studies find that current unlearning methods successfully prevent the model's memorization of content at a significant cost to utility on data not intended for removal [[weijia_cs_3:17]]. To mitigate this, a Retain Set regularizer, which is disjoint from the standard evaluation set, is employed in unlearning training to preserve utility [[weijia_cs_3:17]]. A specific implementation used a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ for the unlearning process [[weijia_cs_3:19]]. These results are not a criticism of the paradigm of machine unlearning, but a study of the potential downsides of existing methods and a call for better algorithms [[weijia_cs_3:17]].

The fundamental objective of machine unlearning is to produce a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set, effectively forcing the model to forget previously learned samples [[weijia_cs_3:24]][[weijia_cs_3:25]]. However, this goal presents a paradoxical challenge because, in stark contrast to the broad goal of machine learning, unlearning requires overfitting [[weijia_cs_3:24]]. This difficulty is magnified in the realm of language models due to the enormity of the training data [[weijia_cs_3:24]]. A significant limitation identified in this process is knowledge entanglement, where attempts to make a model forget one thing often result in the unexpected forgetting of other things [[weijia_cs_3:24]]. This phenomenon supports the necessity of using multiple evaluation datasets to capture the full scope of unlearning effects [[weijia_cs_3:24]].

Evaluating the success of unlearning is complicated by the difficulty of verifying complete knowledge removal, particularly in large-scale models. For instance, audits using the MIN-K% PROB technique on an unlearned LLM trained to forget copyrighted books revealed that the model could still output related copyrighted content [[weijia_cs_3:26]]. Furthermore, higher ROUGE-L recall values indicate a greater degree of overlap, which can signal a higher likelihood of unlearning failure [[weijia_cs_3:26]]. While proposed techniques aim to address the need for auditing machine unlearning to ensure compliance with privacy regulations, the persistence of such outputs highlights the limitations of current methods [[weijia_cs_3:26]]. In specific evaluations, such as the MUSE framework, target metrics may show a score of 0.00, yet the overall study emphasizes that these results are not a criticism of the unlearning paradigm itself, but rather a call for better algorithms to address the potential downsides of existing methods [[weijia_cs_3:27]].

Robustness to adversarial re-learning and the detection of residual knowledge remain open problems. Membership inference attacks demonstrate that adversaries can train inference models to recognize differences in a target model's predictions on inputs it trained on versus those it did not, thereby identifying membership [[weijia_cs_3:28]]. Even simple threshold adversaries can come surprisingly close to the accuracy of more complex attacks, especially given the differences in complexity and requisite adversarial assumptions [[weijia_cs_3:29]]. In the context of text classification, adversarial methods like TextFooler generate adversarial text to fool models, illustrating the vulnerability of models to input shifts [[weijia_cs_3:30]]. The robustness of a model to such input shifts is related to the aliasing phenomenon [[weijia_cs_3:31]]. Although some studies focus on factual recall-oriented problems, the extent to which observations regarding calibration and confidence hold for reasoning-heavy settings remains an interesting open question [[weijia_cs_3:32]].

The provided evidence also includes items that are not directly relevant to the specific limitations of machine unlearning in language models. For example, the robustness of consensus feature ranking in lipid nanoparticle delivery strategies [[weijia_cs_3:33]], the exclusion of MT-Bench due to its limitations [[weijia_cs_3:34]], the inclusion of mathematical problems in the OpenWebMath dataset [[weijia_cs_3:35]], the performance gap in solving challenging mathematical problems [[weijia_cs_3:36]], the improvement in backward rationales via MetaMath [[weijia_cs_3:36]], the parallelization issues in DeepSpeed-Ulysses [[weijia_cs_3:37]], the breakdown of Guanaco on simple problems [[weijia_cs_3:38]], and the loss function for knowledge injection [[weijia_cs_3:39]] do not provide direct evidence regarding the unlearning paradox, adversarial robustness of unlearning, or verification of knowledge removal in LLMs.

While modified prompting language techniques have been shown to have limited effectiveness , the focus of recent work remains on specific bias issues in LLMs for English, with additional languages considered for machine translation and multilingual models . The MUSE framework formally defines different unlearning scopes and corresponding metrics to systematically evaluate these outcomes from both data owners' and deployers' perspectives [1]. A primary metric for assessing the removal of specific content is the Min-K% Prob attack, which measures the probability of the model generating specific tokens from the forget set . In one study, the Min-K% Prob based attack achieved an AUC of approximately 0 on the target function, confirming the effectiveness of that specific unlearning method in preventing memorization [1]. However, other audits using the MIN-K% PROB metric on LLMs trained to forget copyrighted books found that the models could still output related copyrighted content, indicating unlearning failure . This failure is further quantified by ROUGE-L recall values, where higher values signify greater overlap between the model's output and the target data, indicating a higher likelihood of unlearning failure . The ultimate goal of machine unlearning is to obtain a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set [0]. One evaluation approach proposed for the NeurIPS 2023 Machine Unlearning Challenge involves comparing the point-wise distribution of outputs of multiple unlearned and retrained models and performing membership inference attacks [0]. In a membership inference attack, the adversary attempts to infer whether a specific point was included in the dataset used to train a given model . These attacks allow an adversary to detect the presence of a given example in a model's training set . To accurately measure privacy leakage, metrics should use strong attacks rather than incomplete evaluation methodologies that consider average-case success metrics like accuracy or ROC-AUC . While attribute inference is at least as difficult as membership inference, the focus remains on detecting specific training data presence . The challenge of machine unlearning is magnified in language models due to the enormity of the training data [0]. Machine unlearning is a technique that forces a trained model to forget a previously learned sample . One approach involves further fine-tuning the LLMs with alternative labels for specific tokens . However, it is possible that unlearning algorithms only locally modify the model outputs around a particular query, creating a false promise of unlearning [0]. Empirical studies find that current unlearning methods successfully prevent the model's memorization of content at a significant cost to utility on data not intended for removal [1]. To mitigate this, a Retain Set regularizer, which is disjoint from the standard evaluation set, is employed in unlearning training to preserve utility [1]. A specific implementation used a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ for the unlearning process [0]. These results are not a criticism of the paradigm of machine unlearning, but a study of the potential downsides of existing methods and a call for better algorithms [1]. The fundamental objective of machine unlearning is to produce a model that is indistinguishable from one trained exclusively on the retain set, effectively forcing the model to forget previously learned samples [0]. However, this goal presents a paradoxical challenge because, in stark contrast to the broad goal of machine learning, unlearning requires overfitting [0]. This difficulty is magnified in the realm of language models due to the enormity of the training data [0]. A significant limitation identified in this process is knowledge entanglement, where attempts to make a model forget one thing often result in the unexpected forgetting of other things [0]. This phenomenon supports the necessity of using multiple evaluation datasets to capture the full scope of unlearning effects [0]. Evaluating the success of unlearning is complicated by the difficulty of verifying complete knowledge removal, particularly in large-scale models. For instance, audits using the MIN-K% PROB technique on an unlearned LLM trained to forget copyrighted books revealed that the model could still output related copyrighted content . Furthermore, higher ROUGE-L recall values indicate a greater degree of overlap, which can signal a higher likelihood of unlearning failure . While proposed techniques aim to address the need for auditing machine unlearning to ensure compliance with privacy regulations, the persistence of such outputs highlights the limitations of current methods . Robustness to adversarial re-learning and the detection of residual knowledge remain open problems. Membership inference attacks demonstrate that adversaries can train inference models to recognize differences in a target model's predictions on inputs it trained on versus those it did not, thereby identifying membership . Even simple threshold adversaries can come surprisingly close to the accuracy of more complex attacks, especially given the differences in complexity and requisite adversarial assumptions . In the context of text classification, adversarial methods like TextFooler generate adversarial text to fool models, illustrating the vulnerability of models to input shifts . The robustness of a model to such input shifts is related to the aliasing phenomenon . Although some studies focus on factual recall-oriented problems, the extent to which observations regarding calibration and confidence hold for reasoning-heavy settings remains an interesting open question . The provided evidence also includes items that are not directly relevant to the specific limitations of machine unlearning in language models. For example, the robustness of consensus feature ranking in lipid nanoparticle delivery strategies , the exclusion of MT-Bench due to its limitations , the inclusion of mathematical problems in the OpenWebMath dataset , the performance gap in solving challenging mathematical problems , the improvement in backward rationales via MetaMath , the parallelization issues in DeepSpeed-Ulysses , the breakdown of Guanaco on simple problems , and the loss function for knowledge injection do not provide direct evidence regarding the unlearning paradox, adversarial robustness of unlearning, or verification of knowledge removal in LLMs.

question: How to evaluate copyright infringement of image generation models?
raw_answer:
The legal landscape governing the applicability of copyright law and fair use doctrine, also known as “fair dealing,” to language models is largely undetermined [[weijia_cs_4:0]]. In the United States, legal scholars and practitioners have suggested that training models on copyright content might constitute fair use [[weijia_cs_4:0]]. Current fair use doctrine in the United States might allow this training provided that mitigation strategies are used to prevent substantially similar outputs [[weijia_cs_4:1]]. Conversely, in early 2024, Israel and Japan allow copyrighted content to be used for AI training data [[weijia_cs_4:0]]. Despite these varying national stances, the use of specific datasets remains contentious; for example, sources like Books3, which are the center of ongoing legal cases around AI use of copyrighted materials, are avoided in some open corpus efforts despite their use in training models like LLaMA [[weijia_cs_4:0]].

A critical distinction in legal evaluation exists between the usage of training data and the generation of output. Regurgitation of such content may lead to legal intellectual property liability for users and model deployers who further make use of the generated content [[weijia_cs_4:1]]. To address this, intervention techniques that compromise the faithfulness of certain visual aspects are employed for copyright protection [[weijia_cs_4:1]]. Prompt rewriting approaches currently adopted by companies reflect an evaluation framework that encourages policy compliance, such as avoiding the generation of specific copyrighted characters like Mario, while staying close to the user's intent [[weijia_cs_4:1]]. A simple technique for alleviating copyright concerns is effective across all open-source models evaluated, though it remains a mitigation strategy rather than a definitive legal shield [[weijia_cs_4:1]].

Technical methods are being developed to detect potential copyright infringement in training data. MIN-K% PROB can detect potential copyright infringement in training data [[weijia_cs_4:2]]. This method has been used to audit an unlearned LLM that is trained to forget copyrighted books using machine unlearning techniques, finding that such a model could still output related copyrighted content [[weijia_cs_4:2]]. Another approach proposes the use of data watermarks to detect whether a rightholder's document collection is in the training data of a large language model [[weijia_cs_4:3]]. Concurrent work by Meeus et al. (2024) inserts repeated “copyright traps” in a text document to improve membership inference [[weijia_cs_4:3]]. These detection tools are not ethically neutral, as building tools to support copyright law acknowledges the potential for unethical abuse of copyright law, such as enabling censorship [[weijia_cs_4:3]].

The technical mechanisms underlying these legal risks are often linked to model overfitting and memorization. When a learning algorithm is not stable, the models that it produces might overfit to the training data [[weijia_cs_4:4]]. If the model overfits and does not generalize well to inputs beyond its training data, or if the training data is not representative, the model leaks information about its training inputs [[weijia_cs_4:5]]. User-facing applications that use large language models may inadvertently emit data in inappropriate contexts, such as a dialogue system emitting a user's phone number in response to another user's query [[weijia_cs_4:6]]. Different training procedures such as differentially private optimization may prevent watermark memorization, but such optimization may also serve a dual purpose in enabling the fair use of the data [[weijia_cs_4:3]].

The architecture of image generation models presents specific technical contexts for these legal issues. Unlike text-only generation, which is inherently variable-length, token-based image generation produces fixed-size blocks of tokens corresponding to an image [[weijia_cs_4:7]]. Models like CM3 can be prompted to recover the functionality of many other models, including image generation, image captioning, and unconditional image generation [[weijia_cs_4:8]]. CM3 can be prompted for non-trivial image generation, similar to that of DALL-E [[weijia_cs_4:8]]. Similarly, Chameleon performs non-trivial image generation in a single model [[weijia_cs_4:7]]. While these capabilities enable diverse applications, the legal evaluation of infringement remains tied to the distinction between the training process and the resulting outputs, with mitigation strategies and detection tools serving as the primary technical interfaces for legal compliance [[weijia_cs_4:1]][[weijia_cs_4:2]][[weijia_cs_4:3]].

Technical approaches for detecting potential copyright infringement in image generation models rely heavily on embedding space similarity and perceptual hashing techniques to quantify the resemblance between generated outputs and original copyrighted works. A primary method involves computing the cosine similarity between query embeddings and document or character embeddings to identify potential matches [[weijia_cs_4:9]][[weijia_cs_4:10]]. In the context of character generation, candidate keywords are ranked by their embedding's cosine similarity with the character name embedding, which is computed as the averaged token embedding at the last hidden layer [[weijia_cs_4:10]]. If no description with a cosine similarity greater than 0.7 is found, it is concluded that the user query does not intend to generate characters substantially similar to copyrighted ones [[weijia_cs_4:10]]. To facilitate efficient indexing and similarity search of these vectors, libraries such as Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) are used to create databases of embeddings [[weijia_cs_4:11]].

Perceptual hashing and self-supervised descriptors offer another avenue for image copy detection, where similarity normalization consistently improves metrics [[weijia_cs_4:12]]. When applied to contrastive learning, specific regularization acts as a perceptual prior, selecting for stronger copy detection representations [[weijia_cs_4:12]]. Image retrieval within these systems benefits from PCA whitening, and descriptors are often processed at a resolution of $224 \times 224$ [[weijia_cs_4:12]]. While these methods aim to detect copies, the ground-truth labels assigned to matched images may occasionally be incorrect because the labels are generated from LAION captions which may not always contain the artist's name [[weijia_cs_4:13]]. Consequently, numerous images that bear striking stylistic resemblance to the generated images are erroneously labeled as false positives [[weijia_cs_4:13]].

To address the challenge of distinguishing stylistic influence from direct copying, specific thresholds have been proposed for Style Similarity scores. It is hypothesized that a single-image Style Similarity score below 0.5 indicates the absence of the artist's style, whereas a score above 0.8 strongly indicates its presence [[weijia_cs_4:13]]. High image similarity scores are observed in Midjourney generations, and qualitatively these images look stylistically similar to artists' original artworks [[weijia_cs_4:13]]. However, interventions aimed at reducing this similarity, such as adding more fine-grained negative prompts and applying prompt rewriting, significantly reduce the similarity of the generated images to the original copyrighted character [[weijia_cs_4:10]]. Such intervention, however, is compromising the faithfulness of certain visual aspects for copyright protection [[weijia_cs_4:10]].

Beyond image-specific metrics, techniques from large language model (LLM) research provide frameworks for detecting data memorization and membership, which are relevant to understanding how models retain training data. MIN-K% PROB can detect potential copyright infringement in training data [[weijia_cs_4:14]]. Data memorization is defined as a privacy infringement if it causes data to be used outside of its intended context [[weijia_cs_4:15]]. Concurrent work by Meeus et al. (2024) inserts repeated “copyright traps” in a text document to improve membership inference [[weijia_cs_4:16]]. While these methods are primarily text-based, they highlight the broader issue of models retaining specific data points. In contrast, learning from step-by-step explanations, whether generated by humans or more advanced AI models, is a promising direction to improve model capabilities and skills, though this is distinct from the detection of infringement [[weijia_cs_4:17]].

Some detection systems rely on classifiers to identify AI-generated content, with policy models effectively classifying AI-generated utterances even when they differ from the training data distribution [[weijia_cs_4:18]]. In the domain of diffusion models, reverse ODE approximations can give latents with reasonable reconstructions, even with as few as 250 reverse steps, which may be relevant for reconstructing or analyzing generated content [[weijia_cs_4:19]]. Additionally, robust image classifiers can be used as stand-alone generative models, a concept demonstrated by Santurkar et al. [[weijia_cs_4:19]]. While multimodal models like Transfusion achieve similar performance to high-performing image generation models such as DeepFloyd [[weijia_cs_4:20]], and Socratic models use visual search to retrieve related frames [[weijia_cs_4:21]], these generative capabilities do not directly address the metric-based detection of copyright infringement. Irrelevant technical specifications, such as reverse symmetry waveguides in optical biosensors, do not apply to this context [[weijia_cs_4:22]].

Empirical investigations into model memorization reveal that the likelihood of a model reproducing training data is strongly correlated with model scale and training dynamics. Research indicates that larger models initially memorize training data at a slower rate but subsequently reach high proportions of memorization more quickly than smaller counterparts [[weijia_cs_4:23]]. This trend is supported by findings that memorization generally increases as model scale expands [[weijia_cs_4:24]]. In specific evaluations of neural language models, 33% of training sequences in an evaluation set were found to be extractable from a 6-billion parameter model when provided with 50 tokens of context [[weijia_cs_4:25]]. While smaller models may discuss relevant topics, they often lack the coherence of larger models, which can memorize training data verbatim [[weijia_cs_4:25]]. The phenomenon of "eidetic memorization" is defined as data retained by a model despite appearing in only a small set of training instances [[weijia_cs_4:26]]. This memorization is considered an essential component of language models because the training objective inherently seeks to assign high overall likelihood to the training dataset [[weijia_cs_4:26]].

The measurement of memorization is complicated by data duplication and the specific metrics used for evaluation. A strictly larger measurement of memorization can be achieved by accounting for these factors, though the situation becomes complex when considering data duplication due to training set idiosyncrasies [[weijia_cs_4:25]]. One method for identifying duplicates involves marking a sample as a duplicate of another if their trigram multisets are similar, specifically if the intersection of their trigrams is at least half the size of the first sample's trigrams [[weijia_cs_4:26]]. In the context of pretraining data detection, the bound on the total variation distance between model outputs is directly proportional to the occurrence frequency of the example, learning rates, and the inverse of the dataset size [[weijia_cs_4:27]]. Furthermore, membership inference attacks, which determine if specific data points were in the training set, perform better if training datasets overlap, representing a worst-case scenario for the attacker when datasets are distinct [[weijia_cs_4:28]]. To quantify this overlap, researchers have used measures of expected 50-gram overlap against specific corpora such as the Pile [[weijia_cs_4:24]]. The expected overlap for a corpus is calculated using a formula that sums the maximum chains of documents divided by the sum of expected lengths [[weijia_cs_4:24]]. Hypothesis testing methods have also been developed to detect whether a given test set is present in the training data of a language model [[weijia_cs_4:29]].

In the domain of image generation, the nature of memorization differs from verbatim text reproduction, as copyrighted characters are computationally more similar to general concepts that appear in many poses, sizes, and variations within the training data [[weijia_cs_4:30]]. Recent research confirms that generative models, including those for image and video, are susceptible to memorizing and generating entire datapoints or concepts from their training data [[weijia_cs_4:30]]. To evaluate this, frameworks have been developed that consider both the elimination of similar output to copyrighted characters and the generated image's consistency with user input [[weijia_cs_4:30]]. Empirical tests on style similarity in diffusion models have utilized a multiple-choice format where, for each query image, four answer images are provided, with only one originating from the same artist [[weijia_cs_4:31]]. However, these evaluations face limitations, as ground-truth labels assigned to matched images may be incorrect because the labels are often generated from LAION captions that may not always contain the artist's name [[weijia_cs_4:31]].

Mitigation strategies and technical tools for detecting similarity have also been empirically tested. Adding more fine-grained negative prompts and applying prompt rewriting has been shown to significantly reduce the similarity of generated images to original copyrighted characters [[weijia_cs_4:30]]. For detecting image copies, using a single neighbor to normalize similarity works best when the second nearest neighbor is utilized [[weijia_cs_4:32]]. In broader multimodal contexts, models like Chameleon perform non-trivial image generation within a single mixed-modal early-fusion architecture [[weijia_cs_4:33]]. While some studies focus on the overlap between external knowledge bases like Wikipedia and language model training sets [[weijia_cs_4:34]], others note that near-duplicate test questions in training sets can affect evaluation validity, with one study finding that 32.5% of test questions in the Natural Questions dataset overlapped with training sets [[weijia_cs_4:35]]. Additionally, tools like Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) are used to create databases of embeddings for efficient indexing and similarity search [[weijia_cs_4:36]]. Although some research suggests that learning from step-by-step explanations can improve model quality [[weijia_cs_4:37]] and that policy models can classify AI-generated utterances even when they differ from training distributions [[weijia_cs_4:38]], these findings pertain more to model capability and safety classification than to the direct statistical likelihood of copyright infringement through memorization. Legal contexts also vary, with jurisdictions such as Israel and Japan allowing copyrighted content to be used for AI training data [[weijia_cs_4:39]].

Establishing a causal link between training data and specific outputs remains a significant challenge, particularly because large language models will output memorized data even in the absence of an explicit adversary [[weijia_cs_4:40]]. While techniques such as MIN-K% PROB can detect potential copyright infringement in training data, the landscape governing the applicability of copyright law and fair use doctrine to language models is largely undetermined [[weijia_cs_4:41]][[weijia_cs_4:42]]. This legal ambiguity is further complicated by varying international regulations; for instance, in early 2024, Israel and Japan allowed copyrighted content to be used for AI training data [[weijia_cs_4:42]]. Consequently, building tools to support copyright law is not an ethically neutral position, as it carries the potential for unethical abuse, such as enabling censorship [[weijia_cs_4:43]].

Current automated detection tools face inherent limitations in precision and scope. For example, the Self-Supervised Copy Detection (SSCD) method is not precise when matching images composed entirely of text [[weijia_cs_4:44]]. Furthermore, SimCLR often matches images with similar types of distortion together, which may introduce noise into detection results [[weijia_cs_4:44]]. In the context of text-based membership inference, Bloom filters can output false positives but never false negatives, creating an asymmetry in detection reliability [[weijia_cs_4:45]]. Concurrent work by Meeus et al. (2024) attempts to improve membership inference by inserting repeated “copyright traps” in text documents, yet the expected number of matches in such systems is mathematically defined as $E(N,w)=\frac{N-w+1}{w}$ [[weijia_cs_4:43]][[weijia_cs_4:45]].

Despite these challenges, some detection methods have shown promising results in specific contexts. Experiments have provided strong evidence that GPT-3 models may have been trained on copyrighted books [[weijia_cs_4:41]]. Additionally, 5.3% of generated completions have a GPT score similarity to the gold completion that is greater than or equal to 4, indicating a measurable overlap [[weijia_cs_4:41]]. In the domain of image generation, specific intervention techniques have been evaluated, with both methods achieving over 90% accuracy in certain tasks [[weijia_cs_4:46]]. However, such interventions compromise the faithfulness of certain visual aspects for the sake of copyright protection [[weijia_cs_4:46]]. Although this simple technique is effective across all open-source models evaluated, it remains a trade-off between protection and output quality [[weijia_cs_4:46]].

The definition of infringement itself is complex, as data memorization is considered a privacy infringement if it causes data to be used outside of its intended context [[weijia_cs_4:40]]. Evaluating whether an output is supported by evidence requires careful distinction between factual recall and reasoning, as the extent to which observations hold for reasoning-heavy settings remains an interesting open question [[weijia_cs_4:47]]. Current visual instruction tuning models also have limitations, including prolonged training for high-resolution images and a lack of multiple-image understanding [[weijia_cs_4:48]]. These technical constraints, combined with the legal and ethical complexities of defining ground truth for infringement, highlight the need for more robust and legally aligned evaluation frameworks [[weijia_cs_4:42]][[weijia_cs_4:43]].
