question: Data selection has emerged as an important problem for training good language models (i.e., which datapoints to include). Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for LMs (i.e., easy to hard curriculum sequence of data points), such that a LM may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
raw_answer:
Curriculum learning is defined as an effective strategy in machine learning that allows models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [[jacqueline_cs_4:0]]. In the context of neural language models, this approach involves accounting for sample-level ordering, which distinguishes it from methods that do not consider the sequence in which data is presented [[jacqueline_cs_4:1]]. The core objective in language modeling remains the minimization of the negative log-likelihood, expressed as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, <   t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [[jacqueline_cs_4:0]]. While curriculum learning focuses on the temporal progression of difficulty, other training dynamics involve adjusting hyperparameters such as learning rates, where the minimum learning rate is often set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate [[jacqueline_cs_4:2]].

Specific implementations of curriculum learning utilize pacing functions to control the introduction of data over time. For instance, a pacing function can be defined as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ represents the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI tasks, and 3 for addition [[jacqueline_cs_4:1]]. This structured progression contrasts with static data selection or random shuffling, as it explicitly manages the complexity trajectory of the training process [[jacqueline_cs_4:1]][[jacqueline_cs_4:0]]. However, more sophisticated techniques like curriculum learning have been noted to account for sample-level ordering but not necessarily for skills or their dependencies [[jacqueline_cs_4:1]].

The distinction between curriculum learning and other training methodologies is further highlighted by the variety of objectives and parameterizations used in language model training. Different objectives can lead to different sequence lengths and thus different training speeds [[jacqueline_cs_4:3]]. For example, T5 models are trained by removing a random 15% of tokens from each training sequence [[jacqueline_cs_4:4]], while other variants that do not require predicting the full original sequence, such as “replace corrupted spans” and “drop corrupted spans,” make the target sequences shorter and consequently make training faster [[jacqueline_cs_4:3]]. These variations in objective function and sequence length impact the efficiency of training but do not inherently constitute a curriculum based on difficulty progression [[jacqueline_cs_4:3]][[jacqueline_cs_4:4]][[jacqueline_cs_4:3]].

System-level optimizations also influence how sequences are processed during training, which is distinct from the pedagogical ordering of data points. Sequence parallelism has been proposed for training Transformers with longer sequences, addressing limitations where attention-head and depth are much smaller than sequence length [[jacqueline_cs_4:5]]. This approach enables longer sequence training or continual pretraining where the training context length gradually increases over time [[jacqueline_cs_4:6]]. Similarly, DeepSpeed Sequence allows both model size and sequence length to scale near indefinitely unbounded by single GPU memory limitation and at a high fraction of peak compute performance [[jacqueline_cs_4:6]]. These technical advancements facilitate the handling of longer contexts but are separate from the strategic ordering of data points for sample efficiency [[jacqueline_cs_4:5]][[jacqueline_cs_4:6]][[jacqueline_cs_4:5]].

Data selection criteria, such as filtering based on HTML code-to-text ratio or average line length, represent static quality controls rather than dynamic curricula [[jacqueline_cs_4:7]]. For example, Dolma applies filters such as an HTML code-to-text ratio <= 0.2 and an average line length >100 characters [[jacqueline_cs_4:7]]. These static filters determine which data points are included in the corpus but do not dictate the order in which they are presented to the model during training [[jacqueline_cs_4:7]]. In contrast, curriculum learning specifically addresses the ordering of these selected data points to potentially improve learning efficiency [[jacqueline_cs_4:1]][[jacqueline_cs_4:0]].

The evaluation of language models often involves tasks that test specific capabilities, such as reversing letters in a word or solving anagrams, where performance varies across models [[jacqueline_cs_4:8]]. For instance, none of the models tested can reverse the letters in a word, and performance on the more difficult anagram task was 15.1% [[jacqueline_cs_4:8]]. These qualitative and quantitative benchmarks highlight the limitations of current models but do not directly address the training ordering strategies used to achieve those results [[jacqueline_cs_4:8]]. Furthermore, alignment training using reinforcement learning from human feedback has been found to improve performance on almost all NLP evaluations, representing a post-training refinement rather than a pre-training curriculum [[jacqueline_cs_4:9]].

Other approaches to improving language models involve retrieval or memorization, which are distinct from curriculum learning. For example, an approach that can be applied to any neural language model yielded a 2.9 point improvement with no additional training [[jacqueline_cs_4:10]]. Methods for quantifying memorization across neural language models provide a loose lower bound on memorization [[jacqueline_cs_4:4]]. Additionally, it has been found that certain benchmarks, such as the 4 Wikipedia language modeling benchmarks measured in GPT-2 and the Children's Book Test dataset, are almost entirely contained in the training data [[jacqueline_cs_4:8]]. These findings regarding data overlap and memorization underscore the importance of data selection and ordering, though they do not define the curriculum learning framework itself [[jacqueline_cs_4:4]][[jacqueline_cs_4:8]].

Curriculum learning has emerged as an effective strategy in machine learning, allowing models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [[jacqueline_cs_4:11]]. This approach accounts for sample-level ordering, although more sophisticated techniques like curriculum learning do not necessarily account for skills or their dependencies [[jacqueline_cs_4:12]]. The foundational formulation of curriculum learning involves minimizing a loss function defined as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ { T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, <   t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [[jacqueline_cs_4:11]]. In specific implementations, such as the Skill-it! framework, a pacing function is defined as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ is the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, and 3 for addition [[jacqueline_cs_4:12]].

Perplexity serves as a key metric for assessing data difficulty and model performance trajectories. Research indicates that language modeling perplexity correlates well with few-shot in-context learning performance along the trajectory, regardless of model sizes [[jacqueline_cs_4:13]]. Furthermore, the perplexity divergence of correct and incorrect options drives the performance improvement [[jacqueline_cs_4:13]]. However, the use of training curricula remains limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula [[jacqueline_cs_4:14]].

Semantic similarity metrics are another method for determining data relationships and difficulty. To evaluate the similarity between an input image and text, the CLIP model can be used to extract features from both [[jacqueline_cs_4:11]]. In the context of word embeddings, words with similar semantic meanings will have small cosine distance in the embedding space [[jacqueline_cs_4:15]]. Nearest neighbor models have been applied to NLP problems such as part of speech tagging and morphological analysis, but the use of learned representations makes the similarity function much more effective in the case of neural models [[jacqueline_cs_4:16]]. These results strongly suggest that learning similarity between sequences of text is easier than predicting the next word [[jacqueline_cs_4:16]]. Semantic similarity is also central to tasks like SCWS, which requires estimating the semantic similarity of word pairs that occur in context [[jacqueline_cs_4:17]]. In benchmarks like MTEB, an example of Sentence-to-Sentence (S2S) tasks includes all current STS tasks, where the similarity between two sentences is assessed [[jacqueline_cs_4:18]]. However, retrieval and clustering in these benchmarks are English-only [[jacqueline_cs_4:18]]. DINO generates synthetic text pairs for semantic textual similarity [[jacqueline_cs_4:19]].

Length-based and tokenization metrics are also utilized in data processing. The FineWeb datasets include a `token_count` field, which represents the number of tokens when applying the gpt2 tokenizer to a sample [[jacqueline_cs_4:20]]. Additionally, the FineWeb datasets use a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, for processing [[jacqueline_cs_4:20]]. Clustering outperforms Sentence similarity, suggesting it is better at identifying related domains [[jacqueline_cs_4:21]].

Other methods for assigning difficulty include manual estimation. For instance, an estimate of question difficulty may assign a given question to one of five difficulty levels [[jacqueline_cs_4:22]]. In contrast, some approaches involve no gradient updates [[jacqueline_cs_4:14]]. Training configurations often involve specific hyperparameters, such as a minimum learning rate set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate [[jacqueline_cs_4:23]], or a learning rate of 2e-5 [[jacqueline_cs_4:24]]. Data extraction and membership inference also play roles in understanding training data; for a collection of 256 documents, the vocabulary size |V| is roughly 118,000 [[jacqueline_cs_4:25]]. Recent work finds that membership inference methods perform at the level of random chance on pieces of LLM pretraining data [[jacqueline_cs_4:25]]. In data extraction studies, researchers may randomly sample between 5 and 10 tokens of context from scraped data [[jacqueline_cs_4:26]]. Architectural components, such as a convolution module with kernel size 7, are also part of the model training infrastructure [[jacqueline_cs_4:27]].

Curriculum learning is described as an effective strategy in machine learning that allows models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [[jacqueline_cs_4:28]]. In the context of language models, this approach involves accounting for sample-level ordering, although it does not explicitly account for skills or their dependencies [[jacqueline_cs_4:29]]. The loss function used in such training is defined as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, <   t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [[jacqueline_cs_4:28]]. Specific pacing functions have been defined to control this progression, such as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ is the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, and 3 for addition [[jacqueline_cs_4:29]]. Another formulation for pacing involves parameters where $L _ {p} = L _ {\min } + k \Delta L$ and $S _ {p} = S _ {\min } + k \Delta S$ [[jacqueline_cs_4:28]].

While curriculum learning is recognized as an advanced training technique [[jacqueline_cs_4:30]], its application in large-scale language model pretraining is often limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula [[jacqueline_cs_4:31]]. In contrast, standard pretraining approaches, such as those used for the Dolma corpus, involve sampling each source equally rather than applying a specific curriculum [[jacqueline_cs_4:32]]. The impact of data ordering on sample efficiency is further contextualized by findings in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where the sample efficiency is roughly the same on the original crowdworker-written prompt dataset and the model-generated one [[jacqueline_cs_4:33]]. This RLHF training typically uses a learning rate of 0.05 times the pretraining learning rate [[jacqueline_cs_4:33]], or for PMP, a learning rate of 0.1 relative to LM pretraining [[jacqueline_cs_4:33]].

Evidence regarding convergence speed and final performance is mixed across different training paradigms. In knowledge distillation, giving heavy weight to the soft loss at initial training epochs improves the convergence speed [[jacqueline_cs_4:34]], and the proposed method can accelerate convergence speed and improve the final performance of the distilled model [[jacqueline_cs_4:34]]. However, in the context of nearest neighbor language models, a kNN-LM trained on 100M tokens with a datastore of 1.6B tokens already outperforms the LM trained on all 3B tokens, suggesting that data access mechanisms can alter efficiency metrics [[jacqueline_cs_4:35]]. Similarly, adding out-of-domain data to the datastore makes a single LM useful across multiple domains without further training [[jacqueline_cs_4:35]]. For the largest LM in memorization studies, complete memorization occurs after just 33 insertions [[jacqueline_cs_4:36]], and much of the training data extracted is only discovered when prompting the LM with a particular prefix [[jacqueline_cs_4:36]].

Other experimental setups provide additional context on training dynamics. In retrieval-augmented language models, the minimum learning rate is set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate [[jacqueline_cs_4:37]]. In end-task aware training, instead of training the whole network to convergence, the body of the network is fixed at each time-step while a special head is trained to convergence on a small batch of end-task training data [[jacqueline_cs_4:38]]. This approach highlights the power of pretraining and its relative importance over large-scale instruction tuning and reinforcement learning approaches [[jacqueline_cs_4:39]]. Question difficulty estimation has also been applied, assigning questions to one of five difficulty levels [[jacqueline_cs_4:40]]. However, a comprehensive empirical evaluation of all downstream tasks is often beyond the scope of individual works [[jacqueline_cs_4:30]]. Furthermore, empirical results regarding dataset contamination align with theoretical predictions about how detection difficulty changes with dataset size, example frequency, and learning rate [[jacqueline_cs_4:41]].

The implementation of dynamic data reordering and curriculum learning strategies introduces significant computational overhead that often limits their practical adoption in large-scale language model training. For instance, methods like RAIN necessitate a higher computational cost to align models without fine-tuning [[jacqueline_cs_4:42]]. Similarly, increasing the size of models such as T5 yields consistent improvements but comes at a significant computational cost [[jacqueline_cs_4:43]]. In the context of pre-training objectives, choices among denoising tasks are often driven primarily by their computational cost rather than other factors [[jacqueline_cs_4:44]]. Even when considering the detection of pretraining data, pretraining a reference model on the full dataset is described as extremely computationally expensive given the incredible scale of pretraining data [[jacqueline_cs_4:45]]. These costs are further compounded by the need for dynamic batch loading, which updates the composition of sampled data in each training batch based on varying losses across different domains [[jacqueline_cs_4:46]].

Beyond computational expenses, the field lacks robust theoretical guarantees regarding the efficacy of specific ordering strategies, often relying on empirical observations that may not generalize. While curriculum learning has been applied to improve fine-tuning performance in scenarios involving MLLMs [[jacqueline_cs_4:47]], the underlying mechanisms are not always theoretically grounded. For example, in one study, the model's performance improved after introducing curriculum learning, yet it still declined as the data size increased, indicating that the method does not universally resolve scaling issues [[jacqueline_cs_4:47]]. Furthermore, current measures of how well models perform a task have been pointed out to have limitations, which complicates the evaluation of curriculum-based training [[jacqueline_cs_4:48]]. The reliance on empirical results is evident in studies on dataset contamination, where observations align with theoretical predictions about detection difficulty changing with dataset size, example frequency, and learning rate, but these are specific to detection rather than training efficiency [[jacqueline_cs_4:45]].

The sensitivity of results to specific dataset characteristics and the manual curation process presents another major challenge. Advanced training techniques like curriculum learning are often limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula [[jacqueline_cs_4:49]]. This manual dependency is highlighted in frameworks like Skill-it!, where sophisticated techniques account for sample-level ordering but do not inherently account for skills or their dependencies [[jacqueline_cs_4:50]]. The definition of pacing functions, such as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, requires specific parameters like the number of steps and epochs, which vary by task (e.g., 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, 3 for addition) [[jacqueline_cs_4:50]]. Similarly, the linear progression of loss and sample size defined by $L _ {p} = L _ { \min } + k \Delta L \text { and } S _ {p} = S _ { \min } + k \Delta S$ relies on specific assumptions about the data distribution [[jacqueline_cs_4:49]].

Dataset quality and composition significantly influence the outcomes of training, often more than dataset size alone. Research indicates that dataset quality rather than dataset size is critical for mean MMLU accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_4:51]]. While increasing the dataset size and training for more than one epoch helps with MMLU performance, the differences between datasets are far larger, indicating that dataset quality affects MMLU performance more than dataset size [[jacqueline_cs_4:51]]. This is consistent with findings that almost all knowledge in large language models is learned during pretraining, and only limited instruction tuning data is necessary to teach models to produce high-quality output [[jacqueline_cs_4:52]]. The choice of data sources, such as the 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content from FineWeb-Edu, reflects an attempt to curate high-quality data [[jacqueline_cs_4:53]]. However, even with such curated data, the standard practice of training the language model on shuffled training data for one epoch remains a baseline that dynamic methods must compete against [[jacqueline_cs_4:54]].

The interplay between model scale, data selection, and training objectives further complicates the landscape. Very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems [[jacqueline_cs_4:49]]. However, the relationship between dataset and model size often follows log-linear trends, as observed in reinforcement learning from human feedback studies [[jacqueline_cs_4:55]]. In some cases, methods avoid domain-specific data selection by continuing pretraining on the same pretraining data distribution, which simplifies the process but may miss opportunities for targeted curriculum learning [[jacqueline_cs_4:56]]. The stability and accuracy of certain approaches are preferred over others, such as choosing a specific method because it is more stable and accurate than an alternative [[jacqueline_cs_4:57]]. Ultimately, while curriculum learning and advanced training techniques are recognized as important [[jacqueline_cs_4:58]], the lack of unified theoretical frameworks and the high computational and manual costs remain significant barriers to widespread, sample-efficient adoption.
answer_official_all: Curriculum learning is defined as an effective strategy in machine learning that allows models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [0,1]. In the context of neural language models, this approach involves accounting for sample-level ordering, which distinguishes it from methods that do not consider the sequence in which data is presented [3,4,5]. The core objective in language modeling remains the minimization of the negative log-likelihood, expressed as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, < t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [0,1]. While curriculum learning focuses on the temporal progression of difficulty, other training dynamics involve adjusting hyperparameters such as learning rates, where the minimum learning rate is often set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate . Specific implementations of curriculum learning utilize pacing functions to control the introduction of data over time. For instance, a pacing function can be defined as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ represents the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI tasks, and 3 for addition [3,4,5]. This structured progression contrasts with static data selection or random shuffling, as it explicitly manages the complexity trajectory of the training process [3,4,5][0,1]. However, more sophisticated techniques like curriculum learning have been noted to account for sample-level ordering but not necessarily for skills or their dependencies [3,4,5]. The distinction between curriculum learning and other training methodologies is further highlighted by the variety of objectives and parameterizations used in language model training. Different objectives can lead to different sequence lengths and thus different training speeds . For example, T5 models are trained by removing a random 15% of tokens from each training sequence , while other variants that do not require predicting the full original sequence, such as “replace corrupted spans” and “drop corrupted spans,” make the target sequences shorter and consequently make training faster . These variations in objective function and sequence length impact the efficiency of training but do not inherently constitute a curriculum based on difficulty progression . System-level optimizations also influence how sequences are processed during training, which is distinct from the pedagogical ordering of data points. Sequence parallelism has been proposed for training Transformers with longer sequences, addressing limitations where attention-head and depth are much smaller than sequence length . This approach enables longer sequence training or continual pretraining where the training context length gradually increases over time . Similarly, DeepSpeed Sequence allows both model size and sequence length to scale near indefinitely unbounded by single GPU memory limitation and at a high fraction of peak compute performance . These technical advancements facilitate the handling of longer contexts but are separate from the strategic ordering of data points for sample efficiency . Data selection criteria, such as filtering based on HTML code-to-text ratio or average line length, represent static quality controls rather than dynamic curricula . For example, Dolma applies filters such as an HTML code-to-text ratio <= 0.2 and an average line length >100 characters . These static filters determine which data points are included in the corpus but do not dictate the order in which they are presented to the model during training . In contrast, curriculum learning specifically addresses the ordering of these selected data points to potentially improve learning efficiency [3,4,5][0,1]. The evaluation of language models often involves tasks that test specific capabilities, such as reversing letters in a word or solving anagrams, where performance varies across models . For instance, none of the models tested can reverse the letters in a word, and performance on the more difficult anagram task was 15.1% . These qualitative and quantitative benchmarks highlight the limitations of current models but do not directly address the training ordering strategies used to achieve those results . Furthermore, alignment training using reinforcement learning from human feedback has been found to improve performance on almost all NLP evaluations, representing a post-training refinement rather than a pre-training curriculum . Other approaches to improving language models involve retrieval or memorization, which are distinct from curriculum learning. For example, an approach that can be applied to any neural language model yielded a 2.9 point improvement with no additional training . Methods for quantifying memorization across neural language models provide a loose lower bound on memorization . Additionally, it has been found that certain benchmarks, such as the 4 Wikipedia language modeling benchmarks measured in GPT-2 and the Children's Book Test dataset, are almost entirely contained in the training data . These findings regarding data overlap and memorization underscore the importance of data selection and ordering, though they do not define the curriculum learning framework itself . Curriculum learning has emerged as an effective strategy in machine learning, allowing models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [0,1]. This approach accounts for sample-level ordering, although more sophisticated techniques like curriculum learning do not necessarily account for skills or their dependencies [3,4,5]. The foundational formulation of curriculum learning involves minimizing a loss function defined as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ { T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, < t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [0,1]. In specific implementations, such as the Skill-it! framework, a pacing function is defined as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ is the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, and 3 for addition [3,4,5]. Perplexity serves as a key metric for assessing data difficulty and model performance trajectories. Research indicates that language modeling perplexity correlates well with few-shot in-context learning performance along the trajectory, regardless of model sizes . Furthermore, the perplexity divergence of correct and incorrect options drives the performance improvement . However, the use of training curricula remains limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula . Semantic similarity metrics are another method for determining data relationships and difficulty. To evaluate the similarity between an input image and text, the CLIP model can be used to extract features from both [0,1]. In the context of word embeddings, words with similar semantic meanings will have small cosine distance in the embedding space . Nearest neighbor models have been applied to NLP problems such as part of speech tagging and morphological analysis, but the use of learned representations makes the similarity function much more effective in the case of neural models . These results strongly suggest that learning similarity between sequences of text is easier than predicting the next word . Semantic similarity is also central to tasks like SCWS, which requires estimating the semantic similarity of word pairs that occur in context . In benchmarks like MTEB, an example of Sentence-to-Sentence (S2S) tasks includes all current STS tasks, where the similarity between two sentences is assessed . However, retrieval and clustering in these benchmarks are English-only . DINO generates synthetic text pairs for semantic textual similarity . Length-based and tokenization metrics are also utilized in data processing. The FineWeb datasets include a `token_count` field, which represents the number of tokens when applying the gpt2 tokenizer to a sample . Additionally, the FineWeb datasets use a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, for processing . Clustering outperforms Sentence similarity, suggesting it is better at identifying related domains . Other methods for assigning difficulty include manual estimation. For instance, an estimate of question difficulty may assign a given question to one of five difficulty levels . In contrast, some approaches involve no gradient updates . Training configurations often involve specific hyperparameters, such as a minimum learning rate set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate , or a learning rate of 2e-5 . Data extraction and membership inference also play roles in understanding training data; for a collection of 256 documents, the vocabulary size |V| is roughly 118,000 . Recent work finds that membership inference methods perform at the level of random chance on pieces of LLM pretraining data . In data extraction studies, researchers may randomly sample between 5 and 10 tokens of context from scraped data . Architectural components, such as a convolution module with kernel size 7, are also part of the model training infrastructure . Curriculum learning is described as an effective strategy in machine learning that allows models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [0,1]. In the context of language models, this approach involves accounting for sample-level ordering, although it does not explicitly account for skills or their dependencies [3,4,5]. The loss function used in such training is defined as $l _ {j} = - \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \log P _ {\theta} \left(Y _ {j, t} \mid Y _ {j, < t}, X _ {j}\right)$ [0,1]. Specific pacing functions have been defined to control this progression, such as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, where $H$ is the number of steps and $M$ is set to 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, and 3 for addition [3,4,5]. Another formulation for pacing involves parameters where $L _ {p} = L _ {\min } + k \Delta L$ and $S _ {p} = S _ {\min } + k \Delta S$ [0,1]. While curriculum learning is recognized as an advanced training technique , its application in large-scale language model pretraining is often limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula . In contrast, standard pretraining approaches, such as those used for the Dolma corpus, involve sampling each source equally rather than applying a specific curriculum . The impact of data ordering on sample efficiency is further contextualized by findings in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where the sample efficiency is roughly the same on the original crowdworker-written prompt dataset and the model-generated one . This RLHF training typically uses a learning rate of 0.05 times the pretraining learning rate , or for PMP, a learning rate of 0.1 relative to LM pretraining . Evidence regarding convergence speed and final performance is mixed across different training paradigms. In knowledge distillation, giving heavy weight to the soft loss at initial training epochs improves the convergence speed , and the proposed method can accelerate convergence speed and improve the final performance of the distilled model . However, in the context of nearest neighbor language models, a kNN-LM trained on 100M tokens with a datastore of 1.6B tokens already outperforms the LM trained on all 3B tokens, suggesting that data access mechanisms can alter efficiency metrics . Similarly, adding out-of-domain data to the datastore makes a single LM useful across multiple domains without further training . For the largest LM in memorization studies, complete memorization occurs after just 33 insertions , and much of the training data extracted is only discovered when prompting the LM with a particular prefix . Other experimental setups provide additional context on training dynamics. In retrieval-augmented language models, the minimum learning rate is set to 0.1 times the maximum learning rate . In end-task aware training, instead of training the whole network to convergence, the body of the network is fixed at each time-step while a special head is trained to convergence on a small batch of end-task training data . This approach highlights the power of pretraining and its relative importance over large-scale instruction tuning and reinforcement learning approaches . Question difficulty estimation has also been applied, assigning questions to one of five difficulty levels . However, a comprehensive empirical evaluation of all downstream tasks is often beyond the scope of individual works . Furthermore, empirical results regarding dataset contamination align with theoretical predictions about how detection difficulty changes with dataset size, example frequency, and learning rate . The implementation of dynamic data reordering and curriculum learning strategies introduces significant computational overhead that often limits their practical adoption in large-scale language model training. For instance, methods like RAIN necessitate a higher computational cost to align models without fine-tuning . Similarly, increasing the size of models such as T5 yields consistent improvements but comes at a significant computational cost . In the context of pre-training objectives, choices among denoising tasks are often driven primarily by their computational cost rather than other factors . Even when considering the detection of pretraining data, pretraining a reference model on the full dataset is described as extremely computationally expensive given the incredible scale of pretraining data . These costs are further compounded by the need for dynamic batch loading, which updates the composition of sampled data in each training batch based on varying losses across different domains . Beyond computational expenses, the field lacks robust theoretical guarantees regarding the efficacy of specific ordering strategies, often relying on empirical observations that may not generalize. While curriculum learning has been applied to improve fine-tuning performance in scenarios involving MLLMs [0,1], the underlying mechanisms are not always theoretically grounded. For example, in one study, the model's performance improved after introducing curriculum learning, yet it still declined as the data size increased, indicating that the method does not universally resolve scaling issues [0,1]. Furthermore, current measures of how well models perform a task have been pointed out to have limitations, which complicates the evaluation of curriculum-based training . The reliance on empirical results is evident in studies on dataset contamination, where observations align with theoretical predictions about detection difficulty changing with dataset size, example frequency, and learning rate, but these are specific to detection rather than training efficiency . The sensitivity of results to specific dataset characteristics and the manual curation process presents another major challenge. Advanced training techniques like curriculum learning are often limited by the need to manually curate collections of datasets and set up training curricula . This manual dependency is highlighted in frameworks like Skill-it!, where sophisticated techniques account for sample-level ordering but do not inherently account for skills or their dependencies [3,4,5]. The definition of pacing functions, such as $g(i) = \frac{iH}{M}$, requires specific parameters like the number of steps and epochs, which vary by task (e.g., 5 epochs for LEGO and NI, 3 for addition) [3,4,5]. Similarly, the linear progression of loss and sample size defined by $L _ {p} = L _ { \min } + k \Delta L \text { and } S _ {p} = S _ { \min } + k \Delta S$ relies on specific assumptions about the data distribution . Dataset quality and composition significantly influence the outcomes of training, often more than dataset size alone. Research indicates that dataset quality rather than dataset size is critical for mean MMLU accuracy . While increasing the dataset size and training for more than one epoch helps with MMLU performance, the differences between datasets are far larger, indicating that dataset quality affects MMLU performance more than dataset size . This is consistent with findings that almost all knowledge in large language models is learned during pretraining, and only limited instruction tuning data is necessary to teach models to produce high-quality output . The choice of data sources, such as the 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content from FineWeb-Edu, reflects an attempt to curate high-quality data . However, even with such curated data, the standard practice of training the language model on shuffled training data for one epoch remains a baseline that dynamic methods must compete against . The interplay between model scale, data selection, and training objectives further complicates the landscape. Very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems . However, the relationship between dataset and model size often follows log-linear trends, as observed in reinforcement learning from human feedback studies . In some cases, methods avoid domain-specific data selection by continuing pretraining on the same pretraining data distribution, which simplifies the process but may miss opportunities for targeted curriculum learning . The stability and accuracy of certain approaches are preferred over others, such as choosing a specific method because it is more stable and accurate than an alternative . Ultimately, while curriculum learning and advanced training techniques are recognized as important , the lack of unified theoretical frameworks and the high computational and manual costs remain significant barriers to widespread, sample-efficient adoption.

question: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?
raw_answer:
Confidence calibration in the context of Large Language Models (LMs) is defined as the alignment between a model's estimated confidence and the empirical likelihood that its prediction is correct [[jacqueline_cs_5:0]]. Specifically, calibration expresses how closely a model's confidence estimate for a prediction aligns with the true probability that the prediction is correct, as measured by accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_5:1]]. A model is considered perfectly calibrated when the probability of the correct class equals the model's predicted confidence for that class [[jacqueline_cs_5:0]]. In the specific domain of LMs, capability calibration evaluates whether the estimated confidence agrees with the model's likelihood to answer an input correctly [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]]. This form of calibration targets the model's underlying probability of correctness, distinguishing it from response calibration, which penalizes the stochasticity of generated outputs [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]].

The estimation of confidence in LMs can be approached through different levels of probability assessment, primarily distinguishing between token-level and sequence-level or answer-level metrics. Token-level probability estimation relies on the autoregressive nature of language models, where the probability of a specific token depends only on previously seen tokens and retrieved data [[jacqueline_cs_5:3]]. In this framework, a token is assigned a high probability if it has high probability under the base model and specific expert distributions, and low probability under anti-expert distributions [[jacqueline_cs_5:4]]. The overall likelihood of a sequence is often reflected in perplexity; if the perplexity is low, the model is not "surprised" by the sequence and has assigned a high average probability to each subsequent token [[jacqueline_cs_5:5]]. However, relying solely on these internal probabilities can be problematic, as the model's conditional probabilities are often relatively poorly calibrated, whether using the probability of the label given the query or the probability assigned to 'True' given the query and proposed answer [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]].

To address these issues, researchers have explored methods that estimate confidence after the output is generated, such as gray-box methods requiring access to token logprobs [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]]. For instance, P(True) is a gray-box method that requires access to token logprobs to estimate confidence [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]]. Alternatively, some approaches focus on eliciting verbalized confidence from the model itself. Large RLHF-LMs can often directly verbalize better-calibrated confidences, either as a numerical probability or an expression such as 'highly likely,' than the models' internal conditional probabilities [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]]. This verbalization can occur in a one-stage prediction setting, where the model provides an answer and confidence probability or expression together [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]].

Several metrics are used to quantify the degree of calibration. The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is a canonical metric that measures the $L_1$ distance between confidence and accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_5:1]]. A perfectly calibrated model has an ECE of 0, meaning model confidence matches expected accuracy at all confidence levels [[jacqueline_cs_5:1]]. However, ECE has limitations, as it completely fails to capture the confidences' discriminative power [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]]. Another common metric is the Brier score, which quantifies the agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes, with lower values indicating better calibration [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]][[jacqueline_cs_5:7]]. The empirical capability calibration Brier score is specifically defined as the mean squared difference between the confidence score and the empirical accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_5:2]].

Recent works have demonstrated that large language models suffer from significant calibration failures [[jacqueline_cs_5:1]]. To mitigate this, various strategies have been proposed. One approach involves temperature scaling, which fits a single temperature value to the model's confidences to minimize negative log likelihood on the data, thereby adjusting the scaled probability of each class [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]]. Another strategy involves regularizing the model to be less certain during training, which can beneficially smooth probabilities and improve out-of-domain calibration [[jacqueline_cs_5:0]]. Furthermore, models like RoBERTa have been shown to consistently achieve lower in-domain ECE compared to other architectures, suggesting that training dynamics and regularization play a role in calibration performance [[jacqueline_cs_5:0]]. Despite these methods, the challenge remains to ensure that the confidence scores generated by LMs are well-aligned with their actual correctness rates, as standard conditional probabilities often fail to provide reliable confidence estimates [[jacqueline_cs_5:6]].

A model is considered calibrated when its confidence estimates are aligned with the empirical likelihoods of its predictions [[jacqueline_cs_5:8]]. In this context, perfect calibration is achieved when the probability of the correct class equals the model's predicted confidence [[jacqueline_cs_5:8]]. These post-hoc methods typically operate by estimating confidence only after the model output has been generated [[jacqueline_cs_5:9]]. While LLM Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) broadly quantifies the degree of uncertainty towards specific inputs [[jacqueline_cs_5:9]], prior work on LLM calibration has largely focused on response-level confidence, which estimates the correctness of a single generated output [[jacqueline_cs_5:9]]. In contrast, capability calibration targets the model's underlying probability of correctness, whereas response calibration penalizes the stochasticity of generated outputs [[jacqueline_cs_5:9]].

Temperature scaling is a widely used technique that multiplies non-normalized logits by a single scalar hyperparameter to improve in-domain calibration [[jacqueline_cs_5:8]]. This method fits a single temperature value $\beta$ to the model's confidences to minimize negative log likelihood (NLL) on the data, resulting in a scaled probability $\tilde{p}_{i}$ for class $i$ proportional to $p_{i}^{\beta}$ [[jacqueline_cs_5:10]]. Temperature scaling has been shown to be effective at further reducing calibration error in-domain [[jacqueline_cs_5:8]]. To fit the temperature used for computing Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score (BS), data is often split into folds, such as 5 folds, to ensure stability [[jacqueline_cs_5:10]]. Fitting the temperature on 20% of the data yields relatively stable temperatures across these folds [[jacqueline_cs_5:10]]. However, selecting a temperature based on a specific set for temperature scaling may fail to improve ECE over the base LM with a temperature of 1 [[jacqueline_cs_5:11]].

Beyond temperature scaling, prior work has focused on recalibrating neural networks using Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or histogram binning [[jacqueline_cs_5:11]]. Few-shot recalibration offers an alternative approach that improves calibration error for models like PaLM2-Large on MMLU by 16% compared to temperature scaling [[jacqueline_cs_5:11]]. Experiments indicate that this few-shot recalibrator consistently outperforms existing calibration methods [[jacqueline_cs_5:11]]. Overall, the slice-specific recalibrator consistently outperforms existing methods for calibration in all settings and extrapolates well to domains that are unseen at training time [[jacqueline_cs_5:11]].

Ensemble methods and parallel sampling strategies also contribute to post-hoc confidence estimation. For instance, sampling 64 responses in parallel at a higher temperature allows for the post-hoc construction of multi-turn rollouts from independent samples [[jacqueline_cs_5:12]]. In such frameworks, an estimate of question difficulty may assign a given question to one of five difficulty levels [[jacqueline_cs_5:12]]. Additionally, prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options [[jacqueline_cs_5:13]]. In model merging contexts, the estimator may default to the best LLM on the benchmark in cases of low confidence [[jacqueline_cs_5:14]].

Calibration is defined as the alignment of a model's confidence estimates with empirical likelihoods [[jacqueline_cs_5:15]]. Large language models (LLMs) suffer from calibration failure, where they appear well-calibrated on average but are significantly miscalibrated in finer-grained settings [[jacqueline_cs_5:16]]. A perfectly calibrated model achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of zero, meaning model confidence matches expected accuracy at all confidence levels [[jacqueline_cs_5:16]]. While many methods operate post-hoc to estimate confidence after output generation [[jacqueline_cs_5:17]], training-based and fine-tuning approaches seek to incorporate calibration objectives directly into the learning process.

Fine-tuning is a primary mechanism for adapting LLMs, offering strong performance on many benchmarks [[jacqueline_cs_5:18]]. In some fine-tuning regimes, only injected layers are updated while pre-trained ones remain frozen [[jacqueline_cs_5:19]]. For instance, LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B have been trained by fully fine-tuning [[jacqueline_cs_5:20]]. However, the choice of fine-tuning strategy impacts generalization; fine-tuning with In-Context Learning (ICL) is better than directly fine-tuning on generation tasks [[jacqueline_cs_5:21]]. Furthermore, Fine-Tuning with ICL (FTICL) tends to deviate less from the original LLM than vanilla fine-tuning [[jacqueline_cs_5:21]]. Although it was conjectured that large bidirectional models would be stronger at fine-tuning than GPT-3 [[jacqueline_cs_5:18]], no gradient updates are performed in pure few-shot inference scenarios [[jacqueline_cs_5:18]].

Contrastive learning techniques are employed to enhance representation learning and generation quality. In CoNT, increasing the number of contrastive samples continuously boosts performance [[jacqueline_cs_5:22]]. This method focuses on sequence-level contrastive examples, whereas other approaches perform token-level contrastive learning [[jacqueline_cs_5:22]]. The contrastive score in Contrastive Decoding (CD) is defined by dividing the expert probability over amateur probability, which is equivalent to subtraction in the log probability space [[jacqueline_cs_5:23]]. In embedding model training, such as LLM2Vec, positive examples are constructed by applying the LLM's dropout twice on the same input sequence, while other sequences in the batch act as in-batch negatives [[jacqueline_cs_5:24]]. To further enhance representation learning, NV-Embed removes the causal attention mask of LLMs during contrastive training [[jacqueline_cs_5:25]].

Auxiliary loss functions and distillation methods also play a role in shaping model confidence. In Decoupled Knowledge Distillation, the loss weight of well-predicted samples is suppressed by the high confidence of the teacher [[jacqueline_cs_5:26]]. The Non-Confident Knowledge Distillation (NCKD) loss is coupled with $(1 - p_{t}^{\mathcal{T}})$, where $p_{t}^{T}$ represents the teacher's confidence on the target class [[jacqueline_cs_5:26]]. Probing is a white-box method that requires open-weight models [[jacqueline_cs_5:17]]. Training linear probes on LLM activations offers a favorable tradeoff between computational cost and confidence estimation performance [[jacqueline_cs_5:17]].

Fine-tuning with human feedback influences the model's ability to verbalize confidence. The difference between GPT-*, Claude-*, and Llama-2's ability to verbalize confidence is significant [[jacqueline_cs_5:27]]. Models display much lower verbalized confidence on TruthfulQA than on standard factual recall problems [[jacqueline_cs_5:27]]. Prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options [[jacqueline_cs_5:28]]. To account for bias in evaluation, logit-based confidence scores are averaged across two orderings [[jacqueline_cs_5:28]]. In some routing mechanisms, the estimator defaults to the best LLM on the benchmark in cases of low confidence [[jacqueline_cs_5:29]].

Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes a field of methods designed to quantify the degree of uncertainty a model holds towards specific inputs [[jacqueline_cs_5:30]]. A core objective within this domain is calibration, which expresses how closely a model's confidence estimate for a prediction is aligned with the true probability that the prediction is correct, as measured by accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]]. Perfect calibration is mathematically defined as the state where the probability of the correct class given the query equals the model's predicted confidence, i.e., $P(Y = y|Q = q) = q$ [[jacqueline_cs_5:32]]. Well-calibrated models are characterized by lying close to the diagonal $(y = x)$ in reliability diagrams [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]]. Capability calibration is specifically linked to LLM UQ, as it utilizes expected accuracy as the target for the estimated model's uncertainty regarding a specific input [[jacqueline_cs_5:30]].

Recent research indicates that large language models suffer from the same calibration failures observed in other neural architectures [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]]. To address this, various probabilistic and post-hoc frameworks have been developed. Temperature scaling is one such method, which has been shown to be effective at further reducing calibration error in-domain for pre-trained transformers [[jacqueline_cs_5:32]]. In the context of LLMs, these methods typically operate post-hoc, estimating confidence only after the output has been generated [[jacqueline_cs_5:30]]. For instance, prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options, such as in binary choice tasks [[jacqueline_cs_5:33]].

Beyond post-hoc adjustments, researchers have explored eliciting calibrated confidence directly from models fine-tuned with human feedback. This involves prompting the model to assign confidences to its guesses by choosing from a set of linguistic expressions of uncertainty, such as "Almost certain," "Likely," or "Almost no chance" [[jacqueline_cs_5:34]]. Surprisingly, language models can express their uncertainty with numerical probabilities as well or better than with words, despite longstanding difficulties in representing numbers in language models [[jacqueline_cs_5:34]]. This capability allows models to express their uncertainty in words [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]]. The elicitation process can be structured in different ways: one-stage prediction (1S) involves the model providing an answer and confidence probability or expression together, whereas two-stage prediction (2S) requires the model to first give only an answer and then provide a confidence in a second stage [[jacqueline_cs_5:34]].

Alternative approaches focus on recalibrating the model's confidence without altering its underlying predictions. In few-shot recalibration, a function $f$ is applied such that it does not change the prediction of the underlying model $p_{LM}$, only its confidences [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]]. In both settings where capability-calibrated confidence is applied, it leads to improved performance over baselines [[jacqueline_cs_5:30]]. While some studies measure the correlation between verbalized uncertainty and accuracy, others measure the correlation between the uncertainty on two different tasks to evaluate generalizability [[jacqueline_cs_5:33]]. The development of these adaptable, general language systems relies on very large language models as an important ingredient [[jacqueline_cs_5:35]], with specific performance metrics, such as those for GPT-3 13B, providing baseline data for these evaluations [[jacqueline_cs_5:35]]. Although Monte Carlo simulation is used in other domains to predict properties using measurement data [[jacqueline_cs_5:36]] and there is a need for cross-calibration of Monte Carlo methods in high-energy particle interactions [[jacqueline_cs_5:37]], the primary focus for LLM confidence remains on the probabilistic alignment of model outputs with true accuracy [[jacqueline_cs_5:31]][[jacqueline_cs_5:32]].

Recent empirical studies establish that large language models (LLMs) frequently exhibit calibration failures, where their confidence estimates do not align with the true probability of their predictions being correct [[jacqueline_cs_5:38]]. Calibration is formally defined as the alignment between a model's confidence estimates and empirical likelihoods, with perfect calibration occurring when the predicted probability equals the actual conditional probability of the outcome [[jacqueline_cs_5:39]]. This alignment is often quantified using metrics such as the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), where a perfectly calibrated model achieves an ECE of zero, indicating that model confidence matches expected accuracy at all confidence levels [[jacqueline_cs_5:38]]. Another common metric is the Brier score, which measures the mean squared difference between the predicted probability and the observed outcome, serving as a measure of capability calibration linked to uncertainty quantification [[jacqueline_cs_5:40]].

Empirical investigations reveal that LLM outputs are rarely binary, meaning they are neither perfectly deterministic nor consistently correct across multiple inference calls for the same input [[jacqueline_cs_5:40]]. This stochastic nature complicates the assessment of confidence, as methods typically operate post-hoc, estimating confidence only after the output has been generated [[jacqueline_cs_5:40]]. In the context of self-evaluation, LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generations, a bias that can be measured by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options to compute prediction confidence [[jacqueline_cs_5:41]]. While some studies measure the correlation between verbalized uncertainty and accuracy, others focus on the correlation between uncertainty across different tasks, highlighting the complexity of evaluating these judgments [[jacqueline_cs_5:41]].

Several strategies have been proposed to improve calibration, with recent work demonstrating that few-shot recalibration can effectively address these issues. A slice-specific recalibrator has been shown to consistently outperform existing calibration methods in all settings, including extrapolation to domains unseen at training time [[jacqueline_cs_5:38]]. This approach achieves a 16% lower calibration error on test set slices compared to standard methods that use the precision/calibration curve of the combined distribution over all domains [[jacqueline_cs_5:38]]. The effectiveness of this few-shot recalibrator is supported by empirical studies validating the utility of using high-quality data for instruction-tuning and recalibration processes [[jacqueline_cs_5:42]].

Alternative approaches focus on eliciting calibrated confidence scores directly from models fine-tuned with human feedback. Experiments conducted on models such as GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Claude 1, Claude 2, and Llama-2-70B-Chat indicate that directly verbalizing a probability or using linguistic expressions of confidence yields significantly better-calibrated estimates than other methods [[jacqueline_cs_5:43]]. However, the effectiveness of verbalized confidence varies across different LLMs, with results differing between models [[jacqueline_cs_5:40]]. Furthermore, verbalized confidence has been found to achieve results comparable to probe-based methods that require access to internal model states, suggesting that external verbalization can be a viable alternative to internal probing [[jacqueline_cs_5:40]].

Despite these advancements, significant limitations and domain-specific discrepancies remain. Models display markedly lower verbalized confidence on the TruthfulQA benchmark compared to standard factual recall problems, indicating that calibration performance is not uniform across different types of queries [[jacqueline_cs_5:43]]. This gap suggests that the relationship between verbalized confidence and internal probabilities is complex and context-dependent. Additionally, while some systems use confidence to route queries to the best-performing LLM in cases of low confidence, the reliability of these confidence signals remains a subject of ongoing investigation [[jacqueline_cs_5:44]]. The challenge of accurately quantifying model behavior is further complicated by issues such as memorization, where sequences repeated frequently in pretraining data are memorized with high probability, potentially skewing confidence estimates [[jacqueline_cs_5:45]]. Although recent work finds that membership inference methods perform at the level of random chance on pretraining data, the broader implications for calibration in specialized domains like mathematics, where datasets such as OpenWebMath provide extensive problem sets, remain an area for further empirical analysis [[jacqueline_cs_5:46]][[jacqueline_cs_5:47]].
answer_official_all: Confidence calibration in the context of Large Language Models (LMs) is defined as the alignment between a model's estimated confidence and the empirical likelihood that its prediction is correct [3]. Specifically, calibration expresses how closely a model's confidence estimate for a prediction aligns with the true probability that the prediction is correct, as measured by accuracy [1,6,7,8]. A model is considered perfectly calibrated when the probability of the correct class equals the model's predicted confidence for that class [3]. In the specific domain of LMs, capability calibration evaluates whether the estimated confidence agrees with the model's likelihood to answer an input correctly [0,2]. This form of calibration targets the model's underlying probability of correctness, distinguishing it from response calibration, which penalizes the stochasticity of generated outputs [0,2]. The estimation of confidence in LMs can be approached through different levels of probability assessment, primarily distinguishing between token-level and sequence-level or answer-level metrics. Token-level probability estimation relies on the autoregressive nature of language models, where the probability of a specific token depends only on previously seen tokens and retrieved data . In this framework, a token is assigned a high probability if it has high probability under the base model and specific expert distributions, and low probability under anti-expert distributions . The overall likelihood of a sequence is often reflected in perplexity; if the perplexity is low, the model is not "surprised" by the sequence and has assigned a high average probability to each subsequent token . However, relying solely on these internal probabilities can be problematic, as the model's conditional probabilities are often relatively poorly calibrated, whether using the probability of the label given the query or the probability assigned to 'True' given the query and proposed answer [4,5]. To address these issues, researchers have explored methods that estimate confidence after the output is generated, such as gray-box methods requiring access to token logprobs [0,2]. For instance, P(True) is a gray-box method that requires access to token logprobs to estimate confidence [0,2]. Alternatively, some approaches focus on eliciting verbalized confidence from the model itself. Large RLHF-LMs can often directly verbalize better-calibrated confidences, either as a numerical probability or an expression such as 'highly likely,' than the models' internal conditional probabilities [4,5]. This verbalization can occur in a one-stage prediction setting, where the model provides an answer and confidence probability or expression together [4,5]. Several metrics are used to quantify the degree of calibration. The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is a canonical metric that measures the $L_1$ distance between confidence and accuracy [1,6,7,8]. A perfectly calibrated model has an ECE of 0, meaning model confidence matches expected accuracy at all confidence levels [1,6,7,8]. However, ECE has limitations, as it completely fails to capture the confidences' discriminative power [4,5]. Another common metric is the Brier score, which quantifies the agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes, with lower values indicating better calibration [0,2]. The empirical capability calibration Brier score is specifically defined as the mean squared difference between the confidence score and the empirical accuracy [0,2]. Recent works have demonstrated that large language models suffer from significant calibration failures [1,6,7,8]. To mitigate this, various strategies have been proposed. One approach involves temperature scaling, which fits a single temperature value to the model's confidences to minimize negative log likelihood on the data, thereby adjusting the scaled probability of each class [4,5]. Another strategy involves regularizing the model to be less certain during training, which can beneficially smooth probabilities and improve out-of-domain calibration [3]. Furthermore, models like RoBERTa have been shown to consistently achieve lower in-domain ECE compared to other architectures, suggesting that training dynamics and regularization play a role in calibration performance [3]. Despite these methods, the challenge remains to ensure that the confidence scores generated by LMs are well-aligned with their actual correctness rates, as standard conditional probabilities often fail to provide reliable confidence estimates [4,5]. A model is considered calibrated when its confidence estimates are aligned with the empirical likelihoods of its predictions [3]. In this context, perfect calibration is achieved when the probability of the correct class equals the model's predicted confidence [3]. These post-hoc methods typically operate by estimating confidence only after the model output has been generated [0,2]. While LLM Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) broadly quantifies the degree of uncertainty towards specific inputs [0,2], prior work on LLM calibration has largely focused on response-level confidence, which estimates the correctness of a single generated output [0,2]. In contrast, capability calibration targets the model's underlying probability of correctness, whereas response calibration penalizes the stochasticity of generated outputs [0,2]. Temperature scaling is a widely used technique that multiplies non-normalized logits by a single scalar hyperparameter to improve in-domain calibration [3]. This method fits a single temperature value $\beta$ to the model's confidences to minimize negative log likelihood (NLL) on the data, resulting in a scaled probability $\tilde{p}_{i}$ for class $i$ proportional to $p_{i}^{\beta}$ [4,5]. Temperature scaling has been shown to be effective at further reducing calibration error in-domain [3]. To fit the temperature used for computing Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score (BS), data is often split into folds, such as 5 folds, to ensure stability [4,5]. Fitting the temperature on 20% of the data yields relatively stable temperatures across these folds [4,5]. However, selecting a temperature based on a specific set for temperature scaling may fail to improve ECE over the base LM with a temperature of 1 [1,6,7,8]. Beyond temperature scaling, prior work has focused on recalibrating neural networks using Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or histogram binning [1,6,7,8]. Few-shot recalibration offers an alternative approach that improves calibration error for models like PaLM2-Large on MMLU by 16% compared to temperature scaling [1,6,7,8]. Experiments indicate that this few-shot recalibrator consistently outperforms existing calibration methods [1,6,7,8]. Overall, the slice-specific recalibrator consistently outperforms existing methods for calibration in all settings and extrapolates well to domains that are unseen at training time [1,6,7,8]. Ensemble methods and parallel sampling strategies also contribute to post-hoc confidence estimation. For instance, sampling 64 responses in parallel at a higher temperature allows for the post-hoc construction of multi-turn rollouts from independent samples . In such frameworks, an estimate of question difficulty may assign a given question to one of five difficulty levels . Additionally, prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options . In model merging contexts, the estimator may default to the best LLM on the benchmark in cases of low confidence . Calibration is defined as the alignment of a model's confidence estimates with empirical likelihoods [3]. Large language models (LLMs) suffer from calibration failure, where they appear well-calibrated on average but are significantly miscalibrated in finer-grained settings [1,6,7,8]. A perfectly calibrated model achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of zero, meaning model confidence matches expected accuracy at all confidence levels [1,6,7,8]. While many methods operate post-hoc to estimate confidence after output generation [0,2], training-based and fine-tuning approaches seek to incorporate calibration objectives directly into the learning process. Fine-tuning is a primary mechanism for adapting LLMs, offering strong performance on many benchmarks . In some fine-tuning regimes, only injected layers are updated while pre-trained ones remain frozen . For instance, LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B have been trained by fully fine-tuning . However, the choice of fine-tuning strategy impacts generalization; fine-tuning with In-Context Learning (ICL) is better than directly fine-tuning on generation tasks . Furthermore, Fine-Tuning with ICL (FTICL) tends to deviate less from the original LLM than vanilla fine-tuning . Although it was conjectured that large bidirectional models would be stronger at fine-tuning than GPT-3 , no gradient updates are performed in pure few-shot inference scenarios . Contrastive learning techniques are employed to enhance representation learning and generation quality. In CoNT, increasing the number of contrastive samples continuously boosts performance . This method focuses on sequence-level contrastive examples, whereas other approaches perform token-level contrastive learning . The contrastive score in Contrastive Decoding (CD) is defined by dividing the expert probability over amateur probability, which is equivalent to subtraction in the log probability space . In embedding model training, such as LLM2Vec, positive examples are constructed by applying the LLM's dropout twice on the same input sequence, while other sequences in the batch act as in-batch negatives . To further enhance representation learning, NV-Embed removes the causal attention mask of LLMs during contrastive training . Auxiliary loss functions and distillation methods also play a role in shaping model confidence. In Decoupled Knowledge Distillation, the loss weight of well-predicted samples is suppressed by the high confidence of the teacher . The Non-Confident Knowledge Distillation (NCKD) loss is coupled with $(1 - p_{t}^{\mathcal{T}})$, where $p_{t}^{T}$ represents the teacher's confidence on the target class . Probing is a white-box method that requires open-weight models [0,2]. Training linear probes on LLM activations offers a favorable tradeoff between computational cost and confidence estimation performance [0,2]. Fine-tuning with human feedback influences the model's ability to verbalize confidence. The difference between GPT-*, Claude-*, and Llama-2's ability to verbalize confidence is significant [4,5]. Models display much lower verbalized confidence on TruthfulQA than on standard factual recall problems [4,5]. Prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options . To account for bias in evaluation, logit-based confidence scores are averaged across two orderings . In some routing mechanisms, the estimator defaults to the best LLM on the benchmark in cases of low confidence . Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes a field of methods designed to quantify the degree of uncertainty a model holds towards specific inputs [0,2]. A core objective within this domain is calibration, which expresses how closely a model's confidence estimate for a prediction is aligned with the true probability that the prediction is correct, as measured by accuracy [1,6,7,8]. Perfect calibration is mathematically defined as the state where the probability of the correct class given the query equals the model's predicted confidence, i.e., $P(Y = y|Q = q) = q$ [3]. Well-calibrated models are characterized by lying close to the diagonal $(y = x)$ in reliability diagrams [1,6,7,8]. Capability calibration is specifically linked to LLM UQ, as it utilizes expected accuracy as the target for the estimated model's uncertainty regarding a specific input [0,2]. Recent research indicates that large language models suffer from the same calibration failures observed in other neural architectures [1,6,7,8]. To address this, various probabilistic and post-hoc frameworks have been developed. Temperature scaling is one such method, which has been shown to be effective at further reducing calibration error in-domain for pre-trained transformers [3]. In the context of LLMs, these methods typically operate post-hoc, estimating confidence only after the output has been generated [0,2]. For instance, prediction confidence can be computed by normalizing the output probabilities of tokens associated with specific options, such as in binary choice tasks . Beyond post-hoc adjustments, researchers have explored eliciting calibrated confidence directly from models fine-tuned with human feedback.
