question: Find some papers that discuss the methods to suppress multiple light scattering effect on light scattering imaging
raw_answer:
When light propagates through a turbid medium, its un-scattered intensity decays exponentially with distance in accordance with the Beer-Lambert law [[pan_biophysics_1:0]]. In biological tissues, multiple scattering events can lead to small changes in photon trajectories that are difficult to differentiate from directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:0]]. This physical phenomenon results in a situation where the amount of multiply scattered light may greatly exceed the directly scattered light, a condition indicated by a negative value of the parameter P [[pan_biophysics_1:0]]. The presence of multiple scattering in turbid tissue is known to limit both imaging depth and contrast, particularly when it is not accounted for in the model formulation [[pan_biophysics_1:1]]. Furthermore, depolarization in biological tissues can be caused by multiple scattering or by scattering at non-spherical particles such as melanin granules [[pan_biophysics_1:2]].

The impact of multiple scattering on image resolution is evident in optical coherence tomography (OCT), where a photon that undergoes multiple scattering has a longer optical path than single-scattering photons [[pan_biophysics_1:3]]. Consequently, a photon that undergoes multiple scattering at a specific depth appears in the image to be located at a deeper location than its true position [[pan_biophysics_1:3]]. General OCT imaging theory is based on the assumption that most multiple-scattering photons are rejected by a confocal pinhole, such as a single-mode fiber tip, allowing single-scattering photons to govern the imaging process [[pan_biophysics_1:3]]. In turbid samples, the changing light path length amplifies the effect on static intensity [[pan_biophysics_1:4]]. However, in contrast to static experiments, a variation of the light path length in turbid samples has no effect on the decay time, affecting only the intercept [[pan_biophysics_1:4]].

To address these issues, various methods have been developed to suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering. CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques can be used to efficiently suppress these effects [[pan_biophysics_1:5]][[pan_biophysics_1:6]]. One such approach introduces a charge-coupled device (CCD) camera-based detection scheme in dynamic light scattering that provides information on the single-scattered autocorrelation function even for fairly turbid samples [[pan_biophysics_1:6]][[pan_biophysics_1:5]]. In this scheme, a separation comparable to the size of a single-scattering speckle, approximately 30 pixels, serves as a good compromise value for separating single from multiple scattering [[pan_biophysics_1:6]]. For the most turbid samples, with a scattering coefficient of approximately 5.92 cm⁻¹, a noticeable difference is observed due to the loss of the single-scattering signal and an unavoidable increase in error [[pan_biophysics_1:6]].

Structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI) offers another method for suppression, where the suppression of diffuse light performs equally well regardless of whether photons propagate along the incident direction or towards the camera [[pan_biophysics_1:0]]. Increasing the frequency of the incident modulation can improve the sensitivity of the diffuse light filtering capabilities [[pan_biophysics_1:0]]. Studies on elastic scattering and fluorescence have conclusively shown the advantages of SLIPI for imaging within moderately turbid media when probing different particle concentrations and diameters [[pan_biophysics_1:0]].

The optical properties of the media, which influence scattering behavior, are often modeled using phantoms. In glass-based imaging phantoms, the average crystal size has a dominating effect on the reduced scattering coefficient [[pan_biophysics_1:7]]. For the assessment of optical reproducibility, samples with high scattering and absorption are selected as representative for variation in optical properties [[pan_biophysics_1:7]]. In agar-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, intralipid concentration measurements show increased reduced scattering coefficients with an increase in intralipid concentration [[pan_biophysics_1:8]].

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) relies on the principle that multiple scattering (MS) photons are rejected by a confocal pinhole, such as a single-mode fiber tip, allowing single-scattering (SS) photons to govern the imaging process [[pan_biophysics_1:9]]. This rejection is effective because an MS photon travels a longer optical path than SS photons, causing it to appear at a deeper location in the image than its actual scattering depth [[pan_biophysics_1:9]]. The axial resolution of OCT, which is inversely proportional to the light bandwidth, determines the depth resolution of the system [[pan_biophysics_1:10]]. In spectral domain OCT, the choice of spectral window size creates a trade-off where a narrower window provides good spectral resolution but poor spatial resolution, while a longer window improves spatial resolution in the z-direction at the cost of spectral resolution [[pan_biophysics_1:11]]. For instance, an average axial resolution of 2.7 μm in air has been achieved at depths up to 2 mm [[pan_biophysics_1:11]]. However, even with high resolution, OCT faces difficulties visualizing cellular structures due to a lack of scattering contrast [[pan_biophysics_1:12]]. The confocal parameter, which defines the depth of focus, is limited; for example, at a 1 μm focus diameter, the confocal parameter is only 17 μm [[pan_biophysics_1:12]]. To address artifacts and noise, methods such as CLEAN are performed in the spatial image domain to iteratively recover the original image [[pan_biophysics_1:13]]. Additionally, dispersion compensation techniques using time-frequency analysis and iterative optimization have been applied to spectral domain OCT [[pan_biophysics_1:11]]. In some implementations, a ground glass moving diffuser is utilized to reduce speckle, an effect that can also be achieved by other means such as a spatial light modulator [[pan_biophysics_1:14]].

Confocal microscopy provides optical sectioning through the use of an entrance slit or pinhole, which allows for the tracking of membrane protein motion at the apical cell surface [[pan_biophysics_1:15]]. This technique is also employed in Raman spectroscopy, where a laser confocal microscope is used to measure fluorescence intensity with 532 nm excitation light [[pan_biophysics_1:16]]. The ability to isolate specific depths is crucial for suppressing background signals from out-of-focus regions.

Structured Laser Illumination Planar Imaging (SLIPI) offers an alternative approach to suppressing multiple scattering in scattering and fluorescing media [[pan_biophysics_1:17]]. In this method, multiple scattering events that lead to only small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:17]]. Consequently, the local undisturbed amplitude of the modulation serves as a measure of the amount of directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:17]]. The filtering capabilities of SLIPI are independent of the spatial distribution of the diffuse light being detected [[pan_biophysics_1:17]]. The suppression efficiency, denoted as $\varepsilon_{supp}$, is calculated using the formula $\varepsilon_{s u p p}={\frac{I_{C}-I_{S}}{I_{C}}}$ [[pan_biophysics_1:17]].

CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques can efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering [[pan_biophysics_1:18]][[pan_biophysics_1:19]]. In dynamic light scattering based on a digital camera detection scheme, binning leads to partial suppression of multiple scattering by averaging out small speckles [[pan_biophysics_1:19]][[pan_biophysics_1:18]]. This approach utilizes the statistical properties of the scattered light to mitigate the impact of multiple scattering events.

Polarization-sensitive OCT is another technique where multiple scattering in turbid tissue limits imaging depth and contrast if not accounted for in the model formulation [[pan_biophysics_1:20]]. To address this, polarization-insensitive OCT based on partly depolarized light has been developed, where $I_{H}$ represents the signal intensity from the horizontal polarization state [[pan_biophysics_1:21]]. Furthermore, advanced methods such as smart OCT have been proposed, which modulate the pupil using a spatial light modulator (SLM) and a pre-defined reflection matrix to enhance image quality [[pan_biophysics_1:9]].

In the context of signal processing and noise reduction, the contrast of the OCT signal is often characterized by the coefficient of variation, defined as $C = \frac {\sigma}{\mu}$ [[pan_biophysics_1:22]]. Real-time noise reduction can be achieved using ground truth free deep learning for OCT, with imaging depths reaching 6.7 mm [[pan_biophysics_1:23]]. Speckle analysis methods, such as those based on autocorrelation, have been applied to OCT signals, with whole milk (3% fat) used as a scattering media for flow studies [[pan_biophysics_1:24]]. The surface in OCT images is typically defined at the top-most depth where the derivative is larger than a predefined threshold [[pan_biophysics_1:9]].

Wavefront shaping and adaptive optics (AO) are employed to correct for scattering-induced aberrations, with AO specifically noted to provide a lateral resolution of 2 microns, a considerable improvement from the approximately 15-micron lateral resolution of standard optical coherence tomography (OCT) [[pan_biophysics_1:25]]. These systems utilize wavefront correcting components and computational controller software to compensate for aberrations and quality degradation, thereby increasing the quality of OCT images [[pan_biophysics_1:25]]. However, the application of these modalities is limited by the requirement for expensive wavefront manipulation devices, such as a spatial light modulator (SLM) or deformable mirror [[pan_biophysics_1:26]]. Furthermore, state-of-the-art research instruments that incorporate this technology currently employ reduced fields-of-view to keep total imaging times feasible, a limitation that needs to be overcome before they become widely applicable [[pan_biophysics_1:27]].

In the context of dispersion correction, which is critical for maintaining image quality in scattering media, methods often rely on the complex conjugate of the dispersive spectral phase [[pan_biophysics_1:28]][[pan_biophysics_1:29]]. Typically, it is sufficient to compensate for second and third-order dispersion using a phase correction term [[pan_biophysics_1:30]], while other approaches involve numerically compensating residual dispersion using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction [[pan_biophysics_1:31]]. The phase stability required for these corrections is only necessary within a single frame [[pan_biophysics_1:26]].

Alternative methods for suppressing multiple scattering effects include CCD-camera-based light scattering, which can efficiently suppress undesirable effects [[pan_biophysics_1:32]][[pan_biophysics_1:33]]. In dynamic light scattering based on a digital camera detection scheme, binning leads to partial suppression of multiple scattering by averaging out small speckles [[pan_biophysics_1:33]][[pan_biophysics_1:32]]. Structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI) extracts images from three phase-shifted images, where the spatial phase is shifted by 120 degrees [[pan_biophysics_1:34]]. The suppression efficiency in such methods is defined by the ratio of the difference between the clear and scattered intensities to the clear intensity [[pan_biophysics_1:34]]. However, multiple scattering events that lead to small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:34]]. The contribution of multiple scattering depends on particle size, the scattering process involved, and the surrounding media, which makes correction approaches extremely challenging [[pan_biophysics_1:34]].

While wavefront manipulation is a primary method, other techniques such as alignment and normalization schemes allow for measurements on an absolute scale even for samples exhibiting strong multiple scattering [[pan_biophysics_1:35]]. Deep learning approaches, such as SNR-Net, enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of OCT images in deep tissue regions, facilitating the observation of microstructures after brightening [[pan_biophysics_1:36]]. These deep learning models may utilize adaptive learning rate optimization algorithms, such as Adam, as the training optimizer [[pan_biophysics_1:36]]. Real-time noise reduction based on ground truth free deep learning for OCT has been demonstrated with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm and a system sensitivity of 92 dB [[pan_biophysics_1:37]]. As an optical method, the applicability of these techniques is limited to imaging of superficial locations in tissues and other objects [[pan_biophysics_1:38]]. In OCT angiography, specific approaches have the added benefit of removing projection artifacts, since axial resolution can also be improved [[pan_biophysics_1:27]].

Computational reconstruction methods address the limitations imposed by multiple scattering, which is known to limit polarization imaging depth and contrast when not considered in the model formulation [[pan_biophysics_1:39]]. In optical coherence tomography (OCT), multiple scattering specifically limits the observation depth [[pan_biophysics_1:40]], and consequently, multiple scattering events that lead to small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:41]]. To mitigate these effects, CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques have been utilized to efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering [[pan_biophysics_1:42]][[pan_biophysics_1:43]]. One such computational approach involves multi-focus averaging (MFA) for multiple scattering suppression in OCT, where the difference in the number of scattering particles observed between B-MFA and MFA images is attributed to the difference in 1-D and 2-D computational refocusing [[pan_biophysics_1:44]]. However, B-MFA necessitates lateral oversampling due to its utilization of computational refocusing, which may limit the field size [[pan_biophysics_1:44]]. The computational framework for such refocusing relies on the 1-D Fourier transform and its inverse Fourier transform along the fast-scan direction [[pan_biophysics_1:44]].

In the context of inverse problems, the inverse adding-doubling (IAD) method enables the measurement of optical properties of tissue-mimicking phantoms, such as those fabricated from agar [[pan_biophysics_1:45]]. These phantoms are evaluated using technical setups that include a 4-inch integrating sphere with three ports [[pan_biophysics_1:45]]. For spectral domain OCT, dispersion encoding and subsequent reconstruction of a full-range signal is an attractive technique, although it requires more than double the computational effort compared to other methods [[pan_biophysics_1:46]]. The reconstruction process in OCT can be explicitly written using the inverse Fourier transform of the intensity signal, which relates to the reflection coefficients and path lengths [[pan_biophysics_1:47]]. In dynamic light scattering, the inverse relationship between flow and decorrelation time is observed, where decorrelation values are lower for previously studied flows [[pan_biophysics_1:48]].

Deep learning and machine learning approaches have also been applied to computational reconstruction and noise reduction. The entrance of machine learning and deep learning models in data analysis has contributed to overcoming some of the method’s limits [[pan_biophysics_1:49]]. For instance, real-time noise reduction based on ground truth free deep learning for OCT has been implemented with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm [[pan_biophysics_1:50]] and a scanning interval frequency of 70 kHz [[pan_biophysics_1:50]]. Another deep learning model, SNR-Net OCT, is used to brighten and denoise low-light OCT images, trained with a learning rate of $1\times 10^{-4}$ [[pan_biophysics_1:51]] and a batch size of 1 [[pan_biophysics_1:51]]. In the field of dielectric metasurfaces, machine learning has shown the capability for inverse designs of metasurfaces with assigned optical properties [[pan_biophysics_1:52]].

Quantitative metrics are employed to assess the suppression of multiple scattering and image quality. The suppression efficiency is defined by the ratio of the difference between the contrast and signal intensities to the contrast intensity [[pan_biophysics_1:41]]. In the analysis of structured laser illumination, specific parameters such as the total x-distance in millimeters are defined to characterize the imaging geometry [[pan_biophysics_1:41]]. Image quality in OCT is often evaluated using the contrast-to-noise ratio, expressed as the ratio of standard deviation to mean [[pan_biophysics_1:53]], or through specific formulas involving the detector diameter and gamma [[pan_biophysics_1:53]]. Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technique based on light scattering that is subject to these multiple scattering challenges [[pan_biophysics_1:54]].

CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques have been demonstrated to efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering in both static and dynamic contexts [[pan_biophysics_1:55]][[pan_biophysics_1:56]]. In dynamic light scattering, this suppression is achieved through binning, which leads to partial mitigation by averaging out small speckles [[pan_biophysics_1:56]][[pan_biophysics_1:55]]. Furthermore, alignment and normalization schemes associated with these methods allow for measurements on an absolute scale, even for samples exhibiting strong multiple scattering [[pan_biophysics_1:57]]. However, the changes in static scattering intensities are primarily attributed to variations in the detected scattering vector, necessitating corrections such as multiplying static intensities by the sine of the scattering angle to account for changes in the size of the scattering volume [[pan_biophysics_1:57]].

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) faces specific limitations where multiple scattering in turbid tissue restricts imaging depth and contrast if not explicitly considered in the model formulation [[pan_biophysics_1:58]]. As an optical method, the applicability of such techniques is inherently limited to imaging superficial locations in tissues and other objects [[pan_biophysics_1:59]]. In the context of structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI), multiple scattering events that result in only small changes to photon trajectories cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [[pan_biophysics_1:60]]. The contribution of these events depends on particle size, the specific scattering process, and the surrounding media, which makes correction approaches extremely challenging [[pan_biophysics_1:60]]. This fundamental limitation of SLIPI is difficult, if not impossible, to correct for because it may require prior knowledge of the size distribution of the probed sample [[pan_biophysics_1:60]]. Additionally, the suppression capability in such systems is bounded by unavoidable camera noise, with a measured limit of approximately 0.3% correlating well with this noise floor [[pan_biophysics_1:60]].

In optical coherence tomography (OCT), multiple scattering (MS) photons possess a longer optical path than single scattering (SS) photons, causing photons that undergo multiple scattering at a specific depth to appear at a deeper location in the image [[pan_biophysics_1:61]]. Multi-focus averaging (SFA) has been proposed to address this, although it results in lower intensity compared to single acquisition, specifically showing a 2.02-dB reduction in average intensity [[pan_biophysics_1:61]]. Deep learning approaches have also been applied to enhance image quality; for instance, real-time noise reduction based on ground truth-free deep learning has been implemented in systems with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm and a system sensitivity of 92 dB [[pan_biophysics_1:62]]. Similarly, SNR-Net OCT effectively enhances the signal-to-noise ratio in deep tissue regions, facilitating the observation of microstructures after brightening [[pan_biophysics_1:63]]. Technical refinements such as numerical compensation of residual dispersion using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction are also employed to improve imaging fidelity [[pan_biophysics_1:64]].

Alternative methods aim to isolate multiple scattering to reveal deeper volume information; for example, spatially depolarized dynamic speckle techniques remove the large contribution of first-order scattering detected by conventional laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI) to reveal multiple scattering occurring in deeper layers [[pan_biophysics_1:65]]. The choice of wavelength also impacts performance, with in vivo imaging in the near-infrared range (700–900 nm) being superior to the visible spectrum due to low scattering, diminished tissue autofluorescence, and relatively high tissue penetration [[pan_biophysics_1:66]]. Experimental validation of these methods often relies on tissue-mimicking phantoms, such as glass-based phantoms where scattering levels representative of human tissue are induced through controlled crystallization [[pan_biophysics_1:67]]. Agar-based phantoms with varying thicknesses have been used to analyze the depth limitation of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) systems, helping to identify the maximal depth of disease tissue that can be diagnosed [[pan_biophysics_1:68]]. Multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms, which include bulk tissue components, also serve as platforms for evaluating these imaging strategies [[pan_biophysics_1:69]].

In turbid samples, the changing light path length amplifies the effect on static intensity [3]. However, in contrast to static experiments, a variation of the light path length in turbid samples has no effect on the decay time, affecting only the intercept [3]. To address these issues, various methods have been developed to suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering. CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques can be used to efficiently suppress these effects [2][1]. One such approach introduces a charge-coupled device (CCD) camera-based detection scheme in dynamic light scattering that provides information on the single-scattered autocorrelation function even for fairly turbid samples [1][2]. In this scheme, a separation comparable to the size of a single-scattering speckle, approximately 30 pixels, serves as a good compromise value for separating single from multiple scattering [1]. For the most turbid samples, with a scattering coefficient of approximately 5.92 cm⁻¹, a noticeable difference is observed due to the loss of the single-scattering signal and an unavoidable increase in error [1]. Structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI) offers another method for suppression, where the suppression of diffuse light performs equally well regardless of whether photons propagate along the incident direction or towards the camera [4]. Increasing the frequency of the incident modulation can improve the sensitivity of the diffuse light filtering capabilities [4]. Studies on elastic scattering and fluorescence have conclusively shown the advantages of SLIPI for imaging within moderately turbid media when probing different particle concentrations and diameters [4]. The optical properties of the media, which influence scattering behavior, are often modeled using phantoms. In glass-based imaging phantoms, the average crystal size has a dominating effect on the reduced scattering coefficient . For the assessment of optical reproducibility, samples with high scattering and absorption are selected as representative for variation in optical properties . In agar-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, intralipid concentration measurements show increased reduced scattering coefficients with an increase in intralipid concentration . Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) relies on the principle that multiple scattering (MS) photons are rejected by a confocal pinhole, such as a single-mode fiber tip, allowing single-scattering (SS) photons to govern the imaging process [0]. This rejection is effective because an MS photon travels a longer optical path than SS photons, causing it to appear at a deeper location in the image than its actual scattering depth [0]. The axial resolution of OCT, which is inversely proportional to the light bandwidth, determines the depth resolution of the system . In spectral domain OCT, the choice of spectral window size creates a trade-off where a narrower window provides good spectral resolution but poor spatial resolution, while a longer window improves spatial resolution in the z-direction at the cost of spectral resolution . For instance, an average axial resolution of 2.7 μm in air has been achieved at depths up to 2 mm . However, even with high resolution, OCT faces difficulties visualizing cellular structures due to a lack of scattering contrast . The confocal parameter, which defines the depth of focus, is limited; for example, at a 1 μm focus diameter, the confocal parameter is only 17 μm . To address artifacts and noise, methods such as CLEAN are performed in the spatial image domain to iteratively recover the original image . Additionally, dispersion compensation techniques using time-frequency analysis and iterative optimization have been applied to spectral domain OCT . In some implementations, a ground glass moving diffuser is utilized to reduce speckle, an effect that can also be achieved by other means such as a spatial light modulator . Confocal microscopy provides optical sectioning through the use of an entrance slit or pinhole, which allows for the tracking of membrane protein motion at the apical cell surface . This technique is also employed in Raman spectroscopy, where a laser confocal microscope is used to measure fluorescence intensity with 532 nm excitation light . The ability to isolate specific depths is crucial for suppressing background signals from out-of-focus regions. Structured Laser Illumination Planar Imaging (SLIPI) offers an alternative approach to suppressing multiple scattering in scattering and fluorescing media [4]. In this method, multiple scattering events that lead to only small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [4]. Consequently, the local undisturbed amplitude of the modulation serves as a measure of the amount of directly scattered light [4]. The filtering capabilities of SLIPI are independent of the spatial distribution of the diffuse light being detected [4]. The suppression efficiency, denoted as $\varepsilon_{supp}$, is calculated using the formula $\varepsilon_{s u p p}={\frac{I_{C}-I_{S}}{I_{C}}}$ [4]. CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques can efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering [2][1]. In dynamic light scattering based on a digital camera detection scheme, binning leads to partial suppression of multiple scattering by averaging out small speckles [1][2]. This approach utilizes the statistical properties of the scattered light to mitigate the impact of multiple scattering events. Polarization-sensitive OCT is another technique where multiple scattering in turbid tissue limits imaging depth and contrast if not accounted for in the model formulation . To address this, polarization-insensitive OCT based on partly depolarized light has been developed, where $I_{H}$ represents the signal intensity from the horizontal polarization state . Furthermore, advanced methods such as smart OCT have been proposed, which modulate the pupil using a spatial light modulator (SLM) and a pre-defined reflection matrix to enhance image quality [0]. In the context of signal processing and noise reduction, the contrast of the OCT signal is often characterized by the coefficient of variation, defined as $C = \frac {\sigma}{\mu}$ . Real-time noise reduction can be achieved using ground truth free deep learning for OCT, with imaging depths reaching 6.7 mm . Speckle analysis methods, such as those based on autocorrelation, have been applied to OCT signals, with whole milk (3% fat) used as a scattering media for flow studies . The surface in OCT images is typically defined at the top-most depth where the derivative is larger than a predefined threshold [0]. Wavefront shaping and adaptive optics (AO) are employed to correct for scattering-induced aberrations, with AO specifically noted to provide a lateral resolution of 2 microns, a considerable improvement from the approximately 15-micron lateral resolution of standard optical coherence tomography (OCT) . These systems utilize wavefront correcting components and computational controller software to compensate for aberrations and quality degradation, thereby increasing the quality of OCT images . However, the application of these modalities is limited by the requirement for expensive wavefront manipulation devices, such as a spatial light modulator (SLM) or deformable mirror [0]. Furthermore, state-of-the-art research instruments that incorporate this technology currently employ reduced fields-of-view to keep total imaging times feasible, a limitation that needs to be overcome before they become widely applicable . In the context of dispersion correction, which is critical for maintaining image quality in scattering media, methods often rely on the complex conjugate of the dispersive spectral phase . Typically, it is sufficient to compensate for second and third-order dispersion using a phase correction term , while other approaches involve numerically compensating residual dispersion using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction . The phase stability required for these corrections is only necessary within a single frame [0]. Alternative methods for suppressing multiple scattering effects include CCD-camera-based light scattering, which can efficiently suppress undesirable effects [2][1]. In dynamic light scattering based on a digital camera detection scheme, binning leads to partial suppression of multiple scattering by averaging out small speckles [1][2]. Structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI) extracts images from three phase-shifted images, where the spatial phase is shifted by 120 degrees [4]. The suppression efficiency in such methods is defined by the ratio of the difference between the clear and scattered intensities to the clear intensity [4]. However, multiple scattering events that lead to small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [4]. The contribution of multiple scattering depends on particle size, the scattering process involved, and the surrounding media, which makes correction approaches extremely challenging [4]. While wavefront manipulation is a primary method, other techniques such as alignment and normalization schemes allow for measurements on an absolute scale even for samples exhibiting strong multiple scattering [3]. Deep learning approaches, such as SNR-Net, enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of OCT images in deep tissue regions, facilitating the observation of microstructures after brightening . These deep learning models may utilize adaptive learning rate optimization algorithms, such as Adam, as the training optimizer . Real-time noise reduction based on ground truth free deep learning for OCT has been demonstrated with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm and a system sensitivity of 92 dB . As an optical method, the applicability of these techniques is limited to imaging of superficial locations in tissues and other objects . In OCT angiography, specific approaches have the added benefit of removing projection artifacts, since axial resolution can also be improved . Computational reconstruction methods address the limitations imposed by multiple scattering, which is known to limit polarization imaging depth and contrast when not considered in the model formulation . In optical coherence tomography (OCT), multiple scattering specifically limits the observation depth , and consequently, multiple scattering events that lead to small changes in photon trajectory cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [4]. To mitigate these effects, CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques have been utilized to efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering [2][1]. One such computational approach involves multi-focus averaging (MFA) for multiple scattering suppression in OCT, where the difference in the number of scattering particles observed between B-MFA and MFA images is attributed to the difference in 1-D and 2-D computational refocusing [0]. However, B-MFA necessitates lateral oversampling due to its utilization of computational refocusing, which may limit the field size [0]. The computational framework for such refocusing relies on the 1-D Fourier transform and its inverse Fourier transform along the fast-scan direction [0]. In the context of inverse problems, the inverse adding-doubling (IAD) method enables the measurement of optical properties of tissue-mimicking phantoms, such as those fabricated from agar . These phantoms are evaluated using technical setups that include a 4-inch integrating sphere with three ports . For spectral domain OCT, dispersion encoding and subsequent reconstruction of a full-range signal is an attractive technique, although it requires more than double the computational effort compared to other methods . The reconstruction process in OCT can be explicitly written using the inverse Fourier transform of the intensity signal, which relates to the reflection coefficients and path lengths . In dynamic light scattering, the inverse relationship between flow and decorrelation time is observed, where decorrelation values are lower for previously studied flows . Deep learning and machine learning approaches have also been applied to computational reconstruction and noise reduction. The entrance of machine learning and deep learning models in data analysis has contributed to overcoming some of the method’s limits . For instance, real-time noise reduction based on ground truth free deep learning for OCT has been implemented with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm and a scanning interval frequency of 70 kHz . Another deep learning model, SNR-Net OCT, is used to brighten and denoise low-light OCT images, trained with a learning rate of $1\times 10^{-4}$ and a batch size of 1 . In the field of dielectric metasurfaces, machine learning has shown the capability for inverse designs of metasurfaces with assigned optical properties . Quantitative metrics are employed to assess the suppression of multiple scattering and image quality. The suppression efficiency is defined by the ratio of the difference between the contrast and signal intensities to the contrast intensity [4]. In the analysis of structured laser illumination, specific parameters such as the total x-distance in millimeters are defined to characterize the imaging geometry [4]. Image quality in OCT is often evaluated using the contrast-to-noise ratio, expressed as the ratio of standard deviation to mean , or through specific formulas involving the detector diameter and gamma . Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technique based on light scattering that is subject to these multiple scattering challenges . CCD-camera-based light scattering techniques have been demonstrated to efficiently suppress the undesirable effects of multiple scattering in both static and dynamic contexts [2][1]. In dynamic light scattering, this suppression is achieved through binning, which leads to partial mitigation by averaging out small speckles [1][2]. Furthermore, alignment and normalization schemes associated with these methods allow for measurements on an absolute scale, even for samples exhibiting strong multiple scattering [3]. However, the changes in static scattering intensities are primarily attributed to variations in the detected scattering vector, necessitating corrections such as multiplying static intensities by the sine of the scattering angle to account for changes in the size of the scattering volume [3]. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) faces specific limitations where multiple scattering in turbid tissue restricts imaging depth and contrast if not explicitly considered in the model formulation . As an optical method, the applicability of such techniques is inherently limited to imaging superficial locations in tissues and other objects . In the context of structured laser illumination planar imaging (SLIPI), multiple scattering events that result in only small changes to photon trajectories cannot be differentiated from directly scattered light [4]. The contribution of these events depends on particle size, the specific scattering process, and the surrounding media, which makes correction approaches extremely challenging [4]. This fundamental limitation of SLIPI is difficult, if not impossible, to correct for because it may require prior knowledge of the size distribution of the probed sample [4]. Additionally, the suppression capability in such systems is bounded by unavoidable camera noise, with a measured limit of approximately 0.3% correlating well with this noise floor [4]. In optical coherence tomography (OCT), multiple scattering (MS) photons possess a longer optical path than single scattering (SS) photons, causing photons that undergo multiple scattering at a specific depth to appear at a deeper location in the image [0]. Multi-focus averaging (SFA) has been proposed to address this, although it results in lower intensity compared to single acquisition, specifically showing a 2.02-dB reduction in average intensity [0]. Deep learning approaches have also been applied to enhance image quality; for instance, real-time noise reduction based on ground truth-free deep learning has been implemented in systems with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm and a system sensitivity of 92 dB . Similarly, SNR-Net OCT effectively enhances the signal-to-noise ratio in deep tissue regions, facilitating the observation of microstructures after brightening . Technical refinements such as numerical compensation of residual dispersion using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction are also employed to improve imaging fidelity . Alternative methods aim to isolate multiple scattering to reveal deeper volume information; for example, spatially depolarized dynamic speckle techniques remove the large contribution of first-order scattering detected by conventional laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI) to reveal multiple scattering occurring in deeper layers . The choice of wavelength also impacts performance, with in vivo imaging in the near-infrared range (700–900 nm) being superior to the visible spectrum due to low scattering, diminished tissue autofluorescence, and relatively high tissue penetration . Experimental validation of these methods often relies on tissue-mimicking phantoms, such as glass-based phantoms where scattering levels representative of human tissue are induced through controlled crystallization . Agar-based phantoms with varying thicknesses have been used to analyze the depth limitation of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) systems, helping to identify the maximal depth of disease tissue that can be diagnosed . Multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms, which include bulk tissue components, also serve as platforms for evaluating these imaging strategies .

question: Find papers discussing phantom fabrication for bio tissues for imaging
raw_answer:
Bio-tissue phantoms are defined as fabricated structures designed to mimic the physical and optical properties of biological tissues for the evaluation of imaging systems [[pan_biophysics_2:0]][[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. These phantoms serve to validate imaging measurements by providing a stable medium that reflects tissue characteristics more closely than free-diffusion models [[pan_biophysics_2:2]]. The primary materials used in their fabrication include agar, gelatin, glass, epoxy, and silicone-based compounds, each selected to replicate specific tissue attributes such as stiffness, scattering, or structural complexity [[pan_biophysics_2:0]][[pan_biophysics_2:3]][[pan_biophysics_2:4]][[pan_biophysics_2:1]][[pan_biophysics_2:5]].

Agar is a common base material for optical phantoms, where the concentration of the powder directly determines the stiffness of the resulting phantom [[pan_biophysics_2:0]]. By adjusting the agar concentration, researchers can match the mechanical properties of target tissues [[pan_biophysics_2:0]]. Similarly, gelatin solutions are prepared by mixing specific amounts of gelatin powder with de-ionized water to create tissue-mimicking matrices [[pan_biophysics_2:3]]. Water-based phantoms, such as those utilizing agar or gelatin, are noted for their low cost and simple fabrication procedures [[pan_biophysics_2:4]].

For applications requiring specific optical properties, glass-based phantoms have been developed to model the optical characteristics of human tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:4]]. In these glass matrices, scattering levels representative of human tissue are induced through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [[pan_biophysics_2:4]]. The reproducibility of such glass-based phantoms is assessed by measuring attenuation across multiple samples with identical material compositions and fabrication processes [[pan_biophysics_2:4]].

Epoxy is utilized as a reference material in the fabrication of optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, particularly for mimicking pigmentation skin lesions [[pan_biophysics_2:5]]. The use of epoxy helps minimize air bubbles that are often created during the fabrication of thick samples [[pan_biophysics_2:5]]. Specific tissue layers, such as the dermis, can be fabricated using petri dish molding techniques with defined optical parameters [[pan_biophysics_2:5]].

Silicone-based materials, such as Dragon Skin, are employed in multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms to allow for the representation of a wide range of diseased tissue states [[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. The flexibility of these materials and techniques enables the modeling of conditions ranging from benign inflammation to high-grade cancerous lesions [[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. Fast-curing variants of these materials are selected to avoid sagging when applied to non-planar surfaces [[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. These phantoms can incorporate bulk tissue properties using specific pigments, such as blue UV invisible pigment [[pan_biophysics_2:1]].

Existing phantom fabrication techniques and materials have limited capabilities in simultaneously recreating the arbitrary 3D shape of organs, replicating multi-layered tissue structures in 3D, and incorporating multi-stage disease-mimicking regions [[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. Some novel materials have yet to be utilized for phantom fabrication, indicating ongoing development in this field [[pan_biophysics_2:1]]. Biomimetic tumor tissue phantoms have been shown to be stable over periods of up to 10 months, supporting their use in longitudinal validation studies [[pan_biophysics_2:2]]. In the context of image-guided surgery, ex-vivo tests on meningioma samples have demonstrated the feasibility of certain imaging techniques, complementing the use of fabricated phantoms [[pan_biophysics_2:6]].

To model the optical properties of human tissue, researchers have employed various fabrication techniques, including the use of glass matrices and biological emulsions. In one approach, scattering levels representative of human tissue were induced in a glass matrix through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [[pan_biophysics_2:7]]. This glass-based phantom development included reproducibility assessments where attenuation was measured on five samples with the same material composition and fabrication process [[pan_biophysics_2:7]]. The fabrication of a specific high-scattering sample was repeated five times over different days to ensure consistency [[pan_biophysics_2:7]]. For the assessment of optical reproducibility, a sample with high scattering and absorption was selected as the representative for variation in optical properties [[pan_biophysics_2:7]]. The homogeneity of these glass samples was demonstrated by measuring attenuation at five different locations on each of four glass samples [[pan_biophysics_2:7]].

Alternative methodologies utilize agar-based phantoms where specific agents are added to adjust optical features. Intralipid 20% emulsion and Nigrosin were used to adjust the scattering and absorption features of the phantom, respectively [[pan_biophysics_2:8]]. The feasibility of creating such tissue phantoms with varying optical properties was demonstrated, and the Integrated Absorption Difference (IAD) was proved to be versatile in estimating the optical properties of the phantom [[pan_biophysics_2:8]]. Another study fabricated an optical tissue phantom (OTP) mimicking pigmentation skin lesions using epoxy as a reference material, which minimizes air bubbles created during the fabrication of thick samples [[pan_biophysics_2:9]]. Measurements of the optical properties of epoxy and silicone OTPs demonstrated that measured absorption and reduced scattering coefficients were close to the expected values, within 10% [[pan_biophysics_2:9]]. To ensure accuracy, five measurement points were randomly selected per sample during characterization [[pan_biophysics_2:9]].

Multimodal phantoms have also been developed to mimic complex tissue structures, such as cancer. A multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantom utilized bulk tissue components, including blue UV invisible pigment [[pan_biophysics_2:10]]. In this study, the researchers chose to limit their scope to scattering and visual appearance [[pan_biophysics_2:10]]. The attenuation coefficients of this phantom exactly matched the average value previously reported for bladder tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:10]]. However, limitations in earlier works included constraints in the range of possible optical properties needed to mimic various layers of epithelial tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:10]]. Furthermore, an OTP that mimics skin layers has not yet been achieved owing to the intricate optical properties of skin, which are dependent upon the wavelength and the structural inhomogeneity [[pan_biophysics_2:9]].

Regarding acoustic and diffusion properties, a biomimetic tumor tissue phantom was constructed to validate diffusion-weighted MRI measurements [[pan_biophysics_2:11]]. This phantom was designed as a simple mimic of tumor cellular structure, building on a preliminary report of an earlier phantom design [[pan_biophysics_2:11]]. The use of a $128 \times 128$ matrix was noted in the context of this biomimetic tumor tissue phantom [[pan_biophysics_2:11]]. The results indicated that the phantom more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms [[pan_biophysics_2:11]]. While specific acoustic property matching for tissue phantoms is less detailed in the provided excerpts, general acoustic principles involve the velocity of sound, such as $c_{0} = 343 \, m/s$ in air [[pan_biophysics_2:12]]. In non-Hermitian systems, dissipation is numerically modeled by a complex sound velocity, $c = (1 + i\gamma) \times 343$ m/s [[pan_biophysics_2:13]]. Other acoustic phenomena, such as the short wavelength of sound allowing for denser mode spacing than in the purely electromagnetic case [[pan_biophysics_2:14]], and the compactness of acoustic resonators due to the difference between the speeds of sound and light [[pan_biophysics_2:15]], provide context for acoustic wave behavior, though these specific excerpts focus on phononic and electromagnetic comparisons rather than direct tissue phantom fabrication.

Existing phantom fabrication techniques face significant limitations in simultaneously recreating the arbitrary three-dimensional shapes of organs, replicating multi-layered tissue structures, and incorporating multi-stage disease-mimicking regions [[pan_biophysics_2:16]]. To address these challenges, researchers have employed various methods including 3D printing, layering, and embedding to create phantoms with complex anatomical structures or heterogeneous inclusions. One approach utilizes 3D printing to generate molds that mimic complex biological structures, such as vessel networks, which allows for the technical evaluation of optical systems under conditions that resemble actual biological tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:17]]. When combined with 3D printer technology, the applicability of agar-based phantom fabrication protocols can significantly increase [[pan_biophysics_2:17]]. In the context of liver phantoms, 3D printing has been used to create structures where patient and phantom images exhibit similar textures [[pan_biophysics_2:18]]. However, most 3D-printed medical phantoms, even those with patient-specific and tissue-mimicking features, remain only anatomically—and not physiologically—close to human organ structures [[pan_biophysics_2:18]]. Bioprinting technologies offer precise control over the initial cell distribution within the printed construct [[pan_biophysics_2:18]]. Furthermore, the emerging technology of 3D printing fused silica glass enables the development of glass-based phantoms with complex and high-resolution structures [[pan_biophysics_2:19]].

For phantoms requiring specific material properties or non-planar geometries, alternative fabrication methods are employed. In the creation of a multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantom, the fastest-curing Dragon Skin material was selected to avoid sagging while applying it to non-planar surfaces [[pan_biophysics_2:16]]. This phantom incorporated bulk tissue using blue UV invisible pigment from GloMania USA [[pan_biophysics_2:16]]. The fabrication process for this specific phantom also involved the use of a Badger air compressor (model AS180-12) [[pan_biophysics_2:16]]. For optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, epoxy was used as a reference material to fabricate models mimicking pigmentation skin lesions, a choice made to minimize air bubbles created during the fabrication of thick samples [[pan_biophysics_2:20]]. The suitability of reference materials for optical tissue phantom fabrication is qualitatively evaluated by comparing the quality of the resulting models [[pan_biophysics_2:20]]. In glass-based imaging phantoms, the fabrication of specific samples, such as Sample #10, was repeated five times over different days to assess consistency [[pan_biophysics_2:19]].

The construction of phantoms with heterogeneous inclusions often involves specific mechanical and chemical steps to ensure structural integrity and repeatability. A biomimetic tumor tissue phantom designed as a simple mimic of tumor cellular structure was constructed by building on a preliminary report of an earlier phantom design [[pan_biophysics_2:21]]. The construction process for this phantom was found to be repeatable, as evidenced by the similarity in post-immersion $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ values for two phantoms, indicating that samples with comparable sphere sizes can be generated [[pan_biophysics_2:21]]. The phantom utilized a $128 \times 128$ matrix for its design [[pan_biophysics_2:21]], and the volume fraction of inclusions, denoted as $f_i$, was constrained within the range $0.01 \leq f_i \leq 1$ [[pan_biophysics_2:21]]. For magnetic resonance-based magnetic susceptibility imaging, a spherical inclusion phantom was fabricated to allow for more repeatable construction compared to previous phantoms that were mostly cylindrical or elliptical and often utilized elastic bags [[pan_biophysics_2:22]]. The fabrication of this spherical inclusion phantom involved plugging the top hole with hot glue [[pan_biophysics_2:22]], and the phantom was placed inside the coil on a roll of masking tape used as a stand [[pan_biophysics_2:22]].

Characterization of these fabricated phantoms involves specific measurement protocols to validate their optical and structural properties. In the fabrication of agar-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, a protocol for performing computations using the inverse adding-doubling (IAD) method is presented to enable the measurement of the optical properties of the created phantoms [[pan_biophysics_2:17]]. For optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, five measurement points were randomly selected per sample to ensure comprehensive characterization [[pan_biophysics_2:20]].

Empirical validation of tissue-mimicking phantoms across various imaging modalities reveals distinct performance characteristics and limitations regarding their ability to replicate in-vivo data. In the context of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI), a biomimetic tumor tissue phantom was evaluated using a $128 \times 128$ matrix [[pan_biophysics_2:23]]. This phantom demonstrated that it more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms [[pan_biophysics_2:23]]. However, a full validation of the volume fraction for phantom A was precluded by the lack of a ground truth volume fraction [[pan_biophysics_2:23]]. The structural robustness of these phantoms has not been fully evaluated, although initial experience suggests they can be successfully transported between sites without obvious degradation [[pan_biophysics_2:23]]. Long-term stability assessments indicate that the phantom can be used for at least 10 months, though further longitudinal analysis is required to track longer-term stability [[pan_biophysics_2:23]]. The use of such biomimetic phantoms in multi-center studies could enable a more comprehensive validation of DW-MRI, facilitating the comparison of ADC time-dependence and microstructural estimates between scanners [[pan_biophysics_2:23]].

For magnetic susceptibility imaging, a spherical inclusion phantom with a 10 cm diameter was fabricated inside a thin acrylic shell to validate magnetic resonance-based measurements [[pan_biophysics_2:24]]. The theoretical basis for this validation relies on the proton Larmor frequency $\omega_{0} = \gamma B_{0}$, where $\gamma$ is the gyromagnetic ratio [[pan_biophysics_2:24]]. A key limitation of these experiments was that the temperature was not controlled [[pan_biophysics_2:24]]. Despite this, the proposed phantom appears well-suited for cross-sectional comparative studies [[pan_biophysics_2:24]].

In optical imaging, reproducibility and stability are critical metrics for phantom performance. A glass-based imaging phantom was developed to model the optical properties of human tissue, with scattering levels induced through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [[pan_biophysics_2:25]]. The high homogeneity, reproducibility, and long-term stability of these glass samples demonstrate their excellent suitability for use in tissue-mimicking phantoms [[pan_biophysics_2:25]]. Reproducibility was assessed by measuring the attenuation on five samples (#10a - #10e) that shared the same material composition and fabrication process [[pan_biophysics_2:25]]. To ensure consistency, the fabrication of Sample #10 was repeated five times over different days [[pan_biophysics_2:25]]. In contrast, water-based phantoms offer advantages in terms of low cost and simple fabrication procedures [[pan_biophysics_2:25]]. For phantoms containing macrostructure, such as those mimicking pigmentation skin lesions, epoxy was used as a reference material to minimize air bubbles created during the fabrication of thick samples [[pan_biophysics_2:26]]. Measurement protocols for these optical phantoms involved selecting five measurement points randomly per sample [[pan_biophysics_2:26]]. Agar-based tissue-mimicking phantoms have also been employed to assess the imaging depth limitation of hyperspectral imaging systems [[pan_biophysics_2:27]]. Multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms have been developed to address the limitation that most tissue-mimicking phantoms simulate only flat regions of healthy tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:28]]. These multimodal phantoms incorporate bulk tissue components, such as blue UV invisible pigment from GloMania USA [[pan_biophysics_2:28]].

Regarding computed tomography (CT), 3D-printed functional structures have been utilized to create phantoms with heterogeneous backgrounds and realistic pathology similar to real tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:29]]. CT images of a brain phantom showed that the CT number differences of objects of interest were similar to those in patient images [[pan_biophysics_2:29]]. These phantoms could potentially be used for image-quality assessment, radiation dose reduction, and other research and educational activities [[pan_biophysics_2:29]]. While nanoparticles are noted to be superior to conventional imaging equipment such as CT, X-ray, and MRI in terms of imaging positioning [[pan_biophysics_2:30]], the provided evidence does not contain specific empirical findings comparing nanoparticle-based phantoms to in-vivo data for these modalities.

Long-term stability remains a significant challenge for water-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, which, despite their advantages of low cost and simple fabrication, suffer from evaporation over time that limits their suitability for long-term experiments [[pan_biophysics_2:31]][[pan_biophysics_2:32]]. This instability is particularly pronounced in phantoms with high water content, which can experience short-term stability issues if inappropriately stored [[pan_biophysics_2:31]]. In contrast, non-water-based phantoms offer the advantage of long-term stability without significant changes in their properties, although they involve a more complex manufacturing process [[pan_biophysics_2:32]]. For instance, glass-based imaging phantoms have been developed to model the optical properties of human tissue, with their long-term stability examined through accelerated-aging experiments measuring attenuation on multiple samples [[pan_biophysics_2:31]]. The glass matrix in these phantoms is often doped with specific ions, such as nickel, to approximate the absorption of hemoglobin [[pan_biophysics_2:31]].

Material degradation presents another critical limitation, particularly for polymer-based phantoms. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) is known to degrade over time, with many factors influencing the degradation process, which is expected to eventually render the phantom unstable and limit its use as a long-term test object [[pan_biophysics_2:33]]. While one study suggests that a specific biomimetic tumor tissue phantom can be used for at least 10 months, it notes that further longitudinal analysis is required to track longer-term stability [[pan_biophysics_2:33]]. Similarly, in the context of lipid nanoparticle formulations, existing publications often lack information on the stability of lyophilized formulations over time [[pan_biophysics_2:34]].

Temperature sensitivity further complicates the use of these phantoms for consistent imaging validation. For example, in magnetic resonance-based magnetic susceptibility imaging, the phantom temperature should be taken as $11.4 \pm 3$ °C to ensure accurate validation [[pan_biophysics_2:35]]. In other contexts, such as phonon heat transfer studies, frequency shifts correspond to temperature changes of less than 0.02 K, highlighting the precision required in temperature control based on measured frequency–temperature dependence [[pan_biophysics_2:36]].

A major gap exists between the properties of current phantoms and actual biological variability, as most tissue-mimicking phantoms simulate flat regions of healthy tissue rather than complex pathological structures [[pan_biophysics_2:37]]. Earlier works have been limited in the range of possible optical properties needed to mimic various layers of epithelial tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:37]]. Furthermore, an optical tissue phantom that mimics skin layers has not yet been achieved owing to the intricate optical properties of skin, which are dependent upon the wavelength and the structural inhomogeneity [[pan_biophysics_2:38]]. While some phantoms feature heterogeneous backgrounds and realistic pathology similar to real tissue, potentially useful for image-quality assessment and radiation dose reduction, the general challenge of replicating biological complexity remains [[pan_biophysics_2:39]].

To address these variability and stability issues, researchers have explored alternative materials and fabrication methods. Latex, commonly used for some tissue-mimicking phantoms, has sufficient elasticity but is highly absorbing, and its optical properties cannot be tuned to mimic the optical properties of tissue [[pan_biophysics_2:37]]. Consequently, multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms have been developed, though some studies chose to limit their scope to scattering and visual appearance [[pan_biophysics_2:37]][[pan_biophysics_2:38]]. The fabrication of these complex structures often requires specific curing times, such as the use of a slower curing Dragon Skin (30-minute cure time) for layers beneath vessels [[pan_biophysics_2:37]]. In agar-based phantoms, the feasibility of creating phantoms with varying optical properties has been demonstrated, and the IAD method has been proved to be versatile to estimate these properties [[pan_biophysics_2:32]]. However, the assessment of optical reproducibility remains a focus, with specific samples selected to represent variation in optical properties [[pan_biophysics_2:31]]. Measurement protocols often involve selecting multiple points randomly per sample to account for heterogeneity [[pan_biophysics_2:38]]. While some phantoms more closely reflect diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms, as shown by multi-G, multi-Δ data described by microstructural models, the challenge of maintaining stable, biologically representative properties over time persists [[pan_biophysics_2:33]].
answer_official_all: Bio-tissue phantoms are defined as fabricated structures designed to mimic the physical and optical properties of biological tissues for the evaluation of imaging systems [6][4]. These phantoms serve to validate imaging measurements by providing a stable medium that reflects tissue characteristics more closely than free-diffusion models [5]. The primary materials used in their fabrication include agar, gelatin, glass, epoxy, and silicone-based compounds, each selected to replicate specific tissue attributes such as stiffness, scattering, or structural complexity [6][2][3][4][1]. Agar is a common base material for optical phantoms, where the concentration of the powder directly determines the stiffness of the resulting phantom [6]. By adjusting the agar concentration, researchers can match the mechanical properties of target tissues [6]. Similarly, gelatin solutions are prepared by mixing specific amounts of gelatin powder with de-ionized water to create tissue-mimicking matrices [2]. Water-based phantoms, such as those utilizing agar or gelatin, are noted for their low cost and simple fabrication procedures [3]. For applications requiring specific optical properties, glass-based phantoms have been developed to model the optical characteristics of human tissue [3]. In these glass matrices, scattering levels representative of human tissue are induced through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [3]. The reproducibility of such glass-based phantoms is assessed by measuring attenuation across multiple samples with identical material compositions and fabrication processes [3]. Epoxy is utilized as a reference material in the fabrication of optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, particularly for mimicking pigmentation skin lesions [1]. The use of epoxy helps minimize air bubbles that are often created during the fabrication of thick samples [1]. Specific tissue layers, such as the dermis, can be fabricated using petri dish molding techniques with defined optical parameters [1]. Silicone-based materials, such as Dragon Skin, are employed in multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantoms to allow for the representation of a wide range of diseased tissue states [4]. The flexibility of these materials and techniques enables the modeling of conditions ranging from benign inflammation to high-grade cancerous lesions [4]. Fast-curing variants of these materials are selected to avoid sagging when applied to non-planar surfaces [4]. These phantoms can incorporate bulk tissue properties using specific pigments, such as blue UV invisible pigment [4]. Existing phantom fabrication techniques and materials have limited capabilities in simultaneously recreating the arbitrary 3D shape of organs, replicating multi-layered tissue structures in 3D, and incorporating multi-stage disease-mimicking regions [4]. Some novel materials have yet to be utilized for phantom fabrication, indicating ongoing development in this field [4]. Biomimetic tumor tissue phantoms have been shown to be stable over periods of up to 10 months, supporting their use in longitudinal validation studies [5]. In the context of image-guided surgery, ex-vivo tests on meningioma samples have demonstrated the feasibility of certain imaging techniques, complementing the use of fabricated phantoms . To model the optical properties of human tissue, researchers have employed various fabrication techniques, including the use of glass matrices and biological emulsions. In one approach, scattering levels representative of human tissue were induced in a glass matrix through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [3]. This glass-based phantom development included reproducibility assessments where attenuation was measured on five samples with the same material composition and fabrication process [3]. The fabrication of a specific high-scattering sample was repeated five times over different days to ensure consistency [3]. For the assessment of optical reproducibility, a sample with high scattering and absorption was selected as the representative for variation in optical properties [3]. The homogeneity of these glass samples was demonstrated by measuring attenuation at five different locations on each of four glass samples [3]. Alternative methodologies utilize agar-based phantoms where specific agents are added to adjust optical features. Intralipid 20% emulsion and Nigrosin were used to adjust the scattering and absorption features of the phantom, respectively [6]. The feasibility of creating such tissue phantoms with varying optical properties was demonstrated, and the Integrated Absorption Difference (IAD) was proved to be versatile in estimating the optical properties of the phantom [6]. Another study fabricated an optical tissue phantom (OTP) mimicking pigmentation skin lesions using epoxy as a reference material, which minimizes air bubbles created during the fabrication of thick samples [1]. Measurements of the optical properties of epoxy and silicone OTPs demonstrated that measured absorption and reduced scattering coefficients were close to the expected values, within 10% [1]. To ensure accuracy, five measurement points were randomly selected per sample during characterization [1]. Multimodal phantoms have also been developed to mimic complex tissue structures, such as cancer. A multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantom utilized bulk tissue components, including blue UV invisible pigment [4]. In this study, the researchers chose to limit their scope to scattering and visual appearance [4]. The attenuation coefficients of this phantom exactly matched the average value previously reported for bladder tissue [4]. However, limitations in earlier works included constraints in the range of possible optical properties needed to mimic various layers of epithelial tissue [4]. Furthermore, an OTP that mimics skin layers has not yet been achieved owing to the intricate optical properties of skin, which are dependent upon the wavelength and the structural inhomogeneity [1]. Regarding acoustic and diffusion properties, a biomimetic tumor tissue phantom was constructed to validate diffusion-weighted MRI measurements [5]. This phantom was designed as a simple mimic of tumor cellular structure, building on a preliminary report of an earlier phantom design [5]. The use of a $128 \times 128$ matrix was noted in the context of this biomimetic tumor tissue phantom [5]. The results indicated that the phantom more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms [5]. While specific acoustic property matching for tissue phantoms is less detailed in the provided excerpts, general acoustic principles involve the velocity of sound, such as $c_{0} = 343 \, m/s$ in air . In non-Hermitian systems, dissipation is numerically modeled by a complex sound velocity, $c = (1 + i\gamma) \times 343$ m/s . Other acoustic phenomena, such as the short wavelength of sound allowing for denser mode spacing than in the purely electromagnetic case , and the compactness of acoustic resonators due to the difference between the speeds of sound and light , provide context for acoustic wave behavior, though these specific excerpts focus on phononic and electromagnetic comparisons rather than direct tissue phantom fabrication. Existing phantom fabrication techniques face significant limitations in simultaneously recreating the arbitrary three-dimensional shapes of organs, replicating multi-layered tissue structures, and incorporating multi-stage disease-mimicking regions [4]. To address these challenges, researchers have employed various methods including 3D printing, layering, and embedding to create phantoms with complex anatomical structures or heterogeneous inclusions. One approach utilizes 3D printing to generate molds that mimic complex biological structures, such as vessel networks, which allows for the technical evaluation of optical systems under conditions that resemble actual biological tissue [6]. When combined with 3D printer technology, the applicability of agar-based phantom fabrication protocols can significantly increase [6]. In the context of liver phantoms, 3D printing has been used to create structures where patient and phantom images exhibit similar textures [0]. However, most 3D-printed medical phantoms, even those with patient-specific and tissue-mimicking features, remain only anatomically—and not physiologically—close to human organ structures [0]. Bioprinting technologies offer precise control over the initial cell distribution within the printed construct [0]. Furthermore, the emerging technology of 3D printing fused silica glass enables the development of glass-based phantoms with complex and high-resolution structures [3]. For phantoms requiring specific material properties or non-planar geometries, alternative fabrication methods are employed. In the creation of a multimodal 3D cancer-mimicking optical phantom, the fastest-curing Dragon Skin material was selected to avoid sagging while applying it to non-planar surfaces [4]. This phantom incorporated bulk tissue using blue UV invisible pigment from GloMania USA [4]. The fabrication process for this specific phantom also involved the use of a Badger air compressor (model AS180-12) [4]. For optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, epoxy was used as a reference material to fabricate models mimicking pigmentation skin lesions, a choice made to minimize air bubbles created during the fabrication of thick samples [1]. The suitability of reference materials for optical tissue phantom fabrication is qualitatively evaluated by comparing the quality of the resulting models [1]. In glass-based imaging phantoms, the fabrication of specific samples, such as Sample #10, was repeated five times over different days to assess consistency [3]. The construction of phantoms with heterogeneous inclusions often involves specific mechanical and chemical steps to ensure structural integrity and repeatability. A biomimetic tumor tissue phantom designed as a simple mimic of tumor cellular structure was constructed by building on a preliminary report of an earlier phantom design [5]. The construction process for this phantom was found to be repeatable, as evidenced by the similarity in post-immersion $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ values for two phantoms, indicating that samples with comparable sphere sizes can be generated [5]. The phantom utilized a $128 \times 128$ matrix for its design [5], and the volume fraction of inclusions, denoted as $f_i$, was constrained within the range $0.01 \leq f_i \leq 1$ [5]. For magnetic resonance-based magnetic susceptibility imaging, a spherical inclusion phantom was fabricated to allow for more repeatable construction compared to previous phantoms that were mostly cylindrical or elliptical and often utilized elastic bags [2]. The fabrication of this spherical inclusion phantom involved plugging the top hole with hot glue [2], and the phantom was placed inside the coil on a roll of masking tape used as a stand [2]. Characterization of these fabricated phantoms involves specific measurement protocols to validate their optical and structural properties. In the fabrication of agar-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, a protocol for performing computations using the inverse adding-doubling (IAD) method is presented to enable the measurement of the optical properties of the created phantoms [6]. For optical tissue phantoms containing macrostructure, five measurement points were randomly selected per sample to ensure comprehensive characterization [1]. Empirical validation of tissue-mimicking phantoms across various imaging modalities reveals distinct performance characteristics and limitations regarding their ability to replicate in-vivo data. In the context of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI), a biomimetic tumor tissue phantom was evaluated using a $128 \times 128$ matrix [5]. This phantom demonstrated that it more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms [5]. However, a full validation of the volume fraction for phantom A was precluded by the lack of a ground truth volume fraction [5]. The structural robustness of these phantoms has not been fully evaluated, although initial experience suggests they can be successfully transported between sites without obvious degradation [5]. Long-term stability assessments indicate that the phantom can be used for at least 10 months, though further longitudinal analysis is required to track longer-term stability [5]. The use of such biomimetic phantoms in multi-center studies could enable a more comprehensive validation of DW-MRI, facilitating the comparison of ADC time-dependence and microstructural estimates between scanners [5]. For magnetic susceptibility imaging, a spherical inclusion phantom with a 10 cm diameter was fabricated inside a thin acrylic shell to validate magnetic resonance-based measurements [2]. The theoretical basis for this validation relies on the proton Larmor frequency $\omega_{0} = \gamma B_{0}$, where $\gamma$ is the gyromagnetic ratio [2]. A key limitation of these experiments was that the temperature was not controlled [2]. Despite this, the proposed phantom appears well-suited for cross-sectional comparative studies [2]. In optical imaging, reproducibility and stability are critical metrics for phantom performance. A glass-based imaging phantom was developed to model the optical properties of human tissue, with scattering levels induced through controlled crystallization at elevated temperatures [3]. The high homogeneity, reproducibility, and long-term stability of these glass samples demonstrate their excellent suitability for use in tissue-mimicking phantoms [3]. Reproducibility was assessed by measuring the attenuation on five samples (#10a - #10e) that shared the same material composition and fabrication process [3]. To ensure consistency, the fabrication of Sample #10 was repeated five times over different days [3]. In contrast, water-based phantoms offer advantages in terms of low cost and simple fabrication procedures [3]. CT images of a brain phantom showed that the CT number differences of objects of interest were similar to those in patient images [0]. These phantoms could potentially be used for image-quality assessment, radiation dose reduction, and other research and educational activities [0]. While nanoparticles are noted to be superior to conventional imaging equipment such as CT, X-ray, and MRI in terms of imaging positioning , the provided evidence does not contain specific empirical findings comparing nanoparticle-based phantoms to in-vivo data for these modalities. Long-term stability remains a significant challenge for water-based tissue-mimicking phantoms, which, despite their advantages of low cost and simple fabrication, suffer from evaporation over time that limits their suitability for long-term experiments [3][6]. This instability is particularly pronounced in phantoms with high water content, which can experience short-term stability issues if inappropriately stored [3].
