The genome of these cells is more stable than that of cancer cells, which could provide a promising mean to reduce the possibility of mutation induced drug resistance [[pan_biophysics_6:48]]. Nevertheless, physical therapy based on the physical characteristics of nanoparticles tends to be more effective against the tumor stem cells [[pan_biophysics_6:41]].

Overcoming cancer drug resistance requires addressing specific biological mechanisms, including the presence of tumor subpopulations and stromal influences. A small subpopulation of tumor cells possessing stem-like features, such as self-renewal, is often associated with higher therapeutic resistance and tumor relapse [[pan_biophysics_6:49]]. Identifying and eliminating these small populations of cancer cells is considered a significant aid in eliminating drug resistance [[pan_biophysics_6:50]]. Furthermore, tumor stromal factors can promote resistance of cancer cells to therapies, ultimately resulting in deadly diseases such as pancreatic ductal carcinoma (PDAC) [[pan_biophysics_6:51]]. Tumor autophagy is also highly related to the generation of drug resistance, as it can selectively reduce the expression of MHC-I molecules to escape recognition by T cells [[pan_biophysics_6:52]].

Combination therapies are frequently proposed as a primary strategy to manage resistant cancers. The combination therapy is described as the best option for drug-resisted types of cancers [[pan_biophysics_6:50]]. In a mouse model of pancreatic cancer, the combination therapy using cligentide, verapamil, and gemcitabine enhanced survival due to a reduced tumor burden [[pan_biophysics_6:51]]. High-throughput transcript profiling using L1000 can uncover relatively subtle mechanisms of drug sensitivity and resistance based on a comparison of transcriptional and phenotypic responses [[pan_biophysics_6:53]]. In specific cell lines like BT-20, drugs within an equivalence class can substitute for each other in a combination, such as using lapatinib or neratinib for trametinib in a combination that includes alpelisib [[pan_biophysics_6:53]]. When drugs are used in combination, they can elicit a qualitative shift from growth rate reduction to cell death, evidenced by negative growth rate values over a wide range of drug concentrations [[pan_biophysics_6:53]]. However, combination approaches are not without risk; a higher rate of severe fatal toxicity was observed in patients receiving combination therapy without significant clinical benefit response [[pan_biophysics_6:54]]. Additionally, single photothermal therapy (PTT) is easy to induce tumor adaptive resistance, highlighting the need for combined modalities [[pan_biophysics_6:52]].

Targeted inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent another avenue for overcoming resistance, though they face specific challenges. The common payloads used in ADCs, such as MMAE, MMAF, and calicheamicin, can be exported outside cancer cells by ABC transporters, which makes these ADCs show drug resistance [[pan_biophysics_6:54]]. Conversely, the genome of certain targeted cells is more stable than that of cancer cells, which could provide a promising mean to reduce the possibility of mutation-induced drug resistance [[pan_biophysics_6:54]]. The average response time of patients to ADC treatment was 6.7 months [[pan_biophysics_6:54]]. To ensure effective treatments are targeted towards patients who will gain the most benefit, the use of predictive biomarkers or screening tools other than time-intensive immunohistochemistry (IHC) methods will be essential [[pan_biophysics_6:55]].

Predictive biomarkers and computational models are increasingly utilized to personalize medicine and predict drug responses. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) could increase the efficacy of tumors to chemotherapy agents or avoid cancer drug resistance [[pan_biophysics_6:50]]. These small molecules could also serve as a biomarker for prognosis and survival in response to chemotherapy [[pan_biophysics_6:50]]. The combination of chemotherapy agents with RNAi strategies, such as siRNA or miRNA, might be a potential therapy in resisted tumoral cells [[pan_biophysics_6:50]]. In the context of liquid biopsy, the expression of carcinoembryonic antigen and telomerase reverse transcriptase in circulating tumor cells (CTCs) predicted an unfavorable response to nivolumab [[pan_biophysics_6:56]]. Specific ABC transporters, such as ABCB1 encoding P-glycoprotein and ABCG2 identified in mitoxantrone-resistant cells, function to keep cancer stem cells away from chemotherapeutic agents [0]. This efflux activity is not limited to traditional chemotherapies; common payloads used in antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), such as MMAE, MMAF, and calicheamicin, can also be exported outside cancer cells by ABC transporters, leading to drug resistance . The role of P-glycoprotein, also referred to as multidrug resistance associated membrane protein, is further highlighted in the context of the blood-brain barrier, where it transports drugs back into the blood via ATP-dependent efflux pumps . Similarly, in neuro-oncology, the upregulation of efflux pumps removes many larger therapeutic agents from the tumor, even when tight junction loss allows for greater paracellular diffusion of small compounds . The interaction between drug delivery systems and these transporters is significant; for instance, the polarity of spacers in ADC linkers alters the interaction with permeability glycoprotein (Pgp), a major cause of multi-drug resistance in tumor cells . While the mechanism of drug resistance for ADCs is linked to these transporters, it has not been sufficiently characterized, and clinical evidence to confirm these specific mechanisms remains limited . Beyond efflux mechanisms, resistance is driven by genetic mutations that alter drug targets or signaling pathways. For example, the M351 mutation causes weak resistance to imatinib, necessitating an increase in the drug dose to maintain efficacy [0]. This concept of pathway addiction is further illustrated by MDA-MB-231 cells, which carry a KRAS mutation and exhibit high sensitivity to trametinib, implying a reliance on the RAS-MAPK pathway [1]. Cellular heterogeneity and the tumor microenvironment also play critical roles in drug resistance. A small subpopulation of tumor cells possessing stem-like features, including self-renewal, is often associated with higher therapeutic resistance and tumor relapse . plan.title: Mechanisms of Drug Resistance
plan.goal: Define the primary biological mechanisms by which cancer cells evade the effects of anti-cancer drugs, including efflux pumps, target mutation, and metabolic adaptation.
queries: cancer drug resistance mechanisms review
multidrug resistance efflux pumps ABC transporters
target mutation bypass signaling pathways

plan.title: Genomic and Epigenomic Adaptations
plan.goal: Examine how genetic mutations and epigenetic modifications drive the evolution of resistant cell populations under therapeutic pressure.
queries: genomic evolution cancer therapy resistance
epigenetic plasticity tumor adaptation
clonal selection chemotherapy resistance

plan.title: Role of the Tumor Microenvironment
plan.goal: Analyze how stromal cells, immune interactions, and hypoxic conditions within the tumor microenvironment facilitate drug tolerance and survival.
queries: tumor microenvironment drug resistance
hypoxia induced chemoresistance

question: What are major new advanced findings(novelty ) from polarization-sensitive Optical coherence tomography from traditional OCT
raw_answer:
Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is defined as a versatile functional extension of standard OCT technology [[pan_biophysics_7:0]]. This functional extension allows for the extraction of polarization information, where the sample Jones matrix is calculated by dividing the measured Jones matrix by the inverse of the surface Jones matrix [[pan_biophysics_7:0]]. While standard OCT systems often rely on intensity-based detection, PS-OCT requires specific hardware modifications to preserve and measure the polarization state of light, although only few modifications to the standard OCT layout are necessary to achieve this sensitivity [[pan_biophysics_7:0]].

The physical challenge in implementing PS-OCT arises from the fact that OCT systems employing single-mode optical fibers experience considerable variation in the polarization state of the optical signal due to stretching and bending of the fiber [[pan_biophysics_7:1]]. To address this instability, polarization-maintaining (PM) fibers are frequently utilized to overcome such challenges, although their use can introduce artifacts such as polarization crosstalk in the images [[pan_biophysics_7:1]]. In many fiber-based PS-OCT setups, the laser light is initially polarized, and the optical fiber is fixed to prevent changes in the polarization state [[pan_biophysics_7:2]]. Alternatively, another technique minimizes changes in the polarization state of the incident light beam by using a common-path interferometer in conjunction with polarization-maintaining fibers to promote stability of the optical fiber [[pan_biophysics_7:2]].

System architectures for PS-OCT vary between free-space and fiber-optic implementations. Most implementations were done using free-space optics, however, fiber optic prototypes have also been reported based on polarization-maintaining (PM) fiber optics and regular single-mode fibers [[pan_biophysics_7:0]]. For example, a specific setup for imaging depth-resolved collagen organizations utilized a single input configuration with an axial resolution of $7.5\mu \mathrm{m}$ in air [[pan_biophysics_7:3]]. In contrast, other OCT configurations, such as those used for choroidal and retinal disorders, may rely on incoherent illumination and a Linnik interferometer with two microscope objectives in the reference and sample arms [[pan_biophysics_7:2]]. Standard spectral-domain OCT systems, which may serve as a baseline for comparison, often utilize a Michelson interferometer built around a 50/50 fiber coupler made of single-mode optical fiber [[pan_biophysics_7:4]].

Signal detection and noise management are critical components of these architectures. In dual-balanced detection systems, two phase-opposed interferometric spectra are captured simultaneously using two lines of a three-line CCD, sharing identical spectrometer optics, which differs from dual spectrometer OCT systems [[pan_biophysics_7:5]]. The sensitivity of such systems, defined as the measure of the minimum sample signal detectable, has been measured at $105\mathrm{dB}$ at zero optical path difference in polarization-insensitive schemes using partly depolarized light [[pan_biophysics_7:1]]. Other systems report a sensitivity of 92 dB [[pan_biophysics_7:6]]. To mitigate artifacts, such as polarization artifacts in in vivo imaging, techniques like multi-focus averaging (B-MFA) may be employed [[pan_biophysics_7:7]]. Experimental validation of B-MFA-based dynamic OCT is considered a promising avenue for future research [[pan_biophysics_7:7]].

Performance metrics in these advanced systems include high A-line rates, with one system achieving 50,000 A-lines/s [[pan_biophysics_7:7]]. Resolution capabilities vary across different setups; for instance, an OCT setup in tissue measured axial and lateral resolutions of $9.88\mu \mathrm{m}$ and $11.35\mu \mathrm{m}$, respectively [[pan_biophysics_7:8]]. Adaptations of PS-OCT include polarization-sensitive quantitative OCT (PS-QOCT) [[pan_biophysics_7:2]]. Despite these advancements, no available method has been formulated with objective knowledge of the collagen fiber organizations [[pan_biophysics_7:3]]. Furthermore, while PM fibers are used to stabilize polarization, they introduce crosstalk, and standard single-mode fibers suffer from polarization drift, highlighting the ongoing trade-offs in hardware design [[pan_biophysics_7:1]].

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) distinguishes itself from traditional OCT by analyzing the polarization state of backscattered light to measure birefringence within tissue samples [[pan_biophysics_7:9]]. By taking into account the vector nature of the electric field, PS-OCT is capable of detecting the birefringent properties of the sample, which are inaccessible to standard intensity-based measurements [[pan_biophysics_7:10]]. Jones matrix PS-OCT specifically enables the measurement of phase retardation, diattenuation, local birefringence, and local optic axis orientation [[pan_biophysics_7:11]]. While diattenuation in biological tissue is usually very weak and is often assumed negligible for PS-OCT applications, the technology remains capable of quantifying it [[pan_biophysics_7:11]].

The extraction of depolarization metrics provides a particularly useful contrast for assessing the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), especially in clinical cases where pathological eyes make it difficult to distinguish ocular structures [[pan_biophysics_7:11]]. PS-OCT measures and quantifies the polarization and depolarization of tissue to achieve precision, high-quality imaging of retinal pigment epithelium layers [[pan_biophysics_7:9]]. Because the strength of depolarization is proportional to the concentration of polarization scrambling scatterers, depolarization measures such as Degree of Polarization Uniformity (DOPU) can enable a quantitative assessment of melanin concentration in ocular tissues [[pan_biophysics_7:11]].

Birefringence serves as a key diagnostic parameter in various tissue types, as fibrotic tissues containing collagen are particularly birefringent and are thus imaged well by PS-OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:9]]. In vascular applications, the birefringence of vessel walls is a promising diagnostic parameter for arteriosclerotic vascular disease that is accessible by PS-OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:11]]. Furthermore, processes such as demineralization lead to birefringence changes which can be observed by PS-OCT, allowing for the monitoring of structural alterations [[pan_biophysics_7:11]].

Despite the utility of these parameters, standard OCT measurement noise can degrade the quantitative measurement capability of functional OCT, such as polarization sensitive OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:12]]. Techniques like multi-focus averaging have been developed to mitigate this issue; while standard OCT measurement noise may be mitigated in single-focus averaging images due to complex averaging, both measurement noise and multiple scattering signals are mitigated in multi-focus averaging and balanced multi-focus averaging images [[pan_biophysics_7:12]]. Additionally, polarization-dependent image artifacts are common in optical coherence tomography imaging, highlighting the need for careful signal processing [[pan_biophysics_7:13]].

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) represents a functional extension of standard OCT that requires only few modifications to the standard OCT layout to achieve polarization sensitivity [[pan_biophysics_7:14]]. By taking into account the vector nature of the electric field, PS-OCT can detect the birefringent properties of the sample, enabling imaging with enhanced contrast compared to standard OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:15]][[pan_biophysics_7:14]]. The polarimetric approach utilizes Stokes vectors, which, unlike Jones vectors, enable the characterization of light depolarization [[pan_biophysics_7:14]]. The retardation induced by birefringent tissue is related to the angle of rotation of Stokes vectors on the Poincaré sphere [[pan_biophysics_7:14]]. Adaptations of PS-OCT include polarization-sensitive quantitative OCT (PS-QOCT), which measures and quantifies the polarization and depolarization of tissue for precision, high-quality imaging of retinal pigment epithelium layers [[pan_biophysics_7:16]].

Novel computational and hardware techniques have been developed to address polarization-induced artifacts and improve imaging resolution. Polarization-dependent image artifacts are common in optical coherence tomography imaging, often arising from polarization mismatch between the sample and reference beams [[pan_biophysics_7:17]][[pan_biophysics_7:15]]. In particular, OCT systems that employ single-mode optical fibers experience considerable variation in the polarization state of the optical signal arising from stretching and bending of the optical fiber [[pan_biophysics_7:17]]. To mitigate these issues, multi-focus averaging (MFA) has been applied to suppress multiple scattering, and polarization-sensitive B-MFA may mitigate the polarization artifact in in vivo imaging [[pan_biophysics_7:18]]. However, multiple scattering degrades the quantitative measurement capability of functional OCT, such as polarization sensitive OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:18]]. A specific advancement involves a depth-resolved birefringent imaging approach based on the DDG-based PST method, which enables depth-resolved birefringent imaging that only requires one single input polarization state [[pan_biophysics_7:19]]. This single-input approach achieves an axial resolution of $7.5\mu \mathrm{m}$ in air [[pan_biophysics_7:19]].

Signal processing algorithms further refine the extraction of polarization data and flow information. In polarization-insensitive OCT based on partly depolarized light, $I_{H}$ is defined as the signal intensity from the horizontal polarization state [[pan_biophysics_7:17]]. For angiographic applications, PR-OCTA algorithms are based on the observation that reflectance-normalized signal in projection artifacts is smaller than that of true in situ flow in overlying voxels in the same axial line [[pan_biophysics_7:20]]. Speckle analysis methods, such as those based on autocorrelation, calculate the W vector over 1024 consecutive points in time to distinguish between different flow rates through autocorrelation vector analysis [[pan_biophysics_7:21]]. However, the analysis of OCT speckle is currently lacking in validation and information on its reproducibility in vivo, with several reviewed analyses performed only in a theoretical context or using phantoms, indicating that signal-carrying speckle analysis in OCT imaging is still in its early stage [[pan_biophysics_7:22]]. Additionally, noise bias correction is identified as an important processing step in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analyses, especially when averaging weak signals [[pan_biophysics_7:23]]. Dispersion compensation for spectral domain OCT can be achieved through time-frequency analysis and iterative optimization, where the dispersion compensation vector is found to be depth-independent and, once obtained, can compensate for any other measurements [[pan_biophysics_7:24]].

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) distinguishes itself from traditional OCT by analyzing the polarization state of backscattered light to measure birefringence within tissue samples [[pan_biophysics_7:25]]. This capability allows PS-OCT to provide additional contrast for discerning, segmenting, and quantifying ocular structures that exhibit birefringence or depolarization [[pan_biophysics_7:26]]. In the context of glaucoma and retinal disorders, nerve fibers exhibit birefringence, an optical property exploited for quantitative measurements in the retinal nerve fiber layer [[pan_biophysics_7:26]]. PS-OCT measures and quantifies the polarization and depolarization of tissue to achieve precision, high-quality imaging of retinal pigment epithelium layers [[pan_biophysics_7:25]]. The eye features a variety of tissues exhibiting these properties, which enable PS-OCT to resolve structural details that traditional methods may not capture with the same specificity [[pan_biophysics_7:26]].

In preclinical and broader clinical applications, fibrotic tissues containing collagen are particularly birefringent and are thus imaged well by PS-OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:25]]. While traditional PS-OCT provides only accumulated polarization information along depth because back-scattered light must pass through tissue twice before detection, newer adaptations such as polarization-sensitive quantitative OCT (PS-QOCT) have been developed to address imaging needs [[pan_biophysics_7:27]][[pan_biophysics_7:25]]. Recent advancements have achieved an axial resolution of $7.5\mu \mathrm{m}$ in air, facilitating the imaging of depth-resolved collagen organizations [[pan_biophysics_7:27]]. The vector nature of the electric field allows PS-OCT to detect the birefringent properties of the sample, offering insights into tissue microstructure [[pan_biophysics_7:28]].

PS-OCT has shown promising results in cancer imaging, with studies reporting successful applications in the larynx, ovaries, and bladder [[pan_biophysics_7:26]]. Several groups have also successfully studied PS-OCT for imaging breast cancer [[pan_biophysics_7:26]]. These applications leverage the ability of PS-OCT to detect birefringent properties, which can differentiate pathological tissues from healthy ones [[pan_biophysics_7:28]]. However, the implementation of PS-OCT requires only few modifications to the standard OCT layout for polarization sensitivity [[pan_biophysics_7:26]]. Despite these advantages, the interferometric signal of OCT is subjected to polarization-induced artifacts due to polarization mismatch between the sample and reference beams [[pan_biophysics_7:28]]. Polarization-dependent image artifacts are common in optical coherence tomography imaging, which can complicate interpretation [[pan_biophysics_7:29]]. Furthermore, multiple scattering degrades the quantitative measurement capability of functional OCT, such as polarization-sensitive OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:30]].

To mitigate these challenges, signal processing techniques are employed; for instance, in signal-to-noise ratio enhanced spectral domain OCT, the variable gain amplifier (VGA) was rotated by 1.35 degrees to optimize detection [[pan_biophysics_7:31]]. Retinal OCT images may span a dynamic range of 40 dB, with hyperscattering structures such as the nerve fiber layer and the pigment epithelium serving as landmarks for phasor alignment [[pan_biophysics_7:32]]. The signal intensity from the horizontal polarization state, denoted as $I_{H}$, is a fundamental component in polarization-insensitive OCT based on partly depolarized light, highlighting the importance of polarization state analysis [[pan_biophysics_7:29]]. While nanoparticles can be engineered to selectively target cancer cells and create new perspectives for tumor diagnosis, PS-OCT provides a distinct, label-free structural and polarization-based diagnostic modality [[pan_biophysics_7:33]][[pan_biophysics_7:34]]. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) also provides sensitive detection of cancer biomarkers, but PS-OCT offers complementary structural imaging capabilities through its analysis of tissue birefringence [[pan_biophysics_7:35]].

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) requires only few modifications to the standard OCT layout to achieve polarization sensitivity [[pan_biophysics_7:36]]. However, the interferometric signal in OCT is subjected to polarization-induced artifacts due to polarization mismatch between the sample and reference beams [[pan_biophysics_7:37]]. These polarization-dependent image artifacts are common in optical coherence tomography imaging [[pan_biophysics_7:38]]. To overcome such challenges, polarization maintaining (PM) fibers could be used; however, such fibers introduce artifacts such as polarization crosstalk in the images [[pan_biophysics_7:38]]. Additionally, coherent artifacts in OCT images can severely degrade image quality by introducing false targets if no targets are present at the artifact locations [[pan_biophysics_7:39]].

A significant limitation of traditional PS-OCT is that it provides only accumulated polarization information along depth because back-scattered light must pass through tissue twice before detection [[pan_biophysics_7:40]]. This accumulation effect, combined with multiple scattering, degrades the quantitative measurement capability of functional OCT, such as polarization sensitive OCT [[pan_biophysics_7:41]]. To address these issues, adaptations of PS-OCT include polarization-sensitive quantitative OCT (PS-QOCT) [[pan_biophysics_7:42]]. PS-QOCT measures and quantifies the polarization and depolarization of tissue for precision, high-quality imaging of retinal pigment epithelium layers [[pan_biophysics_7:42]]. In specific implementations, $I_{H}$ represents the signal intensity from the horizontal polarization state [[pan_biophysics_7:38]].

Technical challenges also arise from dispersion and motion. Ocular pulsation or drift are sources of bulk motion that affect imaging [[pan_biophysics_7:43]]. Dispersion compensation is critical for image quality; if the optimized order is $a = 1$, the OCT A-scan is dispersion free [[pan_biophysics_7:44]]. Coarse dispersion compensation can be done physically by inserting two BK7 microscope slides into the reference arm [[pan_biophysics_7:44]]. Alternatively, software dispersion compensation tends to be a favored solution since it is low-cost, provides continuous tunability, and can be easily applied to other OCT platforms [[pan_biophysics_7:45]]. This software approach utilizes a dispersion compensation term $\Delta \Phi^{OPT}(k)$, which is an N-pixel vector stored locally and used for future dispersion compensation during routine OCT image reconstruction [[pan_biophysics_7:45]].

Emerging trends in PS-OCT research involve the integration of machine learning and multi-modal approaches. Recent developments on machine learning, namely convolutional neural networks, have reported outperforming results in OCT image analysis in comparison to conventional image processing [[pan_biophysics_7:46]]. For instance, SNR-Net OCT uses a deep learning approach to brighten and denoise low-light optical coherence tomography images, implemented with a Tensorflow (v2.5.0) backend and a batch size of 1 for training [[pan_biophysics_7:47]]. Future research may focus on integrating physics and learning-based approaches to combine their strengths [[pan_biophysics_7:46]].

question: How dynamic signal can be detected from OCT speckle
raw_answer:
In Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), speckle patterns serve a dual role, acting simultaneously as a source of noise that degrades signal quality and as a carrier of information known as signal-carrying speckle [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. The physical mechanism underlying dynamic speckle involves temporal fluctuations in the interference signal caused by moving scatterers, such as red blood cells, within the sample [[pan_biophysics_8:1]][[pan_biophysics_8:2]]. These intensity fluctuations occur because the moving scatterers alter the interference pattern over time, creating a time-varying speckle field [[pan_biophysics_8:1]]. The temporal variation of the OCT signal is primarily driven by the motion of these red blood cells, a principle utilized in techniques like OCT angiography (OCTA) [[pan_biophysics_8:2]].

The relationship between the motion of scatterers and the resulting signal fluctuations is quantitatively described through the concept of decorrelation time. Decorrelation time is defined as the time it takes for the autocorrelation value of the signal to fall to 1/e of its initial value [[pan_biophysics_8:1]]. Analysis based on autocorrelation demonstrates that the intensity fluctuations in time-varying speckle are inversely proportional to flow velocity [[pan_biophysics_8:1]]. Consequently, greater velocities of the scatterers result in lower decorrelation times [[pan_biophysics_8:1]]. This inverse relationship has been experimentally confirmed in studies using milk pumped through microchannels at different velocities, which proved that decorrelation time is inversely proportional to flow velocity [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. For flow rates greater than 1 $\mu$l/min, it is possible to associate the decorrelation time directly with flow velocity [[pan_biophysics_8:1]].

The physical parameters influencing speckle decorrelation include the concentration and size of the particles, as well as velocity field inhomogeneities [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. In tissues that contain both static and flowing scatterers, such as capillaries, the amplitude of the OCT signal can be modeled using the Rician distribution [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. This distinction is critical for separating dynamic signals from static backgrounds, as static scatterers contribute to a stable background while moving scatterers induce the temporal changes necessary for flow detection [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. Speckle variance OCT, for instance, is sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam by measuring the intensity speckle change in the OCT signal [[pan_biophysics_8:2]]. Similarly, the Laser Speckle Optical Coherence Imaging (LSOCI) technique bases its signal on the decorrelation time of the speckle intensity distribution to translate the movements of red blood cells [[pan_biophysics_8:2]].

To enhance the detection of these dynamic signals, various processing methods are employed to manage noise and artifacts. In OCT angiography, the split-spectrum approach calculates the OCT spectrum across multiple sub-bands, where the decorrelation in each sub-band is averaged to form the final decorrelation value, thereby increasing the signal-to-noise ratio [[pan_biophysics_8:3]]. This averaging process helps distinguish true flow signals from noise, as noise is maximally decorrelated and can register large decorrelation values in low-signal regions [[pan_biophysics_8:3]]. Correlation and decorrelation approaches are less likely to misdetect flow in hyperreflective material, improving the specificity of the dynamic signal detection [[pan_biophysics_8:3]]. Additionally, bulk motion contributions can be estimated by considering the statistics of the measured flow signal across all voxels, allowing for the separation of bulk movement from local flow dynamics [[pan_biophysics_8:3]].

The temporal resolution of the OCT system is a critical factor in capturing these dynamic changes. A moving diffuser must be operated at a velocity sufficient to create decorrelated speckle patterns within the acquisition time of a given A-scan; for example, a system with an A-scan rate of approximately 20 kHz requires specific diffuser velocities to ensure decorrelation [[pan_biophysics_8:4]]. If the diffuser moves too fast, it can induce multiple phase changes during the acquisition time, resulting in OCT fringe washout and a decrease in signal intensity [[pan_biophysics_8:4]]. Conversely, speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) can acquire an unlimited number of uncorrelated speckle patterns to effectively remove speckle noise without degrading image resolution [[pan_biophysics_8:4]]. This technique has been demonstrated to produce practically speckle-free high-resolution three-dimensional volumes of turbid media and living tissue [[pan_biophysics_8:4]].

Other methods for analyzing dynamic speckle include quantitative temporal speckle contrast imaging, which depends on the speckle size in the image and the number of images in a sequence [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. Laser speckle flowgraphy is another technique that can be used for ocular blood flow determination, relying on similar principles of speckle dynamics [[pan_biophysics_8:0]]. In experimental phantoms, the total laser speckle contrast index has been shown to be proportional to the speed of blood flow, demonstrating the ability of such phantoms to simulate simple blood circulation [[pan_biophysics_8:5]]. While these methods provide robust measures of flow, they must account for artifacts such as those caused by multiple scattering, where images of scatterers not in a particular B-scan smear into the scan, causing an artifactual increase in the number of scatterers [[pan_biophysics_8:6]]. Furthermore, the use of algorithms like CLEAN has been reported to reduce speckle noise caused by the interference of nonresolvable scatterers in highly scattering tissue [[pan_biophysics_8:7]].

The detection of dynamic signals in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) relies on the dual nature of speckle, which serves both as a source of signal-degrading noise and as a carrier of information [[pan_biophysics_8:8]]. To isolate the dynamic component from static tissue, specific data acquisition parameters must be established to ensure that the temporal resolution is sufficient for the phenomena under investigation. For instance, an effective B-scan rate of 46 Hz has been utilized in scanning microscopic OCT for dynamic contrast analysis [[pan_biophysics_8:9]], while other systems have achieved rates of 108 Hz with total recording times of 1.39 seconds [[pan_biophysics_8:9]]. In spectral domain OCT, a frame rate of 58 frames per second is achievable with 500 consecutive spectra spanning a 3 mm lateral distance [[pan_biophysics_8:10]]. The A-scan repetition rate is a critical determinant of system capability; rates of 16 kHz have been reported when using both backward and forward wavelength scans [[pan_biophysics_8:11]], and 83 kHz A-scan rates have been achieved with 3.6 μm axial resolution [[pan_biophysics_8:12]]. Furthermore, line rates of 76 kHz [[pan_biophysics_8:13]] and maximum acquisition rates of 70 kHz from cameras with 2048 pixels and 12-bit resolution [[pan_biophysics_8:14]] illustrate the high-speed capabilities of modern detectors. However, the temporal resolution of the system becomes a limiting factor at higher flow rates; for example, an 8 kHz sampling rate is unsuitable for high flow regimens, and at 50 μl/min, the acquisition rate is no longer appropriate [[pan_biophysics_8:15]]. Conversely, an acquisition rate of 2.5 kHz is considered sufficient for specific flow regimens as it falls within the range of frequencies properly sampled by the system [[pan_biophysics_8:15]].

Preprocessing strategies are essential to remove static background components and enhance the visibility of dynamic changes. Background subtraction is a common technique where the background signal stored before imaging is subtracted from the acquired data, which greatly attenuates most noise terms, although they are not entirely eliminated [[pan_biophysics_8:10]]. Signal averaging is another method used to improve signal-to-noise ratio; for example, 11 sequential images at the same location may be taken to obtain an averaged image to remove speckle noise [[pan_biophysics_8:16]]. However, averaging techniques such as multi-focus averaging (B-MFA) require the sequential acquisition of a few frames followed by complex averaging, which reduces the effective frame rate and can wash out not only multiple scattering signal components but also dynamic signal components [[pan_biophysics_8:17]]. Speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) offers an alternative by acquiring an unlimited number of uncorrelated speckle patterns to effectively remove speckle noise without degrading image resolution [[pan_biophysics_8:18]]. This technique outperforms other speckle reduction methods by yielding images with uncompromised structural detail, whereas other methods often smooth fine features during noise suppression [[pan_biophysics_8:18]]. In SM-OCT, the movement of the diffuser must be carefully controlled; moving it too fast can induce multiple phase changes during the acquisition time of a given A-scan, resulting in OCT fringe washout and a decrease in signal intensity [[pan_biophysics_8:18]]. To mitigate this, it may be beneficial to synchronize the movement of the diffuser so that it moves only between frame or A-scan acquisitions [[pan_biophysics_8:18]].

Dispersion correction is also a necessary preprocessing step to ensure accurate signal interpretation. In fractional Fourier domain approaches, if the optimized order is $a = 1$, the OCT A-scan is dispersion free [[pan_biophysics_8:14]][[pan_biophysics_8:19]]. While deep learning approaches like SNR-Net can effectively suppress speckle noise and enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of low-light OCT images while retaining detailed information [[pan_biophysics_8:20]], making structures like capillary vessels in the dermis clearer [[pan_biophysics_8:20]], it is important to recognize that speckle noises inherent to OCT images caused by microstructures should be considered inherent structural signals rather than random noises [[pan_biophysics_8:21]]. This distinction is crucial because speckle patterns of static samples do not change between frames [[pan_biophysics_8:21]], implying that dynamic detection relies on the variation of these patterns over time.

The detection of dynamic signals in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) relies on analyzing the temporal variation of the OCT signal, which is caused mainly by moving red blood cells [[pan_biophysics_8:22]]. Among the primary algorithms for quantifying these signals, Speckle Variance OCT (SV-OCT) is a method capable of mapping flow inside a sample by measuring the intensity speckle change in the OCT signal [[pan_biophysics_8:23]][[pan_biophysics_8:22]]. This technique is specifically sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam [[pan_biophysics_8:22]]. In contrast, Doppler OCT combines Doppler velocimetry with OCT to image both blood flow dynamics and tissue structure, providing quantitative information regarding internal flow, including flow velocity and direction [[pan_biophysics_8:22]][[pan_biophysics_8:23]].

The sensitivity of these methods to flow velocity varies based on their underlying statistical or spectral principles. Speckle variance and difference methods exhibit a flow signal that is more strongly coupled to the magnitude of the OCT signal than decorrelation-based methods [[pan_biophysics_8:24]]. This coupling implies that correlation and decorrelation approaches are less likely to misdetect flow in hyperreflective material [[pan_biophysics_8:24]]. Experimental validation using optical tissue phantoms has confirmed that the total laser speckle contrast index is proportional to the speed of blood flow, demonstrating the ability of such phantoms to simulate simple blood circulation [[pan_biophysics_8:25]]. Furthermore, statistical properties of the OCT speckle have been used to infer the dynamic properties of blood samples, indicating that speckle-based techniques may be used to obtain quantitative information of flow in OCT samples [[pan_biophysics_8:26]][[pan_biophysics_8:23]].

Spectral analysis offers another avenue for detecting dynamic signals, where the frequency of signal fluctuations has been measured between 0 and 54 Hz in scanning microscopic OCT [[pan_biophysics_8:27]]. In related optomechanical contexts, power spectral density analysis involves fitting mechanical resonant peaks with a Lorentzian line shape to obtain mechanical Q factors [[pan_biophysics_8:28]]. However, the application of these dynamic detection methods faces challenges in specific imaging configurations. For instance, in Speckle-Modulating OCT (SM-OCT), phase and speckle variance methods encounter additional variations owing to the movement of the diffuser [[pan_biophysics_8:29]]. Additionally, while the rationale behind these techniques has been widely applied to compute OCT angiography (OCTA) from temporal OCT data acquired at the exact same position, further work is needed to validate their applicability and reproducibility in a clinical context [[pan_biophysics_8:26]]. Currently, the analysis of OCT speckle lacks sufficient validation and information on its reproducibility in-vivo [[pan_biophysics_8:26]].

Technical implementation of these detection methods requires careful handling of system artifacts and dispersion. In spectral domain OCT, residual dispersion can be numerically compensated using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction [[pan_biophysics_8:27]]. System sensitivity is a critical parameter, with one system achieving a sensitivity of approximately 110 dB and capable of imaging the eye to a depth of approximately 1.5 mm with 4.0 mW incident light power [[pan_biophysics_8:30]], while another system demonstrated a sensitivity of 89 dB for a power of 2.4 mW on the sample [[pan_biophysics_8:31]]. To ensure accurate signal detection, residual DC signals in the spectral interferogram can be removed by subtracting the moving average of the signal [[pan_biophysics_8:32]]. Specific quantitative results from autocorrelation-based speckle analysis have yielded values such as 2.8x10⁻³ and 1.8x10⁻³ for different conditions [[pan_biophysics_8:23]]. These methods operate within systems that can maintain data streaming rates of 58 fps without disruption [[pan_biophysics_8:33]].

Phase-based methods in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) offer distinct advantages over intensity-based speckle techniques by providing quantitative information regarding internal flow, including both velocity and direction [[pan_biophysics_8:34]]. Unlike intensity-based speckle variance methods, which are sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam by measuring intensity changes [[pan_biophysics_8:35]], Doppler OCT can image both blood flow dynamics and tissue structure by combining Doppler velocimetry with standard OCT imaging [[pan_biophysics_8:35]]. The fundamental principle underlying these phase-based measurements is that the phase shift of an OCT signal is proportional to $2k\Delta z$, where $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the central wavenumber and $\Delta z$ is the axial displacement between successive measurements [[pan_biophysics_8:36]]. This interferometric approach enables detection sensitivities for reflected light signals as low as $10^{-10}$ of the input, contributing to the high sensitivity required for detecting subtle dynamic signals [[pan_biophysics_8:37]].

A significant limitation of standard Doppler OCT is its lack of sensitivity to flows perpendicular to the imaging beam, which is a serious drawback for many applications [[pan_biophysics_8:34]]. In contrast, speckle variance OCT is specifically sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam [[pan_biophysics_8:35]]. To address the directional constraints and enhance flow detection, Phase Resolved Angiography (PRA) and other decorrelation-based methods have been developed. In difference and variance methods, the flow signal is more strongly coupled to the magnitude of the OCT signal than in decorrelation-based methods [[pan_biophysics_8:38]]. This coupling means that correlation-based approaches often introduce amplitude or phase cutoffs that prevent flow detection in hyporeflective regions [[pan_biophysics_8:38]]. Furthermore, re-introducing reflectance magnitude dependence into these approaches can complicate the interpretation of low-velocity flows [[pan_biophysics_8:38]].

The implementation of phase-based OCTA requires careful handling of bulk motion artifacts. Phase signals must be stabilized or compensated by correcting the bulk motion-generated phase shift before computing OCTA signals [[pan_biophysics_8:38]]. However, inclusion of phase noise in the bulk motion estimate tends to lead to underestimates of the true flow [[pan_biophysics_8:38]]. The rationale behind these phase and decorrelation techniques has been widely applied to compute OCT angiography from a set of temporal OCT data acquired at the exact same position [[pan_biophysics_8:39]]. While these methods provide superior directional and quantitative data, they face challenges when combined with speckle-modulating techniques. For instance, phase and speckle variance methods used in Doppler OCT and OCT angiography encounter additional variations owing to the movement of the diffuser in Speckle-Modulating OCT (SM-OCT) [[pan_biophysics_8:40]]. To obtain high-resolution speckle-reduced volume and angiography of the same volume in such systems, the sample must be scanned once with a moving diffuser and a second time with the diffuser either static or removed from the optical path [[pan_biophysics_8:40]].

Signal processing and filtering play critical roles in extracting dynamic signals from phase data. In one study, the measured maximum Doppler shifting frequency was $17\mathrm{kHz}$ [[pan_biophysics_8:41]]. It was found that a high-pass filter tracks the peak Doppler frequency better than a bandpass filter [[pan_biophysics_8:41]]. For low-flow detection, the analysis depends greatly on the sampling rate; however, even at an $8\mathrm{kHz}$ sampling rate, the system remains a good approach for low flows and offers a way to differentiate between flows in OCT without angle dependence and without requiring previous preparation of the sample [[pan_biophysics_8:34]]. This sampling rate makes the system appropriate for differentiating between low flow rates, up to $12\mu l / min$ [[pan_biophysics_8:39]]. In specific experimental procedures, such as those involving autocorrelation analysis, the W vector was calculated over 1024 consecutive points in time, and the procedure was repeated five times and averaged to improve signal quality [[pan_biophysics_8:34]].

Beyond flow dynamics, phase-based methods are also utilized for system calibration and artifact cancellation. Both phase-based methods, such as TSMMR and SAMMR, consider higher-order (greater than 3rd order) dispersion in the OCT system, whereas methods like TSIF only consider up to the third-order dispersion [[pan_biophysics_8:42]]. These phase-based methods could sharpen and symmetrize the Point Spread Function (PSF) [[pan_biophysics_8:42]]. In the context of beam splitting, the light reflected at the refraction plane of the beam splitter experiences a $\pi/2$ phase shift with respect to the light transmitted, a fundamental aspect of the interferometric setup [[pan_biophysics_8:43]]. While dynamic contrast images can be completely free of speckle noise and have remarkably high contrast [[pan_biophysics_8:44]], the integration of phase analysis remains essential for resolving the directional and quantitative aspects of dynamic signals that intensity-based speckle methods cannot fully capture.

The detection of dynamic signals in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is fundamentally complicated by the dual nature of speckle, which acts simultaneously as a source of signal-degrading noise and a carrier of information [[pan_biophysics_8:45]]. While speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) offers a method to acquire uncorrelated speckle patterns and remove noise without degrading resolution, this technique significantly reduces sample-arm input-light power and temporal resolution [[pan_biophysics_8:46]][[pan_biophysics_8:47]]. This reduction in input power and temporal resolution creates inherent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) constraints that limit the reliability of dynamic detection, particularly when compared to standard OCT systems that can detect reflected light signals as low as $10^{-10}$ of the input [[pan_biophysics_8:48]]. Although signal averaging can improve SNR in OCT images, the optimal approach remains an area of investigation regarding contrast-to-noise characteristics and speckle reduction efficiency [[pan_biophysics_8:49]]. Furthermore, the analysis of OCT speckle currently lacks sufficient validation and information on its reproducibility in-vivo, which further complicates the assessment of dynamic signal reliability [[pan_biophysics_8:45]].

Motion artifacts represent a significant limitation in dynamic speckle detection, as bulk motion from sources such as ocular pulsation or drift contributes to the motion contrast signal [[pan_biophysics_8:50]]. Most artifact removal approaches rely on a single test statistic, such as mean, mode, or standard deviation, to estimate this bulk motion contribution [[pan_biophysics_8:50]]. In scanning microscopic OCT, dynamic contrast images are free of speckle noise and have high contrast, but their sensitivity to bulk tissue motion artifacts is reduced by shorter acquisition times and tomographic depth-sectioning, which also simplifies post-processing correction [[pan_biophysics_8:51]]. However, certain multiple scattering suppression techniques, such as multi-focus averaging (B-MFA), are incompatible with functional OCT imaging techniques based on fast sequential acquisition, including Doppler OCT, OCT angiography, and dynamic OCT [[pan_biophysics_8:52]]. Additionally, coherent artifacts caused by the imperfect point spread function of the OCT system can be reduced using nonlinear deconvolution algorithms like CLEAN, but these represent distinct technical challenges in maintaining signal integrity [[pan_biophysics_8:53]].

The "blind spot" issue in low-flow regions is exacerbated by the specific statistical methods used for flow detection. In difference and variance methods, the flow signal is more strongly coupled to the magnitude of the OCT signal than in decorrelation-based methods [[pan_biophysics_8:50]]. Consequently, correlation-based approaches introduce amplitude or phase cutoffs that prevent flow detection in hyporeflective regions, effectively creating blind spots where dynamic signals cannot be reliably identified [[pan_biophysics_8:50]]. While speckle variance OCT is sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam by measuring intensity speckle changes, it does not provide quantitative information, which is a major drawback for the use of speckle-based techniques [[pan_biophysics_8:54]][[pan_biophysics_8:55]]. In contrast, Doppler OCT is capable of providing quantitative information regarding internal flow, including velocity and direction [[pan_biophysics_8:55]].

Sampling rate and temporal resolution further constrain the detection of low-flow dynamics. Autocorrelation-based speckle analysis depends greatly on the sampling rate, although even at 8 kHz, it remains a good approach for low flows that differentiates flow without angle dependence or sample preparation [[pan_biophysics_8:55]]. A sampling rate of 8 kHz is appropriate for differentiating between low flow rates up to $12\mu l / min$ [[pan_biophysics_8:45]]. To improve the robustness of such measurements, procedures may be repeated and averaged, as demonstrated by repeating a procedure five times and averaging the results [[pan_biophysics_8:55]]. The rationale behind these temporal analysis techniques has been widely applied to compute OCT angiography (OCTA) from temporal OCT data acquired at the exact same position [[pan_biophysics_8:45]]. Statistical properties of the OCT speckle have also been used to infer the dynamic properties of blood samples, highlighting the potential of these metrics despite the aforementioned limitations [[pan_biophysics_8:45]]. While OCT and OCTA have been used to visualize and quantify retinal microvasculature, the specific challenges of dynamic speckle detection in these contexts remain subject to the noise, motion, and low-flow constraints described above [[pan_biophysics_8:56]].

Phase-based methods in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) offer distinct advantages over intensity-based speckle techniques by providing quantitative information regarding internal flow, including both velocity and direction [4]. Unlike intensity-based speckle variance methods, which are sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam by measuring intensity changes [3], Doppler OCT can image both blood flow dynamics and tissue structure by combining Doppler velocimetry with standard OCT imaging [3]. The fundamental principle underlying these phase-based measurements is that the phase shift of an OCT signal is proportional to $2k\Delta z$, where $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the central wavenumber and $\Delta z$ is the axial displacement between successive measurements . This interferometric approach enables detection sensitivities for reflected light signals as low as $10^{-10}$ of the input, contributing to the high sensitivity required for detecting subtle dynamic signals . A significant limitation of standard Doppler OCT is its lack of sensitivity to flows perpendicular to the imaging beam, which is a serious drawback for many applications [4]. In contrast, speckle variance OCT is specifically sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam [3]. To address the directional constraints and enhance flow detection, Phase Resolved Angiography (PRA) and other decorrelation-based methods have been developed. In difference and variance methods, the flow signal is more strongly coupled to the magnitude of the OCT signal than in decorrelation-based methods . This coupling means that correlation-based approaches often introduce amplitude or phase cutoffs that prevent flow detection in hyporeflective regions . Furthermore, re-introducing reflectance magnitude dependence into these approaches can complicate the interpretation of low-velocity flows . The implementation of phase-based OCTA requires careful handling of bulk motion artifacts. Phase signals must be stabilized or compensated by correcting the bulk motion-generated phase shift before computing OCTA signals . However, inclusion of phase noise in the bulk motion estimate tends to lead to underestimates of the true flow . The rationale behind these phase and decorrelation techniques has been widely applied to compute OCT angiography from a set of temporal OCT data acquired at the exact same position [1]. While these methods provide superior directional and quantitative data, they face challenges when combined with speckle-modulating techniques. For instance, phase and speckle variance methods used in Doppler OCT and OCT angiography encounter additional variations owing to the movement of the diffuser in Speckle-Modulating OCT (SM-OCT) [2]. To obtain high-resolution speckle-reduced volume and angiography of the same volume in such systems, the sample must be scanned once with a moving diffuser and a second time with the diffuser either static or removed from the optical path [2]. Signal processing and filtering play critical roles in extracting dynamic signals from phase data. In one study, the measured maximum Doppler shifting frequency was $17\mathrm{kHz}$ . It was found that a high-pass filter tracks the peak Doppler frequency better than a bandpass filter . For low-flow detection, the analysis depends greatly on the sampling rate; however, even at an $8\mathrm{kHz}$ sampling rate, the system remains a good approach for low flows and offers a way to differentiate between flows in OCT without angle dependence and without requiring previous preparation of the sample [4]. This sampling rate makes the system appropriate for differentiating between low flow rates, up to $12\mu l / min$ [1]. In specific experimental procedures, such as those involving autocorrelation analysis, the W vector was calculated over 1024 consecutive points in time, and the procedure was repeated five times and averaged to improve signal quality [4]. Beyond flow dynamics, phase-based methods are also utilized for system calibration and artifact cancellation. Both phase-based methods, such as TSMMR and SAMMR, consider higher-order (greater than 3rd order) dispersion in the OCT system, whereas methods like TSIF only consider up to the third-order dispersion . These phase-based methods could sharpen and symmetrize the Point Spread Function (PSF) . In the context of beam splitting, the light reflected at the refraction plane of the beam splitter experiences a $\pi/2$ phase shift with respect to the light transmitted, a fundamental aspect of the interferometric setup . While dynamic contrast images can be completely free of speckle noise and have remarkably high contrast [0], the integration of phase analysis remains essential for resolving the directional and quantitative aspects of dynamic signals that intensity-based speckle methods cannot fully capture. The detection of dynamic signals in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is fundamentally complicated by the dual nature of speckle, which acts simultaneously as a source of signal-degrading noise and a carrier of information [1]. While speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) offers a method to acquire uncorrelated speckle patterns and remove noise without degrading resolution, this technique significantly reduces sample-arm input-light power and temporal resolution [2]. This reduction in input power and temporal resolution creates inherent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) constraints that limit the reliability of dynamic detection, particularly when compared to standard OCT systems that can detect reflected light signals as low as $10^{-10}$ of the input . Although signal averaging can improve SNR in OCT images, the optimal approach remains an area of investigation regarding contrast-to-noise characteristics and speckle reduction efficiency . Furthermore, the analysis of OCT speckle currently lacks sufficient validation and information on its reproducibility in-vivo, which further complicates the assessment of dynamic signal reliability [1]. Motion artifacts represent a significant limitation in dynamic speckle detection, as bulk motion from sources such as ocular pulsation or drift contributes to the motion contrast signal . Most artifact removal approaches rely on a single test statistic, such as mean, mode, or standard deviation, to estimate this bulk motion contribution . In scanning microscopic OCT, dynamic contrast images are free of speckle noise and have high contrast, but their sensitivity to bulk tissue motion artifacts is reduced by shorter acquisition times and tomographic depth-sectioning, which also simplifies post-processing correction [0]. However, certain multiple scattering suppression techniques, such as multi-focus averaging (B-MFA), are incompatible with functional OCT imaging techniques based on fast sequential acquisition, including Doppler OCT, OCT angiography, and dynamic OCT . Additionally, coherent artifacts caused by the imperfect point spread function of the OCT system can be reduced using nonlinear deconvolution algorithms like CLEAN, but these represent distinct technical challenges in maintaining signal integrity . The "blind spot" issue in low-flow regions is exacerbated by the specific statistical methods used for flow detection. In difference and variance methods, the flow signal is more strongly coupled to the magnitude of the OCT signal than in decorrelation-based methods . Consequently, correlation-based approaches introduce amplitude or phase cutoffs that prevent flow detection in hyporeflective regions, effectively creating blind spots where dynamic signals cannot be reliably identified . While speckle variance OCT is sensitive to flow perpendicular to the scanning beam by measuring intensity speckle changes, it does not provide quantitative information, which is a major drawback for the use of speckle-based techniques [3][4]. In contrast, Doppler OCT is capable of providing quantitative information regarding internal flow, including velocity and direction [4]. Sampling rate and temporal resolution further constrain the detection of low-flow dynamics. Autocorrelation-based speckle analysis depends greatly on the sampling rate, although even at 8 kHz, it remains a good approach for low flows that differentiates flow without angle dependence or sample preparation [4]. A sampling rate of 8 kHz is appropriate for differentiating between low flow rates up to $12\mu l / min$ [1]. To improve the robustness of such measurements, procedures may be repeated and averaged, as demonstrated by repeating a procedure five times and averaging the results [4]. The rationale behind these temporal analysis techniques has been widely applied to compute OCT angiography (OCTA) from temporal OCT data acquired at the exact same position [1]. Statistical properties of the OCT speckle have also been used to infer the dynamic properties of blood samples, highlighting the potential of these metrics despite the aforementioned limitations [1]. While OCT and OCTA have been used to visualize and quantify retinal microvasculature, the specific challenges of dynamic speckle detection in these contexts remain subject to the noise, motion, and low-flow constraints described above .

question: What are reprensentative SNR improvement digital method in OCT imaging
raw_answer:
Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) is the most common and widely used image evaluation index in the field of noise reduction for Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) [[pan_biophysics_9:0]]. In this context, SNR serves as a quantitative indicator that measures the signal intensity at a region of interest (ROI) [[pan_biophysics_9:1]]. Generally, a larger value of SNR indicates a better noise reduction effect for the image [[pan_biophysics_9:0]]. However, the definition of SNR may require revision to account for the signal bias $\overline{I_{noise}}$ imposed by the noise floor [[pan_biophysics_9:2]]. To isolate meaningful data, an OCT signal intensity threshold, such as 20 dB above the noise floor, is often used to mask areas of the sample without meaningful signal [[pan_biophysics_9:3]]. While SNR is the primary metric, other image metrics such as contrast-to-noise characteristics and their efficiency in terms of speckle reduction are also investigated [[pan_biophysics_9:2]]. Additionally, evaluation metrics such as the structural similarity index (SSIM) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) are utilized alongside image signal-to-noise ratio [[pan_biophysics_9:1]].

The primary noise sources in OCT include receiver noise and speckle. Receiver noise comprises readout noise, dark noise, and quantization noise, with specific examples including a receiver noise level of $N_{e l}=60e^{-}$ and a full well capacity (FWC) of $100\mathrm{K}e^{-}$ for CCD detectors [[pan_biophysics_9:4]]. Speckle patterns in OCT have a dual role, acting both as a source of noise that degrades signal and as a carrier of information [[pan_biophysics_9:5]]. Many works interpret speckle as a source of noise because it reduces image quality and contrast, making boundaries between tissues less distinguishable [[pan_biophysics_9:5]]. The coefficient of variation (C), defined as $C = \frac {\sigma}{\mu}$, is a metric used to analyze speckle [[pan_biophysics_9:5]]. When the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approaches zero, LOGIV and DLOGIV values approach $\pi^2 /6$ and $\pi^2 /3$, respectively [[pan_biophysics_9:5]].

Digital methods aim to mitigate these noise sources, though their effectiveness varies by noise type. Averaging is a common technique where a mere nine averages can lead to a threefold reduction in speckle noise [[pan_biophysics_9:6]]. However, conventional OCT images exhibited minimal reduction (5.5%) in the coefficient of variation (C) even with extensive averaging (M=100), indicating that speckle noise was not significantly affected by averaging in those specific conditions [[pan_biophysics_9:6]]. This limitation is partly because speckle patterns of static samples do not change between frames [[pan_biophysics_9:0]]. In contrast, deep learning approaches like SNR-Net OCT can achieve brightening of low-light OCT images and speckle-free SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:1]]. Regarding other noise sources, no negative effects of Relative Intensity Noise (RIN) on image quality have been found yet [[pan_biophysics_9:7]].

Signal averaging is a fundamental digital method employed to suppress speckle and improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in optical coherence tomography (OCT) images [[pan_biophysics_9:8]]. The general principle is that a larger value of SNR corresponds to a better noise reduction effect in the resulting image [[pan_biophysics_9:9]]. In conventional OCT systems, extensive averaging has been shown to yield minimal reduction in certain metrics, with only a 5.5% decrease observed even when averaging 100 frames, indicating that standard speckle noise may not be fully affected by simple averaging techniques [[pan_biophysics_9:10]]. However, specific implementations such as speckle-modulating OCT demonstrate that a mere nine averages can lead to a threefold reduction in speckle noise [[pan_biophysics_9:10]].

The choice between complex averaging and magnitude averaging significantly impacts the degree of SNR improvement, particularly for small sample sizes [[pan_biophysics_9:11]]. For small N, complex averaging provides a considerable SNR improvement over magnitude averaging [[pan_biophysics_9:11]]. Quantitative data indicates that for a specific parameter value of 20, the SNR improvement is approximately 12, compared to approximately 5 for other conditions [[pan_biophysics_9:11]]. While deep learning approaches like SNR-Net OCT can achieve brightening of low-light images and speckle-free SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:12]], traditional averaging remains a baseline for comparison. For instance, SNR at indicated fringes of Scotch tape can increase from 14.31 dB to 34.18 dB using advanced processing [[pan_biophysics_9:12]].

Temporal processing and frame averaging are critical for managing motion artifacts and enhancing image quality in volumetric acquisitions. Multi-focus averaging methods utilize sequences of OCT frames to suppress multiple scattering, with specific protocols using a sequence of 32 OCT frames with a frame interval of 204.8 ms [[pan_biophysics_9:13]]. In such systems, each cross-sectional frame consists of 256 A-lines, and the acquisition time of a single frame is 5.12 ms [[pan_biophysics_9:13]]. The sharpness of these averaged images is often evaluated using the information entropy of the OCT images as a metric [[pan_biophysics_9:13]]. Thresholding is applied during this process, with a threshold value of 50 used in arbitrary units, though this value may differ across various OCT systems [[pan_biophysics_9:13]].

Other temporal and iterative digital methods focus on eliminating specific noise artifacts such as autocorrelation noise. A practical approach to eliminate autocorrelation noise terms has been demonstrated for ultrafast and volume-rate OCT imaging [[pan_biophysics_9:14]]. In resonant OCT (ROCT), the overall reduction in autocorrelation noise signal level is nearly 5 dB [[pan_biophysics_9:15]]. Iterative cancellation methods continue processing until the maximum value in the dirty image reaches the noise floor [[pan_biophysics_9:16]]. These techniques complement standard averaging by targeting coherent artifacts that may persist despite temporal averaging.

While ensemble averaging is commonly used in conventional spectrometer-based measurements, newer imaging techniques have illustrated superior sensing performance compared to these methods [[pan_biophysics_9:17]]. Similarly, in surface reaction studies, measurements are in good agreement with rates measured in ensemble averaging techniques [[pan_biophysics_9:18]]. In the context of real-time noise reduction, deep learning models may utilize loss functions such as the sum of squared differences between the noisy image and the denoised image [[pan_biophysics_9:9]]. These models operate within specific imaging depths, such as 6.7 mm [[pan_biophysics_9:9]], and can be combined with hardware adjustments, such as rotating the VGA by 1.35 degrees, to further enhance SNR in spectral domain OCT [[pan_biophysics_9:19]].

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) serves as the most common and widely used image evaluation index in the field of noise reduction for optical coherence tomography (OCT) [[pan_biophysics_9:20]]. In general, a larger value of SNR indicates a better noise reduction effect for the image [[pan_biophysics_9:20]]. While deep learning approaches such as SNR-Net can achieve brightening of low-light OCT images and speckle-free SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:21]], traditional and adaptive digital filtering methods remain critical for enhancing SNR while preserving structural details.

One fundamental digital method for improving SNR is signal averaging, which reduces speckle noise through repeated acquisitions. For instance, a mere nine averages can lead to a threefold reduction in speckle noise [[pan_biophysics_9:22]]. The choice between complex and magnitude averaging significantly impacts the degree of noise reduction; complex averaging reduces the noise variance by $1/N$, providing a much stronger noise reduction than magnitude averaging, which only reduces the noise by $1/\sqrt{N}$ [[pan_biophysics_9:23]]. However, for signals that are comparable to or smaller than the noise level, magnitude averaging yields a better SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:23]]. This averaging procedure can be applied iteratively, such as repeating a speckle analysis procedure five times and averaging the results [[pan_biophysics_9:24]].

Non-linear and adaptive filtering techniques are employed to further refine image quality. Adaptive filtering of the signal is utilized in control loops to address issues such as encoder ripple, which often dominates control system noise [[pan_biophysics_9:25]]. In the context of coherent artifacts, the CLEAN algorithm provides a more robust means to reconstruct the original image [[pan_biophysics_9:26]]. Additionally, specific hardware and signal processing adjustments, such as rotating a VGA by 1.35 degrees, have been implemented in dual-balanced detection systems to enhance SNR [[pan_biophysics_9:27]].

Quantitative metrics and specific system parameters define the performance of these digital methods. The coefficient of variation, defined as $C = \frac {\sigma}{\mu}$, is used to analyze speckle in OCT signals [[pan_biophysics_9:28]]. In systems utilizing resonant OCT (ROCT), the overall reduction in autocorrelation noise signal level is nearly 5 dB [[pan_biophysics_9:29]], with the autocorrelation noise signal appearing much attenuated at a depth of 2 mm [[pan_biophysics_9:29]]. For deep learning-based noise reduction, the loss function is often defined as the sum of squared differences between the noisy and denoised images, expressed as $L _ {2} = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {m - 1} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ I _ {n} (i, j) - I _ {d} (i, j) \right] ^ {2}$ [[pan_biophysics_9:20]].

Performance evaluations of these digital methods demonstrate significant improvements in SNR. In one study, the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image was improved from $8.15\mathrm{dB}$ to $32.66\mathrm{dB}$ using a deep learning approach [[pan_biophysics_9:21]]. Another system achieved a sensitivity of 92 dB with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm [[pan_biophysics_9:20]]. In photothermal OCT, signal spectra corresponding to specific lengths show clear enhancement of SNR for longer signals, leading to images with better SNR and contrast [[pan_biophysics_9:30]]. These digital methods are implemented using various computational backends, such as Tensorflow (v2.5.0) [[pan_biophysics_9:21]], and trained with specific parameters like a batch size of 1 [[pan_biophysics_9:21]] and the adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm (Adam) [[pan_biophysics_9:21]].

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) serves as the most common and widely used image evaluation index in the field of noise reduction, where a larger value generally indicates a better noise reduction effect [[pan_biophysics_9:31]]. Recent developments in machine learning, specifically convolutional neural networks, have reported outperforming results in OCT image analysis compared to conventional image processing methods [[pan_biophysics_9:32]]. For instance, the SNR-Net OCT architecture deeply integrates a conventional OCT setup with a residual-dense-block U-Net generative adversarial network featuring channel-wise attention connections [[pan_biophysics_9:33]]. This model is trained using a customized large speckle-free SNR-enhanced brighter OCT dataset to achieve brightening of low-light OCT images and speckle-free SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:33]]. In one specific application, the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image was improved from 8.15 dB to 32.66 dB using this approach [[pan_biophysics_9:33]]. The training process for this network utilized a batch size of 1 and was implemented based on a Tensorflow (v2.5.0) backend [[pan_biophysics_9:33]].

Other deep learning architectures, such as U-Nets, have also been applied to real-time noise reduction in OCT [[pan_biophysics_9:31]]. In a ground truth-free deep learning framework, a U-net achieved the lowest SNR of 39.01 dB and a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of 41.06 dB, offering the advantage of the shortest computation time of 0.2 seconds [[pan_biophysics_9:31]]. Additionally, conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have been employed to reduce noise in retinal OCT images, with studies indicating that this method outperforms other traditional methods in both performance and generalization ability [[pan_biophysics_9:31]]. In the specific domain of photothermal optical coherence tomography (PT-OCT), artificial neural networks have been utilized to enhance SNR and image contrast, which in turn lowers the required acquisition time [[pan_biophysics_9:34]]. To the best of current knowledge, this represents the first report on utilizing deep learning in the field of PT-OCT for these specific enhancements [[pan_biophysics_9:34]].

These deep learning approaches address challenges inherent in OCT imaging, such as the dominance of multiple scattering photons in deeper regions, which degrades resolution and contrast [[pan_biophysics_9:35]]. While traditional signal averaging can improve SNR in images of scattering structures like the retina, it may be well worth the effort only in specific contexts [[pan_biophysics_9:36]]. For comparison, speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) imaging with equivalent averaging led to a significant 77.8% reduction in speckle noise, whereas a mere nine averages in standard averaging lead to a threefold reduction in speckle noise [[pan_biophysics_9:37]]. Other non-deep learning techniques, such as resonant OCT (ROCT), have achieved an overall reduction in autocorrelation noise signal level of nearly 5 dB [[pan_biophysics_9:38]]. Furthermore, methods for canceling coherent artifacts involve iteration until the maximum value in the dirty image reaches the noise floor [[pan_biophysics_9:39]]. While the provided evidence includes references to generative models and adversarial training concepts in broader computer vision contexts, such as diffusion models and classifier-free guidance, the specific application of these exact architectures to OCT denoising is not detailed in the provided excerpts beyond the use of GANs and U-Nets [[pan_biophysics_9:40]][[pan_biophysics_9:41]][[pan_biophysics_9:42]][[pan_biophysics_9:43]].

The evaluation of digital signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement methods in optical coherence tomography (OCT) relies on specific quantitative metrics, including the structural similarity index (SSIM), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and image signal-to-noise ratio [[pan_biophysics_9:44]]. SSIM is specifically utilized to measure the perceptual visual difference between the predicted image and the ground truth [[pan_biophysics_9:44]]. In general, a larger value of SNR indicates a better noise reduction effect for the image [[pan_biophysics_9:45]]. For instance, the SNR-Net OCT method achieved a significant improvement in the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image, raising it from $8.15\mathrm{dB}$ to $32.66\mathrm{dB}$ [[pan_biophysics_9:44]]. This method is capable of brightening low-light OCT images and achieving speckle-free SNR enhancement [[pan_biophysics_9:44]].

Comparative studies on signal averaging indicate that for small numbers of averages ($N$), complex averaging provides a considerable SNR improvement over magnitude averaging [[pan_biophysics_9:46]]. However, further investigation is needed into other image metrics, such as contrast-to-noise characteristics and efficiency in terms of speckle reduction [[pan_biophysics_9:46]]. In the context of dispersion compensation, SAMMR and TSMMR methods offered greater improvements in image sharpness and SNR when compared with the TSIF method [[pan_biophysics_9:47]]. Regarding relative intensity noise (RIN), no negative effects on image quality have been found yet [[pan_biophysics_9:48]].

Deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks, have reported outperforming results in OCT image analysis compared to conventional image processing [[pan_biophysics_9:49]]. However, these deep learning approaches still lack interpretability and roughly remain a black box, despite recent efforts to address this limitation [[pan_biophysics_9:49]]. A major practical limitation in training these models is the difficulty in obtaining a noisy image and its corresponding clean ground truth [[pan_biophysics_9:45]]. In the field of OCT imaging, acquiring ground truth often requires acquiring multiple frames of B-scan OCT images at the same location, followed by a complicated process of registering and averaging the images [[pan_biophysics_9:45]].

Computational costs and implementation details are also significant factors in the performance of these digital methods. For example, in real-time noise reduction based on ground truth-free deep learning, resizing the input makes the output images cleaner and contributes to a better denoising effect [[pan_biophysics_9:45]]. To manage computational resources, specific allocations of GPU memory may be required, such as allocating 40% for deep learning processing and the remainder for CUDA processing when needed [[pan_biophysics_9:45]]. Training parameters also play a role, with specific configurations such as a batch size of 1 and a learning rate of $\alpha = 1\times 10^{-4}$ being used in SNR-Net OCT [[pan_biophysics_9:44]].

Current limitations also extend to the physical constraints of the imaging process, where deeper regions in an OCT image are more dominated by multiple scattering (MS) photons [[pan_biophysics_9:50]]. This dominance of MS photons degrades the resolution and contrast of the OCT image in these deep regions [[pan_biophysics_9:50]]. While processing an angle-resolved digital image is identified as a better way to deal with multiple scattering problems, this approach has not been realized in some studies [[pan_biophysics_9:51]].
