This averaging procedure can be applied iteratively, such as repeating a speckle analysis procedure five times and averaging the results . Non-linear and adaptive filtering techniques are employed to further refine image quality. Adaptive filtering of the signal is utilized in control loops to address issues such as encoder ripple, which often dominates control system noise . In the context of coherent artifacts, the CLEAN algorithm provides a more robust means to reconstruct the original image . Additionally, specific hardware and signal processing adjustments, such as rotating a VGA by 1.35 degrees, have been implemented in dual-balanced detection systems to enhance SNR [3]. Quantitative metrics and specific system parameters define the performance of these digital methods. The coefficient of variation, defined as $C = \frac {\sigma}{\mu}$, is used to analyze speckle in OCT signals . In systems utilizing resonant OCT (ROCT), the overall reduction in autocorrelation noise signal level is nearly 5 dB , with the autocorrelation noise signal appearing much attenuated at a depth of 2 mm . For deep learning-based noise reduction, the loss function is often defined as the sum of squared differences between the noisy and denoised images, expressed as $L _ {2} = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {m - 1} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ I _ {n} (i, j) - I _ {d} (i, j) \right] ^ {2}$ [4]. Performance evaluations of these digital methods demonstrate significant improvements in SNR. In one study, the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image was improved from $8.15\mathrm{dB}$ to $32.66\mathrm{dB}$ using a deep learning approach [0]. Another system achieved a sensitivity of 92 dB with an imaging depth of 6.7 mm [4]. In photothermal OCT, signal spectra corresponding to specific lengths show clear enhancement of SNR for longer signals, leading to images with better SNR and contrast [1]. These digital methods are implemented using various computational backends, such as Tensorflow (v2.5.0) [0], and trained with specific parameters like a batch size of 1 [0] and the adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm (Adam) [0]. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) serves as the most common and widely used image evaluation index in the field of noise reduction, where a larger value generally indicates a better noise reduction effect [4]. Recent developments in machine learning, specifically convolutional neural networks, have reported outperforming results in OCT image analysis compared to conventional image processing methods . For instance, the SNR-Net OCT architecture deeply integrates a conventional OCT setup with a residual-dense-block U-Net generative adversarial network featuring channel-wise attention connections [0]. This model is trained using a customized large speckle-free SNR-enhanced brighter OCT dataset to achieve brightening of low-light OCT images and speckle-free SNR enhancement [0]. In one specific application, the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image was improved from 8.15 dB to 32.66 dB using this approach [0]. The training process for this network utilized a batch size of 1 and was implemented based on a Tensorflow (v2.5.0) backend [0]. Other deep learning architectures, such as U-Nets, have also been applied to real-time noise reduction in OCT [4]. In a ground truth-free deep learning framework, a U-net achieved the lowest SNR of 39.01 dB and a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of 41.06 dB, offering the advantage of the shortest computation time of 0.2 seconds [4]. Additionally, conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have been employed to reduce noise in retinal OCT images, with studies indicating that this method outperforms other traditional methods in both performance and generalization ability [4]. In the specific domain of photothermal optical coherence tomography (PT-OCT), artificial neural networks have been utilized to enhance SNR and image contrast, which in turn lowers the required acquisition time [1]. To the best of current knowledge, this represents the first report on utilizing deep learning in the field of PT-OCT for these specific enhancements [1]. These deep learning approaches address challenges inherent in OCT imaging, such as the dominance of multiple scattering photons in deeper regions, which degrades resolution and contrast . While traditional signal averaging can improve SNR in images of scattering structures like the retina, it may be well worth the effort only in specific contexts [2]. For comparison, speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) imaging with equivalent averaging led to a significant 77.8% reduction in speckle noise, whereas a mere nine averages in standard averaging lead to a threefold reduction in speckle noise . Other non-deep learning techniques, such as resonant OCT (ROCT), have achieved an overall reduction in autocorrelation noise signal level of nearly 5 dB . Furthermore, methods for canceling coherent artifacts involve iteration until the maximum value in the dirty image reaches the noise floor . While the provided evidence includes references to generative models and adversarial training concepts in broader computer vision contexts, such as diffusion models and classifier-free guidance, the specific application of these exact architectures to OCT denoising is not detailed in the provided excerpts beyond the use of GANs and U-Nets . The evaluation of digital signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement methods in optical coherence tomography (OCT) relies on specific quantitative metrics, including the structural similarity index (SSIM), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and image signal-to-noise ratio [0]. SSIM is specifically utilized to measure the perceptual visual difference between the predicted image and the ground truth [0]. In general, a larger value of SNR indicates a better noise reduction effect for the image [4]. For instance, the SNR-Net OCT method achieved a significant improvement in the SNR of a Scotch tape OCT image, raising it from $8.15\mathrm{dB}$ to $32.66\mathrm{dB}$ [0]. This method is capable of brightening low-light OCT images and achieving speckle-free SNR enhancement [0]. Comparative studies on signal averaging indicate that for small numbers of averages ($N$), complex averaging provides a considerable SNR improvement over magnitude averaging [2]. However, further investigation is needed into other image metrics, such as contrast-to-noise characteristics and efficiency in terms of speckle reduction [2]. In the context of dispersion compensation, SAMMR and TSMMR methods offered greater improvements in image sharpness and SNR when compared with the TSIF method . Regarding relative intensity noise (RIN), no negative effects on image quality have been found yet . Deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks, have reported outperforming results in OCT image analysis compared to conventional image processing . However, these deep learning approaches still lack interpretability and roughly remain a black box, despite recent efforts to address this limitation . A major practical limitation in training these models is the difficulty in obtaining a noisy image and its corresponding clean ground truth [4]. In the field of OCT imaging, acquiring ground truth often requires acquiring multiple frames of B-scan OCT images at the same location, followed by a complicated process of registering and averaging the images [4]. Computational costs and implementation details are also significant factors in the performance of these digital methods. For example, in real-time noise reduction based on ground truth-free deep learning, resizing the input makes the output images cleaner and contributes to a better denoising effect [4]. To manage computational resources, specific allocations of GPU memory may be required, such as allocating 40% for deep learning processing and the remainder for CUDA processing when needed [4]. Training parameters also play a role, with specific configurations such as a batch size of 1 and a learning rate of $\alpha = 1\times 10^{-4}$ being used in SNR-Net OCT [0]. Current limitations also extend to the physical constraints of the imaging process, where deeper regions in an OCT image are more dominated by multiple scattering (MS) photons . This dominance of MS photons degrades the resolution and contrast of the OCT image in these deep regions . While processing an angle-resolved digital image is identified as a better way to deal with multiple scattering problems, this approach has not been realized in some studies .

question: What are ways to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles?
raw_answer:
The center-of-mass (CoM) motion of optically levitated nanoparticles can be controlled to a remarkable degree using active feedback mechanisms and autonomous cavity-assisted cooling schemes, placing the quantum regime of mechanical motion within reach [[shengyan_photonics_1:0]]. Recent experiments have demonstrated quantum ground state cooling of the CoM motion of a single optically levitated nanoparticle in vacuum, providing opportunities for studying macroscopic quantum mechanics and precision measurements [[shengyan_photonics_1:1]]. In one specific implementation, the CoM motion was cooled by measurement-based feedback to an average occupancy of 0.65 motional quanta, corresponding to a state purity of 43% [[shengyan_photonics_1:2]].

Optical trapping forces are fundamental to the levitation and confinement of these particles, with the magnitude of these forces decreasing as particle size decreases [[shengyan_photonics_1:3]]. The stability of optical levitation is dependent on damping conditions; when damping is reduced, optical levitation may no longer be stable, necessitating the use of feedback cooling to stabilize the center-of-mass motions of the microsphere [[shengyan_photonics_1:4]]. The trapping configuration often involves specific optical elements, such as an aspheric trapping lens with a numerical aperture of 0.75 [[shengyan_photonics_1:2]]. In systems involving multiple particles, the total trapping power is split between the traps, with examples showing a total power of approximately 800 mW divided between two traps [[shengyan_photonics_1:5]]. Optical trapping forces can also attract particles to regions of greatest electric field intensity, which results in more uniform step amplitudes in detection signals [[shengyan_photonics_1:3]].

The interaction between light and the particle introduces heating and mechanical effects that influence the CoM dynamics. For a trapping field intensity of 300 mW/µm², the bulk heating rate due to optical absorption is estimated to be approximately 2 K/ms [[shengyan_photonics_1:2]]. While the primary focus is on CoM motion, the optical torque on nonspherical particles scales linearly with optical power in the limit of nearly circularly polarized trapping light, leading to a rotation frequency proportional to the power [[shengyan_photonics_1:0]]. The steady-state rotation frequency scales linearly with the optical trapping power and inversely with pressure, consistent with conservation of angular momentum [[shengyan_photonics_1:0]]. The torsional vibration frequency of nonspherical nanoparticles can be one order of magnitude higher than the CoM motion frequency, which is promising for ground state cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:6]]. The torsional frequency is proportional to the square root of the trapping power [[shengyan_photonics_1:6]]. The alignment of the nanoparticle's long axes with the polarization direction of the trapping laser is indicated by a damping ratio where $\Gamma_{x}/\Gamma_{y}<1$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:6]].

Thermodynamic and quantum limits impose fundamental constraints on the cooling process. The role of fundamental quantum optical effects in mechanical position measurements has led to the understanding of the standard quantum limit and the development of back-action evading measurements [[shengyan_photonics_1:7]]. For levitated particles, quantum back-action is associated with the radiation pressure shot noise arising from the quantization of the light field's linear momentum [[shengyan_photonics_1:2]]. In the weak-coupling regime where $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} \ll \kappa$ and for a detuning $\Delta = \omega_{m}$, the optical back-action damping is given by $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} = 4g^{2}n_{c} / \kappa$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:8]]. Experiments with mechanical mirrors have not yet observed radiation-pressure quantum back-action because it is masked by the random, thermal motion of the mirror [[shengyan_photonics_1:9]]. Quantum optomechanics involves managing various troublesome noises, including measurement and back action, which are typical of quantum measurements [[shengyan_photonics_1:7]].

Active control methods are employed to overcome these limits and stabilize the system. Coherent, off-resonant driving forces can be exerted on the particle, such as at 90 kHz, to manipulate its motion [[shengyan_photonics_1:2]]. The interaction between center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom may allow for studies of spin-orbit coupling in optically levitated systems [[shengyan_photonics_1:0]]. In precession motion experiments, a torque of $1.9 \pm 0.5 \times 10^{-23}$ Nm was measured at a pressure of $1 \times 10^{-1}$ mbar [[shengyan_photonics_1:10]]. At lower pressures, such as $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar, the estimated torque sensitivity reaches $3.6 \pm 1.1 \times 10^{-31}$ Nm/ $\sqrt{Hz}$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:10]].

Active feedback mechanisms and autonomous cavity-assisted cooling schemes have enabled the control of the center-of-mass motion of optically levitated nanoparticles to a remarkable degree, bringing the quantum regime of mechanical motion within reach [[shengyan_photonics_1:11]]. These techniques function analogously to "Stochastic Cooling" of ions in storage rings, utilizing a "pick-up" mechanism, such as an optical cavity interferometer, to measure mechanical motion and a "kicker," such as a radiation-pressure force exerted by a laser, to provide a viscous feedback force [[shengyan_photonics_1:12]][[shengyan_photonics_1:13]]. In the context of cavity optomechanics, this approach relies on the weak-coupling regime where the optomechanical coupling rate is much smaller than the cavity decay rate, and for a specific detuning, the optical back-action damping is determined by the square of the coupling strength and the intracavity photon number [[shengyan_photonics_1:14]].

Two primary variants of active feedback cooling are linear feedback cooling, also known as cold damping, and parametric feedback cooling. In linear feedback cooling, the measured signal is filtered, phase-shifted, and applied as a direct force at the trap frequency of the particle [[shengyan_photonics_1:15]]. Conversely, in parametric feedback cooling, the measured signal is filtered, phase-shifted, and fed back at twice the frequency of particle motion [[shengyan_photonics_1:15]]. Experimental comparisons indicate that parametric feedback cooling along the z-axis is much weaker than linear feedback cooling and can often be safely ignored in the analysis [[shengyan_photonics_1:16]]. The effectiveness of these methods is demonstrated by the ability to cool the center-of-mass motion significantly by applying a feedback damping that is much greater than the initial damping [[shengyan_photonics_1:17]]. For instance, feedback cooling has been used to cool the center-of-mass of a levitated nanodiamond in all three directions, achieving a minimum temperature of about 1.2 K along one direction [[shengyan_photonics_1:18]]. Similarly, feedback cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a levitated nanosphere has been demonstrated to reach approximately 450 μK, corresponding to about 63 phonons at 150 kHz [[shengyan_photonics_1:19]].

The implementation of these feedback loops involves specific operational parameters and constraints. Feedback circuits are typically turned on at pressures of about 20 torr [[shengyan_photonics_1:17]]. In systems utilizing multiple beams, the power of the cooling beams is approximately 1% that of the trapping beams [[shengyan_photonics_1:17]]. While the feedback damping rate at a fixed gain is independent of the pressure, the extraction of this rate is not affected by tweezer modulation [[shengyan_photonics_1:15]]. However, the stability of the closed-loop system is sensitive to the phase slope; for any mode number greater than one, a larger phase slope lowers the value of the feedback gain at which the system becomes unstable, thereby limiting the cooling performance [[shengyan_photonics_1:16]]. Additionally, if the feedback loops are coupled, small correlations can arise between different directions of motion [[shengyan_photonics_1:17]].

In ultrahigh vacuum environments, the intrinsic damping ratio is extremely small, but optical cooling can add equivalent damping that is beneficial for feedback control [[shengyan_photonics_1:20]]. When optimized, the damping ratio can reach approximately 0.65, which is close to the ideal ratio of 0.707 for the feedback control of a typical second-order system [[shengyan_photonics_1:20]]. While some optical tweezers arrays can levitate silica nanoparticles at low pressures without feedback cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:21]], active feedback remains a critical tool for achieving lower temperatures. For example, cavity cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a nanosphere has been demonstrated to reach a few mK [[shengyan_photonics_1:19]], and quantum ground state cavity cooling is achievable for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [[shengyan_photonics_1:22]]. The cooling performance in such cavity systems is measured at specific detunings, such as $\Delta/2\pi = 400$ kHz, whereas other detunings may result in no cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:22]]. The optomechanical damping resulting from the preferential scattering of drive laser photons into the upper-frequency sideband also contributes to cooling the mechanical mode [[shengyan_photonics_1:14]].

Cavity optomechanics provides a route towards quantum optomechanics by utilizing the interaction between light and mechanical motion [[shengyan_photonics_1:23]]. In this regime, the mechanical dissipation rate governs the rate of heating of the mechanical mirror mode by the environment, which limits the effectiveness of optomechanical cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:24]]. For a lower-frequency (red) detuning of the laser from the cavity, the system leads to damping and cooling of the mechanical motion [[shengyan_photonics_1:25]]. Resolved sideband cooling has been demonstrated experimentally, and it has been theoretically shown that ground state cooling is possible in the resolved sideband regime, also known as the good-cavity limit [[shengyan_photonics_1:23]][[shengyan_photonics_1:24]]. In optomechanical sideband cooling within a cavity, the finite Stokes Raman scattering defined by the cavity linewidth combined with shot noise fluctuations dictates a quantum backaction limit, analogous to the Doppler limit of atomic laser cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:26]]. This quantum backaction limit can be circumvented by introducing additional couplings to alter the dynamics of the cavity optomechanical system, such as dissipative optomechanical coupling or measurement and active feedback [[shengyan_photonics_1:26]].

Experimental implementations of cavity cooling for levitated nanoparticles have achieved significant cooling factors. For a particle placed at a node of the cavity field, axial cooling factors beyond 100 have been observed [[shengyan_photonics_1:27]]. The observed performance implies that quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles can be achieved for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [[shengyan_photonics_1:27]]. Maximal damping along the $x$ direction is obtained for minimal coherent scattering powers at $x_0 = \lambda / 4$, while maximal damping along the $z$ direction is obtained for maximal coherent scattering powers at $x_0 = 0$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:27]]. In contrast, dark colors without cooling were observed when the detuning was set to $\Delta / 2\pi = 4$ MHz [[shengyan_photonics_1:27]]. The resonant wavelength of the cavity in torsional optomechanics experiments is 1540 nm, which is different from that of the trapping laser [[shengyan_photonics_1:28]], and another system utilized a wavelength corresponding to $\lambda_{o} = 1537$ nm [[shengyan_photonics_1:25]]. For cavity cooling of a trapped object in vacuum, it is important to use feedback cooling to pre-cool and stabilize the object, in order to have enough time to tune the cavity cooling laser to the correct frequency for efficient cooling [[shengyan_photonics_1:29]]. In two-dimensional optomechanical crystal cavities, a $C_{eff}$ greater than unity under continuous-wave optical pumping has been achieved [[shengyan_photonics_1:30]], although the $\beta = 0$ theoretical curve predicts substantially more cooling of the acoustic mode than measured, and the shape of the measured and theoretical curves are quite different [[shengyan_photonics_1:30]].

Gas damping and viscous drag serve as passive cooling mechanisms in controlled environments. The gas damping rate increases with gas pressure [[shengyan_photonics_1:31]]. At the pressures in typical experiments, mechanical damping $\gamma$ is dominated by the collisions with the surrounding gas [[shengyan_photonics_1:32]]. As expected, the damping time scales inversely with pressure according to $t_{damp} \propto 1/p_{gas}$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:33]]. In ultrahigh vacuum, the damping ratio is extremely small, but optical cooling may add equivalent damping to be beneficial for feedback control [[shengyan_photonics_1:34]]. To reduce the fluctuating force disturbing the motion of levitated nanoparticles, researchers optically trap the particles inside a vacuum chamber connected to a closed-cycle cryostat to lower both the temperature and the pressure of the gas around the particle [[shengyan_photonics_1:35]]. However, the cryocooler periodically compresses and expands the helium gas in the cold head, generating periodic mechanical vibrations on the optical table and the trap itself [[shengyan_photonics_1:35]]. Focused by a high numerical aperture (NA = 0.75) lens, all-optical cold damping has been shown to be scalable for levitated nanoparticles [[shengyan_photonics_1:31]].

Experimental efforts to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles have progressed from millikelvin regimes to the quantum ground state, with recent demonstrations providing opportunities for studying macroscopic quantum mechanics and precision measurements [[shengyan_photonics_1:36]]. Early milestones included feedback cooling of a levitated nanosphere to approximately 450 µK, corresponding to about 63 phonons at 150 kHz, and cavity cooling of the CoM motion to a few mK [[shengyan_photonics_1:37]]. In the context of torsional optomechanics, it was shown that only the torsional mode can be cooled to the ground state using a cavity with a length of 0.5 mm [[shengyan_photonics_1:37]]. This work represented an important step towards quantum ground state cooling of torsional vibration and testing recent theoretical proposals [[shengyan_photonics_1:38]].

More recent experiments have achieved lower temperatures and approached fundamental limits. Using feedback cooling, the CoM of a levitated nanodiamond was cooled in all three directions, reaching a minimum temperature of about 1.2 K along one direction [[shengyan_photonics_1:39]]. In a cryogenic free space environment, an experiment operating at 560 µW of local oscillator power, where optical shot noise was 14 dB above the electronic noise floor, approached the quantum limit to within 30% [[shengyan_photonics_1:40]]. This setup utilized parametric feedback cooling implemented with three phase-locked loops integrated in a lock-in amplifier [[shengyan_photonics_1:40]]. The performance of this system was limited by the fact that for any occupation number n > 1, the larger phase slope lowers the feedback gain at which the closed-loop system becomes unstable, thereby limiting cooling performance [[shengyan_photonics_1:40]]. Environmental conditions in this cryogenic experiment included a cold plate temperature of 6 K and a PEEK lens holder temperature of 57 K when the laser was on [[shengyan_photonics_1:40]].

Cavity cooling techniques have also shown significant potential for reaching the quantum ground state. For a particle placed at a node of the cavity field, axial cooling factors beyond 100 were observed [[shengyan_photonics_1:41]]. The observed performance implies that quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles can be achieved for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [[shengyan_photonics_1:41]]. Scalability of these cooling methods has been demonstrated, with feedback cooling techniques shown to be scalable to two particles [[shengyan_photonics_1:42]]. A protocol combining parametric cooling along the z-axis with all-optical cold damping can achieve 3D cooling of multiple levitated particles by entirely optical means [[shengyan_photonics_1:42]]. However, the relatively heavy mass of levitated nanoparticles, which is several femtograms, requires optical powers greater than 100 mW to trap a single nanoparticle, which is several orders of magnitude larger than for atoms [[shengyan_photonics_1:42]]. Utilizing more efficient feedback cooling schemes and trapping smaller particles can lead to better force detection performance [[shengyan_photonics_1:43]].

Achieving quantum ground state cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a single optically levitated nanoparticle in vacuum has been demonstrated, providing opportunities for studying macroscopic quantum mechanics and precision measurements [[shengyan_photonics_1:44]]. In one such experiment, the center-of-mass motion was cooled by measurement-based feedback to an average occupancy of 0.65 motional quanta, corresponding to a state purity of 43% [[shengyan_photonics_1:45]]. To reduce the fluctuating forces disturbing the particle's motion, nanoparticles are optically trapped inside a vacuum chamber connected to a closed-cycle cryostat with a nominal cold-plate temperature of 4 K, which lowers both the temperature and the pressure of the surrounding gas [[shengyan_photonics_1:45]].

A primary limitation in reaching the quantum regime is the heating induced by gas collisions, where mechanical damping is dominated by collisions with the surrounding gas at typical experimental pressures [[shengyan_photonics_1:46]]. The gas damping rate increases with gas pressure, and in regimes of low feedback gain, the particle center-of-mass temperature is determined by the ratio of gas reheating and feedback cooling rates [[shengyan_photonics_1:47]]. Consequently, quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles is estimated to be achievable only for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [[shengyan_photonics_1:48]]. At this pressure level, the torque sensitivity is limited only by photon shot noise, with an estimated value of $3.6 \pm 1.1 \times 10^{-31}$ Nm/ $\sqrt{Hz}$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:49]].

Optical absorption presents another significant challenge, as the bulk heating rate due to optical absorption is estimated to be approximately 2 K/ms for a trapping field intensity of $300\ mW/\mu m^{2}$ [[shengyan_photonics_1:45]]. This heating effect prevents the simple increase of trapping laser intensity to improve cooling, as it induces heating that subsequently causes the loss of the nanoparticle [[shengyan_photonics_1:50]]. For instance, optically trapped nonspherical nanoparticles such as nanodiamonds and silicon nanorods were lost at about 1 torr due to laser heating [[shengyan_photonics_1:51]]. While coherent scattering schemes offer a significant suppression of laser phase noise heating, which is a specific feature of that approach, the fundamental issue of absorption-induced heating remains a barrier to increasing trap strength [[shengyan_photonics_1:48]].

Technical noise sources further complicate the isolation of the particle from environmental perturbations. In experiments operating at $560 \mu W$ of local oscillator power, the optical shot noise is 14 dB above the electronic noise floor [[shengyan_photonics_1:45]]. Although technical laser noise has been shown to have a negligible impact on sideband asymmetry in some optomechanical crystal resonator systems, the interplay between optical shot noise and electronic noise remains a critical factor in levitated systems [[shengyan_photonics_1:52]]. The field of quantum optomechanics promises motion and force detection near the fundamental limits imposed by quantum mechanics, yet current systems face deviations and errors that must be managed, such as percent errors below 0.6% and deviations of less than 0.3% in related mechanical resonator contexts [[shengyan_photonics_1:53]][[shengyan_photonics_1:54]].

Additional complexities arise from the specific properties of the nanoparticles and their interactions. Particles may carry absolute charges, such as $|q_1| / e = 96 \pm 21$ and $|q_2| / e = 110 \pm 24$, which can influence their dynamics [[shengyan_photonics_1:46]]. For nonspherical particles, achieving quantum ground state cooling of torsional vibration is an important step towards testing recent theoretical proposals, though the specific parameters for torsional optomechanics vary significantly depending on the particle geometry and mode [[shengyan_photonics_1:51]][[shengyan_photonics_1:50]]. The ability to reach the quantum regime is thus constrained by the combined effects of gas pressure, optical absorption heating, and technical noise floors, requiring pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar and careful management of laser-induced heating to prevent particle loss [[shengyan_photonics_1:48]][[shengyan_photonics_1:50]][[shengyan_photonics_1:51]].

For levitated particles, quantum back-action is associated with the radiation pressure shot noise arising from the quantization of the light field's linear momentum [2]. In the weak-coupling regime where $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} \ll \kappa$ and for a detuning $\Delta = \omega_{m}$, the optical back-action damping is given by $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} = 4g^{2}n_{c} / \kappa$ . Experiments with mechanical mirrors have not yet observed radiation-pressure quantum back-action because it is masked by the random, thermal motion of the mirror . Quantum optomechanics involves managing various troublesome noises, including measurement and back action, which are typical of quantum measurements . Active control methods are employed to overcome these limits and stabilize the system. Coherent, off-resonant driving forces can be exerted on the particle, such as at 90 kHz, to manipulate its motion [2]. The interaction between center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom may allow for studies of spin-orbit coupling in optically levitated systems . In precession motion experiments, a torque of $1.9 \pm 0.5 \times 10^{-23}$ Nm was measured at a pressure of $1 \times 10^{-1}$ mbar . At lower pressures, such as $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar, the estimated torque sensitivity reaches $3.6 \pm 1.1 \times 10^{-31}$ Nm/ $\sqrt{Hz}$ . Active feedback mechanisms and autonomous cavity-assisted cooling schemes have enabled the control of the center-of-mass motion of optically levitated nanoparticles to a remarkable degree, bringing the quantum regime of mechanical motion within reach . These techniques function analogously to "Stochastic Cooling" of ions in storage rings, utilizing a "pick-up" mechanism, such as an optical cavity interferometer, to measure mechanical motion and a "kicker," such as a radiation-pressure force exerted by a laser, to provide a viscous feedback force . In the context of cavity optomechanics, this approach relies on the weak-coupling regime where the optomechanical coupling rate is much smaller than the cavity decay rate, and for a specific detuning, the optical back-action damping is determined by the square of the coupling strength and the intracavity photon number . Two primary variants of active feedback cooling are linear feedback cooling, also known as cold damping, and parametric feedback cooling. In linear feedback cooling, the measured signal is filtered, phase-shifted, and applied as a direct force at the trap frequency of the particle [6,7]. Conversely, in parametric feedback cooling, the measured signal is filtered, phase-shifted, and fed back at twice the frequency of particle motion [6,7]. Experimental comparisons indicate that parametric feedback cooling along the z-axis is much weaker than linear feedback cooling and can often be safely ignored in the analysis [2]. The effectiveness of these methods is demonstrated by the ability to cool the center-of-mass motion significantly by applying a feedback damping that is much greater than the initial damping [0,1]. For instance, feedback cooling has been used to cool the center-of-mass of a levitated nanodiamond in all three directions, achieving a minimum temperature of about 1.2 K along one direction . Similarly, feedback cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a levitated nanosphere has been demonstrated to reach approximately 450 μK, corresponding to about 63 phonons at 150 kHz . The implementation of these feedback loops involves specific operational parameters and constraints. Feedback circuits are typically turned on at pressures of about 20 torr [0,1]. In systems utilizing multiple beams, the power of the cooling beams is approximately 1% that of the trapping beams [0,1]. While the feedback damping rate at a fixed gain is independent of the pressure, the extraction of this rate is not affected by tweezer modulation [6,7]. However, the stability of the closed-loop system is sensitive to the phase slope; for any mode number greater than one, a larger phase slope lowers the value of the feedback gain at which the system becomes unstable, thereby limiting the cooling performance [2]. Additionally, if the feedback loops are coupled, small correlations can arise between different directions of motion [0,1]. In ultrahigh vacuum environments, the intrinsic damping ratio is extremely small, but optical cooling can add equivalent damping that is beneficial for feedback control . When optimized, the damping ratio can reach approximately 0.65, which is close to the ideal ratio of 0.707 for the feedback control of a typical second-order system . While some optical tweezers arrays can levitate silica nanoparticles at low pressures without feedback cooling , active feedback remains a critical tool for achieving lower temperatures. For example, cavity cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a nanosphere has been demonstrated to reach a few mK , and quantum ground state cavity cooling is achievable for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [3,4]. The cooling performance in such cavity systems is measured at specific detunings, such as $\Delta/2\pi = 400$ kHz, whereas other detunings may result in no cooling [3,4]. The optomechanical damping resulting from the preferential scattering of drive laser photons into the upper-frequency sideband also contributes to cooling the mechanical mode . Cavity optomechanics provides a route towards quantum optomechanics by utilizing the interaction between light and mechanical motion . In this regime, the mechanical dissipation rate governs the rate of heating of the mechanical mirror mode by the environment, which limits the effectiveness of optomechanical cooling . For a lower-frequency (red) detuning of the laser from the cavity, the system leads to damping and cooling of the mechanical motion . Resolved sideband cooling has been demonstrated experimentally, and it has been theoretically shown that ground state cooling is possible in the resolved sideband regime, also known as the good-cavity limit . In optomechanical sideband cooling within a cavity, the finite Stokes Raman scattering defined by the cavity linewidth combined with shot noise fluctuations dictates a quantum backaction limit, analogous to the Doppler limit of atomic laser cooling . This quantum backaction limit can be circumvented by introducing additional couplings to alter the dynamics of the cavity optomechanical system, such as dissipative optomechanical coupling or measurement and active feedback . Experimental implementations of cavity cooling for levitated nanoparticles have achieved significant cooling factors. For a particle placed at a node of the cavity field, axial cooling factors beyond 100 have been observed [3,4]. The observed performance implies that quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles can be achieved for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [3,4]. Maximal damping along the $x$ direction is obtained for minimal coherent scattering powers at $x_0 = \lambda / 4$, while maximal damping along the $z$ direction is obtained for maximal coherent scattering powers at $x_0 = 0$ [3,4]. In contrast, dark colors without cooling were observed when the detuning was set to $\Delta / 2\pi = 4$ MHz [3,4]. The resonant wavelength of the cavity in torsional optomechanics experiments is 1540 nm, which is different from that of the trapping laser , and another system utilized a wavelength corresponding to $\lambda_{o} = 1537$ nm . For cavity cooling of a trapped object in vacuum, it is important to use feedback cooling to pre-cool and stabilize the object, in order to have enough time to tune the cavity cooling laser to the correct frequency for efficient cooling [0,1]. In two-dimensional optomechanical crystal cavities, a $C_{eff}$ greater than unity under continuous-wave optical pumping has been achieved , although the $\beta = 0$ theoretical curve predicts substantially more cooling of the acoustic mode than measured, and the shape of the measured and theoretical curves are quite different . Gas damping and viscous drag serve as passive cooling mechanisms in controlled environments. The gas damping rate increases with gas pressure [6,7]. At the pressures in typical experiments, mechanical damping $\gamma$ is dominated by the collisions with the surrounding gas . As expected, the damping time scales inversely with pressure according to $t_{damp} \propto 1/p_{gas}$ . In ultrahigh vacuum, the damping ratio is extremely small, but optical cooling may add equivalent damping to be beneficial for feedback control . To reduce the fluctuating force disturbing the motion of levitated nanoparticles, researchers optically trap the particles inside a vacuum chamber connected to a closed-cycle cryostat to lower both the temperature and the pressure of the gas around the particle [2]. However, the cryocooler periodically compresses and expands the helium gas in the cold head, generating periodic mechanical vibrations on the optical table and the trap itself [2]. Focused by a high numerical aperture (NA = 0.75) lens, all-optical cold damping has been shown to be scalable for levitated nanoparticles [6,7]. Experimental efforts to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles have progressed from millikelvin regimes to the quantum ground state, with recent demonstrations providing opportunities for studying macroscopic quantum mechanics and precision measurements . Early milestones included feedback cooling of a levitated nanosphere to approximately 450 µK, corresponding to about 63 phonons at 150 kHz, and cavity cooling of the CoM motion to a few mK . In the context of torsional optomechanics, it was shown that only the torsional mode can be cooled to the ground state using a cavity with a length of 0.5 mm . This work represented an important step towards quantum ground state cooling of torsional vibration and testing recent theoretical proposals . More recent experiments have achieved lower temperatures and approached fundamental limits. Using feedback cooling, the CoM of a levitated nanodiamond was cooled in all three directions, reaching a minimum temperature of about 1.2 K along one direction . In a cryogenic free space environment, an experiment operating at 560 µW of local oscillator power, where optical shot noise was 14 dB above the electronic noise floor, approached the quantum limit to within 30% [2]. This setup utilized parametric feedback cooling implemented with three phase-locked loops integrated in a lock-in amplifier [2]. The performance of this system was limited by the fact that for any occupation number n > 1, the larger phase slope lowers the feedback gain at which the closed-loop system becomes unstable, thereby limiting cooling performance [2]. Environmental conditions in this cryogenic experiment included a cold plate temperature of 6 K and a PEEK lens holder temperature of 57 K when the laser was on [2]. Cavity cooling techniques have also shown significant potential for reaching the quantum ground state. For a particle placed at a node of the cavity field, axial cooling factors beyond 100 were observed [3,4]. The observed performance implies that quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles can be achieved for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [3,4]. Scalability of these cooling methods has been demonstrated, with feedback cooling techniques shown to be scalable to two particles [6,7]. A protocol combining parametric cooling along the z-axis with all-optical cold damping can achieve 3D cooling of multiple levitated particles by entirely optical means [6,7]. However, the relatively heavy mass of levitated nanoparticles, which is several femtograms, requires optical powers greater than 100 mW to trap a single nanoparticle, which is several orders of magnitude larger than for atoms [6,7]. Utilizing more efficient feedback cooling schemes and trapping smaller particles can lead to better force detection performance . Achieving quantum ground state cooling of the center-of-mass motion of a single optically levitated nanoparticle in vacuum has been demonstrated, providing opportunities for studying macroscopic quantum mechanics and precision measurements . In one such experiment, the center-of-mass motion was cooled by measurement-based feedback to an average occupancy of 0.65 motional quanta, corresponding to a state purity of 43% [2]. To reduce the fluctuating forces disturbing the particle's motion, nanoparticles are optically trapped inside a vacuum chamber connected to a closed-cycle cryostat with a nominal cold-plate temperature of 4 K, which lowers both the temperature and the pressure of the surrounding gas [2]. A primary limitation in reaching the quantum regime is the heating induced by gas collisions, where mechanical damping is dominated by collisions with the surrounding gas at typical experimental pressures . The gas damping rate increases with gas pressure, and in regimes of low feedback gain, the particle center-of-mass temperature is determined by the ratio of gas reheating and feedback cooling rates [6,7]. Consequently, quantum ground state cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles is estimated to be achievable only for background pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar [3,4]. At this pressure level, the torque sensitivity is limited only by photon shot noise, with an estimated value of $3.6 \pm 1.1 \times 10^{-31}$ Nm/ $\sqrt{Hz}$ . Optical absorption presents another significant challenge, as the bulk heating rate due to optical absorption is estimated to be approximately 2 K/ms for a trapping field intensity of $300\ mW/\mu m^{2}$ [2]. This heating effect prevents the simple increase of trapping laser intensity to improve cooling, as it induces heating that subsequently causes the loss of the nanoparticle . For instance, optically trapped nonspherical nanoparticles such as nanodiamonds and silicon nanorods were lost at about 1 torr due to laser heating . While coherent scattering schemes offer a significant suppression of laser phase noise heating, which is a specific feature of that approach, the fundamental issue of absorption-induced heating remains a barrier to increasing trap strength [3,4]. Technical noise sources further complicate the isolation of the particle from environmental perturbations. In experiments operating at $560 \mu W$ of local oscillator power, the optical shot noise is 14 dB above the electronic noise floor [2]. Although technical laser noise has been shown to have a negligible impact on sideband asymmetry in some optomechanical crystal resonator systems, the interplay between optical shot noise and electronic noise remains a critical factor in levitated systems . The field of quantum optomechanics promises motion and force detection near the fundamental limits imposed by quantum mechanics, yet current systems face deviations and errors that must be managed, such as percent errors below 0.6% and deviations of less than 0.3% in related mechanical resonator contexts . Additional complexities arise from the specific properties of the nanoparticles and their interactions. Particles may carry absolute charges, such as $|q_1| / e = 96 \pm 21$ and $|q_2| / e = 110 \pm 24$, which can influence their dynamics . For nonspherical particles, achieving quantum ground state cooling of torsional vibration is an important step towards testing recent theoretical proposals, though the specific parameters for torsional optomechanics vary significantly depending on the particle geometry and mode . The ability to reach the quantum regime is thus constrained by the combined effects of gas pressure, optical absorption heating, and technical noise floors, requiring pressures below $1 \times 10^{-7}$ mbar and careful management of laser-induced heating to prevent particle loss [3,4].
