question: What are ways to improve the behavior of the grating couplers?
raw_answer:
Standard uniform grating structures exhibit limited fiber coupling efficiency, a constraint that persists even in theoretical models where achieving fiber-to-chip insertion loss of a few percent is difficult [[hao_photonics_5:0]][[hao_photonics_5:1]]. The primary physical sources of this loss include radiation loss and scattering, which are influenced by the specific geometric design of the grating periods and structural parameters [[hao_photonics_5:2]]. For instance, in dual-layer grating couplers, waves scattered from lower grooves back to the fiber can accumulate a phase shift of $\pi$ relative to waves from adjacent upper grooves when each grating shows an optical thickness of $\lambda /4$, a mechanism that impacts the net coupling efficiency [[hao_photonics_5:2]]. Additionally, back-reflection is a significant factor, as optical fibers are often slightly tilted with respect to the vertical axis specifically to prevent large second-order reflections [[hao_photonics_5:1]].

Design constraints further limit the optimization of these devices, such as the requirement that the waveguide be suspended, which restricts the domain of applicability for certain fiber coupling methods [[hao_photonics_5:0]]. In cryogenic environments, total internal reflection at the fiber/air interface can send light into an on-chip grating coupler at the correct angle for efficient coupling, yet alignment-free coupling from an optical fiber to a silicon optomechanical crystal at 7 mK has been demonstrated with only 25% coupling efficiency [[hao_photonics_5:3]]. Similarly, co-designing the fiber angle (approximately 35.5°) with an apodized grating coupler realizes an optimized coupling efficiency of 52% for 1550 nm light, indicating that angular alignment and grating apodization are critical variables in managing mode mismatch and scattering [[hao_photonics_5:4]].

Despite these fundamental challenges, advanced design strategies and material overlays have improved performance metrics. A high efficiency Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay achieved a fiber coupling efficiency of 78% with a 3 dB optical bandwidth of 85 nm [[hao_photonics_5:1]]. In silicon nitride platforms, a multilayer bottom reflector enabled a peak coupling efficiency of -1.75 dB, corresponding to a measured fiber-to-detector insertion loss of -3.5 dB [[hao_photonics_5:5]]. Fully-automated optimization techniques have also yielded a single-wavelength grating coupler with under 0.2 dB insertion loss, while other implementations achieved an insertion loss of 1.94 dB, an improvement over the 2.12 dB reported in prior work [[hao_photonics_5:6]]. The highest experimentally measured coupling efficiency without the use of embedded back-reflectors is -0.9 dB, representing the current best result in that category [[hao_photonics_5:7]].

Structural modifications to grating couplers include the implementation of dual-layer designs, where the grating structure is defined by specific geometric parameters to enhance performance [[hao_photonics_5:8]]. In one such dual-layer design, the grating consists of 25 periods, with each period characterized by four distinct structural parameters [[hao_photonics_5:8]]. The width of this specific grating structure was measured at $15\mu\mathrm{m}$ [[hao_photonics_5:8]]. To determine the optimal values for these parameters, the design was optimized using the particle swarm algorithm, which employed a preset varying trend of parameters to reduce the number of optimization variables [[hao_photonics_5:8]].

Another approach to structural optimization involves the use of a poly-Silicon overlay on Silicon-on-Insulator platforms [[hao_photonics_5:9]]. In this configuration, the device is assumed to be anti-reflection coated for a wavelength of $1.55\mu\mathrm{m}$ [[hao_photonics_5:9]]. This overlay design achieves a bandwidth that exceeds the $60\mathrm{nm}$ 3dB bandwidth obtained in standard grating coupler structures [[hao_photonics_5:9]].

Multilayer bottom reflectors represent another structural modification, particularly in silicon nitride waveguide grating couplers [[hao_photonics_5:10]]. The design and optimization of such couplers with a bottom multilayer reflector utilize the two-dimensional (2D) finite difference time domain method (FDTD) [[hao_photonics_5:10]]. A specific implementation of this structure features a $13\mu\mathrm{m}$-wide and $30\mu\mathrm{m}$-long geometry [[hao_photonics_5:10]].

Conventional grating coupler designs, such as those for the $220\mathrm{nm}$ SOI platform, typically operate at a 10-degree incident angle with $100\mathrm{nm}$ feature sizes [[hao_photonics_5:11]]. While 2D optimization methods are common, the exact achieved efficiency in three dimensions depends on the length of the coupler in the third dimension [[hao_photonics_5:11]]. Alternative design strategies have been demonstrated to achieve specific performance metrics, including a maximum value of 39.8 [[hao_photonics_5:12]] and a length equal to 5.2 mm [[hao_photonics_5:12]].

The use of high-index contrast materials, such as silicon, has been shown to increase the 3dB bandwidth of grating couplers compared to standard structures [[hao_photonics_5:13]]. Specifically, a high-efficiency Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay achieved a bandwidth larger than the $60\mathrm{nm}$ obtained in standard grating coupler structures, a result attributed to the higher refractive index contrast in the proposed design [[hao_photonics_5:13]]. In contrast, silicon nitride waveguide grating couplers have also been developed to achieve high efficiency, with one design utilizing a multilayer bottom reflector [[hao_photonics_5:14]]. For the fabrication of such silicon nitride devices, a silicon wafer was used as the substrate [[hao_photonics_5:14]]. The number of grating periods in these silicon nitride designs was selected to be 18 or 20 for fabrication purposes [[hao_photonics_5:14]].

Structural parameters and geometric dimensions also play a critical role in the performance of these material systems. A highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler featured a grating width of $15\mu \mathrm{m}$ [[hao_photonics_5:15]]. This specific dual-layer design incorporated a grating with 25 periods, where each period was defined by four structural parameters [[hao_photonics_5:15]]. The coupling efficiency in such vertical configurations depends on the launch conditions, with $y-$ and $x$-polarized $\mathrm{LP}_{01}$ fiber modes being launched from a vertically aligned single-mode fiber having a core diameter of $9\mu \mathrm{m}$ and an index contrast of $0.36\%$ [[hao_photonics_5:15]]. While material contrast influences bandwidth, other design strategies focus on optimizing insertion loss; for instance, a fully-automated optimization approach yielded a single-wavelength grating coupler with under $0.2\mathrm{dB}$ insertion loss [[hao_photonics_5:16]]. Additionally, high-efficiency grating couplers have been demonstrated using a new design strategy that involves a length equal to 5.2 mm [[hao_photonics_5:17]].

Numerical simulation serves as the foundational step in modeling grating couplers, with the two-dimensional (2D) finite difference time domain (FDTD) method frequently employed for design and optimization tasks [[hao_photonics_5:18]]. To reduce computational costs, 2D FDTD is often applied instead of three-dimensional (3D) FDTD, a justification supported by the fact that typical waveguide widths are significantly larger than their heights [[hao_photonics_5:19]]. For instance, in a lithium niobate thin film waveguide design, the waveguide width of approximately $12~\mu\mathrm{m}$ was much bigger than its height of $0.5~\mu\mathrm{m}$, allowing for this simplification [[hao_photonics_5:19]]. While 2D simulations are efficient, 3D FDTD simulations are utilized to verify final performance, such as achieving $92\%$ and $85\%$ efficiencies for $y$- and $x$-polarizations, respectively, in a dual-layer grating coupler [[hao_photonics_5:20]].

Optimization algorithms are critical for navigating the complex parameter spaces of grating couplers, which can include multiple structural parameters per period [[hao_photonics_5:20]]. Genetic algorithms (GA) are particularly effective when the optimal design involves random variations in local grating period and duty cycle [[hao_photonics_5:21]]. In one study, a GA was used to optimize a Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay, with the smallest feature size constrained to $200\mathrm{nm}$ to ensure compatibility with CMOS deep UV lithography [[hao_photonics_5:21]]. The simulation results for such structures, including those with a grating duty cycle of $50\%$, are typically plotted to evaluate performance [[hao_photonics_5:21]]. This approach yielded a $3\mathrm{dB}$ bandwidth larger than the $60\mathrm{nm}$ obtained in standard grating coupler structures [[hao_photonics_5:21]].

Particle swarm algorithms (PSA) represent another robust optimization technique, often implemented within commercial FDTD solvers [[hao_photonics_5:20]]. In the design of a highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler, the first grating was chirped and optimized using the built-in particle swarm algorithm of a commercial FDTD solver in a 2D manner [[hao_photonics_5:20]]. This optimization targeted maximum coupled power at a $1550~\mathrm{nm}$ wavelength using $y$-polarized light [[hao_photonics_5:20]]. To manage the complexity of the optimization, a preset varying trend of parameters was used to thin out the optimization variables [[hao_photonics_5:20]].

Fully-automated optimization workflows have been developed to streamline the design process for specific platforms, such as the $220\mathrm{nm}$ SOI platform [[hao_photonics_5:22]]. In one such automated approach, a conventional grating coupler was designed for a 10-degree incident angle with $100\mathrm{nm}$ feature sizes [[hao_photonics_5:22]]. The total simulation time for these automated optimizations was approximately $2m$ hours on a single 6-core Intel Core i7 machine, where $m$ represents the number of modes [[hao_photonics_5:22]]. To ensure robustness, the optimization process was run 100 times using randomly generated initial conditions [[hao_photonics_5:22]]. These automated methods can also incorporate specific design suggestions, such as designing a blazed grating with a 50-degree slant [[hao_photonics_5:22]].

Recent design strategies have demonstrated that counter-intuitive approaches can yield superior results compared to traditional GA-optimized designs that do not use back-reflectors [[hao_photonics_5:23]]. For example, a high-efficiency grating coupler design achieved a maximum value of 39.8 and a length equal to $5.2~\mathrm{mm}$ [[hao_photonics_5:23]]. These structural designs substantially differ in their photonic response, highlighting the diversity of optimization outcomes [[hao_photonics_5:24]]. Additionally, impedance-matching sets of smaller holes have been used to reduce reflections off the grating, further illustrating the variety of structural modifications explored in numerical studies [[hao_photonics_5:25]].

Experimental and numerical studies on improved grating coupler designs report insertion losses as low as under $0.2\mathrm{dB}$ for single-wavelength devices [[hao_photonics_5:26]]. In a specific high-efficiency design strategy on a 260 nm Si-thick Silicon-on-insulator platform, a numerically demonstrated coupling efficiency of -0.8 dB (83%) closely matched the experimental value of -0.9 dB (81%) [[hao_photonics_5:27]]. The exact achieved efficiency in three-dimensional simulations depends on the length of the coupler in the third dimension [[hao_photonics_5:26]].

Regarding operational bandwidth, a grating coupler with a multilayer bottom reflector and N=20 exhibits a 3 dB bandwidth of 76.34 nm, which covers most of the operation frequencies of the C-band and L-band [[hao_photonics_5:28]]. A dual-layer grating coupler design achieves relatively wide 3 dB bandwidths of 56 nm for y-polarization and 58 nm for x-polarization [[hao_photonics_5:29]]. In contrast, a standard grating coupler structure yields a 60 nm 3 dB bandwidth, which is noted to be smaller than the bandwidth obtained in a poly-Silicon overlay based structure [[hao_photonics_5:30]]. Simulation results for the poly-Silicon overlay structure are plotted for a grating duty cycle of 50% [[hao_photonics_5:30]].

Polarization dependence remains a significant factor in grating coupler performance, as one-dimensional grating couplers are very polarization dependent [[hao_photonics_5:30]]. To address this, a polarization diversity scheme based on a two-dimensional grating coupler can be used in practical applications [[hao_photonics_5:30]]. The highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler demonstrates a polarization-dependent loss (PDL) below 2 dB within a 160 nm spectral bandwidth [[hao_photonics_5:29]]. This design also maintains cross talk between the two polarizations at less than -24 dB [[hao_photonics_5:29]].

Similarly, co-designing the fiber angle (approximately 35.5°) with an apodized grating coupler realizes an optimized coupling efficiency of 52% for 1550 nm light, indicating that angular alignment and grating apodization are critical variables in managing mode mismatch and scattering . Despite these fundamental challenges, advanced design strategies and material overlays have improved performance metrics. A high efficiency Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay achieved a fiber coupling efficiency of 78% with a 3 dB optical bandwidth of 85 nm [6]. In silicon nitride platforms, a multilayer bottom reflector enabled a peak coupling efficiency of -1.75 dB, corresponding to a measured fiber-to-detector insertion loss of -3.5 dB [4]. Fully-automated optimization techniques have also yielded a single-wavelength grating coupler with under 0.2 dB insertion loss, while other implementations achieved an insertion loss of 1.94 dB, an improvement over the 2.12 dB reported in prior work [1]. The highest experimentally measured coupling efficiency without the use of embedded back-reflectors is -0.9 dB, representing the current best result in that category [0]. Structural modifications to grating couplers include the implementation of dual-layer designs, where the grating structure is defined by specific geometric parameters to enhance performance [7]. In one such dual-layer design, the grating consists of 25 periods, with each period characterized by four distinct structural parameters [7]. The width of this specific grating structure was measured at $15\mu\mathrm{m}$ [7]. To determine the optimal values for these parameters, the design was optimized using the particle swarm algorithm, which employed a preset varying trend of parameters to reduce the number of optimization variables [7]. Another approach to structural optimization involves the use of a poly-Silicon overlay on Silicon-on-Insulator platforms [6]. In this configuration, the device is assumed to be anti-reflection coated for a wavelength of $1.55\mu\mathrm{m}$ [6]. This overlay design achieves a bandwidth that exceeds the $60\mathrm{nm}$ 3dB bandwidth obtained in standard grating coupler structures [6]. Multilayer bottom reflectors represent another structural modification, particularly in silicon nitride waveguide grating couplers [4]. The design and optimization of such couplers with a bottom multilayer reflector utilize the two-dimensional (2D) finite difference time domain method (FDTD) [4]. A specific implementation of this structure features a $13\mu\mathrm{m}$-wide and $30\mu\mathrm{m}$-long geometry [4]. Conventional grating coupler designs, such as those for the $220\mathrm{nm}$ SOI platform, typically operate at a 10-degree incident angle with $100\mathrm{nm}$ feature sizes [1]. While 2D optimization methods are common, the exact achieved efficiency in three dimensions depends on the length of the coupler in the third dimension [1]. Alternative design strategies have been demonstrated to achieve specific performance metrics, including a maximum value of 39.8 [0] and a length equal to 5.2 mm [0]. The use of high-index contrast materials, such as silicon, has been shown to increase the 3dB bandwidth of grating couplers compared to standard structures [6]. Specifically, a high-efficiency Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay achieved a bandwidth larger than the $60\mathrm{nm}$ obtained in standard grating coupler structures, a result attributed to the higher refractive index contrast in the proposed design [6]. In contrast, silicon nitride waveguide grating couplers have also been developed to achieve high efficiency, with one design utilizing a multilayer bottom reflector [4]. For the fabrication of such silicon nitride devices, a silicon wafer was used as the substrate [4]. The number of grating periods in these silicon nitride designs was selected to be 18 or 20 for fabrication purposes [4]. Structural parameters and geometric dimensions also play a critical role in the performance of these material systems. A highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler featured a grating width of $15\mu \mathrm{m}$ [7]. This specific dual-layer design incorporated a grating with 25 periods, where each period was defined by four structural parameters [7]. The coupling efficiency in such vertical configurations depends on the launch conditions, with $y-$ and $x$-polarized $\mathrm{LP}_{01}$ fiber modes being launched from a vertically aligned single-mode fiber having a core diameter of $9\mu \mathrm{m}$ and an index contrast of $0.36\%$ [7]. While material contrast influences bandwidth, other design strategies focus on optimizing insertion loss; for instance, a fully-automated optimization approach yielded a single-wavelength grating coupler with under $0.2\mathrm{dB}$ insertion loss [1]. Additionally, high-efficiency grating couplers have been demonstrated using a new design strategy that involves a length equal to 5.2 mm [0]. Numerical simulation serves as the foundational step in modeling grating couplers, with the two-dimensional (2D) finite difference time domain (FDTD) method frequently employed for design and optimization tasks [4]. To reduce computational costs, 2D FDTD is often applied instead of three-dimensional (3D) FDTD, a justification supported by the fact that typical waveguide widths are significantly larger than their heights [5]. For instance, in a lithium niobate thin film waveguide design, the waveguide width of approximately $12~\mu\mathrm{m}$ was much bigger than its height of $0.5~\mu\mathrm{m}$, allowing for this simplification [5]. While 2D simulations are efficient, 3D FDTD simulations are utilized to verify final performance, such as achieving $92\%$ and $85\%$ efficiencies for $y$- and $x$-polarizations, respectively, in a dual-layer grating coupler [7]. Optimization algorithms are critical for navigating the complex parameter spaces of grating couplers, which can include multiple structural parameters per period [7]. Genetic algorithms (GA) are particularly effective when the optimal design involves random variations in local grating period and duty cycle [6]. In one study, a GA was used to optimize a Silicon-on-Insulator grating coupler based on a poly-Silicon overlay, with the smallest feature size constrained to $200\mathrm{nm}$ to ensure compatibility with CMOS deep UV lithography [6]. The simulation results for such structures, including those with a grating duty cycle of $50\%$, are typically plotted to evaluate performance [6]. This approach yielded a $3\mathrm{dB}$ bandwidth larger than the $60\mathrm{nm}$ obtained in standard grating coupler structures [6]. Particle swarm algorithms (PSA) represent another robust optimization technique, often implemented within commercial FDTD solvers [7]. In the design of a highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler, the first grating was chirped and optimized using the built-in particle swarm algorithm of a commercial FDTD solver in a 2D manner [7]. This optimization targeted maximum coupled power at a $1550~\mathrm{nm}$ wavelength using $y$-polarized light [7]. To manage the complexity of the optimization, a preset varying trend of parameters was used to thin out the optimization variables [7]. Fully-automated optimization workflows have been developed to streamline the design process for specific platforms, such as the $220\mathrm{nm}$ SOI platform [1]. In one such automated approach, a conventional grating coupler was designed for a 10-degree incident angle with $100\mathrm{nm}$ feature sizes [1]. The total simulation time for these automated optimizations was approximately $2m$ hours on a single 6-core Intel Core i7 machine, where $m$ represents the number of modes [1]. To ensure robustness, the optimization process was run 100 times using randomly generated initial conditions [1]. These automated methods can also incorporate specific design suggestions, such as designing a blazed grating with a 50-degree slant [1]. Recent design strategies have demonstrated that counter-intuitive approaches can yield superior results compared to traditional GA-optimized designs that do not use back-reflectors [0]. For example, a high-efficiency grating coupler design achieved a maximum value of 39.8 and a length equal to $5.2~\mathrm{mm}$ [0]. These structural designs substantially differ in their photonic response, highlighting the diversity of optimization outcomes . Additionally, impedance-matching sets of smaller holes have been used to reduce reflections off the grating, further illustrating the variety of structural modifications explored in numerical studies . Experimental and numerical studies on improved grating coupler designs report insertion losses as low as under $0.2\mathrm{dB}$ for single-wavelength devices [1]. In a specific high-efficiency design strategy on a 260 nm Si-thick Silicon-on-insulator platform, a numerically demonstrated coupling efficiency of -0.8 dB (83%) closely matched the experimental value of -0.9 dB (81%) [0]. The exact achieved efficiency in three-dimensional simulations depends on the length of the coupler in the third dimension [1]. Regarding operational bandwidth, a grating coupler with a multilayer bottom reflector and N=20 exhibits a 3 dB bandwidth of 76.34 nm, which covers most of the operation frequencies of the C-band and L-band [4]. A dual-layer grating coupler design achieves relatively wide 3 dB bandwidths of 56 nm for y-polarization and 58 nm for x-polarization [7]. In contrast, a standard grating coupler structure yields a 60 nm 3 dB bandwidth, which is noted to be smaller than the bandwidth obtained in a poly-Silicon overlay based structure [6]. Simulation results for the poly-Silicon overlay structure are plotted for a grating duty cycle of 50% [6]. Polarization dependence remains a significant factor in grating coupler performance, as one-dimensional grating couplers are very polarization dependent [6]. To address this, a polarization diversity scheme based on a two-dimensional grating coupler can be used in practical applications [6]. The highly efficient and perfectly vertical chip-to-fiber dual-layer grating coupler demonstrates a polarization-dependent loss (PDL) below 2 dB within a 160 nm spectral bandwidth [7]. This design also maintains cross talk between the two polarizations at less than -24 dB [7].

question: What are ways to modulate the gigahertz surface acoustic waves?
raw_answer:
The modulation of gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) relies on distinct physical mechanisms that allow for the control of amplitude, phase, and frequency through electrical, thermal, and structural means. Electrical modulation is achieved by applying signals to electrodes, where maximum modulation occurs when the traveling acoustic wave and the modulating signal are phase-matched, while zero modulation is observed when they are phase-mismatched by any positive integer number of $2\pi$ phases [[hao_photonics_6:0]]. This electrical control enables the modulation of both the phase and amplitude of acoustic waves, and can be utilized to demonstrate an acoustic frequency shifter via serrodyne phase modulation [[hao_photonics_6:0]]. In such electrical phase modulators, the application of a DC bias voltage on the modulation electrode results in a $\sim \pi /2$ phase shift of the acoustic wave [[hao_photonics_6:0]]. The performance of these electrical modulators is characterized by specific bandwidths; for instance, a 1-cm phase modulator has a measured 3-dB bandwidth of $110\mathrm{kHz}$ [[hao_photonics_6:0]]. While electrical methods offer precise control, alternative approaches such as those relying on thermal excitations of charge carriers in semiconductors inevitably induce loss and noise, and are incompatible with cryogenic temperatures, which precludes their use in quantum applications [[hao_photonics_6:0]].

Thermal modulation provides another mechanism for controlling SAWs, specifically demonstrated on lithium niobate at an input acoustic frequency of 2.45 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:1]]. In thermal phase modulators, the amplitude of the transmission parameter $S_{21}$ remains unchanged when the heater is switched on, while the phase of $S_{21}$ is shifted [[hao_photonics_6:1]]. This indicates that thermal energy primarily affects the phase velocity or propagation characteristics without altering the signal strength in the same manner as amplitude modulators.

Structural and material properties also play a fundamental role in defining the modulation landscape. The velocity of piezoelectric acoustic waves is perturbed when the surface electrical boundary condition of the piezoelectric is changed from electrically open to shorted, a perturbation denoted as $\Delta\nu(0)$ [[hao_photonics_6:2]]. This velocity change is linked to the coupling coefficient $\kappa$, the displacement vector $u$, and the wave vector $k$ in the context of acoustic resonators [[hao_photonics_6:3]]. The geometric design of the devices further dictates their operational parameters; for example, the interdigital transducer (IDT) pitch can be as small as $p = 0.985 \mu m$ [[hao_photonics_6:4]]. Similarly, the operating frequency of nonlinear parity–time symmetric resonators can be adjusted from a hundred megahertz to a few gigahertz by geometrically scaling the design, with 200 MHz chosen for simplicity in electronic circuit design [[hao_photonics_6:5]].

In the domain of quantum and high-frequency applications, the manipulation of SAWs involves complex interactions and specific device architectures. SAW mirrors reflect acoustic waves efficiently within a stop band, such as from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:6]]. The characterization of quantum states in these systems involves amplifier chains defined by an effective amplitude gain $\sqrt{G}$ and an effective added mean photon number $n$ [[hao_photonics_6:7]]. Measurements of these quantum states may utilize optical power meters, whose dynamic range is much larger than that of a voltmeter, allowing for accurate determination of the DC bias voltage of the detector for any amplitude of optical signal [[hao_photonics_6:8]]. Furthermore, multimode entanglement and squeezing of SAW phonons have been observed, with specific mode pairings such as {2}: {1,3,4} yielding a value of -2.4 and {1,2}: {3,4} yielding -2.9 [[hao_photonics_6:7]]. Despite these advances, high-acoustic-index-contrast phononic waveguides remain elusive, preventing intricate manipulation of phonons on par with its photonic counterpart [[hao_photonics_6:9]].

Electrostatic and piezoelectric effects provide mechanisms for dynamically adjusting surface acoustic wave (SAW) properties, with tunable devices historically achieved through mechanical nonlinear deformations, piezoelectrically-actuated deformation, and electro-acoustic effects [[hao_photonics_6:10]]. These conventional approaches have typically required high voltages to achieve a full $\pi$ phase shift [[hao_photonics_6:10]]. In standard substrates such as lithium niobate (LN), the strong piezoelectricity allows for fully tunable gain, loss, and nonlinearity for SAWs using electric circuitry [[hao_photonics_6:11]]. For instance, SAW devices fabricated on a $128^{\circ}$ Y-cut LN substrate with propagation in the X-direction of the crystal leverage these material properties for such modulation [[hao_photonics_6:11]].

Specific electrical control methods rely on non-zero electro-acoustic modulation coefficients, such as $d_{255} = d_{145}$, to interact with acoustic waves [[hao_photonics_6:12]]. In one implementation, an acoustic wave is input at a carrier frequency $f_{\mathrm{c}} \sim 2.5$ GHz, with a device featuring a finger electrode pitch of $650~\mathrm{nm}$ [[hao_photonics_6:12]]. The acoustic group velocity in such devices is inferred to be $v_{g} = 3.36\mathrm{km / s}$, which is consistent with the simulated velocity of $3.38\mathrm{km / s}$ [[hao_photonics_6:12]]. When a DC bias voltage is applied on the modulation electrode, a $\sim \pi /2$ phase shift of the acoustic wave is observed [[hao_photonics_6:12]]. Maximum modulation occurs when the traveling acoustic wave and the modulating signal are phase-matched, whereas zero modulation is observed when they are phase-mismatched by any positive integer number of $2\pi$ phases [[hao_photonics_6:12]].

In advanced semiconductor–piezoelectric heterostructures, electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity offers another avenue for modulation. The perturbation in velocity of the piezoelectric acoustic wave, denoted as $\Delta\nu(0)$, is defined when the surface electrical boundary condition of the piezoelectric is changed from electrically open to shorted [[hao_photonics_6:13]]. In these heterostructures, the acoustic velocity in the silicon can exceed the acoustic velocity for the acoustic modes supported in the $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{3}$ [[hao_photonics_6:13]]. At a velocity ratio equal to 1, the linear acoustoelectric coefficient is zero and the nonlinear acoustoelectric coefficient reaches a minimum value [[hao_photonics_6:13]].

Quantum and high-frequency applications also utilize these tuning principles. SAW cavity modes designed to fall in the band $3.8 - 3.9\mathrm{GHz}$ are used in experiments involving squeezed and multimode entangled phonons [[hao_photonics_6:14]]. In such quantum control experiments, the magnetic flux through a SQUID is modulated without dc flux bias at the frequency of a SAW mode [[hao_photonics_6:14]]. Additionally, SAW mirrors reflect acoustic waves efficiently in the mirror stop band from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:15]]. While thermal modulation on lithium niobate at an input acoustic frequency of 2.45 GHz has been studied with a heater driven at 0.2 W [[hao_photonics_6:10]], the primary focus of electrostatic and piezoelectric tuning remains on the direct electrical manipulation of wave velocity and phase as described in the electrical control and heterostructure studies [[hao_photonics_6:12]][[hao_photonics_6:13]][[hao_photonics_6:11]].

Mechanical and structural modulation of gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) relies on the unique physical properties of acoustic media, where SAWs propagate at a velocity five orders of magnitude smaller than electromagnetic waves at the same frequency [[hao_photonics_6:16]]. This velocity difference results in SAW devices having much smaller wavelengths than their electromagnetic counterparts [[hao_photonics_6:16]], with acoustic waves featuring five-orders-of-magnitude shorter wavelengths and not radiating into free-space compared to gigahertz electromagnetic waves [[hao_photonics_6:17]]. These structural characteristics enable the use of phononic crystals and metamaterials to create specific bandgaps and control wave propagation. For instance, a phononic crystal geometry can be designed with a bandgap extending from approximately 1.90 to 2.50 GHz and a pitch of $a = 900 \, nm$ [[hao_photonics_6:18]]. Similarly, an acoustic shield consisting of a two-dimensional “cross” pattern has been shown to yield a substantial phononic bandgap in the GHz frequency band [[hao_photonics_6:19]]. In other configurations, an acoustic guided-mode bandgap can extend from 10 to 10.6 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:20]].

Structural elements such as SAW mirrors are utilized to reflect acoustic waves efficiently within specific stop bands, such as from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:21]]. The fabrication of these structures often involves precise thickness control; for example, in bulk acoustic-wave resonators, the etching process is stopped when the maximum thickness of the AlN is approximately $\lambda/2$, where $\lambda$ is the acoustic wavelength at the qubit frequency [[hao_photonics_6:22]]. Geometric scaling allows for the adjustment of operating frequencies, as demonstrated in non-reciprocal transmission devices where an operating frequency of 200 MHz can be adjusted from a hundred megahertz to a few gigahertz by geometrically scaling the design [[hao_photonics_6:23]]. These devices are typically fabricated on a $128^{\circ}$ Y-cut lithium niobate (LN) substrate, with the SAW propagating in the X-direction of the crystal [[hao_photonics_6:23]]. The strong piezoelectricity of lithium niobate is leveraged to demonstrate fully tunable gain, loss, and nonlinearity for surface acoustic waves using electric circuitry [[hao_photonics_6:23]].

While most acoustic devices are currently linear, passive, and reciprocal components which limit their functionality [[hao_photonics_6:16]], mechanical and structural approaches offer pathways for modulation. In phononic integrated circuitry, a sinusoidally varying rotation is applied to the system with a peak rate at 0.667 Hz to induce spin–orbit interaction of phonons [[hao_photonics_6:24]]. The structural design of interdigital transducers (IDTs) is critical for defining the acoustic properties, with an IDT pitch of $p = 0.985 \, \mu m$ reported in quantum erasure experiments using entangled surface acoustic phonons [[hao_photonics_6:25]]. These structural and mechanical configurations facilitate the generation and control of quantum states, such as multimode entanglement where specific mode pairs exhibit correlation values like -2.9 for {1,2}: {3,4} [[hao_photonics_6:26]] and -13.7 for {1}: {2,3,4} [[hao_photonics_6:26]]. Although the primary focus here is mechanical and structural modulation, these physical structures often operate in conjunction with electrical or thermal inputs, such as input acoustic frequencies of 2.45 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:16]] or carrier frequencies of $f_{\mathrm{c}} \sim 2.5$ GHz [[hao_photonics_6:17]], to achieve comprehensive control over the SAWs.

Thermal modulation of gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) has been demonstrated on lithium niobate substrates, providing an efficient and stable approach for on-chip control of SAWs [[hao_photonics_6:27]]. In these thermo-acoustic modulators, an input acoustic frequency of 2.45 GHz was utilized to characterize the system response [[hao_photonics_6:27]]. The single pass travel time of the acoustic wave in such configurations is approximately 450 ns [[hao_photonics_6:27]]. Furthermore, amplitude modulation of SAWs was achieved using acoustic Mach Zehnder interferometers [[hao_photonics_6:27]]. While the primary focus of this section is thermal and optical techniques, it is noted that electrical control mechanisms also exist, where maximum modulation is observed when the traveling acoustic wave and the modulating signal are phase-matched, and zero modulation occurs when they are phase-mismatched by any positive integer number of $2\pi$ phases [[hao_photonics_6:28]]. In electrical control devices employing a non-zero electro-acoustic modulation coefficient $d_{255} = d_{145}$, a $\sim \pi /2$ phase shift of the acoustic wave is observed when a DC bias voltage is applied on the modulation electrode [[hao_photonics_6:28]]. The electro-acoustic effect is a parametric process that occurs at both room and millikelvin temperatures and is analogous to the electro-optic effect widely utilized to control the phase and amplitude of optical signals [[hao_photonics_6:28]].

Optical excitation and photoacoustic effects offer another avenue for modulating acoustic waves, although specific gigahertz SAW modulation via this method is less directly detailed in the provided excerpts compared to thermal or electrical methods. The photoacoustic effect, which relies on the excitation of short-pulsed laser light in the NIR range to induce thermoelastic expansion resulting in detectable ultrasound waves, has been applied in medical imaging contexts [[hao_photonics_6:29]]. In the realm of cavity opto-mechanics, it is important to note that despite the small amplitude of mechanical oscillations, the modulation index of the transmitted optical pump wave can be very high, even reaching 100% [[hao_photonics_6:30]]. This high modulation index in optical systems parallels the potential for significant modulation in acoustic systems, though the specific mechanism for gigahertz SAWs via optical pumping is not explicitly detailed in the provided thermal SAW literature.

The modulation of SAWs is also influenced by the structural and material properties of the devices. In semiconductor–piezoelectric heterostructures, the perturbation in velocity of the piezoelectric acoustic wave, denoted as $\Delta\nu(0)$, occurs when the surface electrical boundary condition of the piezoelectric is changed from electrically open to shorted [[hao_photonics_6:31]]. This velocity perturbation is a key parameter in understanding how external conditions modulate the acoustic wave. In compact acoustic resonators, the coupling coefficient $\kappa$, displacement vector $u$, and wave vector $k$ are fundamental parameters in describing the system's behavior [[hao_photonics_6:32]]. For quantum control applications, SAW mirrors reflect acoustic waves efficiently in the mirror stop band, with one example operating from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:33]]. The ripples in the out-of-band mirror reflection in such systems arise from the finite extent of each mirror, which may consist of 500 lines [[hao_photonics_6:33]]. At experiment temperatures of about 10 mK, both the SAWs and the qubit should be in their quantum ground states for quantum control experiments [[hao_photonics_6:33]].

Device geometry and fabrication parameters also play a role in the modulation characteristics. In one electrical control device, the pitch of the finger electrode is 650 nm [[hao_photonics_6:28]]. In another context involving quantum erasure using entangled surface acoustic phonons, the IDT pitch is specified as $p = 0.985 \mu m$ [[hao_photonics_6:34]]. In designs aiming to minimize the reflection effect of IDT2 on the acoustic wave, specific structural considerations are employed [[hao_photonics_6:35]]. Non-reciprocal transmission of microwave acoustic waves in nonlinear parity–time symmetric resonators shows that at a lower input power of 250 nW, SAWs propagating in both directions experience linear gain, and thus no significant nonreciprocity is observed [[hao_photonics_6:36]]. Similar to optical systems, this saturation nonlinearity breaks the time-reversal symmetry for SAWs, but not the dynamic reciprocity [[hao_photonics_6:36]].

In the context of quantum states and entanglement, which can be affected by modulation techniques, specific correlation values have been reported for multimode entanglement of surface acoustic wave phonons. For the partition {2}: {1,3,4}, the value is -2.4 [[hao_photonics_6:37]]. For the partition {1,2}: {3,4}, the value is -2.9 [[hao_photonics_6:37]]. For the partition {1}: {2,3,4}, the value is -13.7 [[hao_photonics_6:37]]. These values indicate the strength of entanglement between different modes, which is a critical aspect of quantum acoustic systems that may be modulated by thermal or optical means.

The modulation of gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) is increasingly enabled by the integration of novel material properties and nanoscale structural designs, which allow for precise control over acoustic propagation, phase, and non-reciprocity. In the domain of electrical modulation, devices utilizing a non-zero electro-acoustic modulation coefficient $d_{255} = d_{145}$ have been developed to manipulate SAWs [[hao_photonics_6:38]]. Experimental observations indicate that maximum modulation occurs when the traveling acoustic wave and the modulating signal are phase-matched, whereas zero modulation is observed when they are phase-mismatched by any positive integer number of $2\pi$ phases [[hao_photonics_6:38]]. Furthermore, the application of a DC bias voltage on the modulation electrode results in a $\sim \pi /2$ phase shift of the acoustic wave [[hao_photonics_6:38]]. This electrical control mechanism is notable for its low noise impact, as the modulation process has been experimentally verified to add less than one noise phonon [[hao_photonics_6:38]].

The strong piezoelectricity of lithium niobate (LN) serves as a foundational material property for these modulation techniques, enabling fully tunable gain, loss, and nonlinearity for surface acoustic waves using electric circuitry [[hao_photonics_6:39]]. Specific device implementations utilize $128^{\circ}$ Y-cut LN substrates, where the SAW propagates in the X-direction of the crystal [[hao_photonics_6:39]]. In such systems, non-reciprocal transmission is achieved when signals applied to succeeding modulation electrode segments are phase delayed by $120^{\circ}$ and the modulation frequency matches the total traveling time of the acoustic wave [[hao_photonics_6:38]]. These electrical modulation strategies operate at specific input acoustic frequencies, such as 2.45 GHz, which are characteristic of gigahertz SAW applications [[hao_photonics_6:40]].

Beyond standard piezoelectric substrates, the incorporation of different materials alters the fundamental acoustic properties of the device. For instance, silicon nitride (SiN) is a harder material with larger stiffness coefficients than LN, which allows for a larger acoustic velocity [[hao_photonics_6:40]]. This material difference contributes to the fact that SAW devices have much smaller wavelengths than their electromagnetic counterparts [[hao_photonics_6:40]]. The structural design of these devices often involves specific geometric parameters, such as an interdigital transducer (IDT) pitch of $p = 0.985 \mu m$ [[hao_photonics_6:41]]. In compact acoustic resonators, the interaction between the coupling coefficient $\kappa$, displacement vector $u$, and wave vector $k$ defines the bound states in the continuum (BIC) [[hao_photonics_6:42]]. While the topological properties of the revealed acoustic BIC remain a matter of further research [[hao_photonics_6:42]], nonperiodic individual optical and mechanical resonators offer the advantage of more easily having confined fields with strong modal intensity at the micro/nanoscale compared to devices based on periodic structures [[hao_photonics_6:43]].

Nanoscale and quantum-scale structures further expand the modulation capabilities of SAWs by enabling quantum control and high-efficiency coupling. SAW mirrors have been designed to reflect acoustic waves efficiently within a stop band ranging from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:44]]. Similarly, SAW cavity modes can be designed to fall within the 3.8 - 3.9 GHz band [[hao_photonics_6:45]]. In quantum experiments, the magnetic flux through a SQUID is modulated without dc flux bias at the frequency of a SAW mode to achieve quantum control [[hao_photonics_6:45]]. These quantum acoustic systems exhibit complex entanglement structures, with specific mode pairings such as {2}: {1,3,4} yielding a value of -2.4 and {1,2}: {3,4} yielding -2.9 [[hao_photonics_6:45]]. The integration of optical and mechanical components at the nanoscale allows for highly efficient coupling, with single pass coupling efficiencies reaching $\eta_{c} \sim 92\%$ in silicon optomechanical cavities [[hao_photonics_6:46]]. Additionally, topological edge states have been directly measured in non-Hermitian systems, matching excellently with non-Bloch topological invariants calculated from localized bulk-state wave functions [[hao_photonics_6:47]].

Modulated gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are utilized in quantum systems where SAW cavity modes are designed to fall within the 3.8–3.9 GHz band [[hao_photonics_6:48]]. In these quantum applications, the IDT pitch is specified as p = 0.985 μm [[hao_photonics_6:49]], and the number of IDT finger pairs is set to N = 20 [[hao_photonics_6:49]]. The frequency dependence of the IDT and mirrors provides a bandwidth of around 40 MHz around the IDT center frequency where SAW modes are overcoupled [[hao_photonics_6:48]]. Experimental results in these multimode systems report specific entanglement values, such as -2.4 for the partition {2}: {1,3,4} [[hao_photonics_6:48]], -2.9 for the partition {1,2}: {3,4} [[hao_photonics_6:48]], and -13.7 for the partition {1}: {2,3,4} [[hao_photonics_6:48]].

For signal processing and modulation, SAW devices operate at carrier frequencies such as $f_{\mathrm{c}} \sim 2.5$ GHz [[hao_photonics_6:50]] or an input acoustic frequency of 2.45 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:51]]. The SAW mirror reflects acoustic waves efficiently in the mirror stop band from 3.96 GHz to 4.04 GHz [[hao_photonics_6:52]]. In electro-acoustic modulators, the number of finger electrode pairs per IDT is 25 [[hao_photonics_6:50]]. Maximum modulation is observed when the traveling acoustic wave and the modulating signal are phase-matched, while zero modulation occurs when they are phase-mismatched by any positive integer number of $2\pi$ phases [[hao_photonics_6:50]]. The modulation efficiency approaches zero every time when the modulation frequency is an integer multiple (N) of $f_{\mathrm{mod}} = 336\mathrm{kHz}$ [[hao_photonics_6:50]].

Thermal modulation of gigahertz SAWs on lithium niobate involves driving a heater at a power of 0.2 W [[hao_photonics_6:51]]. The acoustic-wave bandwidths of these thermo-acoustic modulators are determined by their IDTs [[hao_photonics_6:51]]. This electrical control enables the modulation of both the phase and amplitude of acoustic waves, and can be utilized to demonstrate an acoustic frequency shifter via serrodyne phase modulation [2,3]. In such electrical phase modulators, the application of a DC bias voltage on the modulation electrode results in a $\sim \pi /2$ phase shift of the acoustic wave [2,3]. question: What other systems, besides photonic crystals, have demonstrated bound states in the continuum?
raw_answer:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are defined as a type of eigenstates that possess infinite lifetime while spectrally overlapping with lossy states in the continuum [[hao_photonics_7:0]]. This concept is a general wave phenomenon that was first mathematically proposed in 1929 by von Neumann and Wigner for electronic states [[hao_photonics_7:1]]. According to this definition, a BIC is completely decoupled from all propagating waves of the surrounding space, which means it cannot be excited from the far-field by pressure waves [[hao_photonics_7:2]]. In the context of optical systems, a resonance turns into a BIC when the outgoing power is zero, a condition that occurs if and only if the coefficients $c_{x}$ and $c_{y}$ are both zero [[hao_photonics_7:3]].

The most trivial mechanism for the formation of BICs is due to the symmetry of the structure, where the BIC and the continuous-spectrum modes have incompatible symmetries [[hao_photonics_7:4]]. To date, most experimental demonstrations of BICs in optics and mechanics are based on periodic structures with certain symmetry [[hao_photonics_7:0]]. For such systems, if the structure also has up-down mirror symmetry ($\sigma_{z}$), the outgoing waves on one side of the slab determine those on the other, and BICs are stable because they correspond to the intersections between the nodal line of $c_{x}$ and the nodal line of $c_{y}$ in the $k_{x}-k_{y}$ plane [[hao_photonics_7:3]]. In compact acoustic resonators, the requirement for BIC existence is fulfilled for resonators with an infinite-fold rotation axis-like cylinder, cone, or dimer, which belong to the $D_{\infty h}$ and $D_{\infty v}$ symmetry groups [[hao_photonics_7:2]]. Consequently, genuine acoustic bound states in the continuum may exist in compact solid resonators with a rotational symmetry placed in a gas or nonviscous fluid environment [[hao_photonics_7:2]].

Beyond symmetry-protected mechanisms, topological properties also enable the existence of BICs. In slab-on-substrate photonic crystals, robust existence of accidental mechanical BICs with integer topological charges has been found despite z-symmetry breaking, which contrasts with the optical case [[hao_photonics_7:5]]. When sample periodicity is tuned, BICs with $\pm1$ topological charges can merge into an isolated one with charge +1 [[hao_photonics_7:6]]. In comparison to standard BICs, when there are also off-center BICs at $\pm k_{BIC}$, the inverse quality factor $\sqrt{1/Q}$ becomes proportional to $(k + k_{\mathrm{BIC}})(k - k_{\mathrm{BIC}})k$ [[hao_photonics_7:6]].

Symmetry breaking transforms these ideal states into observable quasi-BICs. By breaking the axial symmetry of the structure, symmetry-protected BICs become quasi-trapped leaky modes coupled to the propagating modes of the waveguides [[hao_photonics_7:4]]. Similarly, breaking the resonator's symmetry turns BICs into quasi-BICs, which manifest themselves in the scattering spectra as high-Q Fano resonances [[hao_photonics_7:2]]. In plasmonic systems, breaking the symmetry by making bars optically different causes hybridized modes to no longer be purely symmetric or anti-symmetric, making interference via radiation possible [[hao_photonics_7:7]]. In contrast to conventional BICs requiring certain symmetry, demonstrated mechanical BICs represent a new paradigm for constructing high-Q micromechanical resonators through symmetry breaking [[hao_photonics_7:0]]. This approach has been utilized in optomechanical crystals empowered by mechanical BICs at 8 GHz [[hao_photonics_7:8]]. While acoustic waves feature five-orders-of-magnitude shorter wavelength than gigahertz electromagnetic waves and do not radiate into free-space [[hao_photonics_7:9]], the relative standard deviation of fitting for observed phonon trapping in the continuum is typically less than 1% [[hao_photonics_7:5]].

Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are defined as eigenstates possessing infinite lifetime while spectrally overlapping with lossy states in the continuum [[hao_photonics_7:10]]. In acoustic and elastic wave systems, these states manifest as mechanical BICs that can be confined within slabs due to symmetry-induced decoupling from the acoustic radiation field [[hao_photonics_7:11]]. For finite-size structures, the existence of BICs is theoretically prohibited by the nonexistence theorem because the number of scattering channels is infinite [[hao_photonics_7:12]]. However, practical implementations utilize compact acoustic resonators that consist of radiative modes and BICs with infinitely high radiative Q factors [[hao_photonics_7:12]]. The mathematical description of these systems involves a coupling coefficient $\kappa$, a displacement vector $u$, and a wave vector $k$ [[hao_photonics_7:12]]. In specific two-dimensional cavity configurations, such as those with a length $L_{y}=2$, transmittance characteristics are analyzed to understand the wave behavior [[hao_photonics_7:13]], often with specific geometric parameters like $d = 1$ [[hao_photonics_7:13]].

Mechanical BICs have been realized in optomechanical microresonators, representing a new paradigm for constructing high-Q micromechanical resonators through symmetry breaking, in contrast to conventional BICs that require certain symmetry [[hao_photonics_7:10]]. In one such implementation, mechanical BICs were observed at 8 GHz [[hao_photonics_7:11]]. The tuning of these resonant frequencies can be achieved by fixing a radius $R = 26.1 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and varying another parameter $r$, which leads to a crossing of resonant frequencies [[hao_photonics_7:10]]. Furthermore, phonon trapping in the continuum has been realized using mechanical BICs with topological features [[hao_photonics_7:14]]. In this paradigm, phonons in the BIC mode are trapped in the unreleased slab without coupling into the substrate, irrespective of the acoustic impedance of the slab and substrate materials [[hao_photonics_7:14]]. Quantitative analysis of these topological phonon trapping systems shows that the relative standard deviation of the fitting is typically less than 1% [[hao_photonics_7:14]].

Topological features also enable ultrahigh-Q guided resonances that are robust to out-of-plane scattering [[hao_photonics_7:15]]. When off-center BICs exist at $\pm k_{BIC}$, the inverse square root of the quality factor, $\sqrt{1/Q}$, becomes proportional to $(k + k_{\mathrm{BIC}})(k - k_{\mathrm{BIC}})k$ [[hao_photonics_7:15]]. More importantly, when multiple BICs are designed to merge, all nearby modes enjoy significant enhancements of their Qs due to a modified scaling rule [[hao_photonics_7:15]]. These elastic wave systems often involve materials with specific anisotropic properties; for instance, sapphire with a trigonal crystal structure has six independent elastic constants and shows anisotropic elastic properties [[hao_photonics_7:16]]. In modeling such systems, silicon may be treated as a hyperelastic material with a user-defined elastic strain energy density [[hao_photonics_7:17]]. Other acoustic wave implementations include non-reciprocal transmission of microwave acoustic waves in nonlinear parity–time symmetric resonators, where the external Bragg mirror consists of 54 grooves [[hao_photonics_7:18]]. Additionally, phononic integrated circuits have demonstrated spin–orbit interaction of phonons, where a sinusoidally varying rotation is applied to the system with a peak rate at 0.667 Hz [[hao_photonics_7:19]], and phase responses are acquired at rotation rates varying from 0.083 Hz to 0.667 Hz [[hao_photonics_7:19]].

Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are defined as eigenstates with infinite lifetime that spectrally overlap with lossy states in the continuum [[hao_photonics_7:20]]. While often associated with photonic crystals, these modes are also manifested in plasmonic and metasurface systems, where they remain ideally confined despite compatibility with free-space radiation [[hao_photonics_7:21]]. In anisotropic plasmonic metasurfaces, the existence of BICs is investigated by varying the period of the unit cell from 2.8 to 3.2 $\mu$m while keeping other parameters fixed [[hao_photonics_7:22]]. Numerical simulations of these systems typically employ periodic boundary conditions in the x- and y-directions and perfectly matched layer (PML) conditions in the z-direction [[hao_photonics_7:22]]. However, the experimental observation of BICs in plasmonic nanostructures is hindered by high losses in the materials [[hao_photonics_7:23]].

In contrast to plasmonic systems, dielectric metasurfaces enable the realization of high-Q resonances with subwavelength confinement. A dielectric metasurface has been demonstrated to provide an experimentally measured Q factor up to 18,511 for operation in the telecommunication wavelength range [[hao_photonics_7:21]]. In aqueous media, such metasurfaces exhibit a resonance dip around 855 nm with a Q factor as high as 144 and a bulk sensitivity of 263 nm.RIU$^{-1}$ [[hao_photonics_7:21]]. The topological nature of these optical BICs is characterized by vorticity in the polarization field, which is a requirement for robust BICs [[hao_photonics_7:24]]. For instance, on a square-lattice photonic crystal slab, five BICs can be identified in the calculated radiative quality factor of the $TM_1$ band within the first Brillouin zone [[hao_photonics_7:24]]. When the grating thickness is set to $h = 1.50a$, two BICs appear on the $k_x$ axis, both carrying topological charges of $q = +1$ [[hao_photonics_7:24]].

The manipulation of topological charges allows for the engineering of ultrahigh-Q guided resonances. By merging multiple topological charges carried by BICs, photonic crystal resonances with record-high quality factors of $Q = 4.9 \times 10^5$ have been experimentally demonstrated, which is over an order of magnitude higher than ordinary designs [[hao_photonics_7:25]]. Specifically, when the sample periodicity is tuned from 519.25 nm to 580 nm, nine BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges merge into an isolated one with a charge of +1 [[hao_photonics_7:25]]. Aside from material absorption and finite sample size, the main limiting factor for the Q of these BICs is out-of-plane scattering losses resulting from fabrication imperfections or disorder [[hao_photonics_7:25]].

Although the section focuses on plasmonic and metasurface systems, the provided evidence also includes data on mechanical BICs in optomechanical crystals, which share similar topological and symmetry-based mechanisms. Mechanical BICs at 8 GHz have been realized in optomechanical crystals, where they are confined in the slab due to symmetry-induced decoupling from the acoustic radiation field [[hao_photonics_7:26]]. Unlike conventional BICs that require certain symmetry, these mechanical BICs represent a new paradigm for constructing high-Q micromechanical resonators through symmetry breaking [[hao_photonics_7:20]]. In millimeter-scale photonic nanocrystals (PnCs), mechanical BICs with $Q \geq 10^7$ are expected to be realized with improved fabrication and material quality [[hao_photonics_7:27]]. The relative standard deviation of the fitting for these phonon trapping results is typically less than 1% [[hao_photonics_7:27]]. Fabrication of such optomechanical structures utilizes electron beam lithography with ZEP520A mask [[hao_photonics_7:26]]. question: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?
raw_answer:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are defined as eigenstates that possess an infinite lifetime while spectrally overlapping with lossy states within the continuum [[hao_photonics_8:0]]. In photonic crystal slabs, the fundamental nature of these states has been identified as topological, where they function essentially as topological defects of polarization directions defined in momentum space [[hao_photonics_8:1]]. The topological charge associated with a BIC is quantified by the rotation of the polarization vector along a closed path in momentum space; specifically, the vector rotates by an angle of $2\pi$ for a topological charge of $q = +1$ or by $-2\pi$ for a topological charge of $q = -1$ [[hao_photonics_8:2]]. This concept extends beyond optics to mechanical systems, where mechanical BICs are associated with transverse topological charges, defined as the winding number of the far-field transverse polarization of Bloch modes in the vicinity, similar to their optical counterparts [[hao_photonics_8:3]].

Mathematically, the winding number of the polarization vector along a closed path is determined by the sum of the topological charges carried by all BICs enclosed within that path [[hao_photonics_8:2]]. When system parameters vary continuously, this winding number remains invariant unless BICs cross the boundary of the path, establishing the topological charge as a conserved quantity [[hao_photonics_8:2]]. This conservation law allows for the merging of multiple BICs in momentum space, a process that enhances the quality factors of nearby resonances [[hao_photonics_8:1]]. For instance, when the sample periodicity is tuned, multiple BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges can merge into an isolated state with a net charge of $+1$ [[hao_photonics_8:1]]. The presence of off-center BICs at specific momentum values further modifies the relationship between the inverse quality factor and momentum, making $\sqrt{1/Q}$ proportional to the product of momentum terms involving the BIC positions [[hao_photonics_8:1]].

While the topological framework is well-established in optical and mechanical domains, its application in acoustic systems presents distinct challenges. Although BICs are generally prohibited in finite photonic, acoustic, and quantum mechanical systems due to the infinite number of scattering channels, acoustics is relieved of these constraints in special cases [[hao_photonics_8:4]]. However, the topological properties of revealed acoustic BICs remain a matter of further research [[hao_photonics_8:4]]. In contrast, mechanical BICs have been successfully realized in optomechanical microresonators, defying conventional wisdom by applying to robust mechanical structures [[hao_photonics_8:0]]. These mechanical BICs, such as those at 8 GHz in optomechanical crystals, enable paradigms of phonon trapping with topological features [[hao_photonics_8:5]][[hao_photonics_8:3]]. Experimental validation of these topological charges in phonon systems has been conducted in vacuum and at low temperatures down to 60 mK, with fitting standard deviations typically less than 1% [[hao_photonics_8:3]].

The theoretical underpinnings of these topological invariants share structural similarities with other non-Hermitian systems, such as the non-Hermitian skin effect. In such contexts, a winding number corresponds to the number of hue cycles crossed along a contour in the complex plane, which relates to the existence of topological edge states in finite open-boundary cases [[hao_photonics_8:6]]. Similarly, the behavior of complex eigenvalues around exceptional points involves loops in the parameter plane that enclose singularities, where eigenvalues switch positions in the complex plane [[hao_photonics_8:7]]. A full loop in the eigenvalue plane requires two loops in the parameter plane, and the behavior of energy levels differs depending on whether the path moves above or below the exceptional point [[hao_photonics_8:8]]. In quantum dynamics, non-Bloch topological invariants calculated from localized bulk-state wave functions correctly predict the existence of topological edge states, whereas Bloch topological invariants fail to do so [[hao_photonics_8:9]].

The topological charge of bound states in the continuum (BICs) is fundamentally defined by the winding number of the polarization vector along a closed path in momentum space [[hao_photonics_8:10]]. Specifically, this charge corresponds to the rotation angle of the polarization vector, where a rotation of $2\pi$ denotes a topological charge of $q = +1$ and a rotation of $-2\pi$ denotes $q = -1$ [[hao_photonics_8:10]]. In systems possessing up-down mirror symmetry ($\sigma_z$), BICs are stable because they correspond to the intersections between the nodal line of $c_x$ and the nodal line of $c_y$ in the $k_x-k_y$ plane [[hao_photonics_8:10]]. This stability is further characterized by the fact that each BIC appears as a topological defect, or vortex, of the polarization long axes, typically carrying an integer topological charge of $\pm 1$ [[hao_photonics_8:11]].

Symmetry plays a critical role in determining the specific values of these topological charges. For instance, in systems with $C_{6v}$ symmetry, a stable BIC with a charge of -2 can arise at the $\Gamma$ point due to the double degeneracy of nodal lines [[hao_photonics_8:10]]. Similarly, $C_4$ rotational symmetry ensures that specific dipole modes are identical under a $90^\circ$ rotation, causing them to share the same complex eigenvalue [[hao_photonics_8:12]]. The conservation of these topological properties is robust; when system parameters vary continuously, the winding number remains invariant unless BICs cross the boundary of the defined path, establishing the topological charge as a conserved quantity [[hao_photonics_8:10]]. This conservation law allows for the merging of multiple BICs; for example, tuning the sample periodicity from 519.25 nm to 580 nm can cause nine BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges to merge into a single isolated BIC with a charge of +1 [[hao_photonics_8:11]].

The concept of topological charges associated with BICs extends beyond optics into mechanical and acoustic domains. In mechanical systems, BICs are associated with transverse topological charges, defined as the winding number of the far-field transverse polarization of Bloch modes, which is similar to their optical counterparts [[hao_photonics_8:13]]. Experimental observations in phonon trapping have confirmed the existence of accidental mechanical BICs with integer topological charges in slab-on-substrate photonic nanocavities, even in the presence of z-symmetry breaking [[hao_photonics_8:13]]. This contrasts with the optical case, where such symmetry breaking often destabilizes the states [[hao_photonics_8:13]]. However, the topological properties of acoustic BICs in compact resonators remain a matter for further research [[hao_photonics_8:14]].

Symmetry breaking significantly affects the stability and nature of BICs. In open acoustic resonators, breaking the axial symmetry of the structure transforms symmetry-protected BICs into quasi-trapped leaky modes that couple to propagating modes of waveguides [[hao_photonics_8:15]]. In optomechanical crystals, the radiation-pressure coupling between mechanical BICs and optical modes strongly depends on the mode symmetry [[hao_photonics_8:16]]. While most experimental demonstrations of BICs in optics and mechanics rely on periodic structures with specific symmetries [[hao_photonics_8:17]], recent work has demonstrated mechanical BICs that do not require such symmetry, representing a new paradigm for constructing high-Q micromechanical resonators through symmetry breaking [[hao_photonics_8:17]]. Furthermore, in systems with in-plane mirror symmetry, unidirectional guided resonances (UGRs) are robust in 2D parameter space along high-symmetric lines [[hao_photonics_8:18]]. These UGRs can be interpreted as points where continuous phase dislocation lines in 3D parameter space pierce a 2D subspace, carrying topological indices defined as the winding numbers in the phase field of the radiation [[hao_photonics_8:18]].

The relationship between topological charges and broader non-Hermitian phenomena is also evident. In non-Hermitian electrical circuits, a winding number of 2 corresponds to a subGBZ loop winding around the north-south axis once on the M-Riemann sphere, which corresponds to two topological edge states in a finite open-boundary case [[hao_photonics_8:19]]. For general sublattice symmetric models, the winding number on the M-Riemann sphere must be calculated around the $\mathbf{d}_{\Gamma}$-axis rather than the Z-axis [[hao_photonics_8:19]]. Under chiral symmetry, topological edge states are necessarily in the coin state $|\pm\rangle$, which are eigenstates of the symmetry operator [[hao_photonics_8:20]]. These findings highlight that the topological classification of BICs and related states is deeply intertwined with the underlying symmetries of the system, whether rotational, mirror, or sublattice-based.

The topological nature of optical bound states in the continuum (BICs) is characterized by the rotation of the polarization vector, which rotates by an angle of $2\pi$ or $-2\pi$, corresponding to topological charges of $q = +1$ or $q = -1$, respectively [[hao_photonics_8:21]]. In this framework, a BIC occurs where all four gray-scale colors meet, with charge $q = +1$ corresponding to the color changing from white to black along a counterclockwise loop, and charge $q = -1$ corresponding to the color changing from black to white [[hao_photonics_8:21]]. A resonance turns into a BIC if and only if the outgoing power is zero, which happens if and only if $c_{x} = c_{y} = 0$ [[hao_photonics_8:21]]. Each BIC appears as a topological defect, or vortex, of polarization long axes characterized by an integer topological charge of $\pm 1$ [[hao_photonics_8:22]].

Accidental BICs exhibit distinct topological behaviors compared to symmetry-protected ones, particularly regarding their existence under broken symmetries. Robust existence of accidental mechanical BICs with integer topological charges has been found in slab-on-substrate photonic crystals despite z-symmetry breaking, which contrasts with the optical case [[hao_photonics_8:23]]. For instance, in a $1 \mu$m-size unit-cell $B_{1}$-BIC mode, the effective mass is noted to be $m_{eff} = 0.51$ pg [[hao_photonics_8:23]]. While the topological properties for revealed acoustic BICs in compact resonators remain a matter of further research [[hao_photonics_8:24]], the definition of a BIC as being completely decoupled from all propagating waves of the surrounding space implies it cannot be excited from the far-field by pressure waves [[hao_photonics_8:24]].

Topological transitions involving accidental BICs are governed by charge conservation laws during parameter changes. As the slab thickness $h$ decreases, two BICs with charge -1 meet with a BIC with charge +1 at the origin, and these three BICs annihilate to yield one BIC with charge -1, as governed by charge conservation [[hao_photonics_8:21]]. Similarly, when the sample periodicity $a$ is tuned from 519.25 nm to 580 nm, 9 BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges merge into an isolated one with charge +1 [[hao_photonics_8:22]]. Specifically, as $a$ increases from 519.25 nm to 531.42 nm, the 8 off-center vortices move towards the center before all 9 of them merge into a single BIC with a charge of +1 as $a$ further increases to 580 nm [[hao_photonics_8:22]]. The overall topological indices raised by unidirectional guided resonances (UGRs) and other singularities remain as a conserved quantity [[hao_photonics_8:25]], and during the evolution, the overall topological index carried by UGRs and other singularities together obeys a conservation law [[hao_photonics_8:25]].

The topological interpretation of UGRs in the view of phase winding $S$ is fully consistent with the previously reported polarization topological charge picture [[hao_photonics_8:25]]. The topological index $S$ depicts how the dislocation line in 3D parameter space penetrates through the 2D subspace $\Sigma$ [[hao_photonics_8:25]]. Along in-plane mirror-symmetric lines, UGRs correspond to robust phase singularities of radiation in parameter space, originated from the piercing behavior of the phase dislocation lines in 3D parameter space [[hao_photonics_8:25]]. It follows from the governing equations that, depending on the sign of parity $p$ or coupling strength $k$, the BIC can be located on either the low- or high-frequency branch in parametric space [[hao_photonics_8:26]]. The quality factor $Q$ is shown to scale quadratically ($\propto 1/k^{2}$) as the distance ($k$) away from a single isolated BIC with charge $\pm 1$ [[hao_photonics_8:22]]. In non-Hermitian systems, theoretically calculated non-Bloch topological invariants correctly predict the existence of topological edge states, whereas Bloch topological invariants fail to do so [[hao_photonics_8:27]].

Experimental investigations into bound states in the continuum (BICs) have identified specific spectral line shapes and near-field behaviors that confirm their topological nature. In optical systems, each BIC appears as a topological defect, or vortex, of the polarization long axes, characterized by an integer topological charge of $\pm 1$ [[hao_photonics_8:28]]. The topological properties of these states are linked to the vanishing of outgoing power; specifically, a resonance turns into a BIC if and only if the coefficients $c_{x}$ and $c_{y}$ are both zero [[hao_photonics_8:29]]. At the nodal line crossing where a BIC is found, the direction of the vector $\mathbf{c}$ becomes undefined [[hao_photonics_8:29]]. When the system is perturbed, a genuine BIC transforms into a quasi-BIC (QBIC), which manifests in the scattering spectrum as a narrow Fano resonance [[hao_photonics_8:30]]. For instance, in compact acoustic resonators, the QBIC corresponding to the irreducible representation $E_{1u}$ appears as a high-$Q$ Fano resonance that collapses as the parameter $e$ tends to zero, manifesting the formation of a genuine BIC [[hao_photonics_8:30]]. Furthermore, an infinite value of the Fano parameter corresponds to a BIC or a supercavity mode [[hao_photonics_8:31]].

The topological charge of BICs has been observed to change through merging processes in photonic structures. When the sample periodicity $a$ is tuned from 519.25 nm to 580 nm, nine BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges merge into an isolated one with a charge of $+1$ [[hao_photonics_8:28]]. This merging behavior affects the quality factor $Q$ of the resonances; when off-center BICs exist at $\pm k_{BIC}$, the quantity $\sqrt{1/Q}$ becomes proportional to $(k + k_{\mathrm{BIC}})(k - k_{\mathrm{BIC}})k$ [[hao_photonics_8:28]]. In the context of non-Hermitian systems, topological edge states have been directly measured and found to match excellently with non-Bloch topological invariants calculated from localized bulk-state wave functions [[hao_photonics_8:32]].

Experimental confirmation extends to mechanical and acoustic domains, where BICs are defined by their decoupling from propagating waves. A BIC is completely decoupled from all propagating waves of the surrounding space and thus cannot be excited from the far-field by pressure waves [[hao_photonics_8:30]]. In optomechanical microresonators, the mechanical BIC was experimentally confirmed by optomechanical measurement of the devices in vacuum [[hao_photonics_8:33]]. For the $1 \mu$m-size unit-cell $B_{1}$-BIC mode, the effective mass $m_{eff}$ was noted to be $0.51$ pg [[hao_photonics_8:34]]. In anisotropic plasmonic metasurfaces, the near-field electric intensity decays much faster than that of the dark mode excited by an out-of-plane electric dipole [[hao_photonics_8:35]]. While these observations confirm the existence of BICs and their associated spectral signatures, the topological properties for revealed acoustic BICs remain a matter of further research [[hao_photonics_8:30]]. Additionally, in experimental observations of the topological structure of exceptional points, no error bars were visible in the reported figures [[hao_photonics_8:36]].

The topological nature of optical bound states in the continuum (BICs) is fundamentally defined by the winding of polarization vectors around vortex centers, where each BIC appears as a topological defect characterized by an integer topological charge of $\pm 1$ [[hao_photonics_8:37]]. This topological interpretation is fully consistent with the phase winding picture, as a resonance turns into a BIC if and only if the outgoing power is zero, which occurs when the complex amplitudes $c_{x}$ and $c_{y}$ are both zero [[hao_photonics_8:38]][[hao_photonics_8:39]]. The robustness of these BICs arises from the existence of conserved and quantized topological charges, which are defined by the number of times the polarization vectors wind around the vortex centers [[hao_photonics_8:39]].

In photonic structures, the topological charge dictates the behavior of lasing emission, where lasing through BICs naturally produces vector beams with a spatial twist in polarization around the center [[hao_photonics_8:39]]. The order number of these vector beams is directly given by the topological charge of the BIC [[hao_photonics_8:39]]. The configuration of these charges can be manipulated by tuning structural parameters; for instance, when the ratio $h/a$ is 1.04, there are two off-$\Gamma$ BICs with charge -1 and a BIC with charge +1 at the $\Gamma$ point [[hao_photonics_8:39]]. As $h/a$ decreases, the two -1 charges move to the center and eventually annihilate with the +1 charge, leaving only one BIC with charge $q = -1$ [[hao_photonics_8:39]]. Similarly, when the sample periodicity $a$ is tuned from 519.25 nm to 580 nm, 9 BICs with $\pm 1$ topological charges merge into an isolated one with charge +1 [[hao_photonics_8:37]].

The topological charge also influences the scattering properties and quality factors of guided resonances. In comparison to standard cases, when there are off-center BICs at $\pm k_{BIC}$, the inverse square root of the quality factor, $\sqrt{1/Q}$, becomes proportional to $(k + k_{\mathrm{BIC}})(k - k_{\mathrm{BIC}})k$ [[hao_photonics_8:37]]. This topological configuration enables resonances to become robust to fabrication imperfections and disorder, as demonstrated numerically for ultrahigh-Q guided resonances [[hao_photonics_8:37]]. While genuine BICs are idealized states, a genuine BIC turns into a quasi-BIC (QBIC), which manifests as a narrow Fano resonance in the scattering spectrum [[hao_photonics_8:40]]. These QBICs are suggested as promising candidates for sensing, lasing, and nonlinear optics applications [[hao_photonics_8:40]].

In the context of non-Hermitian systems and topological design, the robustness of topological features against disorder is a key characteristic. For example, in topological funneling of light, light still moves toward the interface even when combined with a weak disorder $W = 0.1\pi$, demonstrating the robustness of the non-Hermitian Skin effect against a certain degree of disorder [[hao_photonics_8:41]]. From a practical perspective, the bulk-boundary correspondence established in non-Hermitian quantum dynamics, where measured topological edge states match non-Bloch topological invariants, will be useful in open-system-based topological designs such as topological lasers [[hao_photonics_8:42]].

In optomechanical and acoustic domains, the topological properties of BICs and their interaction with other modes are also significant. The radiation-pressure coupling between the mechanical BIC and optical modes strongly depends on the mode symmetry [[hao_photonics_8:43]]. In phonon trapping, the effective mass $m_{eff}$ for the 1 $\mu$m-size unit-cell $B_{1}$-BIC mode is noted to be 0.51 pg [[hao_photonics_8:44]]. However, regarding compact acoustic resonators, the topological properties for the revealed acoustic BIC remain a matter of further research [[hao_photonics_8:40]].
