The interaction between the particle and the cavity can be described using coupled-mode theory, where the frequency shift and linewidth broadening of the hybrid eigenmode induced by nanoparticle coupling match the predictions of Bethe-Schwinger cavity perturbation theory . In specific hybrid systems, a nearby dielectric optical cavity modifies the photonic environment surrounding a plasmonic nanoantenna, presenting opportunities to sculpt its spectral response . A plasmonic nanoparticle can enhance the optical field strength at the microcavity surface, thereby amplifying the resonance wavelength shift upon binding in proportion to the field strength encountered at the binding site . For instance, in a nanoplasmonic-photonic hybrid microcavity, the smooth shell parameter $\xi_{\mathrm{smooth shell}}$ was measured to be 138 . The physical transduction of these optical shifts into mechanical signals is governed by the optical spring effect, where every 1-fm cavity resonance wavelength shift induced by a particle binding event can be transduced to an optomechanical (OMO) frequency change of about 1.5 kHz [4]. An increase in the mechanical oscillation frequency implies a red shift of the cavity resonance wavelength, which corresponds to the binding of a 11.6-nm silica bead on the surface of the microsphere [4]. In practical detection scenarios, binding and dwell states are distinguished by whether the resonance position is above or below a threshold $\Delta \lambda_{\mathrm{th}}$, typically set as half of the maximum shift . The total resonance shift remains approximately the same whether the toroid is exposed to pure Streptavidin or a Streptavidin solution containing additional Tryptophan . Several factors limit the precision and stability of these resonance shifts. Optical losses interact with the whispering gallery mode of the microcavity and are amplified due to the high circulating intensities present within the structure . Absorption in the dielectric cavity causes a local increase in temperature, which is expressed through shifts in the refractive index of the structure . For silica ($\mathrm{SiO}_2$), the refractive index is $n = 1.45$ , and the thermorefractive coefficient is $\frac{dn}{dT} = 1.45\times 10^{-5}\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ . One specific limitation of dielectric microcavities is the mismatch between the high-Q resonances of the cavity and the spectrally wide emission from inhomogeneously broadened fluorescent emitters at room temperature . To enhance sensitivity, researchers utilize materials with a high index of refraction, such as $n\approx 3.42$, which enhances the mechanical resonator's perturbation of the optical cavity's evanescent field . Whispering gallery mode (WGM) Q-factors of $10^{6}-10^{7}$ are common in biosensing applications . In subwavelength dielectric resonators, the quality factor $Q$ is related to the asymmetry parameter by $Q = 0.1\varepsilon^{2.3}$ for $m = 1$ . At a specific geometric ratio of $r / l = 0.703$, the asymmetry parameter tends to infinity and then becomes negative . Furthermore, in systems operating near exceptional points, a small change in the refractive index can remarkably alter the orientation of the elliptical orbit . Even a slight change in the refractive index can significantly alter the size of the ellipse and rotate its orientation angle . The sensitivity, defined as the extent of resonance shifts for a given change in refractive index, depends on the material, geometry, and arrangement of the nanostructures . Cavity optomechanics addresses the radiation-pressure couplings between electromagnetic fields in cavities and the mechanical oscillation of micro- and nano-scale mechanical resonators . Recent advances in micro- and nanofabrication have made it possible to access the regime where the effects of cavity-enhanced radiation pressure alone dominate the mechanical dynamics [5]. This field provides a route towards cavity Quantum Optomechanics . A discernable effect on mirror motion was first demonstrated in the optical bistability resulting from the static elongation of cavity length caused by radiation pressure [5]. Recent experimental advances have allowed studying for the first time the modifications of mechanical dynamics provided by radiation pressure . In optomechanical crystal resonators, a perturbation in the periodicity at the center of the beam results in co-localized optical and mechanical resonances, which are coupled via radiation pressure . The interaction between the optical field and mechanical motion is characterized by specific coupling strengths and damping rates. In the weak-coupling regime where $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} \ll \kappa$ and for a detuning $\Delta = \omega_{m}$, the optical back-action damping is given by $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}} = 4g^{2}n_{c} / \kappa$ . In the resolved sideband limit where $\omega_{m} / \kappa > 1$, driving the system with a laser tuned to the red side of the optical cavity creates an optically-induced damping, $\gamma_{\mathrm{OM}}$, of the mechanical resonance . If the optical pump wave is weak, this damping rate will reflect the intrinsic loss of the mechanical mode . The nature of the radiation pressure force depends on the pump detuning. A pump detuning exists where the radiation-pressure induced mechanical frequency shift is zero, even while the damping/amplification rate is non-zero . For red detuning, the entire radiation pressure force is viscous, contributing only to cooling, whereas for blue detuning, it contributes to amplification . When the optical pump is turned off, the intrinsic loss rate $\gamma_{\mathrm{i}}$ is reduced by a factor of $-3$ and the mechanical frequency redshifts by $-700\mathrm{kHz}$ . It has been observed that the mechanical frequency and intrinsic loss rate are different under different optical powers . For the case where the pump-sideband frequency separation coincides with the mechanical resonance frequency, the optical susceptibility of the cavity is strongly suppressed owing to cancellation of coherent scattering components from the mechanical and optical resonances . Despite these mechanisms, the observation of optomechanical effects at the single-quanta level has long been a problem owing to the coupling strength that is too weak to enter the single-photon strong-coupling regime . Quantum optomechanics, the field that evolved from these developments, promises to provide motion and force detection near the fundamental limits imposed by quantum mechanics [6]. In specific implementations, such as on-chip systems, a force sensitivity of $132\mathrm{aN} / \sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ has been achieved . The coupling strength $g$ in certain detection schemes is quantified by the doublet splitting $g = \pi \delta$, where $\delta$ is the frequency detuning of the SM from the ASM . However, in cavity optomechanical spring sensing, the impact from cavity Q change counteracts that from the cavity resonance wavelength shift, leading to a smaller shift of OMO frequency [4]. Additionally, a variation in the parameter $\varepsilon$ of $1 \mathrm{~nm}$ to $100 \mathrm{~nm}$ induces only a $16\%$ change in resonant wavelength shift . The fundamental physical limits constraining mechanical position measurements in cavity optomechanics are defined by the standard quantum limit, which arises from fundamental quantum optical effects [6]. In the context of optomechanical sideband cooling, the finite Stokes Raman scattering defined by the cavity linewidth combined with shot noise fluctuations dictates a quantum backaction limit, analogous to the Doppler limit of atomic laser cooling . This backaction limit can be circumvented by introducing additional couplings to alter the dynamics of the cavity optomechanical system, such as dissipative optomechanical coupling or measurement and active feedback . For a blue laser detuning of $\Delta = -\omega_{m}$, the optically-induced damping is negative and the photocurrent noise power spectral density is proportional to $S_{b^{\dagger}}(\omega) = (\bar{n} + 1)\gamma/((\omega - \omega_{m})^{2} + (\gamma/2)^{2})$ . Conversely, for a red-sideband detuning $(\Delta = \omega_{m})$, the noise power spectral density of the photocurrent yields a Lorentzian component of the single-sided PSD proportional to $S_{b}(\omega) = \bar{n}\gamma/((\omega - \omega_{m})^{2} + (\gamma/2)^{2})$ . The use of squeezed light can enable surpassing this standard quantum limit [5]. Furthermore, the sensitivity of such systems may be further improved when stretched into the quantum regimes by the implementation of quantum sensing protocols and novel strategies . Technical noise sources, particularly laser phase noise, significantly constrain the minimum detectable mass or binding event. Diode lasers have exhibited excess phase noise that limited sensitivity to a value of about $\delta x_{\mathrm{min}} \cong 5 \cdot 10^{-18} \mathrm{~m} / \sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ . In specific cooling experiments, the level of classical amplitude (phase) noise on the cooling laser was measured to be 0.2% (2%) of shot noise at 5 $\mu$ W, a representative power at which $\bar{n} = n_{ba}$ . However, in pulsed excitation dynamics near the quantum ground state, a quantitative analysis concluded that technical laser noise has a negligible impact on the sideband asymmetry observed . The phase noise of the oscillator has been characterized and observed to obey an inverse power dependence, characteristic of fundamental, Brownian noise [5]. Present-day laser sources are available that offer noise performance that is limited only by quantum noise [5]. In coherent scattering schemes for levitated nanospheres, there is an estimated significant ($>40$ dB) suppression of laser phase noise heating, which is a specific feature of the coherent scattering scheme . Thermal fluctuations and refractive noise within the resonator also impose strict limits on detection capabilities. Measurement noise arising primarily from thermal fluctuations within the resonator and fluctuations in laser frequency often limits the minimum detectable frequency shift to above $5\mathrm{kHz}$, precluding the observation of single molecule binding events . Without plasmonic enhancement, refractive noise could preclude single molecule detection for measurements with $\tau \leq 1\mathrm{ms}$ even when interferometric methods are employed to cancel $\delta \omega_{\Delta \Omega}$ . In cavity optomechanical spring sensing, the Allan deviation includes all noise in the microcavity, implying a detection resolution of $\delta\lambda/\lambda_{0}\approx6\times10^{-12}$ in the device [4]. The impact from cavity Q change counteracts that from the cavity resonance wavelength shift, leading to a smaller shift of the optomechanical oscillator frequency [4]. This effect is observed in systems with an effective mechanical Q of $2.6 \times 10^{6}$ [4] and a cavity linewidth $\kappa_{e}/2\pi = 221$ MHz . Despite these limits, high-Q microcavities offer inherent sensitivity due to the long photon lifetime within the microcavity, which results in an increase in sampling or amplification of the signal without a label on the target molecule . However, these mechanisms assumed that the molecule was non-absorbing . Accurate detection of resonance frequency changes has a higher saturation limit and is less prone to noise than the linewidth measurement . In label-free detection of single proteins using a nanoplasmonic-photonic hybrid microcavity, the largest signal-to-noise ratio in BSA experiments $(S / N \approx 13)$ led to a conservatively estimated new protein limit of detection of 5 kDa . Nevertheless, direct detection of single molecule binding has not been available on a pristine WGM cavity to date . Enhancing the sensitivity of cavity optomechanical sensors for single-protein detection requires strategies that either amplify the light-matter interaction or reduce the noise floor, as the detection limit is fundamentally determined by the strength of this interaction [2]. Improving the detection limit can be accomplished by increasing the sensitivity or reducing the noise level [2]. One approach to enhancing sensitivity involves utilizing exceptional points in microcavity sensors, where a more than threefold enhancement of sensitivity has been observed for single-particle detection . Additionally, photonic-plasmonic hybrids can provide a 10-fold nanoparticle absorption enhancement, leveraging plasmonic properties such as high extinction coefficients and enhanced Raman and fluorescence signals for single-molecule biodetection . In specific hybrid microcavity configurations, wavelength shifts have been enhanced by 240% for Tg and 1500% for BSA compared to earlier work . Signal processing and measurement techniques are critical for overcoming noise limits, particularly when detecting small resonance frequency changes. Accurate detection of resonance frequency changes has a higher saturation limit and is less prone to noise than linewidth measurement . To detect extremely small wavelength shifts, frequency locking combined with filtering techniques can reduce the noise level to $9.6 \times 10^{-4}$ fm over one-millisecond intervals . The temporal confinement of light, characterized by the quality factor (Q-factor) defined by the ratio of resonance frequency and linewidth, is a key parameter in these measurements . In some experiments, the smallest measurable transparency window is on the order of the lock-in detection frequency . However, noise-induced fluctuations can be of the same order of magnitude as small resonance shifts, such as those induced by tryptophan injection, which are negligible compared to shifts induced by Streptavidin . Dynamical back-action offers a mechanism for manipulating mechanical degrees of freedom, allowing for both cooling and amplification of mechanical oscillators [5]. This process exhibits high mechanical spectral selectivity, where the cooling or amplification rates depend on the asymmetry in motional sidebands, allowing the optical linewidth and pump laser detuning to select a particular mechanical mode . For a lower-frequency (red) detuning of the laser from the cavity, dynamical back-action leads to damping and cooling of the mechanical motion . Back-action cooling from a given bath temperature to the quantum ground state requires that $\hbar \kappa \gtrsim k_{B}T_{b} / Q_{m}$ . In the context of acceleration sensing, optical cooling may add equivalent damping that is beneficial for feedback control in ultrahigh vacuum environments where the damping ratio is extremely small . However, combining feedback cooling and feedback control for both sensitivity and practicability remains unexplored, as they are operated at quite different frequencies . Despite these enhancement strategies, practical limitations and discrepancies between theory and experiment persist. In two-dimensional optomechanical crystal cavities, the theoretical curve for $\beta = 0$ predicts substantially more cooling of the acoustic mode than measured, and the shapes of the measured and theoretical curves differ significantly . A significant difference in measurement conditions is that back-action cooling measurements are performed at $\Delta = \omega_{m}$, requiring a 100-fold increase in optical pump power to reach a given intra-cavity photon number compared to measurements of $n_{p}$ and $\gamma_{p}$ . Furthermore, while record sensitivities for nanodetection using microcavity biosensors have been achieved [1], future experiments aim to verify and improve specificity and sensitivity through more complete antibody/linker coverage and experiments with complex solutions, which are critical for practical application as a biosensor . The effective mechanical Q of $2.6 \times 10^{6}$ corresponds to specific sensing conditions in cavity optomechanical spring sensing [4]. Additionally, dielectric metasurfaces enabling advanced optical biosensors have shown resonances at around 1488 nm with a Q factor of 25 . Experimental demonstrations of single-molecule and nanoparticle detection using optical microcavities have achieved significant milestones, with researchers reporting record sensitivity for nanodetection using microcavity biosensors [1]. In one such study, label-free detection of single proteins was accomplished using a nanoplasmonic-photonic hybrid microcavity, yielding signal-to-noise ratios of 22:1 and 13:1 for the respective proteins tested . The high signal-to-noise ratio observed in the Tg experiments provided the experimental rationale for attempting to detect smaller proteins in subsequent trials . Another approach utilizing microtoroid optical resonators enabled the label-free detection of single nanoparticles and biological molecules, with experiments conducted at input powers ranging from 9.3 to 100 $\mu$W at 633 nm . In these microtoroid experiments, a 30-second delay was observed after injection before data recording began . The physical mechanisms underlying these resonance shifts have been characterized through various experimental setups. Early work on nanoparticle-based protein detection by optical shift of a resonant microcavity reported a length scale of $\mathrm{L} \sim 80 \mathrm{~nm}$ at a 1060 nm wavelength, with a quality factor of $\sim 5 \times 10^6$ at the same wavelength . In studies of label-free single-molecule detection with optical microcavities, experimental resonant wavelength shifts were found to be in excellent agreement with the thermo-optic mechanism . Specificity in these microcavity systems is endowed through surface functionalization . For instance, in a study of sensitive optical biosensors for unlabeled targets, the binding stoichiometry of 1:1 between biotin-BSA and streptavidin was estimated from the magnitude of the whispering gallery mode (WGM) shift [2]. Despite these successes, practical implementation in biological environments faces significant challenges related to noise, specificity, and system stability. In microtoroid experiments, unbinding steps observed in interleukin-2 assays were likely due to non-specific adsorption associated with the binding of interleukin-2 to non-functionalized regions of the toroid . This issue of non-specific binding is a broader concern, as further investigations are needed to improve overall performance, including surface chemistry, compatible microfluidics for efficient sample delivery, and detection procedures such as rinsing to minimize non-specific binding [2]. To address noise issues, the combination of frequency locking feedback control and computational filtering has been shown to reduce the noise level to $9.6 \times 10^{-4}$ fm over one-millisecond intervals . The difference in mean noise levels in these systems is clearly apparent, indicating the role of the feedback controller in quenching various noise mechanisms . In the context of on-chip cavity optomechanical coupling, angular and displacement noise floors of 4 nrad/√Hz and 2 fm/√Hz have been demonstrated . Quantitative analysis of noise sources and detection limits reveals both the capabilities and limitations of current devices. A cavity optomechanical spring sensing study reported an Allan deviation that includes all noise in the microcavity, implying a detection resolution of $\delta\lambda/\lambda_{0}\approx6\times10^{-12}$ in the device [4]. In pulsed excitation dynamics of an optomechanical crystal resonator near its quantum ground state of motion, the external coupling rate was measured as $\kappa_{e}/2\pi = 221$ MHz . A quantitative analysis of systematic errors in this system concluded that technical laser noise has a negligible impact on the sideband asymmetry observed . However, modeling assumptions can introduce discrepancies; for example, in performance quantification of resonant refractive index sensors, amplitude noise data points are often drawn from a white Gaussian distribution for simplicity, whereas in reality, shot noise is produced by a Poisson process [0]. Comparisons with other sensing modalities highlight the unique advantages and remaining hurdles for optical microcavities. Compared to nanoelectronic and nanomechanical sensors, nanophotonic sensors are more immune to biological noise and solution ionic strength, making them an appealing tool to study biochemical processes under physiological conditions . In contrast, capacitive sensors are noted to be less prone to nonspecific binding . For digital resolution biomolecular sensing, instrument complexity is not a driving consideration when the main objective is to elucidate biomolecular binding interactions, while assay methods that do not interfere with binding sites are preferred . This type of characterization provides a solution to practical biosensing challenges by quantitatively discriminating between the specific binding signal and non-specific binding background signal, thereby achieving high specificity for single-nucleotide variants . Specificity of binding in related imaging contexts should be validated by comparing the cellular labeling with and without components necessary for binding . Recent advancements have extended the utility of these platforms to more complex biological targets. Single-molecule nucleic acid interactions have been monitored on a label-free microcavity biosensor platform, where high specificity can be achieved by utilizing specific receptors with appreciable dissociation constants, thus separating the need for high specificity from the requirements of high affinity in biosensors . Furthermore, imaging-based spectrometer-less optofluidic biosensors based on dielectric metasurfaces have enabled real-time measurements of extracellular vesicles binding from down to 204 femtomolar solutions . Photonic-plasmonic hybrid single-molecule nanosensors have also been used to measure the effect of fluorescent labels on DNA-protein dynamics .

question: How do exceptional points (EPs) in optical resonators enhance the sensitivity of sensors compared to traditional diabolic points (DPs) for detecting nanoparticles and biomolecules?
raw_answer:
In optical systems, the hybridization of optically identical resonators results in symmetric and antisymmetric modes that cross along a diabolic line as a function of spatial parameters [[yanyu_photonics_4:0]]. At these diabolic points, the resonance frequencies of the hybridized modes are identical, while the loss rates are avoided due to the opposite symmetry of the modes [[yanyu_photonics_4:0]]. This behavior contrasts with exceptional points, which are defined as square root singularities of the eigenvalues as a function of a complex interaction parameter [[yanyu_photonics_4:1]]. Unlike diabolic points, where a genuine degeneracy implies a two-dimensional subspace, the connection at an exceptional point is not of this type [[yanyu_photonics_4:1]]. When an exceptional point involving two coalescing levels is subjected to a perturbation of strength $\varepsilon$, the resulting energy splitting is typically proportional to $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:2]]. Consequently, for sufficiently small perturbations, the splitting at an exceptional point is enhanced compared to a diabolic point, even when exactly the same perturbation is applied [[yanyu_photonics_4:2]].

The mathematical distinction between these degeneracies is rooted in the Hermitian versus non-Hermitian nature of the system's Hamiltonian. In a non-Hermitian regime, such as when $b < g$, the matrix $\vec{K}$ possesses a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues [[yanyu_photonics_4:3]]. In photonic crystal slabs with negligible absorption loss and no artificial gain, exceptional points can exist, indicating that non-Hermiticity does not strictly require artificial gain [[yanyu_photonics_4:4]]. At an exceptional point, the two complex eigenvalues are degenerate, yet the corresponding reflection peaks do not coincide because they represent the eigenvalues of only the Hermitian part of the Hamiltonian, which does not exhibit degeneracy at that specific point [[yanyu_photonics_4:4]]. Generally, reflection peaks occur near the eigenvalues $\Omega_{1,2}$ of the Hermitian part $A$ and are independent of the non-Hermitian part $-iB$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:4]]. Accidental degeneracy in the Hermitian part can be achieved by selecting specific material properties, such as a liquid index of $n = 1.48$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:4]]. The deformation of these structures can arise from dissimilar radiation rates of dipole and quadrupole resonances [[yanyu_photonics_4:4]].

Beyond simple two-level systems, non-Hermiticity fundamentally changes topological band theory, leading to phenomena such as the non-Hermitian skin effect [[yanyu_photonics_4:5]]. In the context of unidirectional guided resonances, non-Hermitian band degeneracies allow resonances to transit from one band to another by crossing Fermi arcs connected by paired exceptional points or topologically trivial band degeneracies protected by in-plane symmetry [[yanyu_photonics_4:6]]. The localization of population distribution serves as an unequivocal manifestation of the localization of bulk eigenstates by the non-Hermitian skin effect [[yanyu_photonics_4:7]]. In contrast to the Hermitian case, probing a non-Hermitian lattice reveals a significant change in propagation dynamics where all eigenmodes are localized at the interface, directing any excitation toward that interface [[yanyu_photonics_4:8]]. Experimental observations of non-Hermitian quantum walks show that the relative height of the domain fits a behavior close to $P_{\mathrm{domain}} / P_{\min} \sim x_0$, as predicted by theory [[yanyu_photonics_4:9]]. These dynamics are calculated by diagonalizing finite domain-wall systems under specific parameters, such as $\theta_{1,2}^{L} = 0.85\pi$, $\theta_{1}^{R} = 0.12\pi$, and $\gamma = 0.8$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:9]][[yanyu_photonics_4:7]].

Mathematical formulations of these non-Hermitian systems involve specific invariants and zero/pole structures. For instance, if $m > n$, $z = 0$ is a zero of $M^2(z)$ of order $m - n$, whereas if $n > m$, $z = 0$ is a pole of $M^2(z)$ of order $n - m$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:10]]. Equation (8) in related models represents the Hermitian $Q$-matrix invariant when the model is Hermitian [[yanyu_photonics_4:10]]. In the context of microcavity sensors, the coupling coefficient is calculated using the beam power, which is $1\mathrm{W}$ when determining $\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:3]]. The general form of the coupling matrix element is given by $A ^ {(N)} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} (V _ {j} - U _ {j}) e ^ {- i 2 m \beta_ {j}}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:2]].

The fundamental distinction between exceptional points (EPs) and diabolic points (DPs) lies in the mathematical nature of their eigenvalue singularities, where EPs are characterized as square root singularities of the eigenvalues as a function of a complex interaction parameter [[yanyu_photonics_4:11]]. When an EP involving two coalescing levels is subjected to a perturbation of strength $\varepsilon$, the resulting energy splitting is typically proportional to $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:12]]. In contrast, the mode splittings at a DP obey a linear law, whereas the mode splittings at an EP obey a square-root law [[yanyu_photonics_4:13]]. This difference in scaling means that for sufficiently small perturbations, the splitting at an EP is enhanced compared to a DP, even though exactly the same perturbation is applied [[yanyu_photonics_4:12]]. Consequently, perturbing a system about an EP splits the degenerate mode in two, and the frequency splitting scales with the square root of the strength of the perturbation [[yanyu_photonics_4:14]].

In the context of microcavity sensors, this square-root scaling results in a larger frequency split at the EP than at the DP when the same perturbation $H_{1}$ is applied, provided the square root term in the relevant equation is larger than unity [[yanyu_photonics_4:12]]. This principle is directly demonstrated in plasmonic nanosensors, where the resonance splitting $\Delta\omega$ is proportional to the square-root of the perturbation $\delta$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:13]]. Experimental observations confirm that the EP sensor produces a larger frequency split than the DP sensor does subject to the same nanoparticles [[yanyu_photonics_4:14]]. Furthermore, it has been confirmed that the EP indeed becomes slightly more sensitive when the perturbation is small [[yanyu_photonics_4:13]].

Beyond frequency splitting, the sensitivity enhancement at EPs extends to the imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, which represent energy loss or gain. A slight increment in a particle's parameter near an EP results in a rapid increase in the imaginary parts of the eigenvalues [[yanyu_photonics_4:15]]. This behavior is linked to the specific mode coupling and radiation characteristics within the resonator. For instance, in systems where rings of exceptional points are spawned out of Dirac cones, the deformation arises from the dissimilar radiation rates of dipole and quadrupole resonances [[yanyu_photonics_4:16]]. The critical coupling strength $\delta_{c}$ in such systems is determined by the geometric mean of the dipole and quadrupole decay rates, given by $\delta_{c} = 2\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{d}}\gamma_{\mathrm{q}}}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:16]]. In optical microcavities, multiple pairs of EPs can emerge as the perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$ ranges from 1 to 11 [[yanyu_photonics_4:15]].

The theoretical framework for these enhancements involves specific coupling coefficients that govern the interaction between modes. For example, coefficients $A^{(N)}$ and $B^{(N)}$ are defined as sums involving the differences between $V_j$ and $U_j$ weighted by phase factors $e^{-i 2 m \beta_{j}}$ and $e^{i 2 m \beta_{j}}$, respectively [[yanyu_photonics_4:12]]. While the primary mechanism for EP-based sensing is the square-root scaling of eigenvalue shifts, other sensing modalities also seek to enhance light-matter interaction. Sensitivity in general optical biosensors can be enhanced by increasing the fraction of light near the sensing surface [[yanyu_photonics_4:17]]. In cavity optomechanics, the optical spring sensing principle has been shown to dramatically enhance sensing resolution by orders of magnitude compared with conventional approaches [[yanyu_photonics_4:18]]. Additionally, resonant enhancement in on-chip cavities scales with the system's optical quality factor, which increases the slope of the resonance [[yanyu_photonics_4:19]].

However, the baseline for detecting such shifts is constrained by the current limits of fractional frequency measurement. Currently, it is possible to detect a fractional frequency change as small as $10^{-8}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:20]]. If the ability to see a shift of a fiftieth of a linewidth is maintained, the least measurable fractional shift would be $10^{-9}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:20]]. In specific experimental setups, such as those calculating the cavity decay rate $\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}$, the beam power is set to $1\mathrm{W}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:15]]. While EPs offer a distinct advantage in sensitivity through non-linear eigenvalue response, other structural modifications also contribute to sensing performance. For example, in optomechanical crystals, the radiation-pressure coupling between mechanical bound states in the continuum and optical modes strongly depends on the mode symmetry [[yanyu_photonics_4:21]]. Similarly, in two-dimensional optomechanical crystal cavities, specific geometric shapes allow for large overlap of acoustic mode stress fields with optical mode intensity, increasing the moving boundary contribution to optomechanical coupling [[yanyu_photonics_4:22]]. In photonic crystal-enhanced fluorescence emission, coupling a leaky mode to an underlying Fabry–Perot-type cavity through a gold mirror reflector can improve enhancement by 360-fold [[yanyu_photonics_4:23]]. Waveguide coupling is also noted as a robust alternative to prisms for integrating optical components [[yanyu_photonics_4:17]]. In semiconductor–piezoelectric heterostructures, the giant electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity yields a value of $5\;\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ from a developed model, compared to $3\;\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ from a perturbative approach [[yanyu_photonics_4:24]].

Experimental comparisons between exceptional point (EP) and diabolic point (DP) sensors reveal distinct differences in frequency splitting magnitudes for specific analytes. In a study involving IgG concentrations, the measured splittings were approximately 2.4 THz for the DP sensor and 5.1 THz for the EP sensor [[yanyu_photonics_4:25]]. These values correspond to the minimum splittings measured at IgG concentrations of 50 aM for the DP sensor and 30 aM for the EP sensor [[yanyu_photonics_4:25]]. The underlying mechanism for this enhanced response is that perturbing a system about an EP splits the degenerate mode in two, with the frequency splitting scaling with the square root of the strength of the perturbation [[yanyu_photonics_4:26]].

Theoretical and experimental investigations of microcavity sensors indicate that operating at an EP can significantly enhance sensitivity compared to traditional configurations. A theoretical study presented that the sensitivity of a microcavity operating at an EP can be significantly enhanced [[yanyu_photonics_4:27]]. This enhancement was quantified as a more than threefold increase in sensitivity [[yanyu_photonics_4:27]]. In specific experimental implementations, an EP emerges around a radius of $r = 0.829\mu \mathrm{m}$ when the incident wavelength is tuned from 1.064 to $1.2\mu \mathrm{m}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:28]]. The condition for the EP to arise is defined by the parameter relationship $b = g$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:28]].

For nanoparticle detection, whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) sensors tuned to an EP have demonstrated superior performance over DP sensors. Yang and colleagues used a WGM sensor tuned to an EP to detect a polystyrene nanoparticle with twice the sensitivity of a DP sensor [[yanyu_photonics_4:26]]. Traditional high-Q microresonators, which operate away from EPs, have established detection limits for dielectric nanoparticles; for a nanoparticle with a refractive index of 1.5, the detection limit is around a radius of $R = 10 \mathrm{~nm}$ using an ultra-high-Q resonance in the 670 nm wavelength band [[yanyu_photonics_4:29]]. In another on-chip single nanoparticle detection setup using an ultrahigh-Q microresonator with $Q = 4 \times 10^{8}$, the theoretical lower limit of measurable radius was estimated to be 9.2 nm for KCl and 8.7 nm for polystyrene at $\lambda = 670\mathrm{nm}$ [[yanyu_photonics_4:30]].

Biomolecular detection using digital resolution methods presents specific challenges regarding noise and sensitivity. The efficacy of single biomolecule detection is often sacrificed due to a complex noise reduction process that influences the sensitivity and multiplexing ability [[yanyu_photonics_4:26]]. question: What are the current state of the art in which photonic metamaterial surfaces are utilized to enhance Label-Free Imaging in Phase Contrast Microscopy and Refractometric Microscopy?
raw_answer:
Label-free imaging techniques, such as photonic crystal enhanced microscopy, enable quantitative, submicron resolution, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions without the use of cytotoxic staining agents or temporally-unstable fluorophores [[yanyu_photonics_5:0]][[yanyu_photonics_5:1]]. This approach allows for the first label-free time-lapse imaging of the attachment localization of living cells during chemotaxis [[yanyu_photonics_5:1]]. In contrast to bright-field microscopy, which primarily relies on variations in optical absorption within the specimen to create image contrast, dark-field microscopy exploits the scattering of incident light from localized variations in the refractive index [[yanyu_photonics_5:2]]. Refractometric sensing is defined by the detection limit (DL), which reports the smallest sample refractive index change that can accurately be measured [[yanyu_photonics_5:3]].

Photonic crystal biosensor surfaces are inexpensively fabricated uniformly over large surface areas by a room temperature nanoreplica molding process [[yanyu_photonics_5:4]]. These surfaces can be integrated into microscopy systems with an effective magnification of $26\times$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:0]][[yanyu_photonics_5:1]]. Image acquisition in these systems involves assembling a series of lines into an image at a rate of $0.1~s$ per line [[yanyu_photonics_5:0]][[yanyu_photonics_5:1]]. A specific modality known as photonic resonator outcoupler microscopy (PROM) operates using an independent sensing mechanism that obtains contrast through the formation of protein clusters at the cell–ECM interface that are capable of outcoupling light from the PC biosensor surface [[yanyu_photonics_5:4]]. As a label-free imaging approach, PROM does not suffer from the limitations of fluorescence-based microscopy, which include photobleaching and stain cytotoxicity [[yanyu_photonics_5:4]]. Structural parameters for such gratings include a depth of $d_{g}=120$ nm [[yanyu_photonics_5:4]].

Dielectric metasurfaces are utilized to enable advanced optical biosensors, providing an experimentally measured Q factor up to 18511 for operation in the telecommunication wavelength range [[yanyu_photonics_5:5]]. The resonance of a single metasurface can be tuned by light incidence angle and polarization to retrieve molecular fingerprint information over a broad spectrum ranging from 1100 to 1800 cm $^{-1}$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:5]]. Diatomic all-dielectric metasurfaces emanated from quasi-BIC modes enable high-performance sensing by supporting high Q resonances with accessible near-fields [[yanyu_photonics_5:6]]. The unique symmetry-breaking design of these metasurfaces makes them more tolerant of nanofabrication [[yanyu_photonics_5:6]].

Planar photonic chips with tailored angular transmission are used for high-contrast-imaging devices, where image contrast is enhanced without altering the specimens and the microscope configurations [[yanyu_photonics_5:7]]. When the numerical aperture (NA) of the imaging objective is <0.7, darkfield imaging can be realized using these chips [[yanyu_photonics_5:7]]. Luminescent surfaces with tailored angular emission are also employed for compact dark-field imaging devices, utilizing bright-field illumination through a water immersion objective with numerical aperture 1.0 [[yanyu_photonics_5:2]]. No data were excluded in the reporting of these luminescent surface results [[yanyu_photonics_5:2]].

The primary limitation of standard bright-field microscopy is its low contrast for thin specimens with weak absorption and biological species whose refractive indices are very close to their surroundings [[yanyu_photonics_5:8]]. In contrast to bright-field microscopy, which relies on variations in optical absorption, dark-field microscopy exploits the scattering of incident light from localized variations in the refractive index [[yanyu_photonics_5:9]]. To address these contrast limitations, planar photonic chips with tailored angular transmission have been developed for high-contrast imaging devices [[yanyu_photonics_5:8]]. Specifically, C-DFM and C-TIRM configurations offer the merits of large illumination area, high imaging contrast, simple configuration, and ease of optical alignment [[yanyu_photonics_5:8]].

Luminescent surfaces with tailored angular emission, such as SLED surfaces, enable compact dark-field imaging by emitting a partially coherent light field [[yanyu_photonics_5:9]]. This illumination allows for the imaging of phase objects analogous to dark-field illumination by translating phase disturbances at the object plane into intensity contrast at the image plane [[yanyu_photonics_5:9]]. For refractive index differences of $\Delta n \leq 0.3$, SLED illumination provides better contrast than bright-field light [[yanyu_photonics_5:9]]. The phase map of the complex amplitude transmission function $A(x,y)$ for a transparent spherical particle with a refractive index of 1.37 illustrates this capability [[yanyu_photonics_5:9]].

Dielectric metasurfaces represent another design strategy for enhancing optical performance in biosensing and imaging applications. The near-zero absorption losses in the constituent materials of dielectric metasurfaces allow for reduced heat generation, while the high refractive index enables profound light confinement [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]]. A biperiodic diamond disk metasurface was proposed theoretically to enhance the averaged C for more than two orders of magnitude in the UV, with local C enhancement reaching 1100 [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]]. Sensitivity, defined as the extent of resonance shifts for a given change in refractive index, depends on the material, geometry, and arrangement of the nanostructures [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]].

High-quality factor (Q) resonances are critical for enhancing phase contrast and sensitivity in these metasurface designs. A diatomic all-dielectric metasurface emanating from quasi-BIC modes enables high-performance sensing by supporting high Q resonances with accessible near-fields [[yanyu_photonics_5:11]]. This design generalizes and expands the concept of BIC developed for asymmetric metasurfaces [[yanyu_photonics_5:11]]. The unique symmetry-breaking design of such structures makes them more tolerant of nanofabrication [[yanyu_photonics_5:11]]. Experimentally, a metasurface provided a measured Q factor up to 18511 for operation in the telecommunication wavelength range [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]]. Owing to high-Q resonances and highly accessible enhanced near-fields, an experimental bulk refractive index sensitivity of 305 nm/RIU was achieved [[yanyu_photonics_5:11]]. These metasurfaces operate in aqueous media with resonances in the visible and near-IR spectral range (600 nm to 850 nm) [[yanyu_photonics_5:11]].

In the context of quantitative analysis, the spatial resolution of dielectric objects in PWV-based PCEM images is directly correlated with the refractive index contrast of the object [[yanyu_photonics_5:12]]. For instance, focal adhesion dynamics have been analyzed using photonic resonator outcoupler microscopy (PROM), where a designated refractive index elevation of $n_{FA} = \sim 1.46$ was observed in contrast to the surrounding medium [[yanyu_photonics_5:12]]. While hyperspectral imaging technology has enabled high-throughput digital biosensing on dielectric metasurfaces at a level of less than three molecules per $\mu m^{2}$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:13]], the integration of dielectric metasurfaces into these systems is still in its infancy [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]]. Furthermore, the utilizations of many other metasurface configurations remain to be explored [[yanyu_photonics_5:10]]. In anisotropic plasmonic metasurfaces, the bright mode exhibits an odd charge distribution with an in-plane dipolar moment, while the dark mode has an even charge distribution and an out-of-plane dipolar moment [[yanyu_photonics_5:14]]. Residual dispersion in related scanning microscopic techniques, such as OCT, has been numerically compensated using a 5th order polynomial for spectral phase error correction [[yanyu_photonics_5:15]].

Refractometric sensitivity in resonant photonic structures is fundamentally defined as the magnitude of the shift in resonant wavelength corresponding to a change in the refractive index of the sample [[yanyu_photonics_5:16]]. This sensitivity serves as a measure of the extent of resonance shifts for a given refractive index change, a parameter that depends on the material, geometry, and arrangement of the nanostructures [[yanyu_photonics_5:17]]. The performance of these sensors is often quantified by the detection limit, which reports the smallest sample refractive index change that can be accurately measured [[yanyu_photonics_5:16]]. This analytical framework is generally applicable to all resonant-based refractive index sensors that conform to standard resonance equations [[yanyu_photonics_5:16]].

Photonic crystal (PC) biosensors represent a novel type of label-free optical biosensing platform that utilizes a photonic crystal surface as a substrate for cell attachment [[yanyu_photonics_5:18]]. These structures are subwavelength nanostructured surfaces with a periodic modulation in the refractive index that acts as a narrow bandwidth resonant optical reflector at one specific resonance wavelength [[yanyu_photonics_5:19]]. By utilizing such a surface, microscopy enables label-free, quantitative, submicron resolution, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions without the need for cytotoxic staining agents or temporally-unstable fluorophores [[yanyu_photonics_5:20]]. This approach has been demonstrated with an effective magnification of $26\times$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:20]]. While the development of PC-based label-free biosensors is still in its initial stage, experimental demonstrations to date indicate that PC structures are a very promising biosensor platform [[yanyu_photonics_5:18]].

Dielectric metasurfaces offer an alternative resonant platform characterized by near-zero absorption losses in their constituent materials, which allows for reducing generated heat, while their high refractive index enables profound light confinement [[yanyu_photonics_5:17]]. These metasurfaces operate in aqueous media with resonances in the visible and near-IR spectral range, specifically between 600 nm and 850 nm [[yanyu_photonics_5:21]]. By generalizing and expanding the concept of Bound States in the Continuum (BIC) developed for asymmetric metasurfaces, researchers have achieved high-Q resonances and highly accessible enhanced near-fields [[yanyu_photonics_5:21]]. This design strategy resulted in an experimental bulk refractive index sensitivity of 305 nm/RIU [[yanyu_photonics_5:21]]. Despite these advancements, the overall performance of dielectric metasurfaces has not yet reached the levels of state-of-the-art plasmonic counterparts [[yanyu_photonics_5:17]], and the integration of dielectric metasurfaces into broader systems is currently in its infancy [[yanyu_photonics_5:17]].

In anisotropic plasmonic metasurfaces, the resonance wavelengths for oblique incidences in the $\Gamma - X$ direction remain hardly unchanged, whereas a red-shift is observed in the $\Gamma - X'$ direction [[yanyu_photonics_5:22]]. The fabrication of such structures can utilize silicon-zirconium hybrid photoresist for laser lithography due to its excellent resistance to shrinkage [[yanyu_photonics_5:22]]. Tuning the period of the unit cell from 2.8 to $3.2\mu \mathrm{m}$, while keeping other parameters fixed, allows for the adjustment of these resonant properties [[yanyu_photonics_5:22]]. Real-time imaging of 100 nm Au-NPs binding in-flow to Au-NHA sensors has been demonstrated on microarrays with dimensions of $100 \times 30 \mu m^{2}$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:23]].

Optical microcavities have successfully demonstrated label-free, single-molecule detection [[yanyu_photonics_5:24]]. In microtoroid optical resonators, label-free detection of single nanoparticles and biological molecules has been achieved, with dwell times scaling with concentration [[yanyu_photonics_5:25]]. In one such experiment, there was a 30-s delay before data recording after injection [[yanyu_photonics_5:25]]. Furthermore, hyperspectral imaging technology introduced by Altug and colleagues enabled high-throughput digital biosensing on dielectric metasurfaces at a level of less than three molecules per $\mu m^{2}$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:26]]. In these digital sensing configurations, as molecules accumulate on the grating, the refractive index changes, resulting in a change in the diffracted light intensity at the photodiode detector [[yanyu_photonics_5:26]].

Experimental investigations into photonic crystal and metasurface-enhanced microscopy have demonstrated the capability for label-free, quantitative, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions with submicron resolution [[yanyu_photonics_5:27]]. This approach eliminates the need for cytotoxic staining agents or temporally unstable fluorophores, offering a distinct advantage over conventional methods that rely on such labels [[yanyu_photonics_5:27]]. In the domain of refractometric sensing, performance is often quantified by the detection limit (DL), which reports the smallest sample refractive index change that can be accurately measured [[yanyu_photonics_5:28]]. Conventional ring resonators, a standard in refractometric sensing, exhibit relatively low sensitivity because only around 1–3% of the optical mode interacts with the sample [[yanyu_photonics_5:28]]. In contrast, dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (quasi-BIC) modes enable high-performance sensing by supporting high Q resonances with accessible near-fields [[yanyu_photonics_5:29]]. One such diatomic all-dielectric metasurface, derived from the generalization of BIC concepts developed for asymmetric metasurfaces, has been implemented for detecting extracellular vesicles [[yanyu_photonics_5:29]]. These metasurfaces operate in aqueous media with resonances in the visible and near-IR spectral range, specifically between 600 nm and 850 nm [[yanyu_photonics_5:29]]. The experimental setup for these imaging-based spectrometer-less optofluidic biosensors comprises a chip with twelve 250 μm by 250 μm sensors arranged in a 3×4 microarray format [[yanyu_photonics_5:29]].

Regarding specific performance metrics, dielectric metasurfaces have achieved an experimentally measured Q factor of up to 18,511 for operation in the telecommunication wavelength range [[yanyu_photonics_5:30]]. While integrating dielectric metasurfaces into advanced optical biosensors is still in its infancy, their overall performance has not yet reached the levels of state-of-the-art plasmonic counterparts [[yanyu_photonics_5:30]]. However, imaging techniques utilizing these metasurfaces illustrate superior sensing performance compared to ensemble averaging methods commonly used in conventional spectrometer-based measurements [[yanyu_photonics_5:30]]. In a related development, hyperspectral imaging technology introduced by Altug and colleagues enabled high-throughput digital biosensing on dielectric metasurfaces at a level of less than three molecules per μm² [[yanyu_photonics_5:31]]. For high-contrast imaging devices, planar photonic chips with tailored angular transmission have been developed, where the roles of the chip as a high-contrast imaging device are confirmed by both theoretical and experimental results [[yanyu_photonics_5:32]]. These devices address the limitation that the coupling efficiency of conventional dark-field microscopy is much lower [[yanyu_photonics_5:32]]. Luminescent surfaces with tailored angular emission have also been designed for compact dark-field imaging devices, with no data excluded from the associated analysis [[yanyu_photonics_5:33]].

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is a critical comparative metric in label-free detection. In a nanoplasmonic-photonic hybrid microcavity used for the label-free detection of single proteins, experimental results yielded signal-to-noise ratios of 22:1 and 13:1 for the associated proteins [[yanyu_photonics_5:34]]. While experimental results in spectral domain optical coherence tomography with dual-balanced detection agreed well with theoretical results, this specific context is distinct from the metasurface-enhanced phase contrast systems discussed here [[yanyu_photonics_5:35]]. Comparative analyses with other conventional techniques highlight that methods like nanobiosensors (NB) suffer from low sensitivity in the nM–pM range, low throughput, and high input RNA requirements, typically on the order of 5–50 μg total RNA per sample [[yanyu_photonics_5:36]]. In diagnostic applications, phage display-based identification has shown a diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of 100% each in comparison to a diagnostic sensitivity of 70% for the CFT and 60% for the cELISA, illustrating the potential for high-accuracy label-free detection when optimized surfaces are utilized [[yanyu_photonics_5:37]].

The integration of dielectric metasurfaces into optical biosensing systems is currently in its infancy, despite the potential for superior sensing performance compared to ensemble averaging methods used in conventional spectrometer-based measurements [[yanyu_photonics_5:38]]. While these surfaces offer advantages such as CMOS-compatible fabrication processes and lower resonance-induced heating compared to plasmonic counterparts, their widespread impact on photonic sensing is still emerging due to compatibility with standard semiconductor fabrication processes, design flexibility, and accessibility to a wider choice of materials [[yanyu_photonics_5:38]].

Current technical limitations are evident in the specific fabrication and operational parameters required for these systems. For instance, photonic resonator outcoupler microscopy (PROM) utilizes specific grating depths of 120 nm and periods of 400 nm to achieve quantitative analysis of focal adhesion dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_5:39]]. Similarly, imaging-based spectrometer-less optofluidic biosensors rely on precise geometrical parameters, such as an ellipticity of 0.44, to fabricate highly uniform silicon metasurfaces operating below 850 nm in aqueous media [[yanyu_photonics_5:40]]. The operational bandwidth of these photonic crystal surfaces is often narrow, with reflectance peaks exhibiting a bandwidth of approximately 4 nm, which constrains the spectral range available for imaging [[yanyu_photonics_5:41]]. Furthermore, the imaging process itself can be time-consuming; for example, one system assembles a series of lines into an image at a rate of 0.1 s per line, while another images in time intervals of 14 s using a CMOS camera [[yanyu_photonics_5:41]][[yanyu_photonics_5:40]].

Field-of-view and magnification constraints also characterize current implementations. Photonic crystal enhanced microscopy systems have been reported with an effective magnification of 26×, which facilitates label-free, quantitative, submicron resolution, time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions without cytotoxic staining agents [[yanyu_photonics_5:41]][[yanyu_photonics_5:42]]. This approach has enabled the first label-free time-lapse imaging of the attachment localization of living cells during chemotaxis [[yanyu_photonics_5:42]]. However, the reliance on specific optical setups, such as collimated linearly polarized laser lines with a 1.75 nm bandwidth at 700 nm collected with a ×10 objective, highlights the specialized nature of these instruments [[yanyu_photonics_5:40]].

Emerging trends in computational imaging and hybrid systems aim to address these limitations. Hyperspectral imaging technology has been introduced to enable high-throughput digital biosensing on dielectric metasurfaces, achieving a sensitivity level of less than three molecules per $\mu m^{2}$ [[yanyu_photonics_5:43]]. Additionally, the concept of bound states in the continuum (BIC) has been generalized and expanded for asymmetric metasurfaces to improve sensing capabilities [[yanyu_photonics_5:40]]. In related optical imaging fields, computational techniques such as interferometric synthetic aperture microscopy (ISAM) are being utilized to enhance depth-independent resolution, representing a primary modality in advanced optical coherence tomography [[yanyu_photonics_5:44]]. While some research areas note that scaling trends can exhibit complex patterns that defy simple trends, and that further improvement may be possible via thorough hyperparameter searches, these specific observations are noted in the context of computational constraints and data distribution complexities [[yanyu_photonics_5:45]][[yanyu_photonics_5:46]].

question: How can all-dielectri photonics crystal enhance fluorescence?
raw_answer:
The spontaneous emission rate of a fluorophore is fundamentally governed by the local density of optical states (LDOS), with the rate being directly proportional to this quantity [[yanyu_photonics_6:0]]. This relationship is derived from Fermi's Golden Rule, which states that the spontaneous emission rate is proportional to the square of the local field of the mode and the number of modes emitting into a given solid angle and frequency range [[yanyu_photonics_6:1]]. In the context of photonic crystals, the electromagnetic density of states can be manipulated; specifically, within a photonic bandgap, the density of states is zero, which inhibits spontaneous emission [[yanyu_photonics_6:1]]. Conversely, the Purcell effect describes a rate enhancement of spontaneous emission, which is distinct from the extraction effect that pertains to overall device efficiency [[yanyu_photonics_6:1]]. Theoretical calculations of the LDOS have been shown to agree with experimental observations of fluorescence lifetime as a function of the crystal lattice parameter [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]].

All-dielectric photonic crystals enhance fluorescence primarily through the Purcell effect, which modifies the quantum efficiency by shortening the spontaneous emission lifetime [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]][[yanyu_photonics_6:3]]. Because dielectric materials are lossless, this enhancement of quantum efficiency occurs without increasing the non-radiative decay rate [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]][[yanyu_photonics_6:3]]. The requirements for noticeable Purcell enhancement include a small mode volume and a high resonance Q-factor, conditions that may not always be met by standard photonic crystal structures [[yanyu_photonics_6:4]]. The decay rate into a specific frequency is maximized when the emitter frequency matches the mode frequency, following a Lorentzian-like dependence on the frequency difference and linewidth [[yanyu_photonics_6:5]]. Theoretically, a dielectric photonic crystal system can provide a 3–5× enhancement to the spontaneous emission rate relative to unpatterned glass [[yanyu_photonics_6:3]]. This enhancement can be significantly improved to a 360-fold increase by coupling the photonic crystal leaky mode to an underlying Fabry–Perot-type cavity through a gold mirror reflector [[yanyu_photonics_6:3]].

Beyond the fundamental Purcell effect, fluorescence enhancement in photonic crystals involves complex interactions with near fields and scattering effects. Enhanced fluorescence emission from quantum dots on a photonic crystal surface has been attributed to a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects, which are linked to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [[yanyu_photonics_6:6]]. A greater density of modes that overlap the emission spectrum of the quantum dots results in stronger scattering and consequently stronger extraction effects [[yanyu_photonics_6:6]]. Experimental measurements have quantified the contribution of near fields, yielding a fluorescence enhancement value of 8.24 ± 0.36 times when comparing resonant and non-resonant angles [[yanyu_photonics_6:6]]. In systems featuring Fano resonances, a significant alteration in the spectral density of states causes an increase in the extraction rate [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]]. The Green's function of the system, from which the local density of states, spontaneous decay rate, and radiative quantum efficiency are derived, can be evaluated by varying the position of the dipole emitter to map these enhancements [[yanyu_photonics_6:7]].

The establishment of a photonic bandgap (PBG) is critical for these mechanisms, requiring a minimum refractive index contrast value of 2.9 to establish a discrete optical band gap [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]]. When such a PBG is observed, it is characterized by a high percentage of reflectance below the critical angle [[yanyu_photonics_6:2]]. Specific structural configurations, such as double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals, have demonstrated remarkable 4.3-fold emission enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_6:8]]. These physical principles underpin the design of universal fluorescence enhancement substrates, such as those based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals with super-wide stopbands [[yanyu_photonics_6:9]].

All-dielectric photonic crystal architectures for fluorescence enhancement are primarily categorized into one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional structures, each supporting distinct resonant modes that modify the local density of optical states. Two-dimensional structures have been utilized extensively in recent literature due to their simple and manufacturable fabrication processes [[yanyu_photonics_6:10]]. In these 2D systems, thin slab photonic crystals possess a bandgap only for TE-polarized guided waves, yet they remain quite useful for enhancing emission [[yanyu_photonics_6:11]]. A specific implementation involves a photonic crystal slab that supports photonic crystal-guided resonances (PCGRs) in a $\mathrm{Si}_3\mathrm{N}_4$ thin-film coating with a refractive index of $n=2.05$ over a periodically modulated $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ substrate with a refractive index of $n=1.46$ [[yanyu_photonics_6:12]][[yanyu_photonics_6:10]]. The geometry of such PC slabs can be defined by specific parameters, such as a slab thickness $h / a = 0.555$ and a hole radius $r / a = 0.225$ [[yanyu_photonics_6:13]].

The resonant modes in these 2D structures, particularly leaky guided modes, play a critical role in extraction efficiency. At specific frequencies, the external emission from leaky guided modes is 20 times more intense than the emission from an unpatterned film [[yanyu_photonics_6:11]]. In the context of quantum dots on a photonic crystal surface, the observed enhancement is attributed to a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects, which are linked to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [[yanyu_photonics_6:14]]. By dividing the total enhancement obtained for the resonant angle by the enhancement obtained for the non-resonant angle, a value of $8.24 \pm 0.36$ times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields was obtained [[yanyu_photonics_6:14]].

Three-dimensional colloidal photonic crystals represent another architectural class, with double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals demonstrating a 4.3-fold emission enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_6:15]]. In the context of universal fluorescence enhancement substrates, multiple heterostructure photonic crystals are designed to feature super-wide stopbands [[yanyu_photonics_6:16]]. For 2D heterostructures, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for E-(CDs@F)-E, whereas a 56-fold enhancement was observed for E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for monolithic (CDs@F) [[yanyu_photonics_6:10]].

Whispering gallery modes (WGMs) are another key resonant mode utilized in dielectric microcavities, where optical losses interact with the WGM and are amplified due to the high circulating intensities present in the microcavity [[yanyu_photonics_6:17]]. While surface-plasmonic whispering-gallery modes have achieved Q factors of $1,376 \pm 65$ in the near infrared at room temperature [[yanyu_photonics_6:18]], purely dielectric microcavities face specific limitations. One limitation of dielectric microcavities is the mismatch between high-Q resonances of the cavity and the spectrally wide emission from inhomogeneously broadened fluorescent emitters at room temperature [[yanyu_photonics_6:12]]. This mismatch is consistent with early fluorescence enhancement methods using dielectric optical microcavities, which showed moderate increases in the emission rate caused by the mismatch between the high-Q cavity resonances and the inhomogeneously broadened emissions [[yanyu_photonics_6:10]].

Theoretical and numerical analyses further characterize these structures. FEM numerical simulations of 1D and 2D cavity structures predict a greatly enhanced thermal conductance coefficient for the quasi-2D cavity, with a ratio of $\epsilon_{2D}/\epsilon_{1D} = 42$ [[yanyu_photonics_6:19]]. The fluorescence enhancement factor is defined by the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the cavity to that in free space, expressed as $F_P = \gamma_{sp} / \gamma^0_{sp}$ [[yanyu_photonics_6:12]].

Experimental investigations into all-dielectric photonic crystals (PCs) have quantified significant enhancements in fluorescence emission, primarily driven by the Purcell effect, which modifies the local density of optical states (LDOS) [[yanyu_photonics_6:20]][[yanyu_photonics_6:21]]. This mechanism results in a reduction of the spontaneous emission lifetime and an increase in quantum efficiency (QE) without elevating the non-radiative decay rate, a benefit attributed to the lossless nature of dielectric materials [[yanyu_photonics_6:20]][[yanyu_photonics_6:22]]. In specific studies involving quantum dots (QDs) on a PC surface with a period of $\Lambda = 300$ nm and a hole radius of $r = 90$ nm, the near-field fluorescence enhancement was calculated to be $8.24 \pm 0.36$ times relative to the non-resonant angle [[yanyu_photonics_6:23]]. The Q-factor for these extraction modes was experimentally determined to be 92 [[yanyu_photonics_6:23]].

Quantitative metrics for single QD systems reveal that the experimental resolved average excitation enhancement factor is approximately 23.14, based on a sample size of 100 individual QDs, which aligns with simulated results [[yanyu_photonics_6:22]]. Concurrently, the QE enhancement factor, defined as the ratio of the PC-enhanced QE to the initial QE, was measured to be 1.67 [[yanyu_photonics_6:22]]. The Purcell factor ($F_P$) is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the PC to that in free space [[yanyu_photonics_6:22]]. These experiments further revealed that the emission lifetime of confined fluorophores is modified over expanded frequency ranges compared to their standard emission profiles in free solution [[yanyu_photonics_6:20]]. The fluorescence lifetime was found to be a function of the crystal lattice parameter, consistent with theoretical calculations of the LDOS [[yanyu_photonics_6:20]]. The temporal resolution of the measurement system used to observe these dynamics was 22 ps [[yanyu_photonics_6:22]].

In more complex heterostructure systems, enhancement factors can reach substantially higher values. For instance, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for the E-(CDs@F)-E configuration, compared to a 56-fold enhancement for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for the monolithic (CDs@F) structure [[yanyu_photonics_6:20]]. Similarly, a double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystal demonstrated a 4.3-fold emission enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_6:21]]. In universal fluorescence enhancement substrates based on multiple heterostructure PCs with super-wide stopbands, the fluorescence enhancement factor reaches a maximum value at a concentration of $100 \times 10^{-6}$ M [[yanyu_photonics_6:24]]. The interaction between dye molecules and the PC structure, which influences the fluorescence quantum yield, varies as the polarity of the dye molecules changes [[yanyu_photonics_6:24]].

Regarding absolute efficiency metrics, thin-film 2-D photonic crystals have been shown to achieve an external quantum efficiency greater than 50% [[yanyu_photonics_6:25]]. In absolute photoluminescence efficiency measurements, such structures have demonstrated a 70% external quantum efficiency, indicating resistance to parasitic absorption effects [[yanyu_photonics_6:25]]. While doping can improve the quantum yield of QDs [[yanyu_photonics_6:26]], the primary enhancement in dielectric PC systems stems from the modification of radiative lifetime due to the redistribution of the density of states (DOS) [[yanyu_photonics_6:21]].

The enhancement of fluorescence via all-dielectric photonic crystals is fundamentally constrained by the spectral bandwidth and the specific overlap between the photonic modes and the emitter's emission spectrum. The Purcell effect, which improves quantum efficiency by shortening the spontaneous emission lifetime, relies on the emitter coupling to specific photonic density of states [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]]. However, defect modes that do not overlap with the band edge cannot exhibit this enhancement effect, indicating a strict spectral alignment requirement [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]]. To achieve enhanced spontaneous emission, the photonic crystal lattice constant must be rescaled to tune the leaky conduction band modes to overlap with the material emission band [[yanyu_photonics_6:28]]. This tuning is particularly challenging when scaling the structure for different wavelengths; for instance, scaling the photonic crystal down for blue light requires a lattice constant of 350 nm, which imposes specific geometric constraints on the design [[yanyu_photonics_6:28]].

Fabrication tolerances and structural imperfections present significant practical challenges for realizing these theoretical enhancements. The performance of the device is sensitive to the precise geometry of the photonic crystal, such as the period and hole radius, where a specific surface structure with a period of 300 nm and a hole radius of 90 nm was utilized to support leaky modes [[yanyu_photonics_6:29]]. In thin-film 2-D photonic crystals, the aspect ratio is a critical parameter, with typical designs assuming a ratio of r/a = 0.37 [[yanyu_photonics_6:28]]. Furthermore, the z-height of the structure, which ranges from 0 nm at the groove to 28 nm at the ridge, must be controlled to ensure proper mode confinement and interaction [[yanyu_photonics_6:30]]. While controlling asymmetry along one axis has been observed to improve tolerance to fabrication imperfections compared to alternative methods, the sensitivity of the system to structural variations remains a key limitation [[yanyu_photonics_6:31]].

Material absorption losses and the complexity of mode coupling further limit the efficiency of fluorescence enhancement. Thin-film photonic crystal modes cannot be classified as pure TE or pure TM, which complicates the analysis and design of polarization-dependent enhancements [[yanyu_photonics_6:28]]. The coupling of emitters to specific modes is not always efficient; for example, quantum dot emission centered at 616 nm can couple to leaky modes supported by the photonic crystal and be extracted, but this requires precise alignment [[yanyu_photonics_6:29]]. In systems where a photonic crystal is coupled to an optical cavity, the sharp resonance and strong evanescent fields are due to the coupling of 1D photonic crystal modes to the modes of the underlying Fabry-Perot type optical cavity, whereas without the photonic crystal, the structure behaves like a weak cavity without strong evanescent fields [[yanyu_photonics_6:32]]. Additionally, Q-matching requirements, specifically that the radiative and non-radiative Q-factors must be equal ($Q_{r}=Q_{nr}$), need to be satisfied for two photonic crystal resonance modes to function optimally [[yanyu_photonics_6:30]].

The magnitude of fluorescence enhancement varies significantly depending on the specific photonic crystal architecture and the emitter-substrate interface. Near-field effects can provide substantial enhancement; for instance, the total enhancement obtained for the resonant angle divided by the non-resonant angle yielded a value of 8.24 ± 0.36 times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields [[yanyu_photonics_6:29]]. In other configurations, a dielectric photonic crystal system theoretically provides a 3–5× enhancement to the spontaneous emission rate relative to the original emission rate on unpatterned glass [[yanyu_photonics_6:30]]. More complex heterostructures can achieve higher gains, such as a 4.3-fold emission enhancement observed in double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals [[yanyu_photonics_6:33]]. In some cases, the enhancement is even more pronounced, with a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement observed for E-(CDs@F)-E heterostructures, compared to 56-fold for E-(CDs@F) and 33-fold for monolithic structures [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]]. These enhancements are often mediated by guided modes excited within the photonic crystal, which create an evanescent field where fluorophores receive greater illumination intensity than on an unpatterned surface [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]].

The integration of emitters into the photonic crystal structure often requires intermediate layers, which can introduce additional variables. For example, radiating dipoles may be embedded in a dielectric matrix, such as PVA polymer, coated with different thicknesses to facilitate coupling [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]]. The maximum emission in such systems can be centered at specific wavelengths, such as 585 nm, depending on the design [[yanyu_photonics_6:34]]. The strength of the simulated modes generally shows good agreement with the data obtained from photonic crystal coupled cavity (PCCE) measurements, validating the theoretical models despite the practical complexities [[yanyu_photonics_6:27]]. However, the radiation-pressure coupling between mechanical bound states in the continuum and optical modes strongly depends on the mode symmetry, highlighting the intricate relationship between structural symmetry and optical performance [[yanyu_photonics_6:35]]. The fluorescence enhancement factor is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the photonic crystal to the rate in free space, $F_P = \gamma_{sp} / \gamma^0_{sp}$, providing a standardized metric for evaluating these challenges [[yanyu_photonics_6:30]].
