question: What are the recent research advancements in enhancing fluorescence for imaging?
raw_answer:
Quantum dots (QDs) are widely utilized to improve fluorescence imaging due to their photochemical stability and strong fluorescence output [[yanyu_photonics_9:0]]. These nanocrystals offer superior performance compared to conventional chemical fluorescent labels, specifically regarding quantum yield and resistance against photobleaching, which is a significant limitation for organic fluorophores in longer-term imaging [[yanyu_photonics_9:1]][[yanyu_photonics_9:2]]. The spectral properties of QDs allow for spectral unmixing and the generation of spectral fingerprints or comparisons of label intensity, facilitating quantitative imaging from single molecules to tissue [[yanyu_photonics_9:2]]. In the context of cancer research, QDs serve as a tool for tumor vascular imaging and multimodal atomic imaging of angiogenesis [[yanyu_photonics_9:0]].

Recent advancements in enhancing QD signal intensity have focused on integrating them with photonic structures. Ganesh et al. demonstrated that the fluorescence intensity of QDs can be enhanced by a factor of up to $10^8$ when placed on a two-dimensional photonic crystal (PC) slab with dual band gaps, compared to QDs on an unpatterned surface [[yanyu_photonics_9:3]][[yanyu_photonics_9:4]]. This enhancement is attributed to leaky-mode-assisted fluorescence extraction from the 2D PC surface [[yanyu_photonics_9:5]]. The near-field contribution to this effect was quantified by dividing the total enhancement at the resonant angle by the enhancement at the non-resonant angle, yielding a value of $8.24 \pm 0.36$ times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields [[yanyu_photonics_9:3]]. In applications involving surface-captured QDs, a $3000\times$ enhancement has been observed compared to free-floating uncaptured QDs [[yanyu_photonics_9:5]]. The magnitude of this strong enhancement factor enables single QD imaging using only a low numerical aperture ($\mathrm{NA} = 0.5$) objective lens [[yanyu_photonics_9:4]].

Beyond standard photonic crystals, hybrid and heterostructure approaches have yielded significant fluorescence enhancements. For carbon dot (CDs) based systems, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for the E-(CDs@F)-E structure, whereas a 56-fold enhancement was noted for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for the monolithic (CDs@F) structure [[yanyu_photonics_9:4]][[yanyu_photonics_9:6]]. Plasmonic nanostructures also contribute to signal amplification; fluorescence lifetime measurements on ensembles of emitters on plasmonic nanoantennas reveal spontaneous emission rate enhancements exceeding 1,000 while maintaining high quantum efficiency ($>0.5$) and directional emission with 84% collection efficiency [[yanyu_photonics_9:7]]. These plasmonic effects are often studied using gold films, such as 50 nm Au films [[yanyu_photonics_9:7]]. Furthermore, photonic–plasmonic hybrids can exhibit a 10-fold nanoparticle absorption enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_9:1]].

Upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) represent another major strategy for enhancing fluorescence imaging by shifting emission wavelengths. Lanthanide-doped UCNPs can transform near-infrared (NIR) light into visible light, enabling deep-tissue imaging [[yanyu_photonics_9:8]]. These nanoparticles can convert long-wavelength light excitation into multiple short wavelengths, allowing the replacement of traditional short-wavelength excitation light with NIR light that possesses strong tissue penetration ability [[yanyu_photonics_9:9]]. Unlike other non-linear optical processes, up-conversion by UCNPs can be efficiently achieved at low excitation density and NIR wavelength, which ameliorates photodamage and autofluorescence effects [[yanyu_photonics_9:1]]. Recent discoveries include the down-conversion luminescence of rare-earth-based probes in the second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1,000–1,700 nm) window for in vivo biological imaging [[yanyu_photonics_9:10]].

In addition to QDs and UCNPs, other nanoparticle systems contribute to fluorescence enhancement and imaging capabilities. Smaller copper nanoparticles demonstrate fluorescence signal and optical imaging capabilities [[yanyu_photonics_9:8]]. In surgical applications, image-guided cancer surgery has been refined using integrated fluorescence imaging, such as adding indocyanine green (ICG) to superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) in a porcine model [[yanyu_photonics_9:10]]. A unique near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence imaging probe, ICG-p28, composed of the clinically nontoxic tumor-targeting peptide p28 and the FDA-approved NIR dye ICG, has been developed to improve the identification of positive margins [[yanyu_photonics_9:11]]. While some studies focus on fluorescence recovery in specific solvent mixtures, such as water/methanol/THF (ratio 1:4:5) [[yanyu_photonics_9:12]], other modalities like magnetic particle imaging offer sensitivity comparable to fluorescence imaging without the need for complex 3D reconstruction [[yanyu_photonics_9:13]].

The primary limitation of conventional organic fluorophores in long-term imaging is their susceptibility to photobleaching, which restricts the duration of observation [[yanyu_photonics_9:14]][[yanyu_photonics_9:15]]. In contrast, quantum dots (QDs) offer superior photostability and brightness compared to fluorescent proteins and organic dyes, enabling more robust quantitative imaging [[yanyu_photonics_9:14]]. This enhanced performance is further exemplified by fluorescent nanoparticles, such as those encapsulating Cy5.5 within a silica core matrix, which exhibit increased brightness and photostability relative to free dyes [[yanyu_photonics_9:16]]. Similarly, semiconducting polymer nanoparticles (SPNs) demonstrate significantly better near-infrared-II (NIR-II) brightness than organic NIR-II agents, attributed to their excellent stability and high quantum yield [[yanyu_photonics_9:17]]. The availability of chemical dyes with diverse spectral properties also facilitates multicolor imaging approaches, expanding the utility of these fluorophores in complex biological contexts [[yanyu_photonics_9:16]].

To address the challenges of signal detection, particularly the requirement for a single spot to accumulate sufficient fluorescent dye to appear brighter than background fluorescence, surface chemistry, and sensor dark noise, photonic crystal substrates have been developed [[yanyu_photonics_9:15]]. These substrates enhance fluorescence emission and suppress blinking, allowing for digital resolution biosensing using inexpensive optics such as low NA objectives, low-power laser diodes, and low EM gain CCDs [[yanyu_photonics_9:18]]. The design of these photonic crystals requires careful consideration of band structures, band gaps, and the absorption and emission maxima of the fluorescent moieties to optimize biosensing strategies, especially for FRET phenomena and quantum dots [[yanyu_photonics_9:19]]. However, experimental artifacts introduced during the fabrication of substrates used for fluorescence-based 'turn-on' (dequenching) and 'turn-off' (quenching) mechanisms remain an area requiring further research [[yanyu_photonics_9:19]]. Additionally, in certain high-contrast imaging devices, scattered light from high-intensity LEDs can excite fluorophores more efficiently than the fluorescence light emitted by QDs [[yanyu_photonics_9:20]].

Bioconjugation strategies are critical for targeting these advanced fluorophores to specific biological structures. Although fluorescent proteins are the only directly genetically expressible fluorophores, small genetically expressible peptides can be utilized to target QDs and organic dyes [[yanyu_photonics_9:14]]. The development of "click" chemistries has emerged as a significant advancement due to their rapidity, high yield, and ease of use at room temperature [[yanyu_photonics_9:14]]. Despite these advances, new bioconjugation chemistries are still necessary to generate QD bioconjugates with the improved precision control and specific functionality required for distinct biological tasks [[yanyu_photonics_9:14]]. The ability to generate stable bioconjugates under mild, near-physiological pH conditions offers numerous advantages over other existing methods [[yanyu_photonics_9:21]]. For instance, silica surfaces possess abundant hydroxyl groups that facilitate the binding of probes or fluorescent groups, providing more flexible functionality for surface modification [[yanyu_photonics_9:22]].

Specific probe designs, such as pH-sensitive dyes, enhance specificity by being fluorescent only in acidic environments, such as the intracellular compartment or the interstitial space of tumors, while remaining non-fluorescent at neutral or basic pH [[yanyu_photonics_9:23]]. These dyes can be bioconjugated to wild-type filamentous bacteriophage to target specific membrane proteins [[yanyu_photonics_9:23]]. In the context of FRET-based sensing, the ratio of acceptor intensity to total emission intensity depends on the proximity between the two fluorophores, providing a mechanism for detecting molecular interactions [[yanyu_photonics_9:15]]. Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime techniques are employed in biological and medical imaging because they display sensitivity to the chemical structures of probes and their microenvironment [[yanyu_photonics_9:16]]. While some studies note slow turn-on times for optical-absorption-induced phonon baths in optomechanical systems [[yanyu_photonics_9:24]], and specific etching processes like C4F8/SF6 chemistry are used in nanosensor fabrication [[yanyu_photonics_9:25]], the core focus remains on the chemical and physical enhancements of fluorophores and their conjugates to improve imaging contrast and specificity.

Deep learning and advanced image reconstruction algorithms are increasingly employed to enhance low-signal fluorescence and optical imaging data, offering improvements in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast without necessarily increasing exposure or relying solely on expensive hardware [[yanyu_photonics_9:26]][[yanyu_photonics_9:27]]. In the domain of optical coherence tomography (OCT), which serves as a parallel example of low-signal interferometric imaging, deep learning methods have demonstrated promising improvements in image quality, particularly in preserving image edge details compared to traditional algorithms [[yanyu_photonics_9:26]]. Specific architectures, such as the modified asymmetric convolution super-resolution residual network (AC-SRResNet), have been trained and evaluated using metrics including SNR, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and edge preservation index (EPI) [[yanyu_photonics_9:26]]. The AC-SRResNet architecture shows a consistent advantage in detail preservation over the standard super-resolution residual network (SRResNet) [[yanyu_photonics_9:26]]. Furthermore, resizing operations within these deep learning pipelines contribute to cleaner output images and better denoising effects [[yanyu_photonics_9:26]].

Recent advancements include the development of SNR-Net, a deep learning approach designed to brighten low-light OCT images and achieve speckle-free SNR enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_9:28]]. The image quality of brightened and denoised images produced by SNR-Net is close to ground truth, indicating strong performance in low-light brightening and denoising tasks [[yanyu_photonics_9:28]]. In the specific field of photothermal optical coherence tomography (PT-OCT), the utilization of artificial neural networks for enhancing SNR and image contrast represents the first report of deep learning application in this modality, which in turn lowers the required acquisition time [[yanyu_photonics_9:27]]. These supervised learning approaches, which address both classification and denoising problems, are solved using specific models such as classifiers and denoisers [[yanyu_photonics_9:29]]. While diffusion models offer high-quality image synthesis, they remain slower than Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) at sampling time due to the requirement of multiple denoising steps [[yanyu_photonics_9:30]]. In broader transfer learning contexts, encoder-decoder architectures with a denoising objective have performed best across various tasks [[yanyu_photonics_9:31]].

In fluorescence microscopy, computational strategies are often paired with hardware modifications to overcome the limitations of traditional high-cost systems. Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy typically achieves single fluorophore resolution by utilizing expensive high NA oil-immersion objectives and electron-multiplying charge-coupled (EM-CCD) cameras, which provide over a 30× increase in signal-to-noise ratio [[yanyu_photonics_9:32]]. In contrast, photonic crystal enhanced microscopy (PCGR) provides TIRF-like z-sectioning that enables the counting of quantum dot (QD) tags within approximately 60 nm of the surface [[yanyu_photonics_9:32]]. This approach allows for the use of inexpensive optics, such as an NA=0.5 objective, low power laser diode, and low EM gain CCD, effectively bypassing the need for TIRF or high gain electron-multiplying cameras [[yanyu_photonics_9:32]]. The use of a low NA lens (NA = 0.5, 50×) in such systems demonstrates that high-resolution biosensing can be achieved without the standard high-end hardware requirements [[yanyu_photonics_9:32]].

Fluorescence lifetime techniques are also utilized in biological and medical imaging due to their sensitivity to the chemical structures of probes and their microenvironment [[yanyu_photonics_9:33]]. Recent fluorescence-imaging techniques employ dyes that absorb near-infrared-II (NIR-II) light in the 1000–1700 nm range, which offers remarkable penetration depth, less photodamage, and low autofluorescence within the extended spectral region [[yanyu_photonics_9:33]]. For super-resolution imaging, the natural blinking of quantum dots has been leveraged to localize individual emitters with separations less than the diffraction limit, a method first proposed and demonstrated by Lidke et al. [[yanyu_photonics_9:34]]. Additionally, Dertinger et al. applied QDs for Super-resolution Optical Fluctuating Imaging (SOFI), where the statistical analysis of fluorescence fluctuations throughout a time series achieves a super-resolution image [[yanyu_photonics_9:34]].

Other optical imaging modalities benefit from specific illumination and detection strategies that complement computational recovery. Structured laser illumination planar imaging in scattering and fluorescing media has been analyzed for multiple scattering suppression, with corresponding fluorescence values reported as 87, 82, and 77 [[yanyu_photonics_9:35]]. Leaky-mode assisted fluorescence extraction in biosensors has revealed differences in enhancement factors across various lattices, with a maximum enhancement factor approaching 220 [[yanyu_photonics_9:36]]. In compact dark-field imaging devices, the resolution obtained with Superluminescent Diode (SLED) illumination is comparable to the resolution in bright-field light [[yanyu_photonics_9:37]]. Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography (PS-OCT) achieves axial resolution in the order of a few micrometers and enables detection sensitivities of reflected light signals as low as $10^{-10}$ of the input, despite high imaging speeds [[yanyu_photonics_9:38]]. TIRFM remains a powerful platform for single-molecule detection, offering both high throughput and high signal-to-background ratio [[yanyu_photonics_9:39]]. Specific experimental setups for real-time imaging of mitochondrial ATP dynamics have utilized GFP excited at 488 nm and MitoTracker Red excited at 561 nm [[yanyu_photonics_9:40]]. While not directly an imaging algorithm, the assessment of miRNA recovery notes that sub-optimal column capacity leads to poor recovery when using very low amounts of cells and plasma, highlighting the importance of signal recovery in low-input scenarios [[yanyu_photonics_9:41]].

The integration of fluorescence with other imaging modalities addresses the inherent limitations of single-modality approaches, particularly the limited sensitivity and lack of specific functional information provided by techniques such as CT and MRI when using non-targeted contrast agents [[yanyu_photonics_9:42]]. While MRI assesses the degree of hydrogen molecule magnetization inside water molecules and allows for simultaneous imaging of soft tissue and interventional equipment, it often lacks the molecular specificity required for detailed disease characterization [[yanyu_photonics_9:43]][[yanyu_photonics_9:44]]. To overcome these constraints, hybrid probes and multimodal strategies have been developed to combine the molecular sensitivity of fluorescence with the deep penetration and anatomical resolution of other modalities.

Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) has emerged as a key complementary modality, employing endogenous and exogenous contrasts to provide insightful data on cellular and molecular properties [[yanyu_photonics_9:44]]. Photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) specifically offers high spatiotemporal resolution, with in-plane resolution of 125-μm and data acquisition rates of 50-μs frame$^{-1}$, along with deep tissue penetration of 48-mm in vivo [[yanyu_photonics_9:45]]. The synergy between fluorescence and photoacoustic imaging is exemplified by ICG-loaded gold nanorod-liposome core-shell nanoparticles, which were developed to integrate both photoacoustic and fluorescence imaging strategies [[yanyu_photonics_9:43]]. Furthermore, near-infrared optical imaging agents with rapid renal clearance can serve as contrast agents for both optical and photoacoustic imaging, while also functioning as photosensitizers for photodynamic or photothermal therapy upon NIR excitation [[yanyu_photonics_9:46]].

Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) represents another hybrid approach, utilizing Janus iron oxides @ semiconducting polymer nanoparticle tracers for cell tracking [[yanyu_photonics_9:47]]. This technique possesses a sensitivity comparable to fluorescence imaging and obviates the need for complex 3D reconstruction [[yanyu_photonics_9:47]]. In the context of image-guided cancer surgery, superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) have been combined with indocyanine green (ICG) to allow for method refinement using integrated fluorescence imaging in porcine models [[yanyu_photonics_9:43]]. Quantum dots (QDs) also serve as versatile tools in this multimodal landscape, providing capabilities for tumor vascular imaging and multimodal atomic imaging of angiogenesis [[yanyu_photonics_9:48]]. QD probes are applicable in techniques that cover all spatiotemporal scales for biological imaging, ranging from single molecules to tissue levels [[yanyu_photonics_9:49]].

Beyond the integration of distinct imaging modalities, significant advancements have been made in enhancing fluorescence emission itself through photonic structures and hybrid materials. Photonic crystals (PCs) have been utilized to enhance fluorescence extraction; for instance, a 108× fluorescence enhancement for a layer of quantum dots was reported using leaky-mode-assisted fluorescence extraction from a 2-dimensional PC surface [[yanyu_photonics_9:50]]. This approach also facilitates blinking suppression for single quantum dot digital resolution biosensing [[yanyu_photonics_9:50]]. In heterostructure designs, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for E-(CDs@F)-E, compared to a 56-fold enhancement for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for monolithic (CDs@F) structures [[yanyu_photonics_9:51]]. The 56-fold enhancement for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure has been specifically noted in the context of anomalous fluorescence enhancement from double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals, which serve as multifunctional fluorescence-based sensor platforms [[yanyu_photonics_9:52]].

The design of these enhanced probes often involves specific material choices to ensure stability and performance. Colloidal CdSe/ZnS quantum dots are frequently chosen for fluorescence measurements due to their ability to perform without significant photo-bleaching [[yanyu_photonics_9:53]]. In the development of QD-tagged ssDNA probes, capture sequences with 5-base oligo(T) linkers are used as spacers to prevent steric effects [[yanyu_photonics_9:50]]. Additionally, fluorescence lifetime techniques are employed in biological and medical imaging because they display sensitivity to the chemical structures of probes and their microenvironment [[yanyu_photonics_9:43]]. answer_official_all: Quantum dots (QDs) are widely utilized to improve fluorescence imaging due to their photochemical stability and strong fluorescence output . These nanocrystals offer superior performance compared to conventional chemical fluorescent labels, specifically regarding quantum yield and resistance against photobleaching, which is a significant limitation for organic fluorophores in longer-term imaging [0]. The spectral properties of QDs allow for spectral unmixing and the generation of spectral fingerprints or comparisons of label intensity, facilitating quantitative imaging from single molecules to tissue [0]. In the context of cancer research, QDs serve as a tool for tumor vascular imaging and multimodal atomic imaging of angiogenesis . Recent advancements in enhancing QD signal intensity have focused on integrating them with photonic structures. Ganesh et al. demonstrated that the fluorescence intensity of QDs can be enhanced by a factor of up to $10^8$ when placed on a two-dimensional photonic crystal (PC) slab with dual band gaps, compared to QDs on an unpatterned surface . This enhancement is attributed to leaky-mode-assisted fluorescence extraction from the 2D PC surface . The near-field contribution to this effect was quantified by dividing the total enhancement at the resonant angle by the enhancement at the non-resonant angle, yielding a value of $8.24 \pm 0.36$ times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields . In applications involving surface-captured QDs, a $3000\times$ enhancement has been observed compared to free-floating uncaptured QDs . The magnitude of this strong enhancement factor enables single QD imaging using only a low numerical aperture ($\mathrm{NA} = 0.5$) objective lens . Beyond standard photonic crystals, hybrid and heterostructure approaches have yielded significant fluorescence enhancements. For carbon dot (CDs) based systems, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for the E-(CDs@F)-E structure, whereas a 56-fold enhancement was noted for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for the monolithic (CDs@F) structure . Plasmonic nanostructures also contribute to signal amplification; fluorescence lifetime measurements on ensembles of emitters on plasmonic nanoantennas reveal spontaneous emission rate enhancements exceeding 1,000 while maintaining high quantum efficiency ($>0.5$) and directional emission with 84% collection efficiency [2]. These plasmonic effects are often studied using gold films, such as 50 nm Au films [2]. Furthermore, photonic–plasmonic hybrids can exhibit a 10-fold nanoparticle absorption enhancement . Upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) represent another major strategy for enhancing fluorescence imaging by shifting emission wavelengths. Lanthanide-doped UCNPs can transform near-infrared (NIR) light into visible light, enabling deep-tissue imaging . These nanoparticles can convert long-wavelength light excitation into multiple short wavelengths, allowing the replacement of traditional short-wavelength excitation light with NIR light that possesses strong tissue penetration ability . Unlike other non-linear optical processes, up-conversion by UCNPs can be efficiently achieved at low excitation density and NIR wavelength, which ameliorates photodamage and autofluorescence effects . Recent discoveries include the down-conversion luminescence of rare-earth-based probes in the second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1,000–1,700 nm) window for in vivo biological imaging . In addition to QDs and UCNPs, other nanoparticle systems contribute to fluorescence enhancement and imaging capabilities. Smaller copper nanoparticles demonstrate fluorescence signal and optical imaging capabilities . In surgical applications, image-guided cancer surgery has been refined using integrated fluorescence imaging, such as adding indocyanine green (ICG) to superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) in a porcine model . A unique near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence imaging probe, ICG-p28, composed of the clinically nontoxic tumor-targeting peptide p28 and the FDA-approved NIR dye ICG, has been developed to improve the identification of positive margins . While some studies focus on fluorescence recovery in specific solvent mixtures, such as water/methanol/THF (ratio 1:4:5) , other modalities like magnetic particle imaging offer sensitivity comparable to fluorescence imaging without the need for complex 3D reconstruction . The primary limitation of conventional organic fluorophores in long-term imaging is their susceptibility to photobleaching, which restricts the duration of observation [0]. In contrast, quantum dots (QDs) offer superior photostability and brightness compared to fluorescent proteins and organic dyes, enabling more robust quantitative imaging [0]. This enhanced performance is further exemplified by fluorescent nanoparticles, such as those encapsulating Cy5.5 within a silica core matrix, which exhibit increased brightness and photostability relative to free dyes . Similarly, semiconducting polymer nanoparticles (SPNs) demonstrate significantly better near-infrared-II (NIR-II) brightness than organic NIR-II agents, attributed to their excellent stability and high quantum yield . The availability of chemical dyes with diverse spectral properties also facilitates multicolor imaging approaches, expanding the utility of these fluorophores in complex biological contexts . To address the challenges of signal detection, particularly the requirement for a single spot to accumulate sufficient fluorescent dye to appear brighter than background fluorescence, surface chemistry, and sensor dark noise, photonic crystal substrates have been developed . These substrates enhance fluorescence emission and suppress blinking, allowing for digital resolution biosensing using inexpensive optics such as low NA objectives, low-power laser diodes, and low EM gain CCDs . The design of these photonic crystals requires careful consideration of band structures, band gaps, and the absorption and emission maxima of the fluorescent moieties to optimize biosensing strategies, especially for FRET phenomena and quantum dots . However, experimental artifacts introduced during the fabrication of substrates used for fluorescence-based 'turn-on' (dequenching) and 'turn-off' (quenching) mechanisms remain an area requiring further research . Additionally, in certain high-contrast imaging devices, scattered light from high-intensity LEDs can excite fluorophores more efficiently than the fluorescence light emitted by QDs . Bioconjugation strategies are critical for targeting these advanced fluorophores to specific biological structures. Although fluorescent proteins are the only directly genetically expressible fluorophores, small genetically expressible peptides can be utilized to target QDs and organic dyes [0]. The development of "click" chemistries has emerged as a significant advancement due to their rapidity, high yield, and ease of use at room temperature [0]. Despite these advances, new bioconjugation chemistries are still necessary to generate QD bioconjugates with the improved precision control and specific functionality required for distinct biological tasks [0]. The ability to generate stable bioconjugates under mild, near-physiological pH conditions offers numerous advantages over other existing methods . For instance, silica surfaces possess abundant hydroxyl groups that facilitate the binding of probes or fluorescent groups, providing more flexible functionality for surface modification . Specific probe designs, such as pH-sensitive dyes, enhance specificity by being fluorescent only in acidic environments, such as the intracellular compartment or the interstitial space of tumors, while remaining non-fluorescent at neutral or basic pH . These dyes can be bioconjugated to wild-type filamentous bacteriophage to target specific membrane proteins . In the context of FRET-based sensing, the ratio of acceptor intensity to total emission intensity depends on the proximity between the two fluorophores, providing a mechanism for detecting molecular interactions . Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime techniques are employed in biological and medical imaging because they display sensitivity to the chemical structures of probes and their microenvironment . While some studies note slow turn-on times for optical-absorption-induced phonon baths in optomechanical systems , and specific etching processes like C4F8/SF6 chemistry are used in nanosensor fabrication , the core focus remains on the chemical and physical enhancements of fluorophores and their conjugates to improve imaging contrast and specificity. Deep learning and advanced image reconstruction algorithms are increasingly employed to enhance low-signal fluorescence and optical imaging data, offering improvements in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast without necessarily increasing exposure or relying solely on expensive hardware . Furthermore, resizing operations within these deep learning pipelines contribute to cleaner output images and better denoising effects . In fluorescence microscopy, computational strategies are often paired with hardware modifications to overcome the limitations of traditional high-cost systems. [0]. Additionally, Dertinger et al. applied QDs for Super-resolution Optical Fluctuating Imaging (SOFI), where the statistical analysis of fluorescence fluctuations throughout a time series achieves a super-resolution image [0]. Other optical imaging modalities benefit from specific illumination and detection strategies that complement computational recovery. Structured laser illumination planar imaging in scattering and fluorescing media has been analyzed for multiple scattering suppression, with corresponding fluorescence values reported as 87, 82, and 77 . Leaky-mode assisted fluorescence extraction in biosensors has revealed differences in enhancement factors across various lattices, with a maximum enhancement factor approaching 220 . question: What are the recent research advancements in enhancing fluorescence for biosensing using photonic crystal?
raw_answer:
The fundamental mechanism underlying fluorescence enhancement in photonic crystal (PC) structures is the modification of the electromagnetic density of states, which directly influences the spontaneous emission rate of fluorophores [[yanyu_photonics_10:0]]. In a photonic bandgap, the electromagnetic density of states is zero, which inhibits spontaneous emission [[yanyu_photonics_10:0]]. Conversely, in artificial photonic band structures, a large density of states, or degeneracy factor, can more than compensate for a large mode volume to provide significant spontaneous emission enhancement [[yanyu_photonics_10:0]]. The spontaneous emission rate is proportional to the local density of states (LDOS), a relationship that is central to understanding these enhancements [[yanyu_photonics_10:1]]. While the well-known Purcell factor, often expressed as Q/V, is a common metric, it is actually only an approximation of the more fundamental quantity, the LDOS [[yanyu_photonics_10:1]]. The influence of the underlying PC on the local density of states and the lifetime of the fluorophores provides significant insights into the enhancement mechanisms [[yanyu_photonics_10:2]].

The Purcell effect specifically refers to a rate enhancement of spontaneous emission, which is distinct from the extraction effect that pertains to overall efficiency [[yanyu_photonics_10:0]]. In dielectric photonic crystals, the Purcell effect improves quantum efficiency by resulting in a shorter spontaneous emission lifetime [[yanyu_photonics_10:2]]. This dielectric PC produces a quantum efficiency enhancement through the Purcell effect, which results in reduced spontaneous emission lifetime and higher quantum efficiency [[yanyu_photonics_10:3]]. The enhancement of quantum dot emission via this effect occurs by modifying quantum efficiency without increasing the non-radiative decay rate, a benefit attributed to the lossless nature of dielectric materials [[yanyu_photonics_10:2]]. Theoretically, such a dielectric PC system can provide a 3–5× enhancement to the spontaneous emission rate relative to the original emission rate on unpatterned glass [[yanyu_photonics_10:3]]. The Purcell factor is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the PC to the original emission rate [[yanyu_photonics_10:3]].

However, the requirements for noticeable Purcell enhancement include a small mode volume and a high resonance Q-factor, conditions that may not always be met by standard photonic crystals [[yanyu_photonics_10:4]]. For instance, in asymmetric structures that cannot possess a bandgap for either transverse electric- or transverse magnetic-like modes, the effect of inhibited spontaneous emission into undetectable waveguide modes is absent [[yanyu_photonics_10:5]]. In such cases, fluorescence enhancement may arise from other mechanisms, such as a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects attributed to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [[yanyu_photonics_10:5]]. Experimental data has shown that the enhancement obtained for the resonant angle divided by the enhancement for the non-resonant angle yields a value of 8.24 ± 0.36 times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields [[yanyu_photonics_10:5]].

Beyond the standard Purcell effect, specific resonant features can further alter the spectral density of states. In the presence of Fano resonances, a significant alteration in the spectral density of states causes an increase in the extraction rate [[yanyu_photonics_10:2]]. The decay rate into a specific frequency is proportional to a Lorentzian-like function that is maximized at the resonance frequency [[yanyu_photonics_10:6]]. In double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals, the cavity layer itself acts as a strong resonator of the emission light, with a partial bandgap overlapping the fluorophore emission wavelength [[yanyu_photonics_10:7]]. These mechanisms collectively demonstrate that while the Purcell effect and LDOS modification are primary drivers, specific structural resonances and near-field effects also contribute significantly to the overall fluorescence enhancement observed in photonic crystal biosensing platforms [[yanyu_photonics_10:5]][[yanyu_photonics_10:2]][[yanyu_photonics_10:7]].

Recent advancements in photonic crystal (PC) biosensing have focused on diverse structural geometries, including one-dimensional (1D), two-dimensional (2D), and three-dimensional (3D) architectures, to optimize light-matter interaction [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]][[yanyu_photonics_10:9]]. Photonic slabs, which include patterned 1D and 2D slabs, are particularly appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to their good sensitivity, simplified optics, and compatibility with substrates [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]]. A specific class of PC biosensors utilizes photonic crystal fiber (PCF), defined as a fiber optic cable with air holes in its cross-section [[yanyu_photonics_10:9]]. In the realm of 2D structures, microcavity biosensors are formed by introducing a point defect into the periodic microstructure, such as increasing or decreasing the central hole [[yanyu_photonics_10:9]]. Another 2D implementation involves a photonic crystal nanobeam cavity consisting of a series of rectangular gratings along a 500-nm-wide, 220-nm-thick waveguide [[yanyu_photonics_10:10]]. For 3D applications, double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals have been developed as multifunctional fluorescence-based sensor platforms [[yanyu_photonics_10:11]]. Additionally, universal fluorescence enhancement substrates based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals with super-wide stopbands have been designed for highly sensitive detection [[yanyu_photonics_10:12]].

Fabrication techniques and material choices significantly influence the performance of these biosensing platforms. A robust, lossless, and practical biosensing platform was developed using a 1DPC, which has the potential to entirely replace the metallic thin films used in surface plasmon resonance (SPCE) platforms [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]]. This approach offers high surface stability compared to metallic thin films, supporting a wide variety of functionalization for the detection of different disease biomarkers [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]]. In another fabrication strategy, a photonic crystal (PC) slab supports photonic crystal-guided resonances (PCGRs) in a Si$_3$N$_4$ thin film ($n=2.05$) coating on a periodically modulated SiO$_2$ substrate ($n=1.46$) [[yanyu_photonics_10:13]]. This specific structure was fabricated by depositing a 130-nm SiO$_2$ thin film onto a 200-mm-diameter glass substrate [[yanyu_photonics_10:13]]. The design of these nano-architectures requires adequate knowledge of the real and imaginary components of the nanomaterials used to achieve excellent performance in biosensing platforms [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]].

The optimization of light-matter interaction through these structural designs yields substantial fluorescence enhancement. A simple photonic biosensor platform utilizing a PC surface achieved an amplification of quantum dot (QD) emission of up to 3000-fold [[yanyu_photonics_10:13]]. This nearly 3000-fold signal enhancement is achieved through multiplicative effects of enhanced excitation, highly directional extraction, quantum efficiency improvement, and blinking suppression [[yanyu_photonics_10:13]]. The fluorescence enhancement factor ($F_P$) is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the presence of the structure to the spontaneous emission rate in free space ($\gamma_{sp} / \gamma^0_{sp}$) [[yanyu_photonics_10:13]]. In a separate study, the total enhancement obtained for the resonant angle divided by the enhancement for the non-resonant angle yielded a value of 8.24 ± 0.36 times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields [[yanyu_photonics_10:14]]. For 3D colloidal photonic crystals, a 4.3-fold emission enhancement was observed, which is considered remarkable [[yanyu_photonics_10:11]]. In heterostructure designs, a 73-fold fluorescence enhancement was observed for E-(CDs@F)-E, whereas a 56-fold enhancement was observed for the E-(CDs@F) heterostructure and a 33-fold enhancement for the monolithic (CDs@F) structure [[yanyu_photonics_10:8]].

Hybrid photonic-plasmonic structures represent another avenue for enhancing light-matter interaction. A photonic-plasmonic hybrid single-molecule nanosensor was utilized to measure the effect of fluorescent labels on DNA-protein dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_10:10]]. In contrast to low-Q photonic crystal nanocavities, research has focused on enhanced light-matter interaction in silica microtoroidal cavities [[yanyu_photonics_10:15]]. A nanoplasmonic-photonic hybrid microcavity enabled label-free detection of single proteins with step heights ranging from 7 to 13 fm [[yanyu_photonics_10:16]]. Furthermore, a nanoparticle-enhanced plasmonic biosensor for digital biomarker detection in a microarray demonstrated that a SiO$_2$ thin film of 5 nm height causes a spectral shift of the Au-NHA transmission resonance peak due to refractive index changes [[yanyu_photonics_10:17]].

These photonic crystal biosensors are a novel type of label-free optical biosensing platform [[yanyu_photonics_10:9]]. The key innovation enabling certain capabilities in this field is the use of noncoherent illumination of a photonic crystal biosensor and a spectroscopic scanning system that couples with a microscope objective [[yanyu_photonics_10:18]]. Regarding theoretical limits, when thin film samples are bonded to a glass hemisphere, a 100% internally efficient, unpatterned, thin film will have a single-sided external efficiency of approximately 0.055 [[yanyu_photonics_10:19]]. Additionally, polarization-splitting grating couplers, such as two-dimensional polarization independence grating coupler and one-dimensional polarization-splitting grating couplers, have been designed and studied on silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates [[yanyu_photonics_10:20]].

Recent empirical studies demonstrate that photonic crystal (PC) enhanced fluorescence significantly improves sensitivity and limit of detection (LOD) across various biosensing platforms. A universal fluorescence enhancement substrate based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals with a super-wide stopband achieved a limit of detection for Cr(VI) of 0.2 ppb [[yanyu_photonics_10:21]]. In this system, the fluorescence enhancement factor reached a maximum value at a concentration of $100 \times 10^{-6}$ M [[yanyu_photonics_10:21]]. The design of the photonic crystal stopband is critical for performance; when the stopband coupled with only excitation light or only emission light, the enhancement factor was improved by approximately 40-fold [[yanyu_photonics_10:21]]. Another study utilizing double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals reported an ultrasensitive detection limit of 91 pM for Hg(II), which is 14-fold lower than the detection limit of carbon dots in suspension [[yanyu_photonics_10:22]].

Quantum dot (QD) based systems have shown substantial improvements in signal-to-noise ratio and detection limits through PC enhancement. The combination of independent multiplicative effects on a PC surface achieved an unprecedented 3000× enhancement in QD emission with blinking suppression [[yanyu_photonics_10:23]]. This enhancement is attributed to a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects, which are linked to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [[yanyu_photonics_10:21]]. The quantum efficiency enhancement factor ($\eta_{\mathrm{QE}}$) was measured to be 1.67 in one such configuration [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]]. The detection scheme inherently incorporates low background fluorescence because QD tags close to the biosensor surface experience maximum fluorescence enhancement, similar to total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy [[yanyu_photonics_10:25]].

Digital resolution biosensing using single quantum dots on photonic crystals has yielded significant advancements in linear dose-response characteristics and detection limits. Direct counting capability yields linear dose-response characteristics on a log-log scale across a target concentration range of 10 aM–1 nM [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]]. This approach provides a 10,000× detection limit improvement compared to analog ensemble intensity measurement [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]]. In contrast, conventional analog intensity measurements require higher laser incident power, such as 5 mW [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]]. The fluorescence enhancement factor ($F_P$) is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate on the PC to that in free space ($F_P = \gamma_{sp} / \gamma^0_{sp}$) [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]]. Experimental data indicated a blank signal level of approximately 5 in these digital resolution assays [[yanyu_photonics_10:24]].

Photonic slabs and patterned 1D and 2D slabs are particularly appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to their good sensitivity, simplified optics, and compatibility with substrates [[yanyu_photonics_10:23]]. A fluorescent sandwich assay on a PC biochip demonstrated a detection limit for Ang2 of $2.5\mathrm{ng / mL}$ within 30 minutes [[yanyu_photonics_10:23]]. In another application, a $\sim 105\times$ improvement in the limit of detection of a fluorophore-tagged protein was demonstrated compared to detection on an unpatterned glass substrate [[yanyu_photonics_10:23]]. The integration of an optical cavity with a photonic crystal led to a 6× increase in the signal-to-noise ratio of a dye-labeled polypeptide compared to ordinary photonic crystal enhanced fluorescence [[yanyu_photonics_10:26]].

Label-free and imaging-based approaches also leverage PC-enhanced fluorescence for biosensing. Photonic crystal biosensors are a novel type of label-free optical biosensing platform [[yanyu_photonics_10:27]]. The key innovation in label-free imaging of cell attachment is the use of noncoherent illumination of a photonic crystal biosensor coupled with a spectroscopic scanning system and a microscope objective [[yanyu_photonics_10:28]]. This same noncoherent illumination and spectroscopic scanning system is identified as the key innovation enabling capabilities in photonic crystal enhanced microscopy for imaging live cell adhesion [[yanyu_photonics_10:29]]. A hybrid system incorporating a high Q-factor ($Q = 8.2 \times 10^{3}$ in buffer) has been reported in the context of digital resolution biomolecular sensing [[yanyu_photonics_10:30]]. While nanoparticle-enhanced plasmonic biosensors have achieved a calculated limit of detection of 69 pg/mL for human CRP, this specific metric is associated with plasmonic rather than purely photonic crystal fluorescence enhancement mechanisms [[yanyu_photonics_10:31]]. Conventional fluorescence spectroscopy using cuvettes suffers from low signal collection efficiency due to the detector being fixed at a particular angle, a limitation that PC-based systems aim to address [[yanyu_photonics_10:23]].

Recent advancements in photonic crystal (PC) biosensing have expanded from general label-free detection to the specific identification of environmental contaminants, disease biomarkers, and cellular dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_10:32]]. A universal fluorescence enhancement substrate based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals with a super-wide stopband has been developed for the highly sensitive detection of hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) [[yanyu_photonics_10:33]]. In the realm of disease biomarker detection, photonic crystal platforms have demonstrated significant improvements in the limit of detection for fluorophore-tagged proteins, achieving a $\sim 105\times$ improvement compared to detection on unpatterned glass substrates [[yanyu_photonics_10:34]]. The high surface stability of these platforms, which is superior to that of metallic thin films, supports a wide variety of functionalization strategies for the detection of different disease biomarkers [[yanyu_photonics_10:34]].

Specific applications in nucleic acid sensing include the ultrasensitive amplified detection of microRNA using a CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated DNA walker, which achieved a limit of detection of $4.1\mathrm{fM}$ [[yanyu_photonics_10:34]]. Another approach utilizes a photonic biosensor platform that provides amplification of quantum dot (QD) emission of up to 3000-fold for digital resolution biosensing [[yanyu_photonics_10:35]]. In this system, the reaction Gibbs energy between the DNA probe and the target was optimized to be approximately zero ($\Delta G^{\prime} \sim 0$) to facilitate specific binding [[yanyu_photonics_10:35]]. The detection target in this specific application was miR-375, which includes 22 nucleobases [[yanyu_photonics_10:35]]. The enhancement of fluorescence emission in these systems is attributed to a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects, which are linked to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [[yanyu_photonics_10:36]]. This enhancement is quantified by the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the presence of the photonic crystal to that in free space, expressed as $F_P = \gamma_sp / \gamma^0_sp$ [[yanyu_photonics_10:35]].

For cellular and protein dynamics, photonic-plasmonic hybrid single-molecule nanosensors have been employed to measure the effect of fluorescent labels on DNA-protein dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_10:37]]. These sensors utilize a photonic crystal nanobeam cavity consisting of a series of rectangular gratings along a 500-nm-wide, 220-nm-thick waveguide [[yanyu_photonics_10:37]]. Additionally, a photonic crystal coupled to an optical cavity has been used to increase the signal-to-noise ratio of a dye-labeled polypeptide by $6\times$ compared to ordinary photonic crystal enhanced fluorescence [[yanyu_photonics_10:38]]. Label-free imaging of cell attachment and adhesion has been achieved using photonic crystal enhanced microscopy, which utilizes noncoherent illumination of a photonic crystal biosensor and a spectroscopic scanning system coupled with a microscope objective [[yanyu_photonics_10:39]][[yanyu_photonics_10:40]]. This method enables label-free, quantitative, submicron resolution, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions without the need for cytotoxic staining agents or temporally unstable fluorophores [[yanyu_photonics_10:39]]. The photonic crystal biosensor strictly limits the lateral propagation of resonantly coupled light, enabling imaging-based detection with sufficient resolution to measure subtle variations in cell adhesion strength within a single cell [[yanyu_photonics_10:40]].

The design of these biosensors varies across different structural configurations. A two-dimensional photonic crystal microcavity biosensor is formed by introducing a point defect into the periodic microstructure, either by increasing or decreasing the central hole [[yanyu_photonics_10:32]]. Another class of PC biosensor is based on photonic crystal fiber (PCF), which is a fiber optic cable with air holes in its cross-section [[yanyu_photonics_10:32]]. The detection scheme for quantum dot-based sensors inherently incorporates low background fluorescence, as QD tags close to the biosensor surface experience maximum fluorescence enhancement, similar to total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy [[yanyu_photonics_10:36]]. These diverse structural and functional approaches address the urgent need for sensor substrates that can enhance excitation, extraction, and quantum efficiency for fluorescent-based detection [[yanyu_photonics_10:34]].

The fabrication of photonic crystal (PC) biosensors involves complex manufacturing processes, which often necessitate specific structural optimizations to maintain feasibility [[yanyu_photonics_10:41]]. For instance, in the development of universal fluorescence enhancement substrates based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals, the optimized film of each homogeneous crystal was fixed at six layers due to the complexity of the manufacturing process [[yanyu_photonics_10:41]]. While some platforms utilize nanoreplica molding to fabricate PC biosensor surfaces uniformly over large areas at room temperature and low cost [[yanyu_photonics_10:42]], other designs, such as photonic crystal nanobeam cavities, require precise construction of rectangular gratings along specific waveguide dimensions [[yanyu_photonics_10:43]]. The integration of microfluidics with these optical platforms remains an area of active development; although early demonstrations integrated microfluidics onto wafers, it is expected that such integration is ultimately required for the effective development of waveguide-based interferometry biosensors [[yanyu_photonics_10:44]]. Furthermore, the integration of dielectric metasurfaces into advanced optical biosensors is currently in its infancy [[yanyu_photonics_10:45]].

Surface functionalization is critical for endowing specificity to microcavity-based sensors [[yanyu_photonics_10:46]]. Photonic crystal platforms offer high surface stability compared to metallic thin films, which supports a wide variety of functionalization strategies for detecting different disease biomarkers [[yanyu_photonics_10:47]]. In specific applications, such as single quantum dot digital resolution biosensing, surface functionalization involves attaching ssDNA probes to a QD-streptavidin surface at a specific ratio [[yanyu_photonics_10:48]]. However, challenges remain in maintaining the stability of these functionalized surfaces for long-term or complex biological assays, as the literature highlights the need for robust interfaces to support diverse detection targets [[yanyu_photonics_10:47]].

Multiplexing capabilities represent a significant frontier for PC-enhanced fluorescence biosensing. The augmented fluorescence enhancements presented with cutting-edge biosensing frameworks using the PCCE platform can be extrapolated for the simultaneous detection of several analytes of interest by tapping different modes of the PCCE substrate [[yanyu_photonics_10:47]]. This approach enables multiplexed sensing by utilizing the distinct optical properties of the photonic crystal structure [[yanyu_photonics_10:47]]. Additionally, photonic-plasmonic hybrid systems have demonstrated the potential for advanced sensing, with 10-fold nanoparticle absorption enhancement observed from such hybrids [[yanyu_photonics_10:49]].

Emerging trends focus on the integration of photonic crystals with microfluidics and advanced imaging systems to enhance biosensing capabilities. Photonic slabs, including patterned 1D and 2D slabs of PCs, are especially appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to their good sensitivity, simplified optics, and compatibility with substrates [[yanyu_photonics_10:47]]. The use of noncoherent illumination of a photonic crystal biosensor coupled with a spectroscopic scanning system and a microscope objective has enabled label-free, quantitative, submicron resolution, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions [[yanyu_photonics_10:50]][[yanyu_photonics_10:51]]. This microscopy approach allows for the detection of subtle variations in cell adhesion strength within a single cell without the need for cytotoxic staining agents or temporally-unstable fluorophores [[yanyu_photonics_10:51]][[yanyu_photonics_10:50]][[yanyu_photonics_10:51]]. For example, mHAT9a cells have been allowed to attach to fibronectin-treated PC biosensor surfaces for extended periods to study cell attachment dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_10:50]]. These developments highlight the potential of PC-enhanced microscopy for live cell imaging and quantitative analysis of focal adhesion dynamics [[yanyu_photonics_10:42]].
answer_official_all: The fundamental mechanism underlying fluorescence enhancement in photonic crystal (PC) structures is the modification of the electromagnetic density of states, which directly influences the spontaneous emission rate of fluorophores . In a photonic bandgap, the electromagnetic density of states is zero, which inhibits spontaneous emission . Conversely, in artificial photonic band structures, a large density of states, or degeneracy factor, can more than compensate for a large mode volume to provide significant spontaneous emission enhancement . The spontaneous emission rate is proportional to the local density of states (LDOS), a relationship that is central to understanding these enhancements . While the well-known Purcell factor, often expressed as Q/V, is a common metric, it is actually only an approximation of the more fundamental quantity, the LDOS . The influence of the underlying PC on the local density of states and the lifetime of the fluorophores provides significant insights into the enhancement mechanisms . The Purcell effect specifically refers to a rate enhancement of spontaneous emission, which is distinct from the extraction effect that pertains to overall efficiency . In dielectric photonic crystals, the Purcell effect improves quantum efficiency by resulting in a shorter spontaneous emission lifetime . This dielectric PC produces a quantum efficiency enhancement through the Purcell effect, which results in reduced spontaneous emission lifetime and higher quantum efficiency . The enhancement of quantum dot emission via this effect occurs by modifying quantum efficiency without increasing the non-radiative decay rate, a benefit attributed to the lossless nature of dielectric materials . Theoretically, such a dielectric PC system can provide a 3–5× enhancement to the spontaneous emission rate relative to the original emission rate on unpatterned glass . The Purcell factor is defined as the ratio of the spontaneous emission rate in the PC to the original emission rate . However, the requirements for noticeable Purcell enhancement include a small mode volume and a high resonance Q-factor, conditions that may not always be met by standard photonic crystals [0]. For instance, in asymmetric structures that cannot possess a bandgap for either transverse electric- or transverse magnetic-like modes, the effect of inhibited spontaneous emission into undetectable waveguide modes is absent [2]. In such cases, fluorescence enhancement may arise from other mechanisms, such as a combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering effects attributed to leaky eigenmodes of the photonic crystal [2]. Experimental data has shown that the enhancement obtained for the resonant angle divided by the enhancement for the non-resonant angle yields a value of 8.24 ± 0.36 times for fluorescence enhancement by the near fields [2]. Beyond the standard Purcell effect, specific resonant features can further alter the spectral density of states. In the presence of Fano resonances, a significant alteration in the spectral density of states causes an increase in the extraction rate . The decay rate into a specific frequency is proportional to a Lorentzian-like function that is maximized at the resonance frequency . In double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals, the cavity layer itself acts as a strong resonator of the emission light, with a partial bandgap overlapping the fluorophore emission wavelength [4]. These mechanisms collectively demonstrate that while the Purcell effect and LDOS modification are primary drivers, specific structural resonances and near-field effects also contribute significantly to the overall fluorescence enhancement observed in photonic crystal biosensing platforms [2][4]. Photonic slabs, which include patterned 1D and 2D slabs, are particularly appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to their good sensitivity, simplified optics, and compatibility with substrates . A specific class of PC biosensors utilizes photonic crystal fiber (PCF), defined as a fiber optic cable with air holes in its cross-section . In the realm of 2D structures, microcavity biosensors are formed by introducing a point defect into the periodic microstructure, such as increasing or decreasing the central hole . Another 2D implementation involves a photonic crystal nanobeam cavity consisting of a series of rectangular gratings along a 500-nm-wide, 220-nm-thick waveguide . For 3D applications, double heterostructure 3D colloidal photonic crystals have been developed as multifunctional fluorescence-based sensor platforms [4]. Additionally, universal fluorescence enhancement substrates based on multiple heterostructure photonic crystals with super-wide stopbands have been designed for highly sensitive detection [3]. queries: 2D photonic crystal nanocavity biosensor design 2023 2024
3D photonic crystal fabrication fluorescence enhancement
one-dimensional photonic crystal thin film biosensing

plan.title: Performance Metrics and Empirical Findings in Biosensing
plan.goal: Summarize key empirical results regarding sensitivity, limit of detection (LOD), and signal-to-noise ratio improvements achieved in recent studies using photonic crystal-enhanced fluorescence.
queries: limit of detection photonic crystal fluorescence biosensor
sensitivity enhancement factor photonic crystal biosensing
empirical comparison photonic crystal vs conventional fluorescence biosensor

plan.title: Applications in Specific Biosensing Targets
plan.goal: Detail recent applications of these enhanced systems for detecting specific biomarkers, pathogens, or environmental contaminants, highlighting real-world utility.
queries: photonic crystal biosensor DNA detection fluorescence
photonic crystal enhanced fluorescence protein biomarker detection
pathogen detection photonic crystal biosensor recent advances

plan.title: Current Limitations and Future Directions
