surface functionalization photonic crystal biosensor stability
future trends photonic crystal biosensing integration microfluidics

question: How can natural language processing and machine learning techniques be leveraged to improve the understanding of medical jargon and research papers for non-experts?
raw_answer:
The scope of medical jargon and technical terminology is defined by specific physical and structural parameters, such as the nano-range size of medical nanocarriers being generally 1–100 nm [[bohao_cs_1:0]]. In the context of medical imaging and research, phantoms are utilized to provide heterogeneous backgrounds and realistic pathology similar to real tissue, serving purposes such as image-quality assessment and radiation dose reduction [[bohao_cs_1:1]]. However, most 3D-printed medical phantoms, even those with patient-specific and tissue-mimicking features, remain only anatomically—and not physiologically—close to human organ structures [[bohao_cs_1:1]]. The complexity of these medical domains is further highlighted by the fundamental shift in medical science caused by nanotechnology [[bohao_cs_1:2]].

Theoretical frameworks for text simplification and readability assessment rely on various automated metrics and evaluation protocols. The jusText tool is one such metric used for text analysis, with a reported score of 31.17 [[bohao_cs_1:3]]. In the domain of generative evaluation, BARTScore introduced an approach that treats text assessment as a generation task, employing the probability of text being generated by BART-based models to assess quality across tasks like machine translation and summarization [[bohao_cs_1:4]]. More recently, the Prometheus model induces fine-grained evaluation capability in language models, utilizing score rubrics that include specific dimensions such as Readability, Comprehension, and Conciseness [[bohao_cs_1:5]]. While automatic metrics are scalable, they do not correlate well with human judgments [[bohao_cs_1:6]]. Furthermore, comparison-based metrics have been found to be significantly more effective at predicting if content was memorized [[bohao_cs_1:7]].

The application of these frameworks to medical texts involves specific data processing and retrieval strategies. Medical examination tasks, such as MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, and MedQA, tend to have a larger proportion of retrieved snippets from textbooks and StatPearls [[bohao_cs_1:6]]. Results indicate that the combination of various medical corpora and retrievers achieves the best performance in benchmarking retrieval-augmented generation for medicine [[bohao_cs_1:6]]. To manage the diversity of source materials, documents are annotated for various filetypes, including.TXT,.DOCX,.PDF,.PPTX,.XLSX,.CSV,.TSV,.PY,.JSON,.JSONL,.HTML, and.XML [[bohao_cs_1:8]]. Language identification is performed using fasttext-based models to categorize documents into 176 languages [[bohao_cs_1:8]], and language prediction scores are reported as floats between 0.0 and 1.0 by the fastText language classifier [[bohao_cs_1:9]].

Data preprocessing and filtering techniques are essential for establishing the quality of text corpora used in these assessments. This includes randomizing whether plain text or Markdown format is used for documents [[bohao_cs_1:3]]. Specific filtering criteria are applied to code-related content, such as requiring a Java, Javascript, or Python code-to-comment ratio to be less than or equal to 0.01 or greater than 0.8 [[bohao_cs_1:10]]. In the context of model training and evaluation, system prompts are used to define the assistant's role, such as identifying summaries for records with binary "Yes" or "No" responses [[bohao_cs_1:11]]. For code-specific tasks, system prompts are employed during rejection sampling to improve code readability, documentation, thoroughness, and specificity [[bohao_cs_1:8]].

Challenges in evaluation include issues of bias and inconsistency in large language models. It is noted that the use of the terminology ‘online’ in reinforcement learning contexts differs from conventional use, referring to retraining a new model per iteration rather than training the same model iteratively [[bohao_cs_1:12]]. Bias in large language models is differentiated between intrinsic bias in the pre-trained model and extrinsic bias arising from fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, though most metrics can measure either [[bohao_cs_1:13]]. Evaluation prompts may take five input strings: metric, metric_definition, aspects, article, and summary [[bohao_cs_1:14]]. Additionally, on reading comprehension tasks such as MultiRC and ReCoRD, machine performance may exceed human performance by a large margin, suggesting that the evaluation metrics used for these tasks may be biased towards machine-made predictions [[bohao_cs_1:15]].

The evolution of natural language processing architectures has shifted from BERT-based models, which were previously considered state-of-the-art for medical question answering, to more advanced transformer-based systems [[bohao_cs_1:16]]. The Transformer architecture relies on a specific attention mechanism defined by the formula $Output\ context = \text{Softmax} ((Q K ^ {T}) / \sqrt {(d)}) V$ [[bohao_cs_1:17]]. To handle the computational demands of these models, system optimizations such as DeepSpeed Ulysses have been developed to enable the training of extreme long sequence transformer models [[bohao_cs_1:17]]. In the context of multimodal applications, the Chameleon model demonstrates that by quantizing images into discrete tokens analogous to words in text, the same transformer architecture can be applied to sequences of both image and text tokens without requiring separate image or text encoders [[bohao_cs_1:18]].

The T5 model, which explores the limits of transfer learning with a unified text-to-text transformer, utilizes a task-specific text prefix added to the original input sequence to specify which task the model should perform [[bohao_cs_1:19]]. This approach leverages pre-training data that is orders of magnitude larger than most datasets, comprising approximately 750 GB of reasonably clean and natural English text [[bohao_cs_1:19]]. While T5 has achieved state-of-the-art results, such as 84.6% in few-shot learning tasks, purely extractive approaches have also been shown to work well on benchmarks like CNN/Daily Mail, which is posed as an abstractive summarization benchmark [[bohao_cs_1:20]][[bohao_cs_1:19]]. The CNN/Daily Mail dataset remains a valuable resource for abstractive multi-sentence summarization, alongside XSum, which is a fundamental resource for the development and assessment of abstractive single-document summarization systems [[bohao_cs_1:21]].

In the domain of summarization, which is critical for abstracting complex information, the paucity of large, labeled datasets has historically limited the application of abstractive neural methods [[bohao_cs_1:22]]. For neural abstractive models, input articles are often truncated to 500 tokens to manage sequence length [[bohao_cs_1:23]]. Evaluation of these systems often relies on metrics like ROUGE, which is suspected to be more appropriate for the relatively uniform style of Wikipedia articles than for general abstractive summarization tasks [[bohao_cs_1:22]]. However, specific heuristics, such as the SUBMODULAR + ABS heuristic for applying a pre-trained abstractive model, have been found not to perform well [[bohao_cs_1:24]]. In contrast, LexRank serves as a graph-based method for computing relative importance in extractive summarization [[bohao_cs_1:23]].

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a key technique for improving performance on various NLP tasks by augmenting language models with relevant information retrieved from knowledge stores [[bohao_cs_1:25]]. In the medical domain, single corpora other than PubMed are generally not recommended for medical QA due to their limited volumes of medical knowledge [[bohao_cs_1:16]]. To address this, recent work has presented the first evaluation of StatPearls in the biomedical NLP community [[bohao_cs_1:16]]. The integration of knowledge graphs is further supported by benchmarks like MKQA, whose grading procedure ensures labels are sufficient to evaluate any QA method, including knowledge graph and generative approaches [[bohao_cs_1:26]].

The quality of the underlying data is crucial for these architectures. The FineWeb datasets utilize a sentence-transformers model, specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, for processing text data at scale [[bohao_cs_1:27]]. Data annotation for large language models like Llama 3 covers a wide range of filetypes, including.TXT,.DOCX,.PDF,.PPTX,.XLSX,.CSV,.TSV,.PY,.JSON,.JSONL,.HTML, and.XML [[bohao_cs_1:28]]. In some data extraction processes, researchers randomly sample between 5 and 10 tokens of context from scraped data [[bohao_cs_1:29]]. The MTEB benchmark quantifies the gains provided by context-aware transformer models compared to word embeddings, although retrieval and clustering tasks within this benchmark are currently English-only [[bohao_cs_1:30]].

Pre-training on domain-specific text has shown benefits for specialized tasks; for instance, pre-training BERT on text from research papers improved its performance on scientific tasks [[bohao_cs_1:19]]. The distinction between reasoning and skills is highlighted by measurements demonstrating that the reasoning graph does not necessarily equal the skills graph [[bohao_cs_1:31]]. While the provided evidence includes examples of simplification in other scientific contexts, such as the simplification of manufacturing processes in antibody–drug conjugates [[bohao_cs_1:32]] and the simplification of experimental implementation in quantum control of nanoparticles [[bohao_cs_1:33]], these specific instances illustrate the concept of simplification in technical domains rather than directly detailing NLP translation methods.

Empirical evaluations of automated text simplification and summarization tools reveal a significant discrepancy between scalable automatic metrics and human judgments, particularly in the context of medical and complex technical content [[bohao_cs_1:34]]. While automatic metrics are valued for their scalability, studies indicate they do not correlate well with human assessments of quality [[bohao_cs_1:34]]. This limitation is further highlighted by the observation that conventional automated evaluation metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE, fail to capture the depth and granularity inherent in human evaluation [[bohao_cs_1:35]]. Although human judgment generally correlates with automatic metrics, this correlation becomes more difficult to distinguish at the higher end of model performance [[bohao_cs_1:36]]. Furthermore, previous evaluation methods often lack explanatory power for their scores, which hinders the human verification of judgments derived from these automated metrics [[bohao_cs_1:37]].

To address the limitations of traditional metrics, recent approaches have leveraged pretrained language models to capture semantic content, aiming to provide a more nuanced and accurate evaluation of summarization system outputs [[bohao_cs_1:38]]. For instance, the FactKB metric has been demonstrated to achieve high correlations with human judgment on summarization datasets, outperforming other metrics such as FACTCC and SUMMAC [[bohao_cs_1:39]]. However, the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as evaluators introduces new biases; LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generations, a phenomenon where ego inflates evaluation scores [[bohao_cs_1:40]][[bohao_cs_1:38]]. This self-preference is compounded by the tendency of contemporary evaluation metrics to lean towards favoring longer summaries, similar to traditional evaluation methods [[bohao_cs_1:38]]. Consequently, the reliability of LLM-based evaluation is further complicated by the fact that LLMs can be inconsistent and biased evaluators, requiring specific prompt structures that take inputs such as metric definitions, aspects, articles, and summaries [[bohao_cs_1:41]].

In the specific domain of medical research, benchmarking retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems presents unique challenges regarding data source and evaluation format. Medical examination tasks, including MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, and MedMCQA, tend to have a larger proportion of retrieved snippets from textbooks and StatPearls [[bohao_cs_1:34]]. Following most other studies, researchers use the format of multi-choice questions for large-scale and automatic evaluation of medical QA [[bohao_cs_1:34]]. However, the rationales generated by systems like MEDRAG remain to be fully evaluated, indicating an open problem in assessing the explanatory quality of medical AI outputs [[bohao_cs_1:34]]. The reliance on multi-choice formats and specific source distributions may not fully capture the complexity of understanding medical jargon for non-experts, especially when considering that automatic metrics do not correlate well with human judgments in this domain [[bohao_cs_1:34]].

Beyond metric selection, the evaluation of model capabilities must account for technical constraints and user-centric factors. For example, when Large Language Models are quantized to 2 bits using GPTQ, they lose their ability to comprehend and follow user instructions, resulting in the generation of incoherent text [[bohao_cs_1:42]]. This degradation in performance underscores the importance of model capacity in maintaining the coherence necessary for simplifying complex medical texts. Additionally, the evaluation of models often involves extracting embeddings for given text, treating written-form input or audio transcripts as if they were generated by the model with an empty user prompt, as seen in the Llama 3 evaluation framework [[bohao_cs_1:43]]. To ensure robustness, results in such evaluations are typically computed over multiple random seeds, such as five, to account for variability [[bohao_cs_1:44]].

User-centric validation also requires attention to the specific needs of different user bases and the distinction between fluency and comprehensibility. A key limitation in current evaluation benchmarks is the lack of a comprehensive study on how model performance impacts different user bases, especially underrepresented groups [[bohao_cs_1:45]]. In the context of machine translation and text simplification, while fluency is a common objective, it may be less important than comprehensibility for users [[bohao_cs_1:46]]. This distinction is critical when re-framing complex tasks, such as video understanding, as reading comprehension problems, where the goal is to make content accessible rather than just fluent [[bohao_cs_1:47]]. The use of specific system prompts, such as those instructing an assistant to identify summaries for records with binary "Yes" or "No" responses, illustrates the structured nature of some evaluation tasks but may not fully capture the nuanced comprehension required for medical jargon [[bohao_cs_1:40]].

The empirical landscape is further complicated by the nature of the source texts and the specific technical contexts in which simplification is applied. For instance, in the field of antibody-drug conjugates, the absence of scrambled disulfide species leads to an overall simplification of the manufacturing process, a technical detail that must be accurately conveyed to non-experts [[bohao_cs_1:48]]. Similarly, in quantum control experiments, using a non-optimal filter results in slightly worse performances but is accompanied by a great simplification of the experimental implementation [[bohao_cs_1:49]]. These examples highlight that "simplification" in technical literature often involves trade-offs between performance and complexity, which automated tools must navigate without losing factual accuracy. The evaluation of such texts requires metrics that can handle the specific terminology and structural nuances of these domains, yet current automatic metrics often fail to align with human perceptions of clarity and accuracy [[bohao_cs_1:34]][[bohao_cs_1:35]].

Finally, the integration of various evaluation strategies reveals a fragmented approach to assessing the effectiveness of NLP tools for medical and technical simplification. While some studies focus on the correlation between automatic metrics and human judgment [[bohao_cs_1:36]][[bohao_cs_1:39]], others highlight the biases inherent in LLM-based evaluators [[bohao_cs_1:38]][[bohao_cs_1:41]]. The use of multi-choice questions for medical QA [[bohao_cs_1:34]] and the reliance on specific datasets like OpenWebMath [[bohao_cs_1:50]] provide benchmarks, but they do not fully address the user-centric goal of improving comprehension for non-experts. The lack of comprehensive studies on underrepresented user groups [[bohao_cs_1:45]] and the potential loss of instruction-following ability in quantized models [[bohao_cs_1:42]] suggest that current empirical evaluations are insufficient for guaranteeing that simplified medical texts are both accurate and comprehensible to all intended audiences.

The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in medical contexts is significantly constrained by the persistent issue of hallucination, where models generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect responses [[bohao_cs_1:51]]. Hallucinations remain a major challenge for these systems, and even models with reduced propensity for such errors, like LLaVA-1.5, are not exempt from producing misinformation and should be used with caution in critical applications such as medicine [[bohao_cs_1:52]]. This risk is compounded by findings that alignment techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), may not always improve factuality; for instance, the factuality score of Llama-2-7b-chat (RLHFed) was lower than that of Vicuna-7b (SFTed), suggesting that RLHF might even cause more hallucination [[bohao_cs_1:53]]. Furthermore, large language models suffer from calibration failures, meaning their confidence levels do not accurately reflect the correctness of their outputs [[bohao_cs_1:54]].

In the specific domain of medical question answering, the reliance on single corpora other than PubMed is discouraged due to their limited volumes of medical knowledge [[bohao_cs_1:51]]. To address these gaps, benchmarks such as the Medical Information Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation (MIRAGE) have been proposed, incorporating 7,663 questions from five medical QA datasets to better assess retrieval-augmented generation [[bohao_cs_1:51]]. Analysis of these tasks reveals that medical examination datasets, including MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, and MedMCQA, tend to have a larger proportion of retrieved snippets from textbooks and StatPearls [[bohao_cs_1:51]]. However, the evaluation of such systems faces methodological hurdles, as researchers must exercise caution regarding construct, content, and ecological validity challenges when assessing bias and fairness [[bohao_cs_1:55]]. Additionally, specific evaluation tools like MT-Bench are sometimes excluded from studies due to their inherent limitations [[bohao_cs_1:56]].

Beyond factual accuracy, the ethical implications of automated medical advice are complicated by the potential for models to learn, perpetuate, and amplify harmful social biases [[bohao_cs_1:55]]. Safety evaluations must determine whether responses avoid unethical or sensitive content, including offensive language, biased statements, or harmful information [[bohao_cs_1:53]]. The risk of data leakage is another critical ethical concern, as large language models have been demonstrated to memorize and leak individual training examples [[bohao_cs_1:57]]. This memorization extends to sensitive information, such as phone numbers, social security numbers, addresses, and medical diagnoses, which are implicitly focused on as sensitive if outputted verbatim [[bohao_cs_1:58]]. While very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems [[bohao_cs_1:59]], their application in medical settings requires rigorous filtering, such as automatically removing answers that are too short (less than 1200 characters) [[bohao_cs_1:60]].

The broader societal and ethical landscape of medical technology is further illustrated by public perception and ethical debates surrounding procedures like xenotransplantation. Surveys indicate that only 34.6% of respondents knew the meaning of xenotransplantation, while 53.8% had a favorable opinion about it being performed as a medical treatment in the future [[bohao_cs_1:61]]. Ethical perspectives on such advances vary, with some arguing that science should never be hampered by ethical considerations despite the controversy surrounding genetic engineering [[bohao_cs_1:62]]. To navigate these complex issues, ethics review committees should be composed of specialized and competent scientific, medical, ethical, and related disciplinary experts [[bohao_cs_1:63]].

Technical and experimental limitations also persist in the underlying technologies and evaluation metrics used in this field. For example, in optical imaging research, limitations in the range of possible optical properties needed to mimic various layers of epithelial tissue have been noted in earlier works [[bohao_cs_1:64]]. Similarly, equipment limitations can prevent the experimental investigation of specific phenomena, such as depth-dependent dispersion compensation in FD-OCT [[bohao_cs_1:65]]. In the context of text generation and summarization, quality is often assessed across five dimensions: Grammaticality, Non-redundancy, Referential clarity, Focus, and Structure and Coherence [[bohao_cs_1:66]]. Specific baseline models, such as SumBasic, have been evaluated with a score of 0 on certain metrics and 16 on others [[bohao_cs_1:66]]. These technical constraints, ranging from hardware limitations to specific scoring baselines, underscore the multifaceted nature of the challenges in developing reliable NLP systems for medical understanding.

The empirical landscape is further complicated by the nature of the source texts and the specific technical contexts in which simplification is applied. For instance, in the field of antibody-drug conjugates, the absence of scrambled disulfide species leads to an overall simplification of the manufacturing process, a technical detail that must be accurately conveyed to non-experts . Similarly, in quantum control experiments, using a non-optimal filter results in slightly worse performances but is accompanied by a great simplification of the experimental implementation . These examples highlight that "simplification" in technical literature often involves trade-offs between performance and complexity, which automated tools must navigate without losing factual accuracy. The evaluation of such texts requires metrics that can handle the specific terminology and structural nuances of these domains, yet current automatic metrics often fail to align with human perceptions of clarity and accuracy . Finally, the integration of various evaluation strategies reveals a fragmented approach to assessing the effectiveness of NLP tools for medical and technical simplification. While some studies focus on the correlation between automatic metrics and human judgment , others highlight the biases inherent in LLM-based evaluators . The use of multi-choice questions for medical QA and the reliance on specific datasets like OpenWebMath provide benchmarks, but they do not fully address the user-centric goal of improving comprehension for non-experts. The lack of comprehensive studies on underrepresented user groups and the potential loss of instruction-following ability in quantized models suggest that current empirical evaluations are insufficient for guaranteeing that simplified medical texts are both accurate and comprehensible to all intended audiences. The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in medical contexts is significantly constrained by the persistent issue of hallucination, where models generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect responses . Hallucinations remain a major challenge for these systems, and even models with reduced propensity for such errors, like LLaVA-1.5, are not exempt from producing misinformation and should be used with caution in critical applications such as medicine . This risk is compounded by findings that alignment techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), may not always improve factuality; for instance, the factuality score of Llama-2-7b-chat (RLHFed) was lower than that of Vicuna-7b (SFTed), suggesting that RLHF might even cause more hallucination . Furthermore, large language models suffer from calibration failures, meaning their confidence levels do not accurately reflect the correctness of their outputs . In the specific domain of medical question answering, the reliance on single corpora other than PubMed is discouraged due to their limited volumes of medical knowledge . To address these gaps, benchmarks such as the Medical Information Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation (MIRAGE) have been proposed, incorporating 7,663 questions from five medical QA datasets to better assess retrieval-augmented generation . Analysis of these tasks reveals that medical examination datasets, including MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, and MedMCQA, tend to have a larger proportion of retrieved snippets from textbooks and StatPearls . However, the evaluation of such systems faces methodological hurdles, as researchers must exercise caution regarding construct, content, and ecological validity challenges when assessing bias and fairness . Additionally, specific evaluation tools like MT-Bench are sometimes excluded from studies due to their inherent limitations . Beyond factual accuracy, the ethical implications of automated medical advice are complicated by the potential for models to learn, perpetuate, and amplify harmful social biases . Safety evaluations must determine whether responses avoid unethical or sensitive content, including offensive language, biased statements, or harmful information . The risk of data leakage is another critical ethical concern, as large language models have been demonstrated to memorize and leak individual training examples . This memorization extends to sensitive information, such as phone numbers, social security numbers, addresses, and medical diagnoses, which are implicitly focused on as sensitive if outputted verbatim . While very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems , their application in medical settings requires rigorous filtering, such as automatically removing answers that are too short (less than 1200 characters) . The broader societal and ethical landscape of medical technology is further illustrated by public perception and ethical debates surrounding procedures like xenotransplantation. Surveys indicate that only 34.6% of respondents knew the meaning of xenotransplantation, while 53.8% had a favorable opinion about it being performed as a medical treatment in the future . Ethical perspectives on such advances vary, with some arguing that science should never be hampered by ethical considerations despite the controversy surrounding genetic engineering . To navigate these complex issues, ethics review committees should be composed of specialized and competent scientific, medical, ethical, and related disciplinary experts . Technical and experimental limitations also persist in the underlying technologies and evaluation metrics used in this field. For example, in optical imaging research, limitations in the range of possible optical properties needed to mimic various layers of epithelial tissue have been noted in earlier works . Similarly, equipment limitations can prevent the experimental investigation of specific phenomena, such as depth-dependent dispersion compensation in FD-OCT . In the context of text generation and summarization, quality is often assessed across five dimensions: Grammaticality, Non-redundancy, Referential clarity, Focus, and Structure and Coherence . Specific baseline models, such as SumBasic, have been evaluated with a score of 0 on certain metrics and 16 on others . These technical constraints, ranging from hardware limitations to specific scoring baselines, underscore the multifaceted nature of the challenges in developing reliable NLP systems for medical understanding.

question: How can we develop effective personalized systems to improve understanding of scientific concepts and jargon across different domains and expertise levels?
raw_answer:
The traditional lecture-textbook-recitation method of teaching, which remains prevalent in high schools, prevents students from applying important scientific, mathematical, and technological skills in a meaningful context [[bohao_cs_2:0]]. To address this, engaging students by using real data to address scientific questions in formal education settings is known to be an effective instructional approach [[bohao_cs_2:0]]. This pedagogical shift aligns with the principle that students learn best if they are not passive recipients of factual information but rather are engaged in the learning process [[bohao_cs_2:0]]. Furthermore, experiences in informal settings can significantly improve science learning outcomes for individuals from groups historically underrepresented in science, such as women and minorities [[bohao_cs_2:0]].

Current scientific literacy levels highlight the need for such adaptive approaches, as a 2015 Pew Charitable Trusts report indicates that 40% of the U.S. public believes that humans coexisted with the dinosaurs [[bohao_cs_2:1]]. Such considerations regarding the integration of ethics and standard scientific theory will not be addressed until the thinking of scientists is radically changed, a goal that can only be accomplished by revolutionary modification of science education [[bohao_cs_2:1]]. In the domain of automated assistance, systems like MAmmoTH2 can assist students in their learning process by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, thus enhancing their understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills [[bohao_cs_2:2]].

The development of personalized systems relies on large language models (LLMs) that must be adapted to specific scientific domains. Pre-training BERT on text from research papers improved its performance on scientific tasks, as found by Beltagy et al. (2019) [[bohao_cs_2:3]]. Similarly, a keyword search is used to generate a dataset of hundreds of relevant scientific papers and pre-loaded into the Llama 3 model inference system [[bohao_cs_2:4]]. However, general models may lack nuanced expertise in particular domains, making them non-specific for specialized scientific tasks [[bohao_cs_2:5]]. To mitigate this, Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters decouples the Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into two parts: the original pre-trained FFNs to maintain the old-domain knowledge and novel domain-specific adapters to inject domain-specific knowledge in parallel [[bohao_cs_2:6]].

Training and aligning these models for personalized scientific instruction involves complex reinforcement learning techniques. Training LLMs with reinforcement learning, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), from human feedback (RLHF) has proven effective in aligning LLMs with human preferences [[bohao_cs_2:7]]. However, RLHF depends on complex reinforcement learning techniques such as PPO, which are challenging to implement and often unstable during training [[bohao_cs_2:8]]. In specific applications like WizardMath, the Integrated Reward Model (IRM) and Process Reward Model (PRM) are integrated within a PPO-based reinforcement learning framework to empower mathematical reasoning [[bohao_cs_2:9]]. Despite these advancements, LLMs may replicate some human-like cognitive biases [[bohao_cs_2:10]], and their factuality is weak, meaning crowdworkers without domain expertise or significant time investments may miss these errors [[bohao_cs_2:10]].

Evaluation and calibration of these personalized systems present additional challenges. GPTScore, including GPT-X and FLAN-T5 models, can perform intricate and personalized assessments without additional training due to an understanding of natural language instructions [[bohao_cs_2:11]]. For retrieval-augmented generation, training a reranker with domain-specific data was more effective than zero-shot reranking [[bohao_cs_2:12]]. Datasets such as SciQ, which contains approximately 14k crowdsourced science exam question-answer pairs, provide benchmarks for evaluating such systems [[bohao_cs_2:13]]. Additionally, the FineWeb-Edu dataset, a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content, serves as a resource for training on educational material [[bohao_cs_2:14]].

Specialized architectures and methods further support the adaptation of scientific content. Socratic Models (SMs) can produce reasonable captions without additional training on domain-specific data [[bohao_cs_2:15]]. In the context of model merging, many MoErging methods do not have user-friendly software implementations available, and applying them often requires technical expertise that many users lack [[bohao_cs_2:16]]. Methods like DAM first compute each domain-specific training set's average embedding from the penultimate layer of the base model to facilitate this process [[bohao_cs_2:16]]. In distillation, each specialist model is initialized with the weights of the generalist model to transfer knowledge [[bohao_cs_2:17]]. These technical adaptations, such as the recent adaptation of the formalism of the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian from quantum mechanics to acoustic resonators [[bohao_cs_2:18]], illustrate the cross-domain transfer of scientific concepts that personalized systems must support.

The extraction and processing of scientific text rely heavily on robust data cleaning and filtering techniques to ensure high-quality input for downstream NLP tasks. For instance, the OpenWebMath dataset utilized specific tools for text extraction, where Trafilatura achieved a score of 63.90, significantly outperforming jusText, which scored 31.17 [[bohao_cs_2:19]]. In the context of large-scale web data decanting, the FineWeb datasets employ a fastText language classifier to assign a language prediction score ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, facilitating the filtering of non-target language content [[bohao_cs_2:20]]. Similarly, the Llama 3 model development process involved annotating data across a wide variety of file types, including.TXT,.DOCX,.PDF,.PPTX,.XLSX,.CSV,.TSV,.PY,.JSON,.JSONL,.HTML, and.XML, to ensure comprehensive coverage of scientific and technical formats [[bohao_cs_2:21]].

To effectively identify and retrieve relevant scientific concepts, researchers utilize keyword search and retrieval-augmented generation strategies. The Llama 3 model inference system, for example, uses keyword search to generate a dataset of hundreds of relevant scientific papers, which are then pre-loaded into the system [[bohao_cs_2:21]]. In retrieval tasks, training a reranker with domain-specific data has been shown to be more effective than zero-shot reranking, highlighting the importance of domain adaptation in retrieval pipelines [[bohao_cs_2:22]]. Furthermore, the MTEB benchmark indicates that scientific datasets such as SciDocsRR, SciFact, and ArxivClustering exhibit high similarities among each other, even when derived from different tasks, suggesting a shared underlying structure in scientific text embeddings [[bohao_cs_2:23]].

Integrating domain-specific knowledge into pre-trained language models is a critical step for accurate jargon handling. The Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters approach decouples the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of the Transformer architecture into two distinct parts: the original pre-trained FFNs, which maintain old-domain knowledge, and novel domain-specific adapters that inject new domain knowledge in parallel [[bohao_cs_2:24]]. This architectural modification allows for the preservation of general linguistic capabilities while enhancing performance on specialized scientific topics. Additionally, the Llama 3 team found that annealing enables the judgment of the value of small domain-specific datasets, providing a method to assess the utility of limited domain data during training [[bohao_cs_2:21]].

Entity linking and disambiguation are essential for linking scientific jargon to broader knowledge bases. The CM3 model, a causal masked multimodal model of the internet, sets the new state-of-the-art for entity linking and entity disambiguation in general through fine-tuning [[bohao_cs_2:25]]. This model also achieves state-of-the-art results in zero-shot summarization, entity linking, and entity disambiguation, demonstrating its versatility across multiple NLP tasks [[bohao_cs_2:25]]. These capabilities are crucial for systems that need to automatically define and link scientific terms without extensive manual annotation.

Graph-based methods and summarization techniques also play a role in extracting and synthesizing scientific concepts. TextRank defines a weighted graph where text units are nodes and edges are defined by a similarity measure based on word overlap, a method used for extracting key phrases and concepts [[bohao_cs_2:26]]. In graph-based neural multi-document summarization, the order of correlation strength for different graph types is found to be PDG > ADG > Cosine Similarity Graph, with models without a graph converging faster and achieving lower training costs than those using Cosine Similarity Graphs or ADGs [[bohao_cs_2:27]]. When generating summaries from long sequences, such as in Wikipedia generation, combining datasets of citations and search results performs best, with the contributions of each source being complementary [[bohao_cs_2:26]].

The evaluation and calibration of these systems require careful consideration of model confidence and bias. Few-shot recalibration allows for the identification of domain-specific confidence thresholds, above which the language model's predictions can be trusted and below which it should abstain, thereby improving reliability in domain-specific applications [[bohao_cs_2:28]]. However, LLMs used as evaluators can exhibit bias, as they recognize and favor their own generations, a phenomenon observed when sampling summaries at temperature zero using simple prompts [[bohao_cs_2:29]]. Prompts for evaluation often take specific input strings, including metric, metric_definition, aspects, article, and summary, to structure the assessment process [[bohao_cs_2:30]].

Cross-cultural and multilingual considerations are also relevant to the development of personalized scientific systems. Analogous to cross-lingual and multilingual NLP, cross-cultural and multicultural NLP considers differences in cultural contexts to better serve users of NLP systems [[bohao_cs_2:31]]. However, a significant challenge remains in the availability of resources, as while Wikipedia and news texts are available for a wide range of languages, texts specifically written for NLP tasks are not available for most languages [[bohao_cs_2:32]]. This scarcity of task-specific multilingual data poses a limitation for developing truly personalized systems across diverse expertise levels and domains.

Finally, the mechanisms by which knowledge is transferred and distilled in these models are an area of ongoing research. Knowledge distillation improves student performance, a phenomenon that has been linked to the regularizing effect of soft labels [[bohao_cs_2:33]]. In the context of improving text embeddings, large language models are used to generate instruction-based queries, where the query is formatted as an instruction followed by the task definition and the original query [[bohao_cs_2:34]]. These techniques, combined with the aforementioned extraction and linking methods, form the foundation for developing effective personalized systems for scientific understanding.

The development of personalized educational systems relies on large-scale datasets that provide the foundational material for generating explanations, such as FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content [[bohao_cs_2:35]]. To facilitate learning, models like MAmmoTH2 are designed to assist students by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, which enhances understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills [[bohao_cs_2:36]]. The generation of such content can be controlled through system instructions that specify the tone, task, format, and limitations of the model’s responses [[bohao_cs_2:37]]. However, methods for “targeting” or “controlling” the content of language models are still at a very early stage [[bohao_cs_2:38]].

In the context of model architecture, Mixture of Experts (MoE) approaches allow for specialized handling of different tasks or user profiles. During MoE training on local data, the global expert remains frozen, while only the local expert and the router are updated to achieve personalization [[bohao_cs_2:39]]. This architecture is particularly relevant in cases where a user-tailored local model is desired and where user data must remain private, often intersecting with Federated Learning (FL) [[bohao_cs_2:39]]. The retrieval of the appropriate expert is critical, as the expert with the most datapoints assigned to it is retrieved [[bohao_cs_2:39]]. Nevertheless, accurate expert retrieval for specific tasks can be challenging, even when relevant experts exist [[bohao_cs_2:39]].

The quality and consistency of generated content are subject to various evaluation metrics and biases. LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, a causal explanation that resists straightforward confounders in controlled experiments [[bohao_cs_2:40]]. In these evaluations, summaries are often sampled from LLMs at temperature zero using simple prompts [[bohao_cs_2:40]]. To assess quality, GPT-4 can be asked to rate its own response from 1 to 10 [[bohao_cs_2:41]], or to rate the quality of generation from another model on a scale of 0 to 10 [[bohao_cs_2:37]]. Additionally, a higher CONS score indicates better consistency with user intent [[bohao_cs_2:42]].

Training strategies for these adaptive systems often involve iterative processes and distillation. The STaR method consists of a loop of self-play by an “apprentice,” followed by imitation learning with feedback from a slower “expert” and then the replacement of the expert with the now-improved apprentice [[bohao_cs_2:43]]. In knowledge distillation, using the discriminative performance of the experts to determine the learned assignments is much better than simply clustering the input vectors and assigning an expert to each cluster [[bohao_cs_2:44]]. Instruction tuning processes may involve generating five responses per question [[bohao_cs_2:41]].

Data quality and filtering are essential for effective content generation. In the OpenWebMath dataset, manual inspection found that content with a score of under 0.2 is very unlikely to contain useful mathematical content [[bohao_cs_2:45]]. In search-augmented instruction learning, such as SAIL, search items must be relevant, otherwise the search item is distracting [[bohao_cs_2:46]]. The memorized content in large language models is highly dependent on the model’s context [[bohao_cs_2:47]], and comparison-based metrics are significantly more effective at predicting if content was memorized [[bohao_cs_2:47]].

Cross-cultural and domain-specific challenges also impact the adaptability of these systems. Data collected from a single culture may contain concepts that do not easily map across cultures, as seen in the MarVL dataset where about a quarter of concepts from non-Western cultures did not map to English concepts [[bohao_cs_2:48]]. In specific scientific domains, such as quantum physics, the creation and destruction of photons are not new concepts [[bohao_cs_2:49]]. In biological contexts, scaffolding proteins like catenins and p120 are main components of adherens junctions in the blood–brain barrier [[bohao_cs_2:50]]. While 3D bioprinting can perform selective surface modification during scaffolding [[bohao_cs_2:51]], medical applications face challenges such as severe adverse events including peripheral sensory neuropathy and neutropenia [[bohao_cs_2:52]].

Performance and computational costs vary across tasks and models. Language models achieve only 15.1% on the more difficult anagram task [[bohao_cs_2:38]]. Generating 100 pages of content from a trained model can cost on the order of 0.4 kW-hr [[bohao_cs_2:38]]. Training processes may involve specific hyperparameters, such as 1500 warmup updates [[bohao_cs_2:53]].

Accurate inference of a user's expertise level is critical for driving personalization, yet current methods often face challenges in scalability and user accessibility. Many Model MoErging methods, which involve recycling and routing among specialized experts for collaborative learning, lack user-friendly software implementations, meaning that applying these techniques often requires technical expertise that many users lack [[bohao_cs_2:54]]. This barrier to entry highlights the need for systems that can assess expertise without demanding advanced technical knowledge from the end-user.

To address the need for scalable expertise assessment across different fields, Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters (MoDA) offers a framework that decouples and injects domain knowledge into pre-trained language models' memories [[bohao_cs_2:55]]. This approach is notable for its scalability, as it scales well to an increasing number of domains [[bohao_cs_2:55]]. By effectively managing domain-specific knowledge, such systems can better adapt to users with varying levels of background in specific scientific or technical areas.

Assessing the difficulty of content is a prerequisite for matching it to a user's current understanding. One method for this involves estimating question difficulty by assigning a given question to one of five distinct difficulty levels [[bohao_cs_2:56]]. This stratification allows for the implementation of curriculum learning, an effective strategy in machine learning that allows models to start with simpler tasks and gradually progress to more complex ones [[bohao_cs_2:57]]. By aligning the complexity of the material with the inferred difficulty level, systems can provide a structured learning path that mirrors the progression from novice to expert understanding.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate responses and infer understanding, but they exhibit specific behavioral biases that must be accounted for. Models tend to be overconfident, even in domains where they have little knowledge [[bohao_cs_2:58]]. This overconfidence can distort expertise assessment if not mitigated. To generate quantitative assessments, systems like Prometheus induce fine-grained evaluation capability in language models, producing outputs that include two components: feedback and a score [[bohao_cs_2:59]]. In similar evaluation frameworks, GPT-4 is asked to rate its own response from 1 to 10 [[bohao_cs_2:60]], and specifically assigns a score $s \in [1, 10]$ for each response [[bohao_cs_2:60]].

These scoring mechanisms are often applied to specific tasks to measure alignment or similarity. For instance, in mathematical reasoning contexts, a score ranging from 1 to 10 is used, where 1 indicates completely different math problem tasks and 10 indicates identical math problem tasks [[bohao_cs_2:61]]. In other contexts, a higher CONS (Consistency) score indicates better consistency with user intent [[bohao_cs_2:62]]. These numerical scores serve as proxies for understanding, allowing systems to track whether a user's responses align with the intended concepts or problem-solving steps.

The integration of these assessment tools into educational systems aims to enhance learning outcomes. MAmmoTH2, for example, can assist students in their learning process by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, thereby enhancing their understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills [[bohao_cs_2:63]]. To support such personalized feedback, system prompts are often written in natural language and separated from the user messages by using the role of “system” in the JSON request, as seen in Orca [[bohao_cs_2:64]]. This structural separation allows the model to maintain a distinct persona or instructional context while processing user inputs.

However, the reliability of these automated assessments is complicated by the nature of the underlying models and data. In standard deep learning, good generalization in practice is often enabled by properties such as the flatness of good solutions, the inductive biases of the network, and the implicit biases of SGD, rather than by solving the optimization problem perfectly [[bohao_cs_2:65]]. Furthermore, the specific data used for training and evaluation can influence performance; for instance, student models trained only on MNIST-orig are evaluated on all three domains to test generalization [[bohao_cs_2:66]]. Similarly, knowledge inheritance (KI) has shown superiority over self-learning, with models like BASE $_{WB}$ achieving improved performance on both domains after being taught by two teachers simultaneously [[bohao_cs_2:67]].

The availability of high-quality educational data is a foundational element for these systems. FineWeb-Edu provides a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content derived from FineWeb, offering a substantial resource for training models on educational material [[bohao_cs_2:68]]. While such large-scale datasets support the development of general-purpose models, the application of specific assessment techniques still faces practical hurdles. For example, in the domain of medical diagnostics, systems like the Cepheid GeneXpert® are fully integrated DNA isolation and real-time PCR systems that can genotype blood samples in 30-40 minutes without user intervention other than sample insertion [[bohao_cs_2:69]]. This level of automation contrasts with the current state of many AI-based expertise assessment tools, which may still require significant user interaction or technical setup.

In specialized scientific domains, the precision of terminology and concepts is paramount. For example, in cancer therapy, ISACs combine the precision of antibody-navigated targeting and the power of small molecule based modulation of the innate and adaptive immune systems [[bohao_cs_2:70]]. Understanding such complex jargon requires a system that can accurately gauge whether a user grasps the specific mechanisms involved. Similarly, in optical coherence tomographic angiography, adaptive optics systems can be used to compensate for aberrations in the eye, increasing system optical resolution and enabling visualization of capillaries at anatomic caliber [[bohao_cs_2:71]]. These examples illustrate the high level of domain-specific knowledge that personalized systems must be capable of assessing and adapting to.

The training of these assessment models involves specific hyperparameter choices that affect their performance. For instance, in training a helpful and harmless assistant with reinforcement learning from human feedback, a learning rate of 0.05 times the pretraining learning rate is used for one component, while a learning rate of 0.1 relative to LM pretraining is used for PMP [[bohao_cs_2:72]]. These technical details underscore the complexity of building robust models that can reliably infer expertise. Additionally, the evaluation of such systems often relies on fundamental resources; for example, XSum is a fundamental resource for the development and assessment of abstractive single-document summarization systems [[bohao_cs_2:73]].

Despite these advancements, security and safety remain concerns. Membership inference attacks against machine learning models exploit the fact that the more classes there are, the more signals about the internal state of the model are available to the attacker [[bohao_cs_2:74]]. This vulnerability is particularly relevant in personalized systems that store detailed user models. Furthermore, alignment techniques like LIMA, while effective in many cases, are more likely to provide unsafe responses when the malicious intent is implicit [[bohao_cs_2:75]]. These limitations highlight the ongoing challenge of creating personalized systems that are not only effective in assessing expertise but also secure and safe for diverse user populations.

Empirical evaluations of personalized learning systems reveal that traditional instructional methods, such as the common lecture-textbook-recitation approach, often prevent students from applying scientific, mathematical, and technological skills in meaningful contexts [[bohao_cs_2:76]]. In contrast, engaging students by using real data to address scientific questions in formal education settings is recognized as an effective instructional approach [[bohao_cs_2:76]]. The effectiveness of modern personalized systems is further supported by empirical studies validating the use of GPT-4-generated data for large language model instruction-tuning [[bohao_cs_2:77]]. Specific models like MAmmoTH2 have been shown to assist students in their learning process by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, thereby enhancing their understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills [[bohao_cs_2:78]]. The quality of the underlying data sources significantly impacts these outcomes, as education website data sources consistently outperform forum data sources, indicating the higher quality of educational questions [[bohao_cs_2:78]]. This is exemplified by the introduction of FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content that was rated as highly educational by a custom classifier [[bohao_cs_2:79]].

Personalization mechanisms in these systems often rely on specific architectural adjustments or assessment capabilities. For instance, in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training on local data, the global expert remains frozen while only the local expert and the router are updated to achieve personalization [[bohao_cs_2:80]]. Additionally, with an understanding of natural language instructions, models such as GPTScore (including GPT-X and FLAN-T5) can perform intricate and personalized assessments without additional training [[bohao_cs_2:81]]. These assessment capabilities are integrated into broader inference systems, where keyword searches are used to generate datasets of hundreds of relevant scientific papers and pre-load them into models like Llama 3 [[bohao_cs_2:82]]. In graph-based summarization, the process of including sentence personalization scores in edge weight assignments leads to a select number of edges gaining markedly large distinction [[bohao_cs_2:83]]. However, the evaluation of these systems is not without challenges, as the use of specific evaluators, such as the Cohere evaluator, is part of the broader landscape of LLM assessment [[bohao_cs_2:81]].

The application of these personalized systems across different scientific domains and user groups faces significant limitations regarding cultural mapping and bias. Data collected from a single culture may contain concepts that do not easily map across cultures, as seen in the MarVL dataset, where about a quarter of concepts from a sample of non-Western cultures did not map to English concepts represented in WordNet [[bohao_cs_2:84]]. Furthermore, the assumptions and values in scientific and computing research tend to reflect those of dominant groups, which can introduce bias into the systems [[bohao_cs_2:85]]. This bias is specifically addressed in alignment datasets like GenderAlign, which include criteria for statements that support or justify gender-based discrimination in the workplace or educational institutions [[bohao_cs_2:86]]. The lack of rigorous empirical justification in some dataset construction processes is also noted, with some choices made without empirical justification and without providing an ablation study [[bohao_cs_2:87]].

The broader context of scientific literacy and education reform highlights the need for these personalized interventions. A 2015 Pew Charitable Trusts report indicates that 40% of the U.S. public believes that humans coexisted with the dinosaurs, underscoring the need for improved scientific understanding [[bohao_cs_2:88]]. Addressing such gaps requires that ethics enter into standard scientific theory and practice, which can only be accomplished by revolutionary modification of science education [[bohao_cs_2:88]]. While specific scientific applications, such as antibody drug conjugates combining the precision of antibody-navigated targeting with the power of small molecule based modulation of immune systems [[bohao_cs_2:89]], or adaptive optics systems compensating for aberrations to increase optical resolution [[bohao_cs_2:90]], represent the complex domains where such understanding is required, the foundational challenge remains the effective delivery of this knowledge through personalized systems. Technical details, such as dialyzing at 4 °C using a 3500 kDa MWCO cellulose membrane [[bohao_cs_2:91]], illustrate the level of specific jargon and procedural knowledge that personalized systems must help users navigate across different expertise levels.

A primary limitation in developing personalized scientific systems is the reliance on large-scale datasets that may not adequately represent the specific educational content required for deep conceptual understanding. While the FineWeb dataset provides a massive corpus, it includes FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion token subset specifically rated as highly educational by a custom classifier, indicating that general web data requires curation to be effective for learning [[bohao_cs_2:92]]. However, training models solely on specific domains, such as mathematics, does not yield substantial gains on broader science and STEM benchmarks, highlighting the critical need for diverse training data to ensure robustness across different scientific fields [[bohao_cs_2:93]]. This challenge is compounded by the fact that language models inherit the biases of the data they are trained on, which can limit their ability to provide neutral and accurate scientific explanations [[bohao_cs_2:94]]. Furthermore, when models are trained to imitate proprietary systems, they inherit the weaknesses and biases of those target models, and their capabilities are roughly upper-bounded by the performance of the proprietary model being imitated [[bohao_cs_2:95]].

The generalization of personalized systems across different domains and tasks remains a significant technical hurdle. Although adding curated high-quality cross-domain data has been proposed as a path towards better zero-shot generalization, the specific prompt format is crucial for cross-task generalization, and identifying a universally effective format remains an open problem [[bohao_cs_2:96]][[bohao_cs_2:97]]. Fine-tuning strategies, such as FTICL trained on generation tasks, have been shown to achieve better cross-task generalization than vanilla fine-tuning, suggesting that the method of adaptation is as important as the data [[bohao_cs_2:97]]. In the context of transfer learning, pre-training BERT on text from research papers improved its performance on scientific tasks, demonstrating the value of domain-specific pre-training for scientific applications [[bohao_cs_2:98]]. However, current adapter approaches for transfer learning do not allow for the sharing of information between tasks, which limits the efficiency of multi-task personalization [[bohao_cs_2:99]]. To address this, methods like AdapterSoup use weight averaging to improve the generalization of pretrained language models, with specific training parameters such as an initial learning rate of 1e-4 used for cross-domain applications [[bohao_cs_2:100]].

Bias and safety concerns further complicate the deployment of personalized AI systems in scientific education. Self-instruct methods, which align language models with self-generated instructions, depend on large language models and will inherit all the limitations that carry over with those base models [[bohao_cs_2:101]]. The decisions of these deep learning systems are not easily interpretable, and they are not necessarily well-calibrated in their predictions on novel inputs, exhibiting much higher variance in performance than humans on standard benchmarks [[bohao_cs_2:94]]. To mitigate these issues, reinforcement learning from human feedback has been used to train assistants that are both helpful and harmless, providing evidence that AI systems can be made safer and more useful simultaneously without incurring performance costs [[bohao_cs_2:102]]. Preference models used in this process have been shown to effectively classify AI-generated utterances, even when those utterances differ from the data distribution on which the models were trained [[bohao_cs_2:102]].

Emerging research directions focus on improving the fidelity, controllability, and evaluation of these systems. Future work on synthetic data should focus on improving the fidelity and controllability of generative models, as well as developing standardized evaluation and contamination protocols and tools [[bohao_cs_2:103]]. In the realm of evaluation, systems like GPTScore, which include GPT-X and FLAN-T5 models, can perform intricate and personalized assessments without additional training by understanding natural language instructions [[bohao_cs_2:104]]. These systems can assign scores on a scale from 1 to 10 for each response, allowing for quantitative assessment of model outputs [[bohao_cs_2:105]]. To facilitate this, system instructions can specify the tone, task, format, and limitations of the model’s responses, enabling more controlled interactions [[bohao_cs_2:106]]. Additionally, instruction tuning processes often involve generating multiple responses per question, such as five responses, to provide a broader range of potential answers for evaluation or selection [[bohao_cs_2:105]].

Specific applications in scientific education and complex problem-solving are also advancing. Models like MAmmoTH2 can assist students in their learning process by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, thereby enhancing their understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills [[bohao_cs_2:93]]. In the domain of visual instruction tuning, robust foundations have been established that have the potential to inform future research in this area [[bohao_cs_2:107]]. However, the integration of such systems into broader scientific and medical contexts faces distinct challenges. For instance, in the field of xenotransplantation, research has faced two important types of challenges: scientific and ethical issues [[bohao_cs_2:108]]. Specifically, China needs to consider how to cope with the scientific, public health, and social ethics challenges of xenotransplantation clinical trials [[bohao_cs_2:108]]. Similarly, xenotransplantation using porcine islets still has important ethical and scientific challenges, especially related to immune rejection and porcine endogenous retroviruses [[bohao_cs_2:109]]. These domain-specific hurdles highlight that while AI systems can provide explanations, the underlying scientific and ethical complexities of fields like biotechnology remain significant barriers to full integration.
answer_official_all: The traditional lecture-textbook-recitation method of teaching, which remains prevalent in high schools, prevents students from applying important scientific, mathematical, and technological skills in a meaningful context . To address this, engaging students by using real data to address scientific questions in formal education settings is known to be an effective instructional approach . This pedagogical shift aligns with the principle that students learn best if they are not passive recipients of factual information but rather are engaged in the learning process . Furthermore, experiences in informal settings can significantly improve science learning outcomes for individuals from groups historically underrepresented in science, such as women and minorities . Current scientific literacy levels highlight the need for such adaptive approaches, as a 2015 Pew Charitable Trusts report indicates that 40% of the U.S. public believes that humans coexisted with the dinosaurs . Such considerations regarding the integration of ethics and standard scientific theory will not be addressed until the thinking of scientists is radically changed, a goal that can only be accomplished by revolutionary modification of science education . In the domain of automated assistance, systems like MAmmoTH2 can assist students in their learning process by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, thus enhancing their understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills . The development of personalized systems relies on large language models (LLMs) that must be adapted to specific scientific domains. Pre-training BERT on text from research papers improved its performance on scientific tasks, as found by Beltagy et al. (2019) . Similarly, a keyword search is used to generate a dataset of hundreds of relevant scientific papers and pre-loaded into the Llama 3 model inference system . However, general models may lack nuanced expertise in particular domains, making them non-specific for specialized scientific tasks . To mitigate this, Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters decouples the Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into two parts: the original pre-trained FFNs to maintain the old-domain knowledge and novel domain-specific adapters to inject domain-specific knowledge in parallel . Training and aligning these models for personalized scientific instruction involves complex reinforcement learning techniques. Training LLMs with reinforcement learning, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), from human feedback (RLHF) has proven effective in aligning LLMs with human preferences . However, RLHF depends on complex reinforcement learning techniques such as PPO, which are challenging to implement and often unstable during training . In specific applications like WizardMath, the Integrated Reward Model (IRM) and Process Reward Model (PRM) are integrated within a PPO-based reinforcement learning framework to empower mathematical reasoning . Despite these advancements, LLMs may replicate some human-like cognitive biases , and their factuality is weak, meaning crowdworkers without domain expertise or significant time investments may miss these errors . Evaluation and calibration of these personalized systems present additional challenges. GPTScore, including GPT-X and FLAN-T5 models, can perform intricate and personalized assessments without additional training due to an understanding of natural language instructions . For retrieval-augmented generation, training a reranker with domain-specific data was more effective than zero-shot reranking . Datasets such as SciQ, which contains approximately 14k crowdsourced science exam question-answer pairs, provide benchmarks for evaluating such systems . Additionally, the FineWeb-Edu dataset, a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content, serves as a resource for training on educational material . Specialized architectures and methods further support the adaptation of scientific content. Socratic Models (SMs) can produce reasonable captions without additional training on domain-specific data . In the context of model merging, many MoErging methods do not have user-friendly software implementations available, and applying them often requires technical expertise that many users lack . Methods like DAM first compute each domain-specific training set's average embedding from the penultimate layer of the base model to facilitate this process . In distillation, each specialist model is initialized with the weights of the generalist model to transfer knowledge . These technical adaptations, such as the recent adaptation of the formalism of the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian from quantum mechanics to acoustic resonators , illustrate the cross-domain transfer of scientific concepts that personalized systems must support. The extraction and processing of scientific text rely heavily on robust data cleaning and filtering techniques to ensure high-quality input for downstream NLP tasks. For instance, the OpenWebMath dataset utilized specific tools for text extraction, where Trafilatura achieved a score of 63.90, significantly outperforming jusText, which scored 31.17 . In the context of large-scale web data decanting, the FineWeb datasets employ a fastText language classifier to assign a language prediction score ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, facilitating the filtering of non-target language content . Similarly, the Llama 3 model development process involved annotating data across a wide variety of file types, including.TXT,.DOCX,.PDF,.PPTX,.XLSX,.CSV,.TSV,.PY,.JSON,.JSONL,.HTML, and.XML, to ensure comprehensive coverage of scientific and technical formats . To effectively identify and retrieve relevant scientific concepts, researchers utilize keyword search and retrieval-augmented generation strategies. The Llama 3 model inference system, for example, uses keyword search to generate a dataset of hundreds of relevant scientific papers, which are then pre-loaded into the system . In retrieval tasks, training a reranker with domain-specific data has been shown to be more effective than zero-shot reranking, highlighting the importance of domain adaptation in retrieval pipelines . Furthermore, the MTEB benchmark indicates that scientific datasets such as SciDocsRR, SciFact, and ArxivClustering exhibit high similarities among each other, even when derived from different tasks, suggesting a shared underlying structure in scientific text embeddings . Integrating domain-specific knowledge into pre-trained language models is a critical step for accurate jargon handling. The Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters approach decouples the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of the Transformer architecture into two distinct parts: the original pre-trained FFNs, which maintain old-domain knowledge, and novel domain-specific adapters that inject new domain knowledge in parallel . This architectural modification allows for the preservation of general linguistic capabilities while enhancing performance on specialized scientific topics. Additionally, the Llama 3 team found that annealing enables the judgment of the value of small domain-specific datasets, providing a method to assess the utility of limited domain data during training . Entity linking and disambiguation are essential for linking scientific jargon to broader knowledge bases. The CM3 model, a causal masked multimodal model of the internet, sets the new state-of-the-art for entity linking and entity disambiguation in general through fine-tuning . This model also achieves state-of-the-art results in zero-shot summarization, entity linking, and entity disambiguation, demonstrating its versatility across multiple NLP tasks . These capabilities are crucial for systems that need to automatically define and link scientific terms without extensive manual annotation. Graph-based methods and summarization techniques also play a role in extracting and synthesizing scientific concepts. TextRank defines a weighted graph where text units are nodes and edges are defined by a similarity measure based on word overlap, a method used for extracting key phrases and concepts . In graph-based neural multi-document summarization, the order of correlation strength for different graph types is found to be PDG > ADG > Cosine Similarity Graph, with models without a graph converging faster and achieving lower training costs than those using Cosine Similarity Graphs or ADGs . When generating summaries from long sequences, such as in Wikipedia generation, combining datasets of citations and search results performs best, with the contributions of each source being complementary . The evaluation and calibration of these systems require careful consideration of model confidence and bias. Few-shot recalibration allows for the identification of domain-specific confidence thresholds, above which the language model's predictions can be trusted and below which it should abstain, thereby improving reliability in domain-specific applications . However, LLMs used as evaluators can exhibit bias, as they recognize and favor their own generations, a phenomenon observed when sampling summaries at temperature zero using simple prompts . Prompts for evaluation often take specific input strings, including metric, metric_definition, aspects, article, and summary, to structure the assessment process . Cross-cultural and multilingual considerations are also relevant to the development of personalized scientific systems. Analogous to cross-lingual and multilingual NLP, cross-cultural and multicultural NLP considers differences in cultural contexts to better serve users of NLP systems . However, a significant challenge remains in the availability of resources, as while Wikipedia and news texts are available for a wide range of languages, texts specifically written for NLP tasks are not available for most languages . This scarcity of task-specific multilingual data poses a limitation for developing truly personalized systems across diverse expertise levels and domains. Finally, the mechanisms by which knowledge is transferred and distilled in these models are an area of ongoing research. Knowledge distillation improves student performance, a phenomenon that has been linked to the regularizing effect of soft labels . In the context of improving text embeddings, large language models are used to generate instruction-based queries, where the query is formatted as an instruction followed by the task definition and the original query . These techniques, combined with the aforementioned extraction and linking methods, form the foundation for developing effective personalized systems for scientific understanding. The development of personalized educational systems relies on large-scale datasets that provide the foundational material for generating explanations, such as FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion token dataset of educational content . To facilitate learning, models like MAmmoTH2 are designed to assist students by offering step-by-step solutions, explanations, and targeted feedback, which enhances understanding of complex concepts and problem-solving skills . The generation of such content can be controlled through system instructions that specify the tone, task, format, and limitations of the model’s responses . However, methods for “targeting” or “controlling” the content of language models are still at a very early stage . In the context of model architecture, Mixture of Experts (MoE) approaches allow for specialized handling of different tasks or user profiles. During MoE training on local data, the global expert remains frozen, while only the local expert and the router are updated to achieve personalization . This architecture is particularly relevant in cases where a user-tailored local model is desired and where user data must remain private, often intersecting with Federated Learning (FL) . The retrieval of the appropriate expert is critical, as the expert with the most datapoints assigned to it is retrieved . Nevertheless, accurate expert retrieval for specific tasks can be challenging, even when relevant experts exist . The quality and consistency of generated content are subject to various evaluation metrics and biases. LLM evaluators have been shown to recognize and favor their own generation, a causal explanation that resists straightforward confounders in controlled experiments . In these evaluations, summaries are often sampled from LLMs at temperature zero using simple prompts . To assess quality, GPT-4 can be asked to rate its own response from 1 to 10 , or to rate the quality of generation from another model on a scale of 0 to 10 . Additionally, a higher CONS score indicates better consistency with user intent . Training strategies for these adaptive systems often involve iterative processes and distillation.
